Wildflower, Read in Order

How to Read This Book

This book reads the Wildflower code in the order its domain tells it. Each part takes one component and starts with an introduction: who is involved, what they ask for, and how the code is layered. Then the part reads the code twice:

  • Bottom up, one chapter per layer, from the domain’s entities through the rules about who may write what, the operations, the HTTP surface and the wiring, down to the SQL. Each chapter needs only the ones before it.
  • Top down, in Integration Tests. Each test gets a section: the promise it holds the server to, the test, and links to the items it relies on.

Read a part top to bottom the first time. Afterwards, it works as a way into a change you are reviewing: every item and test the part covers is shown once, so a change to one points to the place to reread.

How a page reads

A page’s headings follow the code: a module, then the types in it, then their methods. Under each heading, an item reads in the same order every time:

  1. Its doc comment, as prose. What the item means in the domain, in the words the code itself carries.
  2. Its code, under the prose. A struct or enum keeps its fields’ and variants’ doc comments in the code, so they document themselves.
  3. Its tests, one after another, each captioned by its doc comment: the promise that test holds the item to.

The page’s own prose sits between items and says what crosses them: the domain story, why things are as they are, and how the pieces relate. Names in the prose and the doc comments link to where the item they name is shown.

The helpers the tests share, the fixtures that build an entity or a server for a test, are on the Test Fixtures page at the end of each part. A test that first uses one links to it.

The excerpts

Every excerpt is the real source, taken from the commit the book was built from. Nothing is copied by hand, so an excerpt can’t drift from the code; when the code it names moves or is renamed, the book stops building until its chapter follows.

  • An excerpt is a whole item (a function, a type, a method) or the part of one the story needs. A // … line marks where the excerpt skips lines.
  • An item’s doc comment shows as the prose above its code, not in it, and attributes are left out. Ordinary comments stay.
  • The line under each excerpt links to those lines on GitHub, at the commit the book was built from, and to the item’s package in the code index, which shows what the package’s files use and what uses them.

Where the chapters live

Each chapter sits in a docs/Book/ folder beside the code it explains, so a change to the code and to its chapter shows up in the same diff. This book only sets the reading order.

The Authorization Server

This part is a guided read of authorization-server-rust, the server that decides who may use the Owner’s FHIR server. This page is the map: who the actors are, what they ask for, what a yes leaves behind, and how the code is layered.

What this server is for

One person, the Owner, runs a FHIR server on their own devices. Apps, browsers and devices ask for access to it. This server decides who gets in, with what, and for how long. It never decides alone: every access traces back to a moment when the Owner said yes, either just now or earlier, in a way that still stands.

Everything else in the crate serves that sentence.

The cast

WhoWhat they areWhere they are explained
The OwnerThe person whose data this is. Signs in on their own device with a same-device sign-in code, and decides every request.Same-Device Sign-In Codes
A clientAn app (a SMART-on-FHIR app, a Pebble companion, the host app). It has a client_id, maybe a secret, and a registration that is server-defined or trusted on first use.Client
A browser sessionA browser the server has let in, keyed by its sid. Everything minted while using that browser records the sid, so revoking the browser revokes what it earned.Browser Session
A deviceSomething without a good browser (a TV, a watch) that shows a code for the Owner to type in elsewhere.Polled Requests

Three ways to ask

Every request for access is an authorization request, parked until the Owner decides it. There are three flows, each its own type with its own states.

FlowWho asksWhat a yes producesStandard
Authorization codeAn app, running in a signed-in browserA one-minute code, then tokensRFC 6749 §4.1 + PKCE
Device codeA device showing a user codeTokens, collected by the device’s pollRFC 8628
Browser pairingA browser wanting to become a sessionA browser session, collected by its pollOurs, not OAuth

The order matters. A browser signs in or pairs first and then makes app requests, because an app’s code is always issued under the browser session it was requested in.

What a yes leaves behind

ThingLifetimeWhy it exists
GrantUntil revoked“The Owner already said yes to this app at this redirect.” Lets a later request skip asking.
Authorization code60 seconds, single useCarries the approval from the browser to the app’s back end without putting a token in a URL.
Access token15 minutesWhat the app shows the FHIR server. Signed, so anything holding the public key can check it.
Refresh family90 days from the authorization; rotation never extends itOne chain of refresh tokens from one authorization. Replaying an old link ends the whole chain.
Browser sessionEight hours for a same-device session, a day for a paired one, or until revokedThe browser’s standing permission. It caps what any app requested in that browser can receive.

How the code is layered

A request moves through the layers from the top down.

http/routes/…           axum handlers: parse, call ONE capability, render
  └─ domain/capabilities/…   one operation = one store scope (read or write)
       ├─ domain/<entity>         the rules: CodeRequest, BrowserSession, Grant, …
       ├─ domain/authority/…      proofs: "on whose authority is this written?"
       └─ domain/capabilities/writers/…  the ONLY place privileged writes happen
            └─ domain/grant_store/…      the port: GrantStore opens a scope, GrantTx does one statement
                 └─ db/…                 the SQL behind each GrantTx method

Hold on to three rules while you read. Most of the code exists to enforce one of them.

  1. One operation, one scope. A capability opens a single read or write scope at its top, runs the whole flow inside it, and does side effects (notifying the Owner, the revocation store) only after the scope closes.
  2. Every privileged write takes a proof. You can’t call “issue a code” without passing a value that only the rule-checking function can construct. Auditing who can grant access means reading two short lists: the proofs in domain/authority/ and the writers in capabilities/writers/.
  3. A request changes only through its own transitions, and a transition lands only while the row still has the status it was read with. The Authorization Request page shows the guarded replace that makes it so.

How this part is organised

The rest of the part reads the code twice, from opposite ends.

The first pass goes bottom up, one layer per chapter, each needing only the ones before it. A page takes one or a few source files, and its headings follow the code: a module, then its types and free functions, then each type’s methods. Each item shows its doc comment, its source, and right under it the unit tests that hold it, each captioned by the promise it keeps. The page’s own prose says what crosses items: the domain story, why things are as they are, and how the pieces relate. The helpers the tests share are on a Test Fixtures page at the end of the chapter.

  1. Domain: the entities and the rules they own.
  2. Grant Store: what persistence looks like from the domain, one scope per operation.
  3. Authority: the proofs every privileged write demands.
  4. Writers: the only places those writes happen.
  5. Capabilities: the operations, split by what unlocks them.
  6. HTTP: the gates, the extractors and every route.
  7. Assembly: how the crate is put together and handed to the host.
  8. Persistence: the SQLite behind the Grant Store.
  9. Utilities: the small cryptographic helpers.

The second pass, Integration Tests, goes top down. Each file in tests/integration/ gets a page, and each test a section: the promise the test holds the server to, the test itself, and links back to the sections the promise rests on. They follow the order the Domain part builds in, from the tokens’ own checks to the flows. Grant Flows follows one app’s request from the front door to its token.

Domain

The entities in src/domain/ are the rules of the server, with no HTTP and no SQL in them. Each page takes one entity: what it is in the Owner’s world, then its module, types and methods, each with the unit tests that hold it. The pages are in build-up order, so each concept arrives before a later page leans on it.

  • Scopes: how the server compares scope strings, from the shared scopes slice. Every later “covers” means this.
  • Signing Key: the key the server signs its tokens with, and publishes for others to check them.
  • Browser Session: a browser the server has let in, and the scopes that cap what apps requested in it can receive.
  • Access Token: the fifteen-minute signed token an app presents to the FHIR server.
  • Client Credentials: what an app presents when it authenticates.
  • Client: an app that asks for access, the registration that says what it may ask for, and what approving a request would change in it.
  • Grant: the Owner’s standing yes to an app, and when it lets a request skip asking.
  • Launch Context: a SMART launch value, for one app (and maybe one patient) or for a server’s launcher, spent once.
  • Authorization Request: one request for access, and the guarded replace that writes its transitions.
    • Code Request: an app’s request for a code, its limited page, and its resolution against the app’s registration.
    • Polled Requests: a device’s request and a browser’s pairing, which a poll claims once.
  • Errors: the four vocabularies the server says no in.
  • Authorization Code: the one-minute, single-use code that carries an approval to the app’s back end, and the callback that delivers it.
  • Refresh Token: the chain of refresh tokens one authorization starts.
  • Owner Prompt: which waiting request the host asks the Owner about, and the key that names one.
  • Retention: how long each accumulating table keeps a row past its expiry, and the sweep that applies it.
  • Same-Device Sign-In Codes: the codes the base signs the Owner’s browser in with, and where a sign-in may go next.
  • Session Housekeeping: logout’s denylisting and the throttle on a session’s last_seen_at.
  • Source Guards: the tests that hold rules about where code may be written.
  • Test Fixtures: the helpers the Domain tests share.

The capabilities, proofs and writers that put these entities to work (domain/capabilities/, domain/authority/) have chapters of their own, after the Grant Store.

Scopes

Covers scopes-rust/src/smart.rs

Covers scopes-rust/src/lib.rs

A scope names a slice of access: patient/Observation.rs reads and searches one patient’s observations, system/*.cruds does anything to any resource, offline_access asks for a refresh token. Every list of scopes in this server is a list of these strings: what a client’s registration allows, what a request asks for, what a grant, a browser session or a token holds.

The server never compares scopes by spelling. It parses each string into a structured scope and asks whether one covers another: patient/*.rs covers patient/Observation.r, and system/*.cruds covers both. Whenever a later page says a registration, a grant or a browser session “covers” a request, it means allowed_scope_covers. Parsing never fails: a string the grammar can’t read is kept as an unknown scope that covers only itself.

The scopes live in their own slice, slices/scopes/scopes-rust, shared by the server’s Rust slices. This page shows the parts the authorization server uses. Three questions come up again and again:

  • Does one scope cover another? A client’s registration, a standing grant and a browser session each answer it for a request (allowed_scope_covers).
  • What does a list become, widened by another? An approval widens a grant, and a client’s registration trusted on first use, by what it granted (widened_scopes).
  • What may an approval grant? What the Owner ticked, kept only where the request asked for it and a ceiling allows it (grantable_scopes).

wildflowerhealthio_scopes::scope

The structured model the string-facing functions below parse into.

Scope

An OAuth 2.0 / SMART on FHIR scope. Build from a string with From or FromStr (both infallible — parsing is total, falling back to Unknown); render with Display.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum Scope {
    /// A SMART `context/Type.perms` FHIR resource scope.
    FhirResource(FhirResourceScope),
    /// A `wildflower/Resource.perms` scope on one of the app's own resources.
    WildflowerResource(WildflowerResourceScope),
    /// A broadly-known non-resource scope (`openid`, `offline_access`, …).
    Known(KnownScope),
    /// Anything unrecognized, preserved verbatim.
    Unknown(UnknownScope),
}
}

scopes-rust/src/scope/mod.rs lines 47–56 · scopes in the code index

covers

Does this (client-allowed) scope cover other (a requested scope)? Resource scopes compare structurally within their kind; known and unknown scopes — and any cross-kind pair — match exactly.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn covers(&self, other: &Scope) -> bool {
    match (self, other) {
        (Scope::FhirResource(a), Scope::FhirResource(b)) => a.covers(b),
        (Scope::WildflowerResource(a), Scope::WildflowerResource(b)) => a.covers(b),
        (a, b) => a == b,
    }
}
}

Grant

A list of scopes as one value. A token’s scope claim is read into one, and the scope gates check a caller’s authority against it.

An ordered collection of Scopes — a parsed grant. Order is preserved so a grant round-trips through parse → render in the spelling it was given.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct Grant {
    /// The grant's scopes, in their original order.
    pub scopes: Vec<Scope>,
}
}

scopes-rust/src/scope/grant.rs lines 16–19 · scopes in the code index

widen

Fold additional into this grant and collapse the result (collapse) — the structured form of “widen a stored scope list by what was just approved”. Granting again what is already held is a no-op, and a broader addition replaces the narrower entries it supersedes rather than sitting alongside them: widening [patient/Patient.r] by [patient/Patient.cruds] leaves [patient/Patient.cruds], not both.

The result reaches exactly the interactions the two lists reached between them — never a resource, context or interaction neither granted — which is what makes it safe on an authorization ceiling such as a client’s allowed_scopes. It is not string-for-string conservative: see collapse for the one way a merged scope admits a spelling the pair did not.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn widen(&mut self, additional: &Grant) {
    self.scopes.extend(additional.scopes.iter().cloned());
    self.collapse();
}
}

fn widening_replaces_a_narrower_entry_with_the_broader_grant() {

        widened(&["patient/Patient.r", "openid"], &["patient/Patient.cruds"]),
        ["patient/Patient.cruds", "openid"]

scopes-rust/src/scope/grant.rs lines 386–392 · scopes in the code index

Two scopes on one resource, neither covering the other, restate as one scope holding both sets of interactions, in the grammar they share.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn widening_unions_the_interactions_of_one_resource() {
    // Neither covers the other, but both address `patient/Patient` in the
    // letter grammar, so they restate as one scope.
    assert_eq!(
        widened(&["patient/Patient.r"], &["patient/Patient.s"]),
        ["patient/Patient.rs"]
    );
    // Within the v1 word grammar the union lands on `*` (the only word
    // spelling of `read ∪ write`), staying in the grammar it started in.
    assert_eq!(
        widened(&["patient/Patient.read"], &["patient/Patient.write"]),
        ["patient/Patient.*"]
    );
}
}

scopes-rust/src/scope/grant.rs lines 397–410 · scopes in the code index

The grammar guard: a v1 word and a v2 letter bag never fold together, so a word-registered entry can’t be turned into letter-grammar access it never had. Subsumption still crosses the grammars one way.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn widening_never_merges_a_v1_word_into_a_letter_bag() {
    // `.read` (word) and `.c` (letter) each grant what the other doesn't;
    // folding them to `.crs` would newly hand over letter `r`/`s`.
    assert_eq!(
        widened(&["patient/Patient.read"], &["patient/Patient.c"]),
        ["patient/Patient.read", "patient/Patient.c"]
    );
    // But `.cruds` *covers* `.read`, so it absorbs it outright.
    assert_eq!(
        widened(&["patient/Patient.read"], &["patient/Patient.cruds"]),
        ["patient/Patient.cruds"]
    );
    // And the reverse never happens — a word grant can't swallow a letter one.
    assert_eq!(
        widened(&["patient/Patient.cruds"], &["patient/Patient.*"]),
        ["patient/Patient.cruds"]
    );
}
}

A wildcard or a broader context absorbs what it subsumes, but the two are never merged into one — system and user stay distinct spellings unless one genuinely covers the other.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn widening_absorbs_across_resources_and_contexts_by_coverage() {
    assert_eq!(
        widened(
            &["patient/Observation.r", "patient/Condition.rs"],
            &["patient/*.cruds"]
        ),
        ["patient/*.cruds"]
    );
    assert_eq!(
        widened(&["user/Patient.r"], &["system/Patient.cruds"]),
        ["system/Patient.cruds"]
    );
    // `user` does not reach `patient`, so neither absorbs the other.
    assert_eq!(
        widened(&["user/Patient.r"], &["patient/Patient.r"]),
        ["user/Patient.r", "patient/Patient.r"]
    );
}
}

wildflowerhealthio_scopes::smart

The string-facing entry points, which take and return the Vec<String> columns the server stores. The tests here build sets with a small helper.

allowed_scope_covers

Does the scope allowed (a client’s registered scope, or a standing grant’s) cover the scope requested? Both sides are parsed to a Scope and compared with Scope::covers: resource scopes match by context + resource-type (wildcard-aware) + a permission-bit superset — a v2 letter-form allowed covers an equivalent v1 word request, but a v1 word-form allowed never covers a letter request; known and unknown scopes match exactly.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn allowed_scope_covers(allowed: &str, requested: &str) -> bool {
    Scope::from(allowed).covers(&Scope::from(requested))
}
}

widened_scopes

Widen the stored scope list standing by additional, returning the collapsed union as wire strings — the string-facing form of Grant::widen, for callers holding Vec<String> columns (a client’s allowed_scopes, a standing grant’s scopes).

The result grants exactly what the two lists granted between them, stated as shortly as the grammar allows: ["patient/Patient.r"] widened by ["patient/Patient.cruds"] is ["patient/Patient.cruds"], not both. Parsing is total, so an unrecognized string survives as an Unknown scope that only ever collapses against an identical twin.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn widened_scopes(standing: &[String], additional: &[String]) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut grant = Grant::parse(standing);
    grant.widen(&Grant::parse(additional));
    grant.render()
}
}

scopes-rust/src/smart.rs lines 62–66 · scopes in the code index

grantable_scopes

The server calls this through ApprovableScopes::grantable_subset, with the ceiling the request allows: for an app’s request, what its client registration permits.

The scopes an Owner approval can actually grant: those that are both still requested by the pending request and covered by the ceiling (for a consent prompt, the most the client’s registration permits). The Owner can only narrow, never widen, and the ceiling clamp stops a stale request from granting a scope the client’s policy no longer permits.

Both sides match by coverage, not exact equality (each parsed to a Scope and compared with Scope::covers). Coverage on the requested side is what lets an Owner narrow: an approved patient/Observation.s is still ⊆ a requested patient/Observation.rs, so it’s granted where exact equality would drop it. Coverage is wildcard/context-aware and bridges grammars one way — a v2 letter scope covers the equivalent v1 word, but not the reverse (known/unknown match exactly — see Scope::covers).

Every kept scope is rendered back to its own approved wire spelling (v1↔v2 back-compat — see Permission), de-duplicated by rendered form (first-seen order). An empty grant stays empty (approve handlers treat “nothing granted” as a deny).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn grantable_scopes(
    approved: Vec<String>,
    requested: &HashSet<&str>,
    ceiling: &HashSet<&str>,
) -> Vec<String> {
    let requested: Vec<Scope> = requested.iter().map(|&s| Scope::from(s)).collect();
    let ceiling: Vec<Scope> = ceiling.iter().map(|&s| Scope::from(s)).collect();

    let mut seen: HashSet<String> = HashSet::new();
    let mut granted: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
    for approved_scope in approved.into_iter().map(|s| Scope::from(s.as_str())) {
        let is_requested = requested.iter().any(|r| r.covers(&approved_scope));
        let is_under_ceiling = ceiling.iter().any(|c| c.covers(&approved_scope));
        if is_requested && is_under_ceiling {
            let rendered = approved_scope.to_string();
            if seen.insert(rendered.clone()) {
                granted.push(rendered);
            }
        }
    }
    granted
}
}

scopes-rust/src/smart.rs lines 447–457 · scopes in the code index

with_alternate_canonical_forms

The server mints a token’s scope claim through this, so the FHIR server, which reads only the letter grammar, honours a grant spelled in words.

Append each scope’s equivalent alternate spelling, where it has one (see Scope::as_alternate_canonical_form) — today, a resource scope in SMART v1 word form gaining its canonical v2 letter form.

Some consumers parse only one spelling — notably helios-auth’s SmartPermissions, which HFS uses to authorize FHIR requests and which reads only the SMART v2 letter grammar, silently dropping a .read/.write/.* segment. Emitting both spellings into a token’s scope claim means such a consumer still honors the grant, while consumers that read the original spelling keep working (the originals are preserved verbatim). Only the extra alternates are added — de-duplicated against the input, order-preserving, and idempotent.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn with_alternate_canonical_forms(scopes: &[String]) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut out: Vec<String> = Vec::with_capacity(scopes.len());
    for s in scopes {
        out.push(s.clone());
        if let Some(alternate) = Scope::from(s.as_str()).as_alternate_canonical_form() {
            let alternate = alternate.to_string();
            // Skip an alternate the caller already granted (idempotency) or that
            // an earlier original in this pass already produced.
            let already_granted = scopes.iter().any(|x| x == &alternate);
            if !already_granted && !out.contains(&alternate) {
                out.push(alternate);
            }
        }
    }
    out
}
}

scopes-rust/src/lib.rs lines 23–25 · scopes in the code index

Signing Key

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/signing_key.rs

Every access token the server issues is a JWT signed with an RSA key the server holds, and every token presented back is checked against those keys. A signing key is that key at rest: one row, with its private half, in the server’s own database. The server signs with its one active key and verifies against every key it holds. It publishes the public half of every key at its JWKS endpoint, so anything else that checks its tokens can do the same.

The server makes its key itself. On a boot that finds no active key, it generates one and stores it as active (ensure_some_active_signing_key); on every later boot it leaves the keys alone.

Private key material is handled with two habits that recur across the crate: it is scrubbed from memory when dropped, and it never prints, so a key formatted into a log line or a panic shows only its public parts.

domain::signing_key

SigningKey

An RSA signing key used to mint and verify access tokens; is_active marks the one key that signs, and every key verifies. Diesel-mapped 1:1 to the signing_keys table; values maps to the values_json JSON TEXT column.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct SigningKey {
    /// A random id, written into each token's JWS `kid` header so a verifier
    /// can pick the key that signed it.
    pub kid: String,
    /// JWK key type — always `"RSA"` for keys produced here.
    pub kty: String,
    /// JWS signing algorithm — always `"RS256"` for keys produced here.
    pub alg: String,
    /// RSA key components: public (`n`, `e`) and private (`d`, `p`, `q`).
    pub values: SigningKeyValues,
    /// Whether this key signs new tokens. A key that isn't active still
    /// verifies, and stays published in the JWKS.
    pub is_active: bool,
}
}

From an RSA key

A key generated by the rsa crate becomes a SigningKey with its components base64url-encoded and a new kid, not yet active.

Wrap private as a SigningKey with base64url-encoded JWK components and a new kid. The key starts inactive.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn from(private: &RsaPrivateKey) -> Self {
    let primes = private.primes();
    let p = &primes[0];
    let q = &primes[1];
    // The private components (`d`, `p`, `q`) pass through big-endian byte
    // buffers on their way to base64url; scrub those transient copies so the
    // only surviving plaintext is the `SigningKeyValues` (itself
    // zero-on-drop). `n`/`e` are public and need no scrubbing.
    let d_bytes = Zeroizing::new(private.d().to_bytes_be());
    let p_bytes = Zeroizing::new(p.to_bytes_be());
    let q_bytes = Zeroizing::new(q.to_bytes_be());
    SigningKey {
        kid: Uuid::new_v4().to_string(),
        kty: "RSA".to_string(),
        alg: "RS256".to_string(),
        values: SigningKeyValues {
            n: base64::url_safe_no_pad_encode(&private.n().to_bytes_be()),
            e: base64::url_safe_no_pad_encode(&private.e().to_bytes_be()),
            d: base64::url_safe_no_pad_encode(&d_bytes),
            p: base64::url_safe_no_pad_encode(&p_bytes),
            q: base64::url_safe_no_pad_encode(&q_bytes),
        },
        is_active: false,
    }
}
}

A token signed with a generated key’s signing half verifies with its verifying half, and every claim comes back as it went in.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn round_trip_sign_verify() {
    use jsonwebtoken::{Algorithm, Header, Validation};
    let key = SigningKey::generate().expect("generate");
    let enc = EncodingKey::try_from(&key).expect("enc");
    let dec = DecodingKey::try_from(&key).expect("dec");
    let mut header = Header::new(Algorithm::RS256);
    header.kid = Some(key.kid.clone());
    let claims = serde_json::json!({ "sub": "alice", "exp": 9_999_999_999u64 });
    let token = jsonwebtoken::encode(&header, &claims, &enc).expect("encode");
    let mut validation = Validation::new(Algorithm::RS256);
    validation.validate_aud = false;
    let decoded =
        jsonwebtoken::decode::<serde_json::Value>(&token, &dec, &validation).expect("decode");
    // Assert the whole round trip in one line so every claim is checked,
    // not just `sub`.
    assert_eq!(decoded.claims, claims);
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/signing_key.rs lines 294–310 · authorization-server in the code index

Reconstruct an RsaPrivateKey from key’s base64url JWK components. Every decoded private component is scrubbed if a later one fails.

Errors

A KeyMaterialError when a component isn’t base64url, or the five don’t compose into a private key.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn try_from(key: &SigningKey) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
    // Keep every decoded component wrapped in `Zeroizing` until all five
    // succeed: if a later `?` bails out, the private BigUints decoded so
    // far (`d`, `p`) still scrub on their way out of scope rather than
    // dropping as raw plaintext. Once all are in hand, `std::mem::take`
    // moves each value out (leaving a zeroed `BigUint::default()` behind,
    // which the wrappers then scrub) so `from_components` receives the
    // integers without cloning.
    let mut n = base64_url_to_biguint(&key.values.n)?;
    let mut e = base64_url_to_biguint(&key.values.e)?;
    let mut d = base64_url_to_biguint(&key.values.d)?;
    let mut p = base64_url_to_biguint(&key.values.p)?;
    let mut q = base64_url_to_biguint(&key.values.q)?;
    RsaPrivateKey::from_components(
        std::mem::take(&mut *n),
        std::mem::take(&mut *e),
        std::mem::take(&mut *d),
        vec![std::mem::take(&mut *p), std::mem::take(&mut *q)],
    )
    .map_err(KeyMaterialError::Compose)
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/signing_key.rs lines 201–221 · authorization-server in the code index

Reconstruct an RsaPublicKey from key’s public JWK components (n, e).

Errors

A KeyMaterialError when n or e isn’t base64url, or the two don’t compose into a public key.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn try_from(key: &SigningKey) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
    // `n`/`e` are public, so scrubbing is unnecessary here — but
    // `base64_url_to_biguint` returns `Zeroizing` uniformly; move the
    // integers out of the (harmless) wrappers before composing.
    let mut n = base64_url_to_biguint(&key.values.n)?;
    let mut e = base64_url_to_biguint(&key.values.e)?;
    RsaPublicKey::new(std::mem::take(&mut *n), std::mem::take(&mut *e))
        .map_err(KeyMaterialError::Compose)
}
}

SigningKeyValues

The base64url-encoded RSA key components stored in the values_json column of a signing_keys row.

Holds the private RSA exponents (d, p, q) in plaintext, so #[derive(ZeroizeOnDrop)] scrubs every component string from memory when the value is dropped. n/e are public but are zeroed alongside them — one blanket scrub is simpler than carving out the public halves.

fn main() {
fn debug_redacts_private_exponents() {
    let values = SigningKeyValues {
        n: "public-modulus".to_string(),
        d: "PRIVATE-D-SECRET".to_string(),
        e: "public-exp".to_string(),
        p: "PRIVATE-P-SECRET".to_string(),
        q: "PRIVATE-Q-SECRET".to_string(),
    };
    let rendered = format!("{values:?}");
    // The private exponents must never surface in a formatted value.
    assert!(
        !rendered.contains("PRIVATE-D-SECRET"),
        "d leaked: {rendered}"
    );
    assert!(
        !rendered.contains("PRIVATE-P-SECRET"),
        "p leaked: {rendered}"
    );
    assert!(
        !rendered.contains("PRIVATE-Q-SECRET"),
        "q leaked: {rendered}"
    );
    assert!(
        rendered.contains("<redacted>"),
        "no redaction marker: {rendered}"
    );
    // Public components stay visible so a logged value is still identifiable.
    assert!(rendered.contains("public-modulus"), "n hidden: {rendered}");
    assert!(rendered.contains("public-exp"), "e hidden: {rendered}");
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/signing_key.rs lines 315–344 · authorization-server in the code index

base64_url_to_biguint

Decode a base64url JWK component into a big-endian BigUint, wrapped in Zeroizing so the value scrubs on drop.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn base64_url_to_biguint(s: &str) -> Result<Zeroizing<BigUint>, KeyMaterialError> {
    // Scrub the decoded bytes on the way out — for the private components
    // (`d`, `p`, `q`) they are plaintext key material. `rsa::BigUint` is
    // `num_bigint_dig::BigUint`, which implements `Zeroize` (rsa 0.9 enables
    // num-bigint-dig's `zeroize` feature), so the reconstructed integer is
    // zeroizable too — return it wrapped so a caller that drops it before
    // handing it to `RsaPrivateKey` (e.g. an error partway through decoding the
    // five components) still scrubs the plaintext. Wrapping the public `n`/`e`
    // is harmless.
    let bytes =
        Zeroizing::new(base64::url_safe_no_pad_decode(s).map_err(KeyMaterialError::Decode)?);
    Ok(Zeroizing::new(BigUint::from_bytes_be(&bytes)))
}
}

KeyMaterialError

Failure modes when round-tripping a SigningKey through jsonwebtoken/rsa — bad JWK components, DER encode, RSA composition, or fresh-key generation.

Each variant keeps the original source error (#[source]) so the full cause chain survives for logging rather than being flattened to a string. Compose and Generate both wrap rsa::Error, so neither uses #[from] (two From<rsa::Error> impls would conflict) — call sites construct them explicitly to keep the two failure modes distinct. A key that fails here is the operator’s problem, not the caller’s: minting and verifying report it as an unreadable signing key.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum KeyMaterialError {
    /// A stored component isn't valid base64url.
    Decode(#[source] base64::DecodeError),
    /// The components don't make an RSA key.
    Compose(#[source] rsa::Error),
    /// The rebuilt key couldn't be DER-encoded for `jsonwebtoken`.
    Encode(#[source] rsa::pkcs1::Error),
    /// Generating a fresh RSA key failed.
    Generate(#[source] rsa::Error),
}
}

Browser Session

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/browser_session.rs

A browser session is a browser the server has let in. It is keyed by its sid, and everything minted while using that browser records the sid: each authorization code, access token and refresh-token family. That is what makes a browser revocable as a unit: revoking the session ends what it earned.

A browser gets a session one of two ways. The Owner’s browser, on the server’s own device, signs in with a same-device sign-in code, and its session lasts eight hours (SAME_DEVICE_SESSION_TTL), or until the server’s last launch view closes, which ends it by expiring it, or it goes stale, as when the server restarts with no launch view open that it signed in. Any other browser pairs: it shows a code, the Owner approves it and chooses what it may hold, and its session lasts a day (PAIRED_SESSION_TTL).

A session’s scopes cap what any app requested in it can receive. The Owner may approve an app for more, but the code issued under the session carries only what the session also covers. A browser paired with read-only access earns no app write access, whoever approved the request. This is also why a browser signs in or pairs before it makes app requests: a code is always issued under the session its request was made in.

        vec!["system/*.cruds".to_owned()],

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn is_live_at(
    &self,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
    stale_session_cutoff: &StaleSessionCutoff,
) -> bool {
    self.revoked_at.is_none()
        && self.expires_at > now
        && !stale_session_cutoff.makes_stale(self)
}
}

fn main() {
fn a_session_is_live_until_it_expires_or_is_revoked() {
    let now = Utc::now();
    let cutoff = StaleSessionCutoff::none();
    let session = BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), now);
    assert!(session.is_live_at(now, &cutoff));
    assert!(!session.is_live_at(session.expires_at, &cutoff));
    let revoked = BrowserSession {
        revoked_at: Some(now),
        ..session
    };
    assert!(!revoked.is_live_at(now, &cutoff));
}
}

fn main() {
fn a_cutoff_makes_stale_only_unexempt_same_device_sessions_before_it() {
    let invalidate_sessions_before = Utc::now();
    let earlier = invalidate_sessions_before - Duration::hours(1);
    let stale = BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), earlier);
    let exempt = BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), earlier);
    let paired = BrowserSession::new_paired_session(
        "Firefox on Linux".to_owned(),
        vec![],
        Duration::hours(24),
        earlier,
    );
    let since = BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(
        vec![],
        Duration::hours(8),
        invalidate_sessions_before,
    );

    let cutoff = StaleSessionCutoff::new(
        invalidate_sessions_before,
        HashSet::from([exempt.sid.clone()]),
    );

    assert!(!stale.is_live_at(invalidate_sessions_before, &cutoff));
    assert!(exempt.is_live_at(invalidate_sessions_before, &cutoff));
    assert!(paired.is_live_at(invalidate_sessions_before, &cutoff));
    assert!(since.is_live_at(invalidate_sessions_before, &cutoff));
}
}

StaleSessionCutoff

A same-device session created before the cutoff is stale, unless its sid is exempt. A stale session isn’t live: its cookie is refused, the Browsers list leaves it out, and a request made in it is denied. Nothing is written for it, so its row is left as it was. Paired sessions are never stale. Setup builds the one cutoff the server holds.

The cutoff before which a same-device session is stale: one created before invalidate_sessions_before whose sid isn’t among exempt_sids. A stale session isn’t live (BrowserSession::is_live_at): the token verifier refuses its cookie, as it does an expired session’s, the Browsers list leaves it out, and the request approver denies a request made in it. Its row is left as it was, so making a session stale writes nothing. Paired sessions are never stale.

Access Token

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/claims.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/mint.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/verify.rs

An access token is what an app shows the FHIR server to be let in. It is a JWT the server signs with its active signing key, and it states everything the server decided: which app it was issued to, the scopes it carries, the SMART patient, and the browser session it was earned under. Whoever holds the token has that access until it expires or is revoked, so it is short-lived, and each one carries an id of its own so it can be revoked alone.

This page is the token as a value: its claims, minting one, and checking a presented one’s signature and claims. Revocation is checked on top of that, by TokenVerifier::verify: a token whose jti is denylisted, whose app’s revocation epoch post-dates it, or whose browser session is revoked is refused even though its signature is good. Three claims are there for revocation’s sake, one per way to revoke: the jti names one token, the sub and iat place it before or after its app was revoked, and the sid names the browser it was earned in.

fn main() {
fn deserialize_audience<'de, D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Vec<String>, D::Error>
where
    D: Deserializer<'de>,
{
    enum StringOrVec {
        One(String),
        Many(Vec<String>),
    }
    match StringOrVec::deserialize(deserializer)? {
        StringOrVec::One(s) => Ok(vec![s]),
        StringOrVec::Many(v) => Ok(v),
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/mint.rs lines 12–27 · authorization-server in the code index

mint_access_token

The jti and the times are the mint’s own, never the caller’s, so no mint site can forget them or reuse an id. The server’s own minter, AccessTokenMinter::mint, sets the issuer and audience to the server’s origin.

Mint a signed access token using signing_key and the supplied claim inputs.

The jti and the times are the mint’s own, never the caller’s, so no mint site can forget them or reuse an id: a fresh random jti, iat from the mint’s clock, and exp the caller’s ttl after it.

Errors

Returns AccessTokenMintError::SigningKeyUnreadable if signing_key’s material cannot be turned into an EncodingKey, or AccessTokenMintError::JwsEncodeFailed if encoding the JWS fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn mint_access_token(
    signing_key: &SigningKey,
    args: &NewAccessTokenArgs<'_>,
) -> Result<String, AccessTokenMintError> {
    let now = Utc::now();
    let claims = AccessTokenClaims {
        issuer: args.issuer.to_string(),
        subject: args.client_id.to_string(),
        // A fresh random `jti` per mint — generated here, not taken from
        // `NewAccessTokenArgs`, so *every* mint site (the OAuth token response, the
        // refresh/token-exchange path) gets a unique id
        // without having to remember to pass one.
        jti: uuid::Uuid::new_v4().to_string(),
        audience: args.audience.unwrap_or(args.issuer).to_string(),
        expires_at: now + args.ttl,
        issued_at: now,
        scope: args.scopes.join(" "),
        patient: args.patient.map(str::to_string),
        sid: args.sid.map(str::to_string),
    };
    let mut header = Header::new(Algorithm::RS256);
    header.kid = Some(signing_key.kid.clone());
    let enc =
        EncodingKey::try_from(signing_key).map_err(AccessTokenMintError::SigningKeyUnreadable)?;
    jsonwebtoken::encode(&header, &claims, &enc).map_err(AccessTokenMintError::JwsEncodeFailed)
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/mint.rs lines 67–92 · authorization-server in the code index

Any minted token verifies against its key, issuer and audience (the issuer when none is named), and carries back exactly the claims it was minted with, living exactly its TTL from about now.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn mint_and_verify_round_trip(
    client_id in "[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,32}",
    scopes in prop::collection::vec("[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,15}", 0..5),
    ttl_seconds in 1i64..=3600,
    origin in "https://[a-z]{3,16}\\.[a-z]{2,8}",
    audience_suffix in prop::option::of("/[a-z]{2,16}"),
    patient in prop::option::of("[a-zA-Z0-9-]{1,32}"),
    sid in prop::option::of("[a-zA-Z0-9-]{1,36}"),
) {
    let key = shared_key();
    let audience: Option<String> = audience_suffix.map(|s| format!("{origin}{s}"));
    let expected_aud = audience.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| origin.clone());

    let before = Utc::now();
    let token = mint_access_token(
        key,
        &NewAccessTokenArgs {
            client_id: &client_id,
            scopes: &scopes,
            ttl: Duration::seconds(ttl_seconds),
            issuer: &origin,
            audience: audience.as_deref(),
            patient: patient.as_deref(),
            sid: sid.as_deref(),
        },
    ).expect("mint");

    let verified_claims = verify_access_token(
        &token,
        std::slice::from_ref(key),
        &AccessTokenVerifyOptions {
            expected_issuer: &origin,
            accepted_audiences: std::slice::from_ref(&expected_aud),
        },
    ).expect("verify");

    // Compare the whole struct so a Debug diff names every wrong field at once.
    let expected = VerifiedClaims {
        issuer: origin.clone(),
        subject: client_id.clone(),
        audience: vec![expected_aud],
        scope: Some(scopes.join(" ")),
        patient: patient.clone(),
        sid: sid.clone(),
        // `jti` is a fresh random id we can't predict, so mirror what
        // was minted; asserted non-empty separately below. Cloned (not
        // spread) because `Option<String>` isn't `Copy` — a bare
        // `..verified_claims` would partially move it and break the
        // `&verified_claims` comparison that follows.
        jti: verified_claims.jti.clone(),
        // Spread verified_claims for timestamps through —
        // they come from `Utc::now()` so we can't predict them
        ..verified_claims
    };
    prop_assert_eq!(&verified_claims, &expected);
    // Every mint stamps a non-empty `jti` (uniqueness is covered by
    // `each_mint_carries_a_unique_jti`).
    prop_assert!(verified_claims.jti.as_deref().is_some_and(|jti| !jti.is_empty()));

    let iat = verified_claims.issued_at.expect("iat present");
    let exp = verified_claims.expires_at.expect("exp present");
    prop_assert_eq!(exp - iat, Duration::seconds(ttl_seconds));
    // JWT timestamps are second-precision; allow a small slack window
    // around the wall-clock `before`/`now` envelope.
    prop_assert!((iat - before).num_seconds().abs() <= 2);
}
}

Every mint stamps a distinct jti: minting the same inputs twice must still yield two different ids (the id is random, not derived from the claims). This is the property the per-token denylist relies on — two live tokens can’t collide on one revocation handle.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn each_mint_carries_a_unique_jti(
    client_id in "[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,32}",
    origin in "https://[a-z]{3,16}\\.[a-z]{2,8}",
    mints in 2usize..=16,
) {
    let key = shared_key();
    let mut seen = std::collections::HashSet::new();
    for _ in 0..mints {
        let token = mint_access_token(key, &owner_args(&client_id, &origin)).expect("mint");
        let claims = verify_access_token(
            &token,
            std::slice::from_ref(key),
            &AccessTokenVerifyOptions {
                expected_issuer: &origin,
                accepted_audiences: std::slice::from_ref(&origin),
            },
        )
        .expect("verify");
        let jti = claims.jti.expect("minted token carries a jti");
        prop_assert!(!jti.is_empty(), "jti must be non-empty");
        prop_assert!(seen.insert(jti), "jti must be unique across mints");
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/verify.rs lines 12–17 · authorization-server in the code index

verify_access_token

Verify a JWT against possible_signing_keys, returning the decoded claims on success.

If the header carries a kid that matches any of the supplied keys, only those keys are tried; otherwise every key is attempted (allowing for rotation overlap).

Errors

Returns AccessTokenVerifyError::NoSigningKeysConfigured if possible_signing_keys is empty, AccessTokenVerifyError::SigningKeyUnreadable if a candidate key’s material cannot be turned into a DecodingKey, or AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected if the token is empty, its header cannot be decoded, or no candidate key validates it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn verify_access_token(
    token: &str,
    possible_signing_keys: &[SigningKey],
    opts: &AccessTokenVerifyOptions<'_>,
) -> Result<VerifiedClaims, AccessTokenVerifyError> {
    let token = token.trim();
    if token.is_empty() {
        return Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected);
    }
    if possible_signing_keys.is_empty() {
        return Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::NoSigningKeysConfigured);
    }
    let header =
        jsonwebtoken::decode_header(token).map_err(|_| AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected)?;

    let kid = header.kid.as_deref();
    let mut kid_matched = possible_signing_keys
        .iter()
        .filter(move |k| kid.is_some_and(|target| k.kid == target))
        .peekable();
    let mut candidates: Box<dyn Iterator<Item = &SigningKey> + '_> = if kid_matched.peek().is_some()
    {
        Box::new(kid_matched)
    } else {
        Box::new(possible_signing_keys.iter())
    };

    let mut validation = Validation::new(Algorithm::RS256);
    validation.set_issuer(&[opts.expected_issuer]);
    let audiences: Vec<&str> = opts.accepted_audiences.iter().map(String::as_str).collect();
    validation.set_audience(&audiences);
    validation.validate_exp = true;

    let try_verifying_with =
        |key: &SigningKey| -> Result<Option<VerifiedClaims>, AccessTokenVerifyError> {
            let dec =
                DecodingKey::try_from(key).map_err(AccessTokenVerifyError::SigningKeyUnreadable)?;
            Ok(
                jsonwebtoken::decode::<VerifiedClaims>(token, &dec, &validation)
                    .ok()
                    .map(|d| d.claims),
            )
        };

    candidates
        .find_map(|key| try_verifying_with(key).transpose())
        .unwrap_or(Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected))
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn verify_accepts_legacy_token_without_jti() {
    let key = SigningKey::generate().expect("gen");
    let origin = "tauri://localhost";
    let now = Utc::now();
    // A claims object with the same shape as a minted token minus `jti`.
    let legacy_claims = serde_json::json!({
        "iss": origin,
        "sub": "legacy-client",
        "aud": origin,
        "exp": (now + Duration::seconds(60)).timestamp(),
        "iat": now.timestamp(),
        "scope": "system/*.read",
    });
    let mut header = Header::new(Algorithm::RS256);
    header.kid = Some(key.kid.clone());
    let enc = EncodingKey::try_from(&key).expect("encoding key");
    let token = jsonwebtoken::encode(&header, &legacy_claims, &enc).expect("encode legacy");

    let claims = verify_access_token(
        &token,
        &[key],
        &AccessTokenVerifyOptions {
            expected_issuer: origin,
            accepted_audiences: &[origin.to_string()],
        },
    )
    .expect("legacy no-jti token must still verify");
    assert_eq!(claims.jti, None, "a legacy token surfaces no jti");
    assert_eq!(claims.subject, "legacy-client");
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/access_token/verify.rs lines 207–236 · authorization-server in the code index

AccessTokenVerifyError

The answers split by whose fault they are. A bad token and a revoked one are the caller’s, a 401, kept distinct so the logs can tell them apart. Everything else is the server’s, a 500, and a store that can’t say whether a token is revoked refuses it. verify_access_token itself answers only TokenRejected, NoSigningKeysConfigured and SigningKeyUnreadable; the rest come from the revocation checks in TokenVerifier.

Failures while verifying an access token.

verify_access_token itself answers only TokenRejected, NoSigningKeysConfigured and SigningKeyUnreadable. The rest come from the TokenVerifier capability, which runs it with the stored keys: KeyStoreUnavailable when it can’t read those keys, and Revoked, RevocationStoreUnavailable and BrowserSessionStoreUnavailable from its revocation checks.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum AccessTokenVerifyError {
    /// Token did not pass cryptographic or claim validation, or it is a
    /// browser session's own token and the session has expired; surface as
    /// 401.
    TokenRejected,
    /// No signing keys are configured — operator misconfiguration, surface as 500.
    NoSigningKeysConfigured,
    /// The signing-key store could not be read (e.g. the database query
    /// failed) — distinct from a key whose material is corrupt. Surface as 500.
    /// Wraps the domain [`AuthorizationServerError`]
    /// the store surfaced, so no database error type appears here.
    KeyStoreUnavailable(#[source] AuthorizationServerError),
    /// A configured signing key's material could not be turned into a
    /// `DecodingKey`.
    SigningKeyUnreadable(#[source] KeyMaterialError),
    /// The token verified cryptographically but has since been revoked — its
    /// `jti` is on the denylist, the subject's revocation epoch post-dates
    /// the token's `iat`, or the browser session its `sid` names is revoked. Surface as 401. Distinct from [`Self::TokenRejected`]
    /// so the caller and the logs can tell a revoked token from a bad one.
    Revoked,
    /// The revocation store could not be read (e.g. the database query failed)
    /// while checking whether a token was revoked. An operator problem, and we
    /// **fail closed** — surface as 500 rather than admit a possibly-revoked
    /// token — matching how [`Self::KeyStoreUnavailable`] is treated.
    RevocationStoreUnavailable(String),
    /// The browser session a token's `sid` names could not be read while
    /// checking whether it was revoked. Fails closed like
    /// [`Self::RevocationStoreUnavailable`].
    BrowserSessionStoreUnavailable(#[source] AuthorizationServerError),
}
}

Client Credentials

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/client_credentials.rs

An app that can keep a secret authenticates at /oauth/token by presenting its client_id and that secret; one that can’t presents its client_id alone. This page is the pair as the domain sees it, before anything checks it. The authenticated-client proof checks it against the app’s client row, which stores only a hash of the secret.

The secret is the one piece of client material the server ever holds in plaintext, and only for the length of one request. It gets the same two habits as a signing key’s private parts: scrubbed when dropped, and never printed.

domain::client_credentials

ClientCredentials

A client’s presented credentials. The plaintext client_secret is scrubbed from memory when the value is dropped (ZeroizeOnDrop) — defense in depth that shortens the window the secret sits on the heap after the request that verified it completes; it does not eliminate every copy (the raw request body and header still live in axum’s buffers upstream). client_id is not secret and is skipped.

Client

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/client/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/essential_client.rs

A client is an app that asks for access to the Owner’s FHIR server: a SMART app in a browser, a Pebble companion, the host app. It names itself with a client_id on every request. A client that can keep a secret is confidential and authenticates with its credentials; a client that can’t (a single-page app, a native app) is public.

Every client has a registration: the redirect URIs it may send a browser back to, the scopes it may ask for, and the grant types it may use at /oauth/token. Who defines the registration decides how a request is judged against it. A few clients belong to the server itself, and their registration is fixed: a request is held to it as it stands. Every other client is trusted on first use. An app the server has never seen isn’t turned away at /oauth/authorize. Its request goes to the Owner with a warning, and the Owner’s approval writes the registration, or widens it when a known app steps outside what it registered.

That warning is the presented client change: what approving the request would change in the app’s registration. Nothing, if the request stays inside it; create it, for an app the Owner has never approved; or widen it, by a new redirect, new scopes, or both. The change is derived from the current row on every read, never stored, so a consent prompt opened after the row moved shows the move. A request that would change the registration never skips the Owner, even when a standing grant would cover it.

Two clients the Owner can’t switch off at all, because they are how the Owner gets in: they are essential.

    /// Who defines the registration: the server, which seeds it and holds

The tests judge requests at the presented-change fixtures’ redirect, against clients built from the shared client fixture.

PresentedClientChange

What approving an authorization-code request would change in its client’s registration: the registration it presents (see PresentedClientRegistration) judged against the current clients row. The consent prompt renders it as the Owner-facing warning.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum PresentedClientChange {
    /// The row exists, the `redirect_uri` is on its allowlist, and every
    /// requested scope is covered by `allowed_scopes`: approving changes
    /// nothing. The only change that may take the existing-grant fast path at
    /// `/authorize`.

    /// No row exists for this `client_id`: approving would create one. Nothing
    /// is persisted for such a client until the Owner approves.
    WouldCreate,
    /// The row exists but the presented registration steps outside it, so
    /// approving would widen the row (for a client trusted on first use).
    WouldWiden {
        /// The presented `redirect_uri` is not on the allowlist.

        /// The requested scopes no `allowed_scopes` entry covers, in request
        /// order. Empty when only the redirect changed.

    },
}

from_presented_registration

Judge presented_registration against its current client row.

@returns WouldCreate when no row exists, NoChange when the redirect is on the allowlist and every requested scope is covered, and WouldWiden otherwise — carrying which of the two stepped outside the registration.

Scope coverage is the same coverage-aware check the rest of the slice uses (wildflowerhealthio_scopes::allowed_scope_covers): a client allowed a broad scope also covers a narrower same-grammar request. An unparseable scope parses to an Unknown scope that only covers itself, so it is reported as new unless the registration lists it verbatim — deliberately, since the Owner should see an unrecognized scope string.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn from_presented_registration(
    presented_registration: &PresentedClientRegistration<'_>,
) -> PresentedClientChange {
    let Some(existing_client) = presented_registration.maybe_existing_client else {
        return PresentedClientChange::WouldCreate;
    };
    let redirect_uri_is_new =
        !existing_client.allows_redirect_uri(presented_registration.redirect_uri);
    let unregistered_requested_scopes = uncovered_scopes(
        &existing_client.allowed_scopes,
        presented_registration.scopes,
    );
    if redirect_uri_is_new || !unregistered_requested_scopes.is_empty() {
        PresentedClientChange::WouldWiden {
            redirect_uri_is_new,
            unregistered_requested_scopes,
        }
    } else {
        PresentedClientChange::NoChange
    }
}
}

The change is exactly one of the three, and each is decided by the two facts it reports: NoChange iff the redirect is allowlisted and nothing is uncovered, and a WouldWiden change never carries both “nothing new” flags (that would be NoChange). The reported unregistered_requested_scopes are always a subset of what was requested, in request order.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn the_change_agrees_with_what_it_reports(
    registered in prop::collection::vec(arb_plain_scope(), 0..5),
    requested in prop::collection::vec(arb_plain_scope(), 0..5),
    allowlisted in any::<bool>(),
) {
    let mut app = client("app", &[]);
    app.allowed_scopes = registered;
    if !allowlisted {
        app.redirect_uris = Vec::new();
    }
    let change = PresentedClientChange::from_presented_registration(&PresentedClientRegistration {
        maybe_existing_client: Some(&app),
        redirect_uri: &redirect(),
        scopes: &requested,
    });
    let uncovered = uncovered_scopes(&app.allowed_scopes, &requested);
    match change {
        PresentedClientChange::WouldCreate => prop_assert!(false, "a known client never WouldCreate"),
        PresentedClientChange::NoChange => {
            prop_assert!(allowlisted);
            prop_assert!(uncovered.is_empty());
        }
        PresentedClientChange::WouldWiden { redirect_uri_is_new, unregistered_requested_scopes } => {
            prop_assert_eq!(redirect_uri_is_new, !allowlisted);
            prop_assert_eq!(&unregistered_requested_scopes, &uncovered);
            prop_assert!(redirect_uri_is_new || !unregistered_requested_scopes.is_empty());
            // A subset of the request, in request order.
            let mut remaining = requested.iter();
            for new_scope in &unregistered_requested_scopes {
                prop_assert!(remaining.any(|r| r == new_scope));
            }
        }
    }
}
}

Grant

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant.rs

A grant is the Owner’s standing yes. When the Owner approves an app’s request, the server records a grant alongside the one-off approval: “this app may have these scopes, here”. The grant lasts until the Owner revokes it. Nothing about it expires.

There are two kinds, one per flow that has an Owner to ask. An authorization-code grant is keyed on the app and the exact redirect URI it asked from. A device grant is keyed on the app and the device’s name. It is the Owner’s record of which devices they have paired, and it never skips a prompt.

When a grant skips the Owner

A later request from the same app, at the same redirect, may get its code at /oauth/authorize without asking the Owner. That takes all of these at once:

  • The request changes nothing in the app’s registration: its presented client change is NoChange. A new app, a new redirect or a new scope always goes back to the Owner, however much an old grant covers.
  • The standing grant covers every requested scope. A grant that covers only some of them pre-ticks those on the consent card, and the Owner decides the rest.
  • The request’s browser session holds what the request needs, or has gone on past its limited page for this app before, so the request isn’t waiting there. The code then carries only what the session also covers.
  • A launch’s patient, if it bound one, is the grant’s patient. Otherwise the Owner decides.

The proof that the first two hold is GrantCoverage::resolve; the request’s limited page is on the Code Request page. A code issued this way stamps the grant’s last_used_at. A device grant’s is stamped instead when a refresh family it earned rotates.

Revoking a grant ends what it earned. GrantsRevoker::revoke revokes every access token the app holds, deletes the row, and expires every refresh family issued to the app.

domain::grant

AuthorizationCodeGrant

A standing authorization-code consent: client X may have scopes Y at redirect URI Z. A later request from the client at that redirect gets its code without asking the Owner only when it changes nothing in the client’s registration, this grant covers every requested scope, its browser session is live and holds what it asks for (or its browser has gone on past the limited page for this client), and a launch’s patient, if any, is this grant’s. A grant covering only some scopes pre-ticks them on the consent card.

One grant per (client_id, redirect_uri). Diesel-mapped 1:1 to the authorization_code_grants table; on the wire it rides inside Grant::AuthorizationCode.

CumulativeConsent

The re-approval rule both grant kinds share — behaviour, not structure: consent is cumulative. A later approval unions its scopes into the standing set (order-preserving, no duplicates) and refreshes the consent instant and patient context; approving a narrower request never withdraws previously-consented scopes — revoking the grant is the way to withdraw.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub trait CumulativeConsent {
    /// Fold a re-approval into this standing grant: union `additional` scopes
    /// in, stamp `granted_at = at`, and adopt the re-approval's `patient`.
    /// `last_used_at` is left as it was.
    fn absorb_reapproval(
        &mut self,
        additional: &[String],
        patient: Option<&str>,
        at: DateTime<Utc>,
    );
}
}

fn absorb_reapproval(
    &mut self,
    additional: &[String],
    patient: Option<&str>,
    at: DateTime<Utc>,
) {
    union_scopes_into(&mut self.scopes, additional);
    self.granted_at = at;
    self.patient = patient.map(str::to_owned);
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn absorb_reapproval_unions_scopes_and_refreshes_consent() {
    let later: DateTime<Utc> = "2025-06-01T00:00:00Z".parse().expect("timestamp");

    let mut code = code_grant();
    code.absorb_reapproval(
        &["read".to_owned(), "write".to_owned()],
        Some("pat-2"),
        later,
    );
    assert_eq!(
        code.scopes,
        vec![
            "read".to_owned(),
            "offline_access".to_owned(),
            "write".to_owned()
        ],
    );
    assert_eq!(code.granted_at, later);
    assert_eq!(code.patient.as_deref(), Some("pat-2"));

    let mut device = device_grant();
    device.absorb_reapproval(&["read".to_owned()], None, later);
    assert_eq!(
        device.scopes,
        vec!["read".to_owned(), "offline_access".to_owned()],
        "a narrower re-approval never un-approves earlier consent",
    );
    assert_eq!(device.granted_at, later);
    assert_eq!(device.patient, None);
}
}

Launch Context

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/launch_context.rs

A launch context is a SMART App Launch launch value this server handed out, and what it binds. When an app is launched, from the apps launch route or from the base, the server mints an opaque value and gives it to the app. The app echoes it back at /oauth/authorize, and the request that presents it consumes it, once. A second presentation, from anyone, is refused. A launch that isn’t consumed within five minutes expires.

A launch is either for one app or for a server’s launcher. The base launches a server’s launcher without knowing which app the Owner set as the launcher, so that launch is open to any app. A launch for one app can’t be spent by another: an /oauth/authorize from a different client is refused, and the launch stays consumable by its own app.

Only a launch for one app can bind a patient. When it does, the code request it starts records that patient, and an approval must name the same one. The server’s in-process mints, LaunchContexts::mint and LaunchContexts::mint_for_server_launcher, bind no patient.

domain::launch_context

LaunchContext

One SMART App Launch launch value this server handed out, and what it binds. Minted in-process (the apps launch route, the base’s launch) through the LaunchContexts capability, and consumed single-use by the /oauth/authorize request that presents it. Diesel-mapped 1:1 to the launch_contexts table.

A launch is for one OAuth client (LaunchContext::for_client) or for a server’s launcher, which any client may consume (LaunchContext::for_server_launcher). Only a launch for one client can bind a patient: the client and patient fields are private so no other shape can be built, and the table’s CHECK holds the same rule.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct LaunchContext {
    /// Primary key — the opaque `launch` value the app is handed and echoes
    /// back at `/oauth/authorize`.
    pub nonce: String,
    /// The OAuth client the launch is for; an authorize from any other client
    /// can't consume it. `None` for a launch minted for the server launcher,
    /// which any client may consume.
    client_id: Option<String>,
    /// The patient the launch binds, if any. When set, the request it starts
    /// records that patient, and the consent approval must name the same one.
    /// Set only alongside `client_id`.
    patient: Option<String>,
    /// When the launch was minted.
    pub created_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    /// Instant after which the launch can no longer be consumed.
    pub expires_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    /// When `/oauth/authorize` consumed the launch; `None` while unused.
    pub consumed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,
}
}

Authorization Request

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/approval.rs

Every request for access is parked as an authorization request until someone decides it: an app at /oauth/authorize asking for a code, a device asking for a token, a browser asking the Owner for a browser session. The Owner (or, for an app’s request, a browser allowed to decide for them) answers it once. Each flow is its own type, with its own fields, states and transitions:

FlowTypeKeyed byStored inEnds
Authorization codeCodeRequestan internal UUIDcode_authorization_requestsapproved or denied; its code is what is redeemed
Device codeDeviceRequestthe device’s device_codeuser_code_requestsclaimed once by the device’s poll
Browser pairingPairingRequestthe page’s pairing codeuser_code_requestsclaimed once by the pairing page’s poll

A code request has one state the others don’t: when its browser session holds less than it asks for, it first waits on that browser’s limited page, which asks the person at the browser whether to go on, and the Owner isn’t asked about it until they do. The device and pairing flows share their shape instead: a user_code the Owner enters at the device page, and a poll that waits for the decision and then claims it. Their pages are Code Request and Polled Requests.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> AwaitingLimitedPage: a code request whose session falls short
    [*] --> Pending: any other request
    AwaitingLimitedPage --> Pending: Continue
    AwaitingLimitedPage --> Denied: Cancel
    Pending --> Approved: approve
    Pending --> Denied: deny
    Approved --> Claimed: a device's or pairing's poll

There’s no expired state. Expiry is a fact about time, so it is worked out from expires_at whenever someone asks, and never written. A code request stays approved for good: its single use is the code it earned, not the request.

Transitions and the guarded replace

A request is started by its flow’s new and changed only by its flow’s transitions. A transition writes nothing. It reads the request as loaded, takes now, and answers with the changed request, or a refusal such as NotPending when it no longer applies. The store then writes the changed request over the row with a guarded replace, one UPDATE that lands only while the row still has the status the request was read with:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn replace_code_request(
    &mut self,
    read: &CodeRequest,
    changed: &CodeRequest,
) -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError> {
    if changed.id != read.id {
        return Err(replaced_by_another(&read.id, &changed.id));
    }
    let affected = diesel::update(
        code_authorization_requests::table
            .find(&read.id)
            .filter(code_authorization_requests::status.eq(read.state.status())),
    )
    .set(CodeAuthorizationRequestRow::from(changed))
    .execute(self.conn)
    .map_err(failed("replace_authorization_request failed"))?;
    Ok(affected == 1)
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/db/authorization_requests/mod.rs lines 384–401 · authorization-server in the code index

One affected row means “you won”. None means someone moved the row first. A decision that loses is answered as not found, since the request is no longer there for that caller; a claim that loses gets nothing; a poll stamp that loses is dropped. The same mechanism settles three races:

  • Two decisions on one request. Both read it pending; the first write moves the status, and the second no longer matches.
  • Continue racing Cancel on the limited page. Both read it awaiting the page; whichever lands moves the status, to pending or to denied, and the other no longer matches.
  • A poll stamp racing an approval. A stamp leaves the status pending, so an approval read before the stamp still lands. A stamp read before the approval no longer matches, so it can’t write the request back to pending.

The port declares one guarded replace per flow, AuthorizationRequestsTx::replace_code_request and its two siblings. Approving is the one transition that grants anything, so a source guard holds every approve and claim call to the writers and the proofs that may make them (tests::APPROVAL_CONSTRUCTIONS).

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/approval.rs lines 9–14 · authorization-server in the code index

Code Request

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/code/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/code/resolved.rs

A code request is an app’s request for an authorization code (RFC 6749 §4.1), parked by /oauth/authorize until it is decided. It is always made in a browser session: /oauth/authorize sends a browser without one to sign in or pair first. The code it earns is issued under that session, not the approver’s, and carries only what that session also covers.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> AwaitingLimitedPage: new, the session falls short
    [*] --> Pending: new
    AwaitingLimitedPage --> Pending: acknowledge_session_shortfall (Continue)
    AwaitingLimitedPage --> Denied: deny_on_limited_page (Cancel)
    Pending --> Pending: raise_for_owner
    Pending --> Approved: approve
    Pending --> Denied: deny

The limited page

Suppose the browser’s session lacks a scope the app asks for: a laptop paired read-only, an app that wants write. The request starts awaiting the limited page, and the browser is sent there. The page says what’s missing and offers Continue or Cancel. Until the browser goes on, the Owner isn’t asked about the request and nothing decides it. Continue makes it pending with a fresh lifetime; Cancel denies it. Once a browser has pressed Continue for an app, its later requests for that app start pending: the page is shown once per browser per app. Both buttons are transitions read from the same status, so of two tabs pressing them at once only the first lands (the guarded replace).

Who decides

A pending request is decided by the Owner, or by the browser that made it when that browser’s session may decide consents and holds what approving takes: then the browser shows the consent card itself. A browser that can read the request but not approve it can raise it for the Owner, after which the host notifies the Owner about it. When a standing grant covers the request, nobody decides: the request is parked and approved at once.

Resolving against the registration

Every step that judges a code request, /oauth/authorize, the limited page’s Continue, and the consent read and approval, learns what the app’s client row says about it in one place: a resolved code request. It is worked out from the row as it stands on every read, never stored, so a consent prompt opened after the row moved shows the move. The most an approval may grant comes from ApprovableScopes::for_code, which caps a fixed registration at itself.

pub fn new(args: NewCodeRequestArgs, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> Self {

resolve

Resolve a request from client_id presenting redirect_uri and requested_scopes against the client’s row maybe_existing_client.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn resolve(
    client_id: &str,
    redirect_uri: &Url,
    requested_scopes: &[String],
    maybe_existing_client: Option<&Client>,
) -> Self {
    match maybe_existing_client {
        // Trusted on first use: an unknown client is named by its
        // `client_id`, and approving its request would create its row.
        None => ResolvedCodeRequest {
            client_name: client_id.to_owned(),
            client_disabled: false,
            registration_is_fixed: false,
            redirect_is_registered: false,
            presented_client_change: PresentedClientChange::WouldCreate,
            approvable_scopes: ApprovableScopes::for_code(requested_scopes, None, false),
        },
        Some(existing_client) => {
            let registration_is_fixed = existing_client.is_registration_fixed();
            ResolvedCodeRequest {
                client_name: existing_client.name.clone(),
                client_disabled: existing_client.disabled_at.is_some(),
                registration_is_fixed,
                redirect_is_registered: existing_client.allows_redirect_uri(redirect_uri),
                presented_client_change: PresentedClientChange::from_presented_registration(
                    &PresentedClientRegistration {
                        maybe_existing_client: Some(existing_client),
                        redirect_uri,
                        scopes: requested_scopes,
                    },
                ),
                approvable_scopes: ApprovableScopes::for_code(
                    requested_scopes,
                    Some(existing_client),
                    registration_is_fixed,
                ),
            }
        }
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/code/resolved.rs lines 131–133 · authorization-server in the code index

Polled Requests

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/polled.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/device.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_request/pairing.rs

Two flows ask from something that can’t show the Owner a consent card itself, and so wait by polling:

  • A device request (RFC 8628): a TV or a watch asks for a token, shows its user a short user_code, and polls /oauth/token with its device_code until the Owner decides.
  • A browser pairing: a browser that isn’t on the server’s own device asks for a browser session at /oauth/pair, shows a user_code, and polls with its pairing code. Pairing is no OAuth grant: its claim starts a paired session, and nothing is redeemed at /oauth/token.

Both are decided at the server’s device page, where the Owner enters or confirms the user_code. The key the poll uses, the device_code or the pairing code, is a 256-bit secret only the poller holds; the user_code is short enough to type, and only finds the request for the Owner.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: new
    Pending --> Pending: stamp_poll
    Pending --> Approved: approve
    Pending --> Denied: deny
    Approved --> Claimed: claim, by the next poll

An approval is redeemed once. The poll after the Owner approves claims the request; a second claim finds it claimed and gets nothing. A claimed request keeps its approval, and an approved request past its expiry can’t be claimed. A poll is stamped, so the next one can be told to slow down when it comes sooner than DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL after it. A stamp leaves the request pending, so an approval read before the stamp still lands after it (the guarded replace).

domain::authorization_request::polled

The tests run on a fixed clock, with the polled-request fixtures.

Polled

What a device request and a browser pairing share: the code the Owner enters, the poll that waits on the decision, and the claim that redeems it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub trait Polled: Sized {
    /// What the Owner's approval carries for this flow.
    type Approval: Clone;

    /// The code the device page looks the request up by, which the Owner
    /// enters or confirms there.
    fn user_code(&self) -> &str;

    /// The last poll, for the slow-down; `None` before the first.
    fn last_polled_at(&self) -> Option<DateTime<Utc>>;

    /// The instant the request stops waiting for a decision.
    fn expires_at(&self) -> DateTime<Utc>;

    /// Where the request stands.
    fn state(&self) -> &PolledState<Self::Approval>;

    /// Claim the approved request at `now`, once: the poll that redeems the
    /// Owner's approval.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`NotClaimable`] for a request not approved, or past its expiry.
    fn claim(&self, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> Result<Self, NotClaimable>;

    /// Whether the request is past its expiry at `now`.
    fn is_expired_at(&self, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> bool {
        self.expires_at() <= now
    }

    /// Whether the request waits for the Owner's decision at `now`: pending
    /// and unexpired.
    fn is_pending_at(&self, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> bool {
        matches!(self.state(), PolledState::Pending) && !self.is_expired_at(now)
    }

    /// Whether a poll at `now` comes sooner than [`DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL`]
    /// after the last one, which answers `slow_down` (RFC 8628 §3.5).
    fn is_polled_too_soon_at(&self, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> bool {
        self.last_polled_at()
            .is_some_and(|last_polled_at| now - last_polled_at < DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL)
    }
}
}
