#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn claim_redeems_an_approved_request_once() {
    let request = device_request();
    let approved = request.approve(approval(), None, at(1)).expect("approves");
    let claimed = approved.claim(at(2)).expect("claims");
    assert_eq!(claimed.state, PolledState::Claimed(approval()));
    assert_eq!(claimed.state.status(), RequestStatus::Claimed);
    assert_eq!(claimed.state.approval(), Some(&approval()));
    assert_eq!(claimed.claim(at(2)), Err(NotClaimable));
    assert_eq!(request.claim(at(2)), Err(NotClaimable));
    assert_eq!(approved.claim(at(300)), Err(NotClaimable));
}
}

claimed_state

The claimed state of request at now: its approval, redeemed. The flows’ Polled::claim build on it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) fn claimed_state<P: Polled>(
    request: &P,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<PolledState<P::Approval>, NotClaimable> {
    match request.state() {
        PolledState::Approved(approval) if !request.is_expired_at(now) => {
            Ok(PolledState::Claimed(approval.clone()))
        }
        _ => Err(NotClaimable),
    }
}
}

pub fn approve(

    approval: Approval,
    device_name: Option<String>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Self, NotPending> {
    self.require_pending(now)?;
    Ok(DeviceRequest {
        device_name: device_name.or_else(|| self.device_name.clone()),
        state: PolledState::Approved(approval),
        ..self.clone()
    })

The Owner may settle the name the browser goes by on the Owner’s list of browsers. The session itself starts later, when the pairing page’s poll claims the request.

Approve the pairing at now with approval, naming the browser browser_name (None keeps the name it has).

Errors

NotPending for a pairing no longer pending at now.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn approve(
    &self,
    approval: PairingApproval,
    browser_name: Option<String>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Self, NotPending> {
    self.require_pending(now)?;
    Ok(PairingRequest {
        browser_name: browser_name.unwrap_or_else(|| self.browser_name.clone()),
        state: PolledState::Approved(approval),
        ..self.clone()
    })
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn approve_records_the_approval_and_the_browser_s_name() {
    let request = started();
    let renamed = request
        .approve(approval(), Some("Ruth's laptop".to_owned()), at(1))
        .expect("approves");
    assert_eq!(renamed.state, PolledState::Approved(approval()));
    assert_eq!(renamed.browser_name, "Ruth's laptop");
    let kept_name = request.approve(approval(), None, at(1)).expect("approves");
    assert_eq!(kept_name.browser_name, "Firefox on Linux");
    assert_eq!(renamed.approve(approval(), None, at(1)), Err(NotPending));
}
}

The server says no in four vocabularies, one per audience:

  • AuthorizationServerError to the Owner’s UI on the /authorization surface, and from every operation when the store fails;
  • OAuthErrorCode to an app, as the error of an OAuth response;
  • AuthorizeRefusal to the person at the browser, or the app, when /oauth/authorize refuses a request;
  • TokenExchangeError to an app at /oauth/token, with the specific reason kept for the operator’s log.

None of them knows about HTTP. Each is a domain fact, and the HTTP layer decides the status and the body (Errors and Wire Shapes). The two that reach an app are built so that nothing from the request is echoed back: a code is one of a closed set, and a description is one of the server’s fixed sentences.

domain::authorization_server_error

AuthorizationServerError

The semantic variants are decided one layer up from the store, in the capabilities, so the SQLite adapter and the in-memory test fake speak only the port’s primitive contract, and the store produces nothing but Infrastructure. Display gives each variant a sentence for the logs.

The ways an authorization server domain operation can fail. The *NotFound variants are semantic, client-facing outcomes that are part of the wire contract (each renders as a structured JSON 404 keyed by the resource’s identifying field); Infrastructure is an opaque infrastructure failure rendered as a logged, empty 500. Its audience is the Owner’s UI on the /authorization surface, which acts on the semantic variants, and every operation when the store fails. Each semantic 4xx renders as JSON naming the variant in error, with the identifying field beside it, so the Owner’s UI can tell which thing went missing.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum AuthorizationServerError {
    /// No pending, unexpired authorization-code consent has this id — the
    /// Owner-facing `/authorization/oauth-consents/{id}` surface's 404.
    OAuthConsentNotFound {
        /// The authorization request id the Owner's UI asked for.
        id: String,
    },
    /// No pending, unexpired device-code consent has this user code — the
    /// Owner-facing `/authorization/devices/{userCode}` surface's 404.
    DeviceConsentNotFound {
        /// The user code the Owner's UI asked for.
        user_code: String,
    },
    /// No standing grant has this id — the `/authorization/grants/{id}` 404.
    GrantNotFound {
        /// The grant id the Owner's UI asked for.
        id: String,
    },
    /// No standing browser session has this `sid` — the
    /// `DELETE /authorization/browser-sessions/{sid}` 404.
    BrowserSessionNotFound {
        /// The session id the Owner's UI asked to revoke.
        sid: String,
    },
    /// No registered client has this `client_id` — the
    /// `PATCH /authorization/clients/{clientId}` 404.
    ClientNotFound {
        /// The client the Owner's UI asked to change.
        client_id: String,
    },
    /// The Owner tried to disable an essential client — the
    /// `PATCH /authorization/clients/{clientId}` **409**. Disabling it would
    /// leave the Owner no way in (see
    /// `is_essential_client`).
    /// Nothing is written when it is raised.
    EssentialClient {
        /// The essential client the Owner tried to disable.
        client_id: String,
    },
    /// No authorization request has this id — the `/oauth/authorize/{id}`
    /// polling endpoint's 404, which the wait page's poll hears.
    AuthorizationRequestNotFound {
        /// The authorization request id the wait page polled.
        id: String,
    },
    /// The caller authenticated, but their token doesn't cover the scope(s) the
    /// `/authorization` operation requires — the surface's **403**. `missing_scopes`
    /// are the rendered scopes the caller must additionally hold. Raised when the
    /// [`Scoped`](wildflowerhealthio_scope_capabilities::Scoped) extractor rejects (via
    /// `From<MissingScopes>`), and when a consent approval's approver lacks one
    /// of the request's approval scopes (`wildflower/Grant.c` for a standing
    /// grant, `wildflower/Client.c` and `wildflower/Client.u` for a
    /// registration trusted on first use, a code request's resource scopes),
    /// which depend on the request and so are checked per call. Nothing is
    /// written when an approval raises it.
    InsufficientScope {
        /// The rendered scopes the caller lacks.
        missing_scopes: Vec<String>,
    },
    /// An approver tried to grant a client more than they themselves hold —
    /// the consent approve surfaces' **403**. `approver_missing_scopes` are the rendered
    /// scopes the approval would grant that the approver's own token does not
    /// cover ("you can't delegate more permission than you have"). Semantic and
    /// client-facing: the approver must step up (or narrow their approval).
    /// It renders as the same 403 body as
    /// [`InsufficientScope`](AuthorizationServerError::InsufficientScope).
    InsufficientApproverScope {
        /// The rendered scopes the approval would grant beyond the approver's
        /// own token.
        approver_missing_scopes: Vec<String>,
    },
    /// The Owner approved an authorization-code consent whose client is new to
    /// this authorization server (or whose redirect / scopes step outside its
    /// registration) without acknowledging that warning — the consent approve
    /// surface's **409**. Semantic and client-facing: the launcher must show the
    /// registration warning and send
    /// `acknowledgedRegistrationChange: true`. Nothing is written when it is raised.
    RegistrationNotAcknowledged {
        /// The authorization request the Owner approved.
        id: String,
    },
    /// The Owner approved an authorization-code consent whose SMART launch
    /// bound a patient, naming a different patient (or none) — the consent
    /// approve surface's **409**. Nothing is written when it is raised.
    LaunchPatientMismatch {
        /// The authorization request the Owner approved.
        id: String,
    },
    /// An infrastructure failure in the backing store (a lock, query, or
    /// mapping error) — opaque to clients: the HTTP layer logs `context` +
    /// `source` and answers an empty 500. The cause is captured as text so
    /// this type stays free of the store's database error types.
    Infrastructure {
        /// A fixed phrase saying what the store was doing when it failed.
        context: &'static str,
        /// The cause's `Display` text. Kept as text, not an error source, so
        /// no database error type reaches the routes.
        source: String,
    },
}
}

domain::oauth_error_code

OAuthErrorCode

A code from the closed set of OAuth error codes the authorization server’s JSON error surface may emit. Its AsRef<str>/Display impls (derived by strum from the snake_case variant names) yield the exact RFC wire value. Its audience is an app, as the error of an OAuth response: from /oauth/token, or on its callback redirect.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) enum OAuthErrorCode {
    /// RFC 6749 §5.2 — the request is missing a required parameter, malformed,
    /// or otherwise invalid.
    InvalidRequest,
    /// RFC 6749 §5.2 — client authentication failed.
    InvalidClient,
    /// RFC 6749 §5.2 — the provided grant (authorization code, refresh token,
    /// device code) is invalid, expired, revoked, or does not match.
    InvalidGrant,
    /// RFC 6749 §5.2 — the authenticated client is not authorized to use this
    /// grant type.
    UnauthorizedClient,
    /// RFC 6749 §5.2 — the requested scope is invalid, unknown, or exceeds what
    /// the client may hold.
    InvalidScope,
    /// RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 — the authorization server does not support obtaining an
    /// authorization code using this `response_type`. Surfaced on the
    /// authorization-endpoint redirect, never the JSON token surface.
    UnsupportedResponseType,
    /// RFC 6749 §5.2 — the server encountered an unexpected condition.
    ServerError,
    /// RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 — the resource owner (or authorization server) denied
    /// the request, or it ended before it could be approved (its browser
    /// session ended, or its browser cancelled on the limited page).
    AccessDenied,
    /// RFC 8628 §3.5 — the device authorization is still pending the user's
    /// action; the client should keep polling.
    AuthorizationPending,
    /// RFC 8628 §3.5 — the client is polling faster than the permitted interval
    /// and must back off.
    SlowDown,
    /// RFC 8628 §3.5 — the `device_code` has expired and the device-flow
    /// authorization session is no longer valid.
    ExpiredToken,
}
}

Each variant’s wire value must match its exact RFC string — this guards the strum serialize_all rule (and any variant rename) from silently changing what ships on the wire.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn as_ref_matches_rfc_wire_values() {
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::InvalidRequest.as_ref(), "invalid_request");
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::InvalidClient.as_ref(), "invalid_client");
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::InvalidGrant.as_ref(), "invalid_grant");
    assert_eq!(
        OAuthErrorCode::UnauthorizedClient.as_ref(),
        "unauthorized_client"
    );
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::InvalidScope.as_ref(), "invalid_scope");
    assert_eq!(
        OAuthErrorCode::UnsupportedResponseType.as_ref(),
        "unsupported_response_type"
    );
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::ServerError.as_ref(), "server_error");
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::AccessDenied.as_ref(), "access_denied");
    assert_eq!(
        OAuthErrorCode::AuthorizationPending.as_ref(),
        "authorization_pending"
    );
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::SlowDown.as_ref(), "slow_down");
    assert_eq!(OAuthErrorCode::ExpiredToken.as_ref(), "expired_token");
}
}

domain::authorize_refusal

RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 lets a refusal go back to the app only once its redirect_uri is trusted. Before that point, or for a redirect nobody has vouched for, the refusal is a local page in the browser. Either way the reason is the same sentence.

AuthorizeRefusal

Why /oauth/authorize refused a request: shown on the local page, or sent back to a trusted redirect as the error_description. Its audience is the person at the browser, or the app once its redirect is trusted. The local page is titled for the refusal, with Self::description as its body.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum AuthorizeRefusal {
    /// The `redirect_uri` is not a well-formed URL, so there is nowhere
    /// trusted to send the refusal.
    InvalidRedirectUri,
    /// The `redirect_uri` is not `http` or `https`.
    InvalidScheme,
    /// The request comes from a client the Owner has disabled.
    DisabledClient,
    /// The `redirect_uri` is not on a server-defined registration. A client
    /// trusted on first use is never refused for this: its new redirect goes
    /// to the Owner instead.
    RedirectUriNotAllowed,
    /// `response_type` is not `code`.
    UnsupportedResponseType,
    /// `code_challenge_method` is not `S256`.
    UnsupportedCodeChallengeMethod,
    /// `code_challenge` is not a well-formed S256 challenge.
    InvalidCodeChallenge,
    /// `launch` names no launch this client may see: never minted, pruned
    /// after expiring, or another app's, which reads exactly like one that
    /// doesn't exist.
    LaunchUnknown,
    /// `launch` names this client's launch, which was consumed already.
    LaunchAlreadyUsed,
    /// `launch` names this client's launch, which is past its expiry.
    LaunchExpired,
    /// `aud` does not name this server's origin, its FHIR base.
    InvalidAudience,
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorize_refusal.rs lines 15–43 · authorization-server in the code index

description

Every sentence is a fixed string, never request input, and valid error_description text, so nothing an attacker sends is echoed back and no sentence breaks the redirect’s grammar. The tests check every sentence against the RFC’s grammar with a small predicate, including the three fixed sentences of the client callback.

The sentence saying why: the local page’s body, and the error_description when the refusal goes back to the client. Plain ASCII without " or \, as RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 requires of an error_description.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn description(self) -> &'static str {
    match self {
        AuthorizeRefusal::InvalidRedirectUri => {
            "The supplied redirect_uri is not a well-formed URL."
        }
        AuthorizeRefusal::InvalidScheme => "The supplied redirect_uri must use http or https.",
        AuthorizeRefusal::DisabledClient => "The supplied client_id has been disabled.",
        AuthorizeRefusal::RedirectUriNotAllowed => {
            "The supplied redirect_uri is not registered for this client."
        }
        AuthorizeRefusal::UnsupportedResponseType => {
            "The app asked for a kind of sign-in this server doesn't support."
        }
        AuthorizeRefusal::UnsupportedCodeChallengeMethod => {
            "The app's sign-in request uses a security method this server doesn't support."
        }
        AuthorizeRefusal::InvalidCodeChallenge => {
            "The app's sign-in request has a malformed security check."
        }
        AuthorizeRefusal::LaunchUnknown => "This launch isn't recognized. Open the app again.",
        AuthorizeRefusal::LaunchAlreadyUsed => {
            "This launch was already used. Open the app again."
        }
        AuthorizeRefusal::LaunchExpired => "This launch has expired. Open the app again.",
        AuthorizeRefusal::InvalidAudience => {
            "The app asked for a different server than this one."
        }
    }
}
}

domain::token_exchange_error

The app hears less than the log. The HTTP layer collapses the specific reasons a grant was refused onto a few generic descriptions (invalid_grant_description), so a response doesn’t say which check a code failed, and a refresh token presented by the wrong app reads exactly like an unknown one. Two reasons record what was done as well as what was found: a code that is unknown or already redeemed has revoked any refresh family minted from it, and a consumed refresh token presented again has revoked its whole family.

The token exchanger and the redemption proofs raise each variant, and their tests show them.

InvalidGrantReason

Why a grant presented at /oauth/token was refused as invalid_grant. The specific reason goes to the operator’s log; the app hears one generic description per family of reasons. The fields carry only what an operator needs to tell the cases apart — never the code, verifier, challenge, or token.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) enum InvalidGrantReason {
    /// The authorization code is unknown or already redeemed — a possible
    /// replay; any refresh family minted from the code has been revoked.
    CodeNotFoundOrRedeemed,
    /// The code was issued to a different client.
    CodeClientMismatch {
        /// The client the code was issued to.
        code_client_id: String,
        /// The client that presented it.
        presented_client_id: String,
    },
    /// The presented `redirect_uri` is not the one the code was issued for.
    CodeRedirectMismatch {
        /// The redirect the code was issued for.
        code_redirect_uri: String,
        /// The redirect the redeemer named.
        presented_redirect_uri: String,
    },
    /// The code's lifetime has passed.
    CodeExpired {
        /// When the code stopped being redeemable.
        expires_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    },
    /// The PKCE `code_verifier` does not hash to the parked challenge.
    PkceMismatch {
        /// The client that presented the code.
        client_id: String,
    },
    /// No device request matches the `device_code` for this client: none
    /// exists, or it belongs to another client, which reads the same.
    DeviceRequestNotFound {
        /// The client that presented the `device_code`.
        presented_client_id: String,
    },
    /// Two polls raced for one approved device request; this one lost.
    DeviceCodeAlreadyRedeemed {
        /// The client the device request belongs to.
        client_id: String,
    },
    /// No live refresh token has this value.
    RefreshTokenNotFound,
    /// The refresh token belongs to a different client — answered exactly like
    /// not-found so a stranger can't probe validity.
    RefreshTokenClientMismatch {
        /// The client the family was issued to.
        family_client_id: String,
        /// The client that presented the token.
        presented_client_id: String,
    },
    /// The family's absolute deadline passed, or it was ended (revoked or
    /// replayed), which moves the deadline to that moment.
    RefreshTokenExpired,
    /// The browser session the family was minted under has been revoked, or
    /// no longer exists.
    RefreshTokenSessionRevoked {
        /// The family whose browser session ended.
        family_id: String,
    },
    /// The family began before its client's revocation epoch: bumping the
    /// epoch revoked every token the client held then.
    RefreshTokenClientRevoked {
        /// The family issued before the client's tokens were revoked.
        family_id: String,
    },
    /// A consumed refresh token was presented again — theft signal; the whole
    /// family has been revoked.
    RefreshTokenReplayed {
        /// The family that has been revoked.
        family_id: String,
        /// The client the family was issued to.
        client_id: String,
    },
    /// The token vanished between lookup and rotation.
    RefreshTokenVanished {

Authorization Code

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authorization_code.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/client_redirect.rs

An authorization code carries an approved code request from the browser to the app’s back end. The browser is sent back to the app’s redirect URI with the code in the URL; the app’s back end then trades the code at /oauth/token for tokens. The URL holds only the code, never a token, and the code is worth nothing to anyone who sees it without the app’s PKCE verifier.

A code lives 60 seconds and is redeemed once. It is issued in one place, RequestApprover::approve_for_code, on either authority, the Owner’s approval or a standing grant, and everything the redemption will check is fixed on it then.

Redeemed once

Redemption reads and deletes the code in one statement, so of two redemptions of the same code only one gets it back. The other sees nothing, just as for a code that was never issued:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// A concurrent redemption of the same code can only succeed once, so
// any racer past this point sees `None` (RFC 6749 §10.5).
let Some(code) = tx.redeem_authorization_code(presented.code)? else {
    tx.expire_refresh_token_families_for_authorization_code(
        &token_storage_hash(presented.code),
        now,
    )?;
    return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
        InvalidGrantReason::CodeNotFoundOrRedeemed,
    )));
};
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/redemption.rs lines 192–202 · authorization-server in the code index

A code presented a second time ends what the first redemption started. The refresh family a redemption begins records a hash of its code, and a code that comes back unknown expires every family carrying that hash before the refusal. A code stolen and replayed after the app redeemed it therefore takes the app’s refresh token down with it; the app runs the flow again. A code that never existed matches no family, and the refusal is the same invalid_grant either way.

A request too malformed to check (a verifier of the wrong length, a redirect that isn’t a URL) is refused before the code is touched. Past that, the code is spent whatever happens next: a redemption that names the wrong app or redirect, arrives late, or fails PKCE has already deleted it. auth_code_grant_replay_rejected and auth_code_replay_revokes_issued_refresh_family hold the server to both rules.

The client callback

A code request ends with the browser sent back to the app’s redirect_uri (RFC 6749 §4.1.2): with a code and the app’s state when it was approved, or with an error, an error_description and the state when it wasn’t. These builders are the one place that URL is made. /oauth/authorize, the wait page’s status poll, the Owner’s consent decision and the limited page’s Cancel all hand back the URL built here, so the app sees the same shape whichever path settled its request.

They take a redirect_uri that is already parsed and already trusted: deciding whether a redirect may receive anything is the registration’s job, not theirs.

Everything the redemption checks is fixed on the code when it is issued. Diesel-mapped 1:1 to the authorization_codes table.

Refresh Token

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/refresh_token.rs

An access token lasts minutes. An app the Owner allowed offline_access also gets a refresh token, which it trades at /oauth/token for a new access token, and a new refresh token, without asking anyone again. The first refresh token comes from redeeming an authorization code or from a device’s successful poll; every later one replaces the one before it.

That chain is a refresh family: every refresh token descended from one redemption. The family holds what they all share (the app, the scopes, the patient, the browser session, the deadline), and each token in it is one link. Only the newest link works. Presenting an older one kills the whole family, because a link presented twice means either a copy is loose or the app is broken, and either way the chain can’t be trusted. The app then has to run the authorization flow again.

A family is never deleted when it ends. Ending it moves its deadline to now and spends its live link, so the chain stays readable after the fact, and a replayed link still finds its dead family rather than reading as unknown. The retention sweep removes it later.

Before a presented link is spent, it is refused outright if its family belongs to another app, has passed its deadline (which covers a family already ended), was minted under a revoked browser session, or was begun before the app’s tokens were revoked (ValidatedRefreshToken::validate).

RefreshTokenFamily

One authorization’s refresh-token lineage (RFC 6749 §6). The family owns every fact shared by all the tokens rotated under it — client, scopes, patient context, and the absolute deadline — so those are stated exactly once. Tokens (RefreshToken) reference it by family_id.

fn main() {
pub struct RefreshTokenFamily {
    /// Primary key — lineage id shared by every token descended from one
    /// authorization.

    /// Client the family was issued to; only it may refresh. A refresh token
    /// presented by any other client reads exactly like an unknown one.
    pub client_id: String,
    /// Scopes carried forward to every access token minted from this family,
    /// copied from the redemption that started it.
    pub scopes: Vec<String>,
    /// SMART-on-FHIR patient context recorded at authorization, if any.
    pub patient: Option<String>,
    /// When the family was created: the redemption or device poll that
    /// started it. Revoking the client refuses every family issued before
    /// that moment.
    pub issued_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    /// Absolute deadline for the whole family — rotation never extends it;
    /// past this the client must re-run the authorization flow. Ending the
    /// family (a replay, a revocation) moves it to the moment it ended,
    /// rather than deleting the row; the retention sweep removes it later.
    pub expires_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    /// SHA-256 base64url hash of the authorization `code` that minted this
    /// family, or `None` for grants with no authorization code (the
    /// device-code flow). On a detected code replay the family is revoked via
    /// this hash (RFC 6749 §4.1.2 / OAuth 2.1 §4.1.2.1). The plaintext code is
    /// never stored.
    pub authorization_code_hash: Option<String>,
    /// The [`Grant`](crate::domain::grant::Grant) that authorized this family,

    /// `None` when no matching grant was found at exchange time (e.g. a grant
    /// revoked between approval and the token poll). No FK: families outlive

    pub grant_id: Option<String>,

    /// prunes an ended session only once no live family names it.

Consume a live refresh token in the caller’s write scope, reporting which of the three RefreshTokenConsumeOutcome states the presented token was in. The guarded stamp and the existence probe run under the scope’s write lock, so of two concurrent redeemers of the same token exactly one stamps the live row (Consumed), and the other sees the row still present but no longer live (Replayed); an unknown hash is NotFound.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure if the stamp or the existence probe fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn consume_refresh_token(
    tx: &mut impl RefreshTokensTx,
    token_hash: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<RefreshTokenConsumeOutcome, AuthorizationServerError> {
    if tx.stamp_refresh_token_consumed_if_live(token_hash, now)? {
        Ok(RefreshTokenConsumeOutcome::Consumed)
    } else if tx.has_refresh_token(token_hash)? {
        Ok(RefreshTokenConsumeOutcome::Replayed)
    } else {
        Ok(RefreshTokenConsumeOutcome::NotFound)
    }
}
}

Owner Prompt

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/owner_prompt.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/consent_key.rs

The Owner is asked about one request at a time: the newest one waiting for them, of any flow. A request waits for the Owner while it is pending, unexpired, and from a client that isn’t disabled; a code request still on its browser’s limited page doesn’t, yet. It works like a stack: a new request takes over from the one before it, and deciding it brings back the newest of those still waiting. The Jargon says how the host learns of it.

The three flows share no lookup key. A device request and a browser pairing are found by the user_code the Owner types at the device page; a code request by its id, at its consent card. So both types here are discriminated by flow, each variant carrying the key its consent surface already fetches by:

  • an Owner prompt is what the host shows: the key, plus the name of what asks, for the notification;
  • a consent key names one request by the same key, without the name. The host’s server status carries it, and asks the store whether the request it names is still awaiting the Owner.

The store answers both: AuthorizationRequestsTx::owner_prompt reads the newest waiting request of each flow and keeps the later, and AuthorizationRequestsTx::is_awaiting_owner reads the one a key names. Their tests are with the SQLite adapter.

domain::owner_prompt

OwnerPrompt

What the host asks the Owner next: the newest authorization request waiting for the Owner’s decision. The host shows one notification for it, which opens the request’s consent surface.

A request whose client is disabled is not prompted for: its consent prompt answers not found, so the host is never asked about it (a client with no row, trusted on first use, stays a candidate). The store’s owner_prompt applies it in its reads, filtering on the left-joined client’s disabled_at; is_awaiting_owner and raising a prompt for the Owner apply it through is_client_disabled.

Discriminated because the flows share no lookup key, nor what asks: each variant carries the key its consent surface already fetches by, and the name of what asks, for the host’s notification.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn for_request(
    request: &AuthorizationRequest,
    registered_client_name: Option<String>,
) -> Self {
    let client_name = registered_client_name.unwrap_or_else(|| request.client_id().to_owned());
    match request {
        AuthorizationRequest::Code(code_request) => OwnerPrompt::AuthorizationCode {
            id: code_request.id.clone(),
            client_name,
            decidable_in_requesting_browser: code_request.decidable_in_requesting_browser,
        },
        AuthorizationRequest::Device(device_request) => OwnerPrompt::DeviceCode {
            user_code: device_request.user_code.clone(),
            client_name,
        },
        AuthorizationRequest::Pairing(pairing_request) => OwnerPrompt::BrowserPairing {
            user_code: pairing_request.user_code.clone(),
            browser_name: pairing_request.browser_name.clone(),
        },
    }
}
}

Retention

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/retention.rs

Why the server deletes rows on a timer, why the windows are 90 days, 7 days and a day, and why they are measured past each row’s expiry rather than from now.

Tables that only grow

Most of the server’s tables limit themselves: a grant is deleted when it is revoked, and an authorization code when it is redeemed. These don’t:

  • refresh_token_families and refresh_tokens. Rotation adds a link per generation, and ending a family deliberately deletes nothing: it pulls the family’s deadline back and spends its live link. Keeping the rows is what lets a replayed link still resolve to its dead family, which is how reuse detection knows to end a lineage rather than shrug at an unknown hash.
  • code_authorization_requests and user_code_requests. Nothing moves a request the person simply walked away from. It stays pending, and expired, for good.
  • authorization_codes. Redemption deletes a code, so only the codes nobody came back for pile up.
  • browser_sessions. Every sign-in and pairing adds a row, and revoking a session stamps it rather than deleting it, so the tokens it minted can still be refused by its sid.

None of this is a correctness problem: every read already checks expiry, so a stale row is inert. It is a storage problem, and on a single-user desktop app the storage is the Owner’s disk.

A window past expiry, not now

The plain sweep would be “delete where expires_at is before now”. It reclaims the most, and it is the wrong tool, because these rows have audit value after they stop being usable. “Why did that device lose access on Tuesday?” is answerable only while Tuesday’s lineage is still there. A cutoff at now destroys the record at the moment it stops being state and becomes evidence.

So each window is measured past the row’s own expiry: the retention clock starts when the row stopped being usable, not when it was made. For a browser session that is its expiry or its revocation, whichever came first. Two things follow:

  • Nothing live is ever in range. A live family’s deadline is in the future, and a cutoff of now less 90 days is behind now. The sweep can’t delete something in use even with every window set to zero.
  • A revoked family gets its full window too. Ending a family pulls its deadline back to the moment it ended, so the clock starts there. The reuse-detection case, the one most worth auditing, is kept 90 days from the event.

A family is deleted with every link in it, links first, since every pooled connection enforces foreign keys. Leaving orphaned links would be worse than keeping everything: an orphan reads as an unknown token, which is exactly the answer that makes replay detection do nothing.

When the sweep runs

spawn_retention_sweep sweeps once at startup and then daily. The desktop app has no cron and shouldn’t need one. Daily is far finer than the coarsest window, so no row outstays its policy by much, and a machine switched off for a month sweeps once on its next boot rather than catching up a month of missed ticks. The deletes run in one write scope, so a failure rolls back to the set before the sweep; the failure is logged, and the next tick tries again. A sweep is logged only when it reclaimed something.

The insert’s narrow prune

One delete happens outside the sweep. A device request or pairing is keyed for the Owner by its user_code, and a partial unique index holds at most one pending request per user_code. An expired request still pending under a user_code occupies that index until the sweep reaches it, so inserting a new request under the same code would fail. The insert (SqliteGrantTx::insert_user_code_row) therefore first clears exactly that: rows holding this request’s user_code that are still pending and had already expired when this request started. The condition mirrors the index. A decided row is left for the sweep, since it isn’t in the index and could never collide, and a live pending one is never dropped to make room: that collision stays an error.

It is a guard on the index, not a step the flow relies on. generate_unique_user_code already draws a code no request of any status holds.

purge_expired

Delete every row that has aged past its retention window as of now, in one write scope, and report what went. Idempotent — a second pass at the same now matches nothing.

now is a parameter rather than a Utc::now() inside, so the whole pass reads one instant and tests can place rows either side of a window without sleeping. Each window is turned into a cutoff here; the store primitives never see a policy constant.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure if the scope or any of the deletes fails — rolled back, so a failure leaves the retained set as it was.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn purge_expired(
    store: &impl GrantStore,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<PurgedCounts, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let family_cutoff = now - REFRESH_TOKEN_FAMILY_RETENTION;
    let authorization_cutoff = now - AUTHORIZATION_RETENTION;
    let browser_session_cutoff = now - BROWSER_SESSION_RETENTION;
    store.write(|tx| {
        Ok(PurgedCounts {
            refresh_token_families: tx
                .delete_refresh_token_families_expired_before(family_cutoff)?,
            code_authorization_requests: tx
                .delete_code_requests_expired_before(authorization_cutoff)?,
            user_code_requests: tx.delete_polled_requests_expired_before(authorization_cutoff)?,
            authorization_codes: tx
                .delete_authorization_codes_expired_before(authorization_cutoff)?,
            browser_sessions: tx.delete_browser_sessions_ended_before(browser_session_cutoff)?,
        })
    })
}
}

Same-Device Sign-In Codes

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/same_device_sign_in_codes.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/sign_in_redirect.rs

The Owner signs a browser in by asking the base, the Wildflower app on the device that runs the server. The base mints a same-device sign-in code in-process and opens GET /oauth/sign-in?code=…&next=… in a browser. Whoever presents the code there first, in time, starts a same-device browser session in that browser. Only the base can mint a code, and the base runs on the server’s own device, so redeeming one stands for “this browser is on the Owner’s device”. The same-device sign-in proof is that redemption; this page is the codes it redeems from, and where the browser may be sent once it is signed in.

A code is single-use, short-lived, and never stored in the clear. Each is 256 random bits, redeemable once, for a minute. The outstanding codes live only in the server’s memory and only as SHA-256 hashes: a restart drops them all, and reading the server’s memory yields none.

The set follows each code past its redemption, by the same hash: while the session it starts is being stored, for a minute at most, after which a sign-in that never finished is given up on, and then which session it started, until that session expires. The base holds each code it minted as a SameDeviceSignInCode: the code with the set of the run that minted it, and nothing of the run’s store, so it outlives that run. Through it the base withdraws the code once the view it was opened in closes: an unredeemed code is no longer redeemable, and a code withdrawn while its session is still being stored signs nobody in, the session never landing. Through it the same-device session ender finds the session to end once the server’s last launch view closes, and setup the session to exempt from the next run’s stale-session cutoff while a view is still open. A code forgets its session only once the ending has landed, so a failed ending can be tried again.

Where a sign-in may send the browser

A sign-in URL carries a next: where the browser goes once its session has started. A next is held to an allow-list, so a sign-in link can’t be turned into a redirect to anywhere. A next is allowed when it is

  • a path on this server: it starts with / but not //, and still names this server’s origin once resolved against it;
  • a URL under the hosted launcher or the Wildflower Authorization app;
  • a URL under the pages the host opens for this server, its own launcher and Authorization app: the page itself, whatever its query, or a URL within it as a folder.

Each is judged by the URL a browser would make of it, parsed as the WHATWG URL standard says, so spellings a browser reads as another host (/\evil.example, a tab inside //, user@host) resolve to that host here too, and are refused. The redirect is the parsed URL re-serialized, never the raw next. The sign-in checks next before it touches the code, so a refused next leaves the code redeemable.

A browser pairing’s next is held tighter: a paired browser is only ever sent on to this server’s own /oauth/authorize.

insert

Minting a code. The base’s minter, SameDeviceSignInCodeMinter, calls this with each code it generates.

Keep code redeemable until SAME_DEVICE_SIGN_IN_CODE_TTL past now. The codes already expired at now, the sign-ins given up on by now, and the sessions already expired at now, are dropped, so only live ones are kept.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn insert(&self, code: &str, now: DateTime<Utc>) {
    let mut sign_in_by_code_hash = self.sign_in_by_code_hash.lock();
    sign_in_by_code_hash.retain(|_, sign_in| match sign_in {
        CodeSignIn::Outstanding { expires_at }
        | CodeSignIn::SigningIn { expires_at }
        | CodeSignIn::WithdrawnWhileSigningIn { expires_at }
        | CodeSignIn::SignedIn { expires_at, .. } => *expires_at > now,
    });
    sign_in_by_code_hash.insert(
        token_storage_hash(code),
        CodeSignIn::Outstanding {
            expires_at: now + SAME_DEVICE_SIGN_IN_CODE_TTL,
        },
    );
}
}

fn main() {
fn minting_gives_up_on_the_sign_ins_that_never_finished() {
    let codes = SameDeviceSignInCodes::new();
    let redeemed_at = Utc::now();
    let session =
        BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), redeemed_at);
    for code in ["signing-in", "withdrawn"] {
        codes.insert(code, redeemed_at);
        assert!(codes.take(code, redeemed_at));
    }
    codes.withdraw("withdrawn");
    codes.insert("fresh", redeemed_at + SAME_DEVICE_SIGN_IN_CODE_TTL);
    {
        let sign_in_by_code_hash = codes.sign_in_by_code_hash.lock();
        assert_eq!(sign_in_by_code_hash.len(), 1);
        assert!(sign_in_by_code_hash.contains_key(&token_storage_hash("fresh")));
    }
    assert!(!codes.session_stored("signing-in", &session));
    assert_eq!(codes.signed_in_sid("signing-in"), None);
}

take

Redeeming a code.

Redeem presented: whether it was outstanding, and unexpired at now. Redeemed, its session is being stored until session_stored or session_not_stored says how that went, or, past SAME_DEVICE_SIGN_IN_CODE_TTL from now, the sign-in is given up on as one that never finished; an expired one is dropped. Either way it is no longer outstanding, so a code is redeemed at most once and an expired one is spent by the attempt. The presented code is hashed before the lookup, which compares hashes, never the code itself.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn take(&self, presented: &str, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> bool {
    let mut sign_in_by_code_hash = self.sign_in_by_code_hash.lock();
    let code_hash = token_storage_hash(presented);
    match sign_in_by_code_hash.get(&code_hash) {
        Some(CodeSignIn::Outstanding { expires_at }) if *expires_at > now => {
            sign_in_by_code_hash.insert(
                code_hash,
                CodeSignIn::SigningIn {
                    expires_at: now + SAME_DEVICE_SIGN_IN_CODE_TTL,
                },
            );
            true
        }
        Some(CodeSignIn::Outstanding { .. }) => {
            sign_in_by_code_hash.remove(&code_hash);
            false
        }
        _ => false,
    }
}
}

session_stored

The sign-in calls this once the session it started is stored.

The session the redeemed code started has been stored: remember it, so the code finds its sid, and return true; or, when the code was withdrawn meanwhile, or its sign-in given up on, forget the code and return false, for the caller to roll the session back.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn session_stored(&self, code: &str, session: &BrowserSession) -> bool {
    let mut sign_in_by_code_hash = self.sign_in_by_code_hash.lock();
    let code_hash = token_storage_hash(code);
    if !matches!(
        sign_in_by_code_hash.get(&code_hash),
        Some(CodeSignIn::SigningIn { .. })
    ) {
        sign_in_by_code_hash.remove(&code_hash);
        return false;
    }
    sign_in_by_code_hash.insert(
        code_hash,
        CodeSignIn::SignedIn {
            sid: session.sid.clone(),
            expires_at: session.expires_at,
        },
    );
    true
}
}

withdraw

Withdraw code: an outstanding code is no longer redeemable, and one whose session is being stored signs nobody in. A code that signed a browser in keeps its session, for signed_in_sid to find.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn withdraw(&self, code: &str) {
    let mut sign_in_by_code_hash = self.sign_in_by_code_hash.lock();
    let code_hash = token_storage_hash(code);
    match sign_in_by_code_hash.get(&code_hash) {
        Some(CodeSignIn::Outstanding { .. }) => {
            sign_in_by_code_hash.remove(&code_hash);
        }
        Some(CodeSignIn::SigningIn { expires_at }) => {
            let expires_at = *expires_at;
            sign_in_by_code_hash.insert(
                code_hash,
                CodeSignIn::WithdrawnWhileSigningIn { expires_at },
            );
        }
        Some(CodeSignIn::WithdrawnWhileSigningIn { .. } | CodeSignIn::SignedIn { .. })
        | None => {}
    }
}
}

A code that signed a browser in finds its session until the session is forgotten, and only that code finds it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn a_signed_in_session_is_found_by_its_own_code_until_forgotten() {
    let codes = SameDeviceSignInCodes::new();
    let now = Utc::now();
    let first = BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), now);
    let second = BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), now);
    for (code, session) in [("code-1", &first), ("code-2", &second)] {
        codes.insert(code, now);
        assert!(codes.take(code, now));
        assert!(codes.session_stored(code, session));
    }
    codes.withdraw("code-1");
    assert_eq!(
        codes.signed_in_sid("code-1"),
        Some(first.sid),
        "withdrawing keeps a session signed in"
    );
    codes.forget_session("code-1");
    assert_eq!(codes.signed_in_sid("code-1"), None, "forgotten");
    assert_eq!(codes.signed_in_sid("code-3"), None, "signed nobody in");
    assert_eq!(codes.signed_in_sid("code-2"), Some(second.sid));
}
}

fn main() {
enum CodeSignIn {
    /// Minted and not yet presented.
    Outstanding {

    },

        /// When the sign-in is given up on, as one that never finished.
        expires_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    },
    /// Signed a browser in.
    SignedIn {
        /// The session's `sid`.
        sid: String,
        /// When the session expires, after which it needs no ending.
        expires_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    },
}
}

fn main() {
pub(crate) fn allow(&self, next: &str) -> Option<SignInRedirect> {
    if next.starts_with('/') {
        return self.path_on_this_server(next);
    }
    let url = Url::parse(next).ok()?;
    let is_allowed = [
        self.launcher.as_url(),
        self.authorization_app.as_url(),
        &self.launcher_url,
        &self.authorization_url,
    ]
    .into_iter()
    .any(|page| is_under(&url, page));
    is_allowed.then(|| SignInRedirect(url.into()))
}
}

    url.origin() == page.origin()
        && url.username().is_empty()
        && url.password().is_none()
        && (url.path() == page.path() || url.path().starts_with(&folder))

Session Housekeeping

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/session.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/last_seen_throttle.rs

Two chores around a signed-in caller that never decide anything on their own. Logout denylists the access token the caller presented, so a leaked copy of it can’t be replayed afterwards. Cookie use moves a browser session’s last_seen_at, so the Owner’s list of browsers shows when each was last used; a throttle keeps a page load’s burst of requests to one write.

Neither may get in the way of the request it rides on. A logout succeeds even when the denylist can’t be written, and a request on a session cookie goes ahead whether or not its use is recorded.

domain::session

revoke_session_token

The token goes to the host’s revocation store, through the Revocation port. The session ender calls this, and only for a token that carries both a jti and an expiry. The tests stand a recording fake in for the store.

Denylist the logged-out session token’s jti until expires_at, so a leaked copy of the token can’t be replayed after logout.

Best-effort by design: the /authorization gate already verified the request’s token, so this only recovers the trusted jti + exp to denylist; any store hiccup (already revoked, transient failure) must never fail the logout — the client has already forgotten the token — so a failure is logged and swallowed rather than returned.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn revoke_session_token(
    revoker: &(impl Revocation + ?Sized),
    jti: &str,
    expires_at: DateTime<Utc>,
) {
    if let Err(error) = revoker.revoke_jti(jti, expires_at, "logout") {
        tracing::warn!(%error, "logout: failed to revoke presented token jti");
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/last_seen_throttle.rs lines 25–29 · authorization-server in the code index

admit

Whether a use of session sid at now goes on to the update: none was let through in the LAST_SEEN_RESOLUTION before now. One that goes on is noted at now, and every note older than the window is dropped, so the map holds only the sessions let through within the last window: at most the live sessions, since a sid reaches here only from a token the gates accepted.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn admit(&self, sid: &str, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> bool {
    let window_start = now - LAST_SEEN_RESOLUTION;
    let mut admitted_at_by_sid = self.admitted_at_by_sid.lock();
    if admitted_at_by_sid
        .get(sid)
        .is_some_and(|admitted_at| *admitted_at > window_start)
    {
        return false;
    }
    admitted_at_by_sid.retain(|_, admitted_at| *admitted_at > window_start);
    admitted_at_by_sid.insert(sid.to_owned(), now);
    true
}
}

Source Guards

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/mod.rs

Some of the crate’s rules are about where code may be written, not what it does. A route handler never reaches the store except through a capability. A privileged write never happens outside a writer. The domain never imports the transport layer. The compiler can’t hold those, so source-guard tests do: each enumerates the source files and fails on a line that breaks the rule, so a new file is guarded the day it is added.

They are advisory-strength, and say so. The needles are text, not types: a guard catches the ordinary way of breaking its rule, not a determined one. What keeps them honest is that they scan production code only. Comments and string literals may name anything, and every #[cfg(test)] item (the unit-test module, a test-only method, a test-only use) may arrange state directly, planting rows or building proofs, without being the production path the guard pins.

The domain module

src/domain/mod.rs is also the domain’s front page. Nothing in the domain depends on crate::http. The entities carry diesel derives naming their crate::db tables, and that is the domain’s only reach into the adapter.

  • The entities, one module each, own their rules. An authorization request owns its lifecycle: each change is a transition, and the store writes it back only while the row still has the status it was read with.
  • The port, the grant store, is persistence as the domain sees it: one scope per operation, read or write, handing out single-statement primitives, one trait per table.
  • The capabilities are the operations. Each opens its one scope at its top, runs its flow inside to an outcome, and acts on the outcome (republishing, the revocation store) once the scope has closed (Capabilities).
  • The authority proofs are what every privileged write demands (Authority), and the writers are the one place those writes happen (Writers).

Everything fails with the domain’s own AuthorizationServerError.

The guards

Two guards sit here, and three more beside the layers they guard:

  • production_code_precedes_the_test_module: no file under src/ has production code after its unit-test module.
  • domain_never_references_crate_http: no file under src/domain/ names crate::http.
  • source_guards::handlers_reach_the_state_only_through_capabilities: no route handler names the router state or one of its fields; it reaches them only through a capability extractor (Capabilities).
  • source_guards::middleware_verifies_only_through_the_token_verifier: no middleware names the store or the revocation store; the gates verify a token through the token verifier.
  • tests::privileged_store_calls_happen_only_in_writers: the calls that grant authority, and the building of an approved or claimed request, appear only in the writers and the few files allowed them (Writers).

The handler, middleware and writer guards also fail when they find fewer files than expected, so a moved directory can’t make them pass by scanning nothing.

What this module adds is reading Rust as production code. Its own tests trim each scanned line with a small helper, so assertions read the code as written.

production_lines

The lines a guard scans.

The production code of a source file, one entry per line that has any, numbered from 1. A guard scans these: comments and string literals may name anything (they are blanked out, so a trailing // … never trips a needle), and every #[cfg(test)]-gated item — the unit-test module, a test-only helper method, a test-only use — may arrange state directly (planting rows, constructing proofs) without being the production path the guard exists to pin. Only the gated item itself is skipped, so production code after it is still scanned.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn production_lines(source: &str) -> Vec<(usize, String)> {
    let code = code_only(source);
    let test_items = cfg_test_items(&code);
    code.iter()
        .enumerate()
        .filter(|(i, _)| !test_items.iter().any(|item| item.lines.contains(i)))
        .filter(|(_, line)| !line.trim().is_empty())
        .map(|(i, line)| (i + 1, line.clone()))
        .collect()
}
}

cfg_test_items

Every #[cfg(test)]-gated item in code (the output of code_only, so braces inside comments and strings are already gone).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn cfg_test_items(code: &[String]) -> Vec<CfgTestItem> {
    let mut items = Vec::new();
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < code.len() {
        if code[i].trim() != "#[cfg(test)]" {
            i += 1;
            continue;
        }
        let start = i;
        // Skip any further attributes and blank lines to the item itself.
        let mut item_start = i + 1;
        while item_start < code.len() {
            let trimmed = code[item_start].trim();
            if trimmed.is_empty() || trimmed.starts_with("#[") {
                item_start += 1;
            } else {
                break;
            }
        }
        let end = item_end(code, item_start);
        let is_inline_module = code
            .get(item_start)
            .is_some_and(|line| is_mod_header(line) && line.contains('{'));
        items.push(CfgTestItem {
            lines: start..end,
            is_inline_module,
        });
        i = end;
    }
    items
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/mod.rs lines 176–206 · authorization-server in the code index

item_end

The line after the item that starts at start: the line where its braces balance again, or — for a braceless item (use …;, mod x;) — the line holding its terminating ;.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn item_end(code: &[String], start: usize) -> usize {
    let mut depth: usize = 0;
    let mut opened = false;
    for (i, line) in code.iter().enumerate().skip(start) {
        for ch in line.chars() {
            match ch {
                '{' => {
                    depth += 1;
                    opened = true;
                }
                '}' => depth = depth.saturating_sub(1),
                ';' if !opened => return i + 1,
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        if opened && depth == 0 {
            return i + 1;
        }
    }
    code.len()
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn is_mod_header(line: &str) -> bool {
    let trimmed = line.trim_start();
    let after_visibility = if let Some(rest) = trimmed.strip_prefix("pub") {
        let rest = rest.trim_start();
        match rest.strip_prefix('(') {
            Some(scoped) => scoped.split_once(')').map_or(rest, |(_, after)| after),
            None => rest,
        }
    } else {
        trimmed
    };
    after_visibility.trim_start().starts_with("mod ")
}
}

code_only

source, line for line, with every comment and every string / char literal replaced by spaces, so what remains is code alone. Handles line and (nested) block comments, escaped and raw strings (r#"…"#, byte variants), and tells a char literal ('{') from a lifetime ('a). Line numbers still match the file, and blanking literals also blanks the braces inside them, which keeps cfg_test_items’ brace count true.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn code_only(source: &str) -> Vec<String> {
    let chars: Vec<char> = source.chars().collect();
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(source.len());
    let mut i = 0;
    let blank = |c: char| if c == '\n' { '\n' } else { ' ' };
    while i < chars.len() {
        let c = chars[i];
        let next = chars.get(i + 1).copied();
        if c == '/' && next == Some('/') {
            while i < chars.len() && chars[i] != '\n' {
                out.push(' ');
                i += 1;
            }
        } else if c == '/' && next == Some('*') {
            let mut depth = 0;
            while i < chars.len() {
                if chars[i] == '/' && chars.get(i + 1) == Some(&'*') {
                    depth += 1;
                    out.push_str("  ");
                    i += 2;
                } else if chars[i] == '*' && chars.get(i + 1) == Some(&'/') {
                    depth -= 1;
                    out.push_str("  ");
                    i += 2;
                    if depth == 0 {
                        break;
                    }
                } else {
                    out.push(blank(chars[i]));
                    i += 1;
                }
            }
        } else if let Some(hashes) = raw_string_hashes(&chars, i) {
            // `r`/`br`, the hashes, the opening quote, then up to the
            // closing quote followed by as many hashes.
            let mut j = i;
            while chars[j] != '"' {
                j += 1;
            }
            j += 1;
            let closing: Vec<char> = std::iter::once('"')
                .chain(std::iter::repeat_n('#', hashes))
                .collect();
            while j < chars.len() && !chars[j..].starts_with(&closing) {
                j += 1;
            }
            let end = (j + closing.len()).min(chars.len());
            out.extend(chars[i..end].iter().map(|&c| blank(c)));
            i = end;
        } else if c == '"' {
            out.push(' ');
            i += 1;
            while i < chars.len() && chars[i] != '"' {
                if chars[i] == '\\' {
                    out.push(' ');
                    i += 1;
                }
                if let Some(&escaped) = chars.get(i) {
                    out.push(blank(escaped));
                }
                i += 1;
            }
            out.push(' ');
            i += 1;
        } else if c == '\'' {
            // A char literal is `'x'` or `'\…'`; anything else is a lifetime.
            let literal_len = match next {
                // Past the escaped char, so `'\''` closes on its last quote.
                Some('\\') => chars
                    .get(i + 3..)
                    .and_then(|rest| rest.iter().position(|&c| c == '\''))
                    .map(|close| close + 4),
                Some(_) if chars.get(i + 2) == Some(&'\'') => Some(3),
                _ => None,
            };
            match literal_len {
                Some(len) => {
                    out.extend(std::iter::repeat_n(' ', len));
                    i += len;
                }
                None => {
                    out.push(c);
                    i += 1;
                }
            }
        } else {
            out.push(c);
            i += 1;
        }
    }
    out.lines().map(str::to_owned).collect()
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/mod.rs lines 387–398 · authorization-server in the code index

raw_string_hashes

The number of #s when a raw string literal (r"…", r#"…"#, br#"…"#) starts at i, else None. An identifier that merely ends in r (for, bar#) is not a raw string.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn raw_string_hashes(chars: &[char], i: usize) -> Option<usize> {
    let prefix_len = match (chars.get(i), chars.get(i + 1)) {
        (Some('r'), _) => 1,
        (Some('b'), Some('r')) => 2,
        _ => return None,
    };
    let preceded_by_ident = i
        .checked_sub(1)
        .and_then(|p| chars.get(p))
        .is_some_and(|&p| p.is_alphanumeric() || p == '_');
    if preceded_by_ident {
        return None;
    }
    let hashes = chars[i + prefix_len..]
        .iter()
        .take_while(|&&c| c == '#')
        .count();
    (chars.get(i + prefix_len + hashes) == Some(&'"')).then_some(hashes)
}
}

        let relative = relative_to(&path, src).expect("enumerated under src");
        let source =
            std::fs::read_to_string(&path).unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("read {relative}: {e}"));
        if let Some(line) = production_code_after_test_module(&source) {
            violations.push(format!("{relative}:{line}"));
        }
    }
    assert!(
        violations.is_empty(),
        "production code after the unit-test module (move it above the tests): {violations:?}",
    );
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/mod.rs lines 460–475 · authorization-server in the code index

domain::http_free_guard

domain_never_references_crate_http

The guard’s needle is assembled from parts, so its own source doesn’t trip it.

domain/ must never depend on crate::http — the capabilities live here and are built from crate::live_bindings, so a stray use crate::http::… would re-couple the domain to the transport layer. This test enumerates the domain/ tree and fails if any non-comment line names crate::http, so the invariant can’t silently regress.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn domain_never_references_crate_http() {
    // Assembled from parts so this guard's own source doesn't contain the
    // literal it scans for (which would make it flag itself).
    let needle = concat!("crate", "::", "http");
    let domain_dir = std::path::Path::new(concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), "/src/domain"));
    for path in rs_files_under(domain_dir).expect("enumerate domain_dir") {
        let source = std::fs::read_to_string(&path)
            .unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("read {}: {e}", path.display()));
        for (n, line) in production_lines(&source) {
            assert!(
                !line.contains(needle),
                "domain/ file {} line {n} imports the transport layer (`{needle}`) — domain \
                 must stay transport-free; route the dependency through a port or `crate::live_bindings`",
                path.display(),
            );
        }
    }
}
}

            .bytes()
            .all(|byte| matches!(byte, 0x20..=0x21 | 0x23..=0x5B | 0x5D..=0x7E))
}
}

seeded puts one row of each kind on each side of its window: a family 91 days dead and one 89 days dead, a live family minted under the session named; requests and codes 8 days dead, 6 days dead, and live; sessions ended 25 hours ago, 23 hours ago, and 10 days ago (named).

Seed one row of each kind on each side of its window, plus a genuinely live refresh-token family, and return the store.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn seeded() -> FakeGrantStore {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    // Past the 90-day window (its deadline is 91 days behind `now`).
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_refresh_token_family_row(&family("old", now() - Duration::days(91)))
        .expect("seed old family");
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_refresh_token(&token("old-token", "old"))
        .expect("seed old token");
    // Dead, but only 89 days dead — still inside the window.
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_refresh_token_family_row(&family("recent", now() - Duration::days(89)))
        .expect("seed recent family");
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_refresh_token(&token("recent-token", "recent"))
        .expect("seed recent token");
    // Live: deadline still ahead of `now`, and minted under the session
    // `named`.
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_refresh_token_family_row(&RefreshTokenFamily {
            sid: Some("named".to_string()),
            ..family("live", now() + Duration::days(30))
        })
        .expect("seed live family");
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_refresh_token(&token("live-token", "live"))
        .expect("seed live token");

    store
        .tx()
        .insert_device_request(&request("old", now() - Duration::days(8)))
        .expect("seed old request");
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_code_request(&code_request(
            "old-code",
            RequestStatus::Denied,
            now() - Duration::days(8),
        ))
        .expect("seed old code request");
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_device_request(&request("recent", now() - Duration::days(6)))
        .expect("seed recent request");
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_device_request(&request("live", now() + Duration::minutes(5)))
        .expect("seed live request");

    // Ended a day and an hour ago — past the 24-hour window; an hour short
    // of it; and long ago, but named by the live family.
    for (sid, expires_at) in [
        ("old", now() - Duration::hours(25)),
        ("recent", now() - Duration::hours(23)),
        ("named", now() - Duration::days(10)),
    ] {
        store
            .tx()
            .insert_browser_session(&session(sid, expires_at))
            .expect("seed session");
    }

    store
        .tx()
        .issue_authorization_code(&code("old", now() - Duration::days(8)))
        .expect("seed old code");
    store
        .tx()
        .issue_authorization_code(&code("recent", now() - Duration::days(6)))
        .expect("seed recent code");
    store
        .tx()
        .issue_authorization_code(&code("live", now() + Duration::minutes(1)))
        .expect("seed live code");
    store
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/mod.rs lines 378–383 · authorization-server in the code index

Grant Store

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/store.rs

The grant store is everything the server remembers: the apps it knows, the browsers it has let in, the requests waiting on the Owner, the codes and refresh tokens it has handed out, the Owner’s standing grants, and the keys it signs with. This part is the port: the shape the domain asks of that memory, with no SQL in it. The Persistence part is the SQLite adapter that fills it, and the test fake is the in-memory one every domain unit test runs against.

The port has two halves. A scope is one unit of store work: a run of reads and writes on one connection that, for a write, either all happen or none do. A primitive is one thing done to one table inside a scope: load a client, redeem a code, end a refresh family. Scopes come from GrantStore; primitives come from the handle a scope lends, GrantTx.

One operation, one scope. A capability method (an app exchanging a code, the Owner approving a request) opens exactly one scope, at its top. Everything beneath it, the proofs in domain/authority/ and the writers, takes the handle the scope lends, never the store, so nothing below a capability can open a second scope and see the world change between two of its own reads. A method reads as: open the scope, run the flow inside it to an outcome value, then act on the outcome outside it.

What acts outside the scope is a side effect: republishing the Owner prompt to the host, and writing to the host’s revocation store. Inside the scope, a side effect would run before the commit: a republish reads the store on another pooled connection, which would still see the rows as they stood before this scope. Signing a token isn’t a side effect. It is pure computation over the key the scope loaded, so it runs inside the scope, and a signing failure rolls the scope back.

A refusal that must keep what the scope wrote is an Ok outcome, not an Err, since an Err rolls a write scope back: a presented authorization code that fails a check stays spent, and a refused device poll stays stamped. That is why many flows return Result<Result<T, Refusal>, AuthorizationServerError>: the outer Err is “the store failed, undo everything”, the inner one is “the answer is no, keep what we did”.

Two scopes in one operation

Two operations open a read scope and then a write scope, for the same reason: each also reads or writes the revocation store, which is another connection to the same SQLite file, and touching it while holding this store’s write lock could stall both connections for the busy timeout.

  • Exchanging a refresh token validates the token in a read scope, its app’s revocation epoch included. A write scope then checks the store-only facts again (the family may have ended between the two), rotates the token and mints.
  • Revoking a grant loads the grant in a read scope to learn its app, bumps that app’s revocation epoch, then deletes the grant and ends the app’s refresh families in a write scope.

domain::grant_store::store

GrantStore

The transaction seam: the two scopes a capability runs its store work in. Each capability method opens exactly one, at its top, and everything beneath it (the flow, the authority proofs, the writers) takes the GrantTx the scope hands out, never the store.

A scope’s closure may fail with any error a flow defines, as long as an AuthorizationServerError converts into it; an Err rolls a write scope back. A refusal that must keep what the scope wrote (a spent code, a stamped poll) is an Ok outcome, not an Err.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub trait GrantStore {
    /// The connection-scoped handle a scope hands its closure: for the
    /// `SQLite` adapter a checked-out diesel connection, for the fake the
    /// in-memory maps.
    type Tx<'a>: GrantTx
    where
        Self: 'a;

    /// Run `f` on one connection in autocommit, for an operation that only
    /// reads: no lock is held between its statements.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// Whatever `f` returns, plus [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`]
    /// if a connection can't be acquired.
    fn read<T, E: From<AuthorizationServerError>>(
        &self,
        f: impl FnOnce(&mut Self::Tx<'_>) -> Result<T, E>,
    ) -> Result<T, E>;

    /// Run `f` inside one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, for an operation
    /// that writes: the write lock is taken before the first read, so a read
    /// that decides a write sees the row the write lands on. Committed when
    /// `f` returns `Ok`, rolled back when it returns `Err`.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// Whatever `f` returns, plus [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`]
    /// if the connection, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` or `COMMIT` fails.
    fn write<T, E: From<AuthorizationServerError>>(
        &self,
        f: impl FnOnce(&mut Self::Tx<'_>) -> Result<T, E>,
    ) -> Result<T, E>;
}
}

domain::grant_store

GrantTx

The handle is a bundle of one trait per table, each on a page of its own, in the order the Domain part introduces the entities they hold:

  • Clients: the registered apps, and the switch that disables one.
  • Browser Sessions: the browsers the server has let in, and the apps each has gone on past its limited page for.
  • Authorization Requests: the requests the Owner decides, and each flow’s guarded replace.
  • Launch Contexts: SMART launch values, each spent once.
  • Grants: the Owner’s standing consent, per app and redirect or per app and device.
  • Authorization Codes: issued codes, each redeemed once.
  • Refresh Tokens: refresh families and their rotation lineage, ended rather than deleted.
  • Signing Keys: the keys tokens are signed and checked with.
  • Test Fake: the in-memory store, and the fixtures the crate’s unit tests share.

Every per-table primitive, on one connection-scoped handle: what a GrantStore scope hands its closure. Implemented for any type that implements every concern trait.

pub trait GrantTx:
    ClientsTx
    + SigningKeysTx
    + AuthorizationRequestsTx
    + AuthorizationCodesTx
    + LaunchContextsTx
    + BrowserSessionsTx
    + RefreshTokensTx
    + GrantsTx
{
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/mod.rs lines 54–64 · authorization-server in the code index

Clients

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/clients.rs

The clients table holds every app the server knows, as a Client: its registration, and whether it is disabled. Rows arrive two ways: boot-time seeding writes the server’s own clients, and the Owner’s approval of an app trusted on first use writes or widens that app’s registration. The Owner can disable an app and enable it again; nothing deletes one.

A missing row is a fact the domain uses, not an error. An app trusted on first use has no row until the Owner first approves it, so its request goes to the Owner rather than being turned away, and it reads as enabled. Rewriting a registration never re-enables a disabled app or changes when the app first arrived: seeding relies on that to make each server-defined client match the code on every boot, and the grant recorder relies on it when an approval widens a registration.

pub trait ClientsTx {
    /// Look up a registered client by its `client_id`, or `None` when no client
    /// has this id.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the read fails or a returned row
    /// cannot be mapped to a [`Client`].
    fn client_by_id(&mut self, client_id: &str)
        -> Result<Option<Client>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Whether `client_id`'s client is disabled. A client with no row is not:
    /// one trusted on first use has none until the Owner approves it.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the read fails.
    fn is_client_disabled(&mut self, client_id: &str) -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Insert a client, or update its policy fields if one with the same
    /// `client_id` already exists (`ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE`), preserving
    /// `registered_at` and `disabled_at`. Used by the seeding every boot runs,
    /// so a seeded client's definition always matches the code, and by the
    /// grant recorder to create or widen a registration trusted on first use.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the upsert fails.
    fn upsert_client(&mut self, client: &Client) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Every registered client, ordered by `client_id` — the Owner's "Trusted
    /// apps" list. Disabled clients are included (their `disabled_at` is set).
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the read fails or any returned row
    /// cannot be mapped to a [`Client`].
    fn list_clients(&mut self) -> Result<Vec<Client>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Set (`Some`) or clear (`None`) a client's `disabled_at`, touching no other

    /// stamp re-enables it with its registration intact.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the update fails.
    fn set_client_disabled(
        &mut self,
        client_id: &str,
        disabled_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,
    ) -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError>;
}

Browser Sessions

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/browser_sessions.rs

The browser_sessions table holds every browser session the server has started: the Owner’s signed-in browser and each paired one. A session is revoked by stamping it, never by deleting it, because everything minted under it carries its sid, and the token verifier and a refresh must still be able to tell that the session ended. That is also why a sid with no row counts as revoked. A same-device session can also end early by expiring: its expires_at moves back to now once the server’s last launch view closes. A server start cuts off the rest but those a launch view still open signed in, without writing: the others are stale, and the token verifier refuses them as it does an expired one. Expiring it isn’t revoking it: its own token stops working, but the tokens and refresh families apps were issued under it don’t end with it. Rows go only in the retention sweep, once nothing they minted can still be live: a session a live refresh family names is kept.

The table’s companion, session_shortfall_acknowledgements, records per session the apps it has gone on past the limited page for: the page a browser sees when an app asks for more than the session holds. Continue records it, in the same write scope as the request’s acknowledgement, and only once that acknowledgement has landed. Once the person at the browser has gone on for an app, that app’s later requests from the same browser skip the page.

last_seen_at moves two ways. The server accepting the session’s cookie passes seen_before as now less LAST_SEEN_RESOLUTION, so the column is written at most once per resolution. A refresh family under the session rotating passes now for both, so it always moves unless a later use is already recorded.

    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the update fails.

        now: DateTime<Utc>,
    ) -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError>;

    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the update fails.

    ///
    /// # Errors
