Authorization Requests

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/authorization_requests.rs

Every authorization request lives here from the moment it starts until the retention sweep removes it, in one of two tables: code_authorization_requests for an app’s code request, and user_code_requests for the device requests and browser pairings a poll claims. A request’s row is the shared record that the app or device polling, the browser waiting and the Owner deciding all read and write.

The rule these tables keep is that a decision lands once: a transition is written only over the row as it was read. That guarded replace, and the races it settles, are on the domain page: Transitions and the guarded replace.

Only one pending request may hold a given user_code. The Owner types the code at the device page, and the pending lookup is what finds the request, so a finished request holding the same code must never answer for a live one. Minting a fresh code takes the other lookup, which sees every status: a candidate is used only if no request, live or finished, already bears it.

The two reads that span flows serve the host: owner_prompt is the one request the host notifies about and opens for the Owner, and is_awaiting_owner tells the host whether the consent it holds open is still undecided.

domain::grant_store::authorization_requests

AuthorizationRequestsTx

The authorization requests the Owner decides. Every method is one primitive on the caller’s GrantStore scope: a single statement, or a few that land together within that scope.

Every read fails with AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure when the read fails or a returned row is malformed (a column its flow requires is missing, or its approval disagrees with its status), rather than reading as absent.

The replace_* writes are each flow’s guarded replace: write changed over the row of read’s id, but only while that row still has read’s status, returning whether it landed. Of two transitions read from one row, the first to land wins and the other answers false. The write is the whole row, so a transition read before a poll stamp landed writes the stamp’s last_polled_at back as it read it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub trait AuthorizationRequestsTx {
    /// Load the request of any flow whose key is `id` (a `device_code`, a
    /// pairing code, or a code request's UUID), or `None` when absent.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn authorization_request_by_id(
        &mut self,
        id: &str,
    ) -> Result<Option<AuthorizationRequest>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Load the code request `id`, in whatever state, or `None` when there is
    /// no code request with that id.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn code_request_by_id(
        &mut self,
        id: &str,
    ) -> Result<Option<CodeRequest>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Load the device request keyed by `device_code`, in whatever state, or
    /// `None` when there is no device request with that key.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn device_request_by_id(
        &mut self,
        device_code: &str,
    ) -> Result<Option<DeviceRequest>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Load the browser pairing keyed by `pairing_code`, in whatever state,
    /// or `None` when there is no pairing with that key.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn pairing_request_by_id(
        &mut self,
        pairing_code: &str,
    ) -> Result<Option<PairingRequest>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Load *any* device request or pairing bearing the human-typed
    /// `user_code`, regardless of status, or `None` when absent. Callers that
    /// need a live request must use
    /// [`Self::pending_polled_request_by_user_code`].
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn polled_request_by_user_code(
        &mut self,
        user_code: &str,
    ) -> Result<Option<PolledRequest>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Load the *pending* device request or pairing for `user_code` (the
    /// status filter stops a stale terminal row from shadowing a live one),
    /// or `None` when none is pending.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn pending_polled_request_by_user_code(
        &mut self,
        user_code: &str,
    ) -> Result<Option<PolledRequest>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// The newest request waiting for the Owner at `now` — pending and
    /// unexpired, so not a code request still on its browser's limited page —
    /// as the host notifies and opens it, or `None` when there is none.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn owner_prompt(
        &mut self,
        now: DateTime<Utc>,
    ) -> Result<Option<OwnerPrompt>, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Whether the request `consent_key` names is still undecided at `now`
    /// ([`AuthorizationRequest::is_undecided_at`]: a code request still on
    /// its browser's limited page included), and its client not disabled
    /// (the rule on [`OwnerPrompt`]). A request that isn't there, or is
    /// decided or expired, isn't.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// See the [trait](Self).
    fn is_awaiting_owner(
        &mut self,
        consent_key: &ConsentKey,
        now: DateTime<Utc>,
    ) -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Persist a freshly started code request.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the insert fails (for
    /// example a unique-constraint violation on the id).
    fn insert_code_request(
        &mut self,
        request: &CodeRequest,
    ) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Persist a freshly started device request.
    ///
    /// Bulk reclamation of expired rows belongs to
    /// `domain::retention::purge_expired`, not here — an insert leaves

    /// row holding this request's `user_code` that had expired by the time
    /// this request started, since that row occupies the partial unique

    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the insert fails (for
    /// example a unique-constraint violation on the id, or a collision with

    fn insert_device_request(
        &mut self,
        request: &DeviceRequest,
    ) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// Persist a freshly started browser pairing, as
    /// [`insert_device_request`](Self::insert_device_request) does a device
    /// request.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// As [`insert_device_request`](Self::insert_device_request).
    fn insert_pairing_request(
        &mut self,
        request: &PairingRequest,
    ) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError>;

    /// The code flow's guarded replace (see the [trait](Self)).
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure`] if the update fails, or
    /// `changed` has another id than `read`.

        &mut self,

Launch Contexts

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/launch_contexts.rs

The launch_contexts table holds the SMART launch values the server has handed out, as launch contexts, keyed by the value itself (the nonce). The rule this table keeps is that a launch is spent once, by the app it is for, or by any app for one for the server’s launcher. The check and the spend are one statement, so two /oauth/authorize requests presenting the same launch can’t both get it, and a launch presented by the wrong app stays spendable by its own.

A spent launch keeps its row, stamped consumed, until it expires. Every mint prunes the launches already expired, in the same write scope as its insert, so they don’t pile up and need no sweeper of their own. A launch pruned this way is gone, so presenting it later reads as unknown rather than expired.

The read by nonce comes only after a consume found nothing, to say why: unknown, another app’s, already used, or expired, in that order, so another app’s launch never reveals whether it was used. That classification is consume_launch, and the refusals are the domain’s LaunchRefusal.

Grants

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/grants.rs

The Owner’s standing consent lives in two tables, one per kind of grant: authorization_code_grants, one per app and redirect, and device_grants, one per app and device name. Each pair is unique in its table, so a re-approval updates the one grant rather than adding a second. A grants view unions the two for the reads that don’t care which kind: the Owner’s list and a lookup by id. Grant ids are UUIDs unique across both tables.

Which table a write lands in is decided in the domain, by the caller handing over the concrete grant, never by the store inspecting a Grant. So there is a create, an update, a use stamp and a delete per kind. The read-then-create-or-update of a re-approval belongs to the grant recorder, inside one write scope, folding the approval in with absorb_reapproval so consent only accumulates. Revoking a grant runs both deletes, since at most one hits; when neither does, the grant vanished since it was read, and the revoke answers “no such grant”.

The code grant lookup by app and redirect is asked in three places: /oauth/authorize asks whether a request is covered by a standing grant so it can skip the Owner, the grant recorder asks whether an approval updates a grant or creates one, and redeeming a code asks for the grant behind it, to record its id on the refresh family it starts.

Authorization Codes

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/authorization_codes.rs

The authorization_codes table holds the authorization codes the server has issued and no app has yet redeemed. The request approver issues a code in the same write scope as the approval, and the browser waiting on the request finds it again by the request’s id when it polls for where to go next. The rule this table keeps is that a code redeems once: redeeming reads and deletes it in one statement, so of two apps presenting the same code at once, exactly one gets it. The redemption proof treats a miss as a replay and ends every refresh family the code started.

Refresh Tokens

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/refresh_tokens.rs

Two tables hold an app’s standing credentials, the refresh families: refresh_token_families, one row per authorization (its app, scopes, absolute deadline, and the browser session, code and grant it came from), and refresh_tokens, one row per token in the family’s rotation, keyed by the token’s hash.

Two rules live here. A token is consumed once: the guarded stamp lets exactly one presentation of a live token through, and the existence probe after a failed stamp tells a replay, which ends the family, from a token never issued (consume_refresh_token). A family is ended, not deleted: ending pulls its deadline back to now and stamps its live token consumed, keeping the lineage readable, and only the retention sweep deletes it.

A family ends four ways, all through the same expire-and-stamp: a replayed token, the app revoking its own refresh token, the Owner revoking a grant (every family the app holds, in the same write scope as the grant’s delete, so consent and the credentials it earned end together), and a code presented again after it was redeemed (every family that code started).

Signing Keys

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/grant_store/signing_keys.rs

The signing_keys table holds the server’s signing keys, one row per key, keyed by kid. The active key signs every new token; every key in the table is published and verified against, so a token signed by a key since rotated out still checks. Boot-time seeding makes sure an active key exists, and nothing else in the server writes one.

The access token minter loads the active key inside the scope that mints, and with none it refuses. /oauth/authorize asks only whether one exists, before starting or continuing a code request: a server that couldn’t sign the token at the end doesn’t start the flow.

Test Fake

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/test_fake/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/test_fake/tx.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/test_fake/fixtures.rs

Every unit test in src/domain/ runs against FakeGrantStore: the grant store port kept in memory, one map per table, with no diesel and no database. It exists so a test of a rule (a code redeems once, a decision lands once, a revoked session fails closed) reads as the rule, and runs in microseconds. It models the guarantees the domain relies on, not the SQL: each primitive does what its port promises, in plain Rust over the maps. The SQL that keeps the same promises, with real locks and real constraints, is tested in the Persistence part.

This page is also the appendix of the fixtures the crate’s unit tests share, the second half below.

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/test_fake/mod.rs lines 42–45 · authorization-server in the code index

The scopes

A write scope rolls back on Err, as SQLite’s would: it snapshots every map before running the closure and restores them when the closure fails, so a test never sees half of a failed operation. That is the one property of a write scope the fake models. It takes no lock, as the fake is single-threaded, so a race is tested by ordering: read a request, move it with another transition, then write the first.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn write<T, E: From<AuthorizationServerError>>(
    &self,
    f: impl FnOnce(&mut Self::Tx<'_>) -> Result<T, E>,
) -> Result<T, E> {
    // No real locking (the fake is single-threaded); the snapshot models
    // the one property the flows rely on, rollback on error, so a
    // partially applied scope never leaks into a later assertion.
    let snapshot = self.tables.snapshot();
    let result = f(&mut FakeGrantTx {
        store: &self.tables,
    });
    if result.is_err() {
        self.tables.restore(snapshot);
    }
    result
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn replace_code_request(
    &mut self,
    read: &CodeRequest,
    changed: &CodeRequest,
) -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError> {
    if changed.id != read.id {
        return Err(replaced_by_another(&read.id, &changed.id));
    }
    let mut requests = self.store.code_authorization_requests.borrow_mut();
    let Some(stored) = requests.get_mut(&read.id) else {
        return Ok(false);
    };
    if stored.state.status() != read.state.status() {
        return Ok(false);
    }
    *stored = changed.clone();
    Ok(true)
}
}

The guarded replace of a device request or pairing: write changed over the entry of read_id while it is still of changed’s flow and has read_status.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn replace_user_code_request(
    &self,
    read_id: &str,
    read_status: RequestStatus,
    changed: PolledRequest,
) -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError> {
    if changed.id() != read_id {
        return Err(replaced_by_another(read_id, changed.id()));
    }
    let mut requests = self.store.user_code_requests.borrow_mut();
    let Some(stored) = requests.get_mut(read_id) else {
        return Ok(false);
    };
    let stored_as_read = match (&*stored, &changed) {
        (PolledRequest::Device(stored), PolledRequest::Device(_)) => {
            stored.state.status() == read_status
        }
        (PolledRequest::Pairing(stored), PolledRequest::Pairing(_)) => {
            stored.state.status() == read_status
        }
        _ => false,
    };
    if stored_as_read {
        *stored = changed;
    }
    Ok(stored_as_read)
}
}

fn consume_launch_context(
    &mut self,
    nonce: &str,
    client_id: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Option<LaunchContext>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let mut contexts = self.store.launch_contexts.borrow_mut();

The Owner is asked about the newest request still waiting

A disabled app’s request is skipped, and an app with no registration is kept with no registered name, as the SQL’s left join to clients does.

Mirrors the adapter’s two reads: the newest candidate from each map (of two started at once, the greater id), keeping the later by requested_at, and on a tie the code request.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn owner_prompt(
    &mut self,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Option<OwnerPrompt>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let clients = self.store.clients.borrow();
    // Mirrors the SQL: a disabled client's request is skipped, a client
    // with no row's kept.
    let is_candidate = |request: &AuthorizationRequest| {
        request.is_pending_at(now)
            && clients
                .get(request.client_id())
                .is_none_or(|client| client.disabled_at.is_none())
    };
    let newest = |requests: Vec<AuthorizationRequest>| {
        requests
            .into_iter()
            .filter(is_candidate)
            .max_by(|a, b| (a.requested_at(), a.id()).cmp(&(b.requested_at(), b.id())))
    };
    let code = newest(
        self.store
            .code_authorization_requests
            .borrow()
            .values()
            .cloned()
            .map(AuthorizationRequest::Code)
            .collect(),
    );
    let polled = newest(
        self.store
            .user_code_requests
            .borrow()
            .values()
            .cloned()
            .map(AuthorizationRequest::from)
            .collect(),
    );
    let later = match (code, polled) {
        (Some(code), Some(polled)) if polled.requested_at() > code.requested_at() => {
            Some(polled)
        }
        (Some(code), _) => Some(code),
        (None, polled) => polled,
    };
    Ok(later.map(|request| {
        // Mirrors the SQL left join: a client with no registration has no
        // registered name.
        let registered_client_name = clients
            .get(request.client_id())
            .map(|client| client.name.clone());
        OwnerPrompt::for_request(&request, registered_client_name)
    }))
}
}

A session outlives its end while a live family names it

Its limited-page acknowledgements go with it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn delete_browser_sessions_ended_before(
    &mut self,
    cutoff: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<usize, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let named_by_a_family_alive_at_cutoff: Vec<String> = self
        .store
        .families
        .borrow()
        .values()
        .filter(|family| family.expires_at >= cutoff)
        .filter_map(|family| family.sid.clone())
        .collect();
    let mut sessions = self.store.browser_sessions.borrow_mut();
    let before = sessions.len();
    sessions.retain(|sid, session| {
        let ended_before_cutoff = session.expires_at < cutoff
            || session
                .revoked_at
                .is_some_and(|revoked_at| revoked_at < cutoff);
        !ended_before_cutoff || named_by_a_family_alive_at_cutoff.contains(sid)
    });
    self.store
        .session_shortfall_acknowledgements
        .borrow_mut()
        .retain(|(sid, _)| sessions.contains_key(sid));
    Ok(before - sessions.len())
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/test_fake/tx.rs lines 636–662 · authorization-server in the code index

Where the fake is looser than SQLite

The fake leaves out what no domain rule rests on, so a test can’t lean on these:

  • No unique constraints. An insert of a repeated key (a sid, a code, a second pending request with the same user_code) overwrites the old entry instead of failing, and the signing-key insert appends.
  • Updates insert. update_authorization_code_grant and update_device_grant write the grant whether or not it was there.
  • Orderings differ. all_grants sorts by grant id, where SQLite orders by granted_at; all_signing_keys keeps insertion order, where SQLite puts the active key first, then orders by kid.
  • No locks. Concurrency is tested in SQLite; the fake only sequences.

fn main() {
pub(crate) fn code_with_status(request: CodeRequest, status: RequestStatus) -> CodeRequest {
    let decided_at = request.expires_at - Duration::milliseconds(1);
    match status {
        RequestStatus::Pending => request,
        RequestStatus::AwaitingLimitedPage => CodeRequest {
            state:
                crate::domain::authorization_request::code::CodeRequestState::AwaitingLimitedPage,
            ..request
        },
        RequestStatus::Approved => request
            .approve(fixture_approval(&request.requested_scopes), decided_at)
            .expect("a pending fixture approves"),
        RequestStatus::Denied => request.deny(decided_at).expect("a pending fixture denies"),
        RequestStatus::Claimed => panic!("a code request is never claimed"),
    }
}
}

fn main() {
pub(crate) fn device_with_status(request: DeviceRequest, status: RequestStatus) -> DeviceRequest {
    let decided_at = request.expires_at - Duration::milliseconds(1);
    let approve = |request: &DeviceRequest| {
        request
            .approve(
                fixture_approval(&request.requested_scopes),
                None,
                decided_at,
            )
            .expect("a pending fixture approves")
    };
    match status {
        RequestStatus::Pending => request,
        RequestStatus::Approved => approve(&request),
        RequestStatus::Denied => request.deny(decided_at).expect("a pending fixture denies"),
        RequestStatus::Claimed => approve(&request)
            .claim(decided_at)
            .expect("an approved fixture is claimed"),
        RequestStatus::AwaitingLimitedPage => panic!("a device request has no limited page"),
    }
}
}

Approve the request id stored in store now, granting granted_scopes and naming its device or browser requester_name (None keeps its own), as an approval through the consent surfaces would.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn approve_stored(
    store: &FakeGrantStore,
    id: &str,
    granted_scopes: &[&str],
    requester_name: Option<&str>,
) {
    let mut tx = store.tx();
    let request = tx
        .authorization_request_by_id(id)
        .unwrap()
        .expect("the request is stored");
    let approval = Approval {
        granted_scopes: owned_scopes(granted_scopes),
        patient: None,
    };
    let now = Utc::now();
    let requester_name = requester_name.map(str::to_owned);
    let landed = match request {
        AuthorizationRequest::Code(read) => {
            let approved = read.approve(approval, now).expect("pending");
            tx.replace_code_request(&read, &approved)
        }
        AuthorizationRequest::Device(read) => {
            let approved = read
                .approve(approval, requester_name, now)
                .expect("pending");
            tx.replace_device_request(&read, &approved)
        }
        AuthorizationRequest::Pairing(read) => {
            let approval = PairingApproval {
                granted_scopes: approval.granted_scopes,
            };
            let approved = read
                .approve(approval, requester_name, now)
                .expect("pending");
            tx.replace_pairing_request(&read, &approved)
        }
    };
    assert!(landed.unwrap());
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn redeemed_code(
    store: &FakeGrantStore,
    client_id: &str,
    granted_scopes: &[&str],
) -> RedeemedAuthorizationCode {
    const VERIFIER: &str = "verifier-verifier-verifier-verifier-verifier-1";
    let redirect_uri = Url::parse("https://example.com/cb").unwrap();
    let authenticated = authenticated_public_client(store, client(client_id, granted_scopes));
    let now = Utc::now();
    let code = generate_authorization_code();
    store
        .tx()
        .issue_authorization_code(&AuthorizationCode {
            code: code.clone(),
            request_id: "req".to_owned(),
            client_id: client_id.to_owned(),
            redirect_uri: redirect_uri.clone(),
            code_challenge: compute_code_challenge(VERIFIER),
            granted_scopes: owned_scopes(granted_scopes),
            patient: Some("pat-1".to_owned()),
            issued_at: now,
            expires_at: now + AUTHORIZATION_CODE_TTL,
            sid: FIXTURE_SID.to_owned(),
        })
        .unwrap();
    RedeemedAuthorizationCode::redeem(
        &mut store.tx(),
        &authenticated,
        &PresentedAuthorizationCode {
            code: &code,
            code_verifier: VERIFIER,
            redirect_uri: redirect_uri.as_str(),
        },
        now,
    )
    .expect("the fake store does not fail")
    .expect("a freshly issued code redeems")
}
}

Authority

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/mod.rs

Every row that hands out access is written on some authority. Approving a request, issuing a code, recording or widening a grant, widening an app’s registration, starting a browser session, minting a token: each happens because someone was entitled to cause it. An authority proof is that entitlement as a value. A privileged write takes a proof as its argument, so it can’t happen without one.

A proof has private fields and one constructor, which is the check for the rule it stands for. There is no other way to build one, so holding the value is the evidence that the check ran. The constructors that read the store take the calling capability’s open scope from the Grant Store, so the proof is checked against the same rows the operation then writes, under the same lock.

That makes the audit two short lists: the constructors on these pages, and the writers, the one place a privileged store call may appear. A source guard in the writers’ module fails when a privileged store method is called anywhere else in production code, so a new flow can’t reach around a writer and the proof it demands.

Where a writer accepts more than one kind of proof, the set is an enum, not a trait: TokenEntitlement for the access-token minter, GrantRedemption for the refresh-family writer, and the request approver’s CodeAuthority. A closed list in one place is what an audit reads, and a new source of authority has to be added to it by name.

Some writes need no proof. The request transitions that grant nothing (parking a request, stamping a poll, denying, raising a request for the Owner, the limited page’s Continue and Cancel) go through the guarded replace. Whether the Owner acknowledged a change to an app’s registration is a consent-card rule, checked before anything is written.

The pages, in the order the proofs build on each other:

  • Authenticated Client: the app exists, is enabled, and, if it keeps a secret, presented it. Anything an app does on its own behalf takes one.
  • Delegated Scopes: an approver passes on only what the prompt may grant and what it holds itself, and holds the power to create what approving creates. A code carries only what the requesting browser also holds.
  • Standing Grant: a standing grant already covers every scope of a request that changes nothing in the app’s registration, so /oauth/authorize may issue a code with nobody asked.
  • Redemption: a code, an approved device request or a refresh token was redeemed at /oauth/token by the app it belongs to; the token carries what the record behind it recorded.
  • Same-Device Sign-In: a sign-in code the base minted was presented once and in time, so the browser is on the server’s own device and is the Owner’s.
  • Browser Pairing: a pairing the Owner approved was claimed, once, by the page that started it, so that browser gets a session with what the Owner granted.
  • Token Entitlement: the closed list of proofs a token may be minted under, each carrying the token’s claims.
  • Test Fixtures: the helpers the Authority tests share.

Authenticated Client

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/authenticated_client.rs

An app’s back end calls the server on its own behalf: it redeems a code or a refresh token at /oauth/token, or starts a device pairing at /oauth/device_authorization. Before it may, the app must be one the server knows, still enabled, and, if it keeps a secret, it must present that secret. An authenticated client is the proof that it did. Every operation an app does on its own behalf takes one, so no flow can act for an app whose secret was never checked.

What the app presents is its client credentials; what they are checked against is its client row, which stores only a hash of the secret. The capability that runs the check, in a read scope, is the Client Authenticator.

The tests present credentials and register a confidential app with the authenticated-client fixtures, over the shared client fixture.

A client whose credentials have been verified. It answers the questions a flow asks of the client it acts for (its id, name, and what its registration allows); the row itself is private and there is no other constructor.

authenticate

An unknown app is refused, then a disabled one, before any secret is looked at. A secret a public app sends anyway is ignored: it can’t keep one, so it has nothing to prove with it.

Look up the client the credentials name and verify them: unknown and disabled clients are refused; a public client passes on identity alone; a confidential client must present the secret matching its stored argon2id PHC string (compared in constant time inside the verifier). A secret a public client sends anyway is ignored.

Errors

A ClientAuthenticationError naming the failed check.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn authenticate(
    tx: &mut impl ClientsTx,
    presented: &ClientCredentials,
) -> Result<Self, ClientAuthenticationError> {
    let client = tx
        .client_by_id(&presented.client_id)
        .map_err(ClientAuthenticationError::Store)?
        .ok_or(ClientAuthenticationError::UnknownClient)?;
    if client.disabled_at.is_some() {
        return Err(ClientAuthenticationError::Disabled);
    }
    if matches!(client.kind, ClientKind::Public) {
        return Ok(AuthenticatedClient { client });
    }
    let stored_hash = client
        .secret_hash
        .as_deref()
        .ok_or(ClientAuthenticationError::SecretNotConfigured)?;
    let secret = presented
        .client_secret
        .as_deref()
        .ok_or(ClientAuthenticationError::SecretRequired)?;
    let matches = verify_client_secret(secret, stored_hash)
        .map_err(|e| ClientAuthenticationError::Verification(e.to_string()))?;
    if !matches {
        return Err(ClientAuthenticationError::SecretMismatch);
    }
    Ok(AuthenticatedClient { client })
}
}

fn a_confidential_client_needs_the_matching_secret() {

        .upsert_client(&confidential("app", "s3cret"))

fn the_proof_answers_for_its_registration() {

Delegated Scopes

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/delegated_scopes.rs

When a request is approved, someone is handing on access: the Owner, or a browser the Owner paired. No one can delegate more than they hold. This page holds the scope rules the whole server leans on for that, in three parts.

  • What a prompt may grant at most. Each consent prompt has a ceiling, set by its flow and the app’s registration. Whatever the approver ticks is clamped to it.
  • What the approver must hold. To approve a prompt at all, the approver holds its approval scopes: the power to decide the request and to create what approving it creates. And every piece of access it passes on, it must hold itself.
  • What the browser holds. A code issued for an app carries only what the browser session the request was made in also holds, and the browser is told beforehand what it lacks, on the limited page.

Delegated scopes are the proof of the first two: a scope set the approver has approved and is entitled to delegate. The writers that record grants, write registrations and issue codes on an approval accept nothing else. The third part is two free functions, applied when a code is issued and when /oauth/authorize decides where to send the browser.

Every “covers” on this page is the scope coverage the Scopes page explains: by permission, not by spelling.

domain::authority::delegated_scopes

The tests build prompts and approvers with the delegated-scopes fixtures.

ApprovalFlow

A prompt belongs to one of three flows, and the flow decides both its ceiling and its approval scopes.

The flow a consent prompt belongs to, which decides its ceiling, its approval scopes, and whether approving it writes the client registration.

  • A code prompt for a client trusted on first use records a grant, writes the registration, and its approver must hold what is asked.
  • A code prompt for a server-defined (fixed) registration records a grant and its approver must hold what is asked, but it writes no registration.
  • A device prompt records a grant only; its consent is expandable, so the approver need not hold what the device asked for.
  • A browser pairing records no grant and writes no registration; like a device prompt it is expandable.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
enum ApprovalFlow {
    /// An authorization-code prompt, whose approval records a standing grant
    /// and approves the request as asked.
    Code {
        /// Whether the client's registration is server-defined, which an
        /// approval never writes. When it is not, the client is trusted on
        /// first use, so approving creates or widens its registration.
        registration_is_fixed: bool,
    },
    /// A device-code prompt: approving records a standing device grant.
    Device,
    /// A browser pairing: approving records no grant and registers no client.
    BrowserPairing,
}
}

The scopes one consent prompt may grant at most, decided by its flow. An approved scope must be covered by a scope of the request and by a scope of the registration ceiling (the most the client’s registration permits for this approval); each constructor names the policy that fills those two halves.

The flow also decides the prompt’s approval scopes, what its approver must hold to approve it at all (missing_approval_scopes).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) struct ApprovableScopes {
    /// The half that bounds a tick by what was asked: the request's scopes for
    /// a code prompt, so a code prompt never grants past what the client asked
    /// for. An expandable prompt fills it with its ceiling instead: a device
    /// prompt's registered scopes, a pairing's the Owner's scopes.
    requested_scopes: Vec<String>,
    /// The most the client's registration permits for this approval: a fixed
    /// registration's scopes, a registration trusted on first use's scopes
    /// plus what the request asks for, a device client's registered scopes, or
    /// the Owner's scopes for a pairing.
    registration_ceiling_scopes: Vec<String>,
    /// The prompt's flow, which sets its approval scopes and whether approving
    /// it writes the registration.
    flow: ApprovalFlow,
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/delegated_scopes.rs lines 89–103 · authorization-server in the code index

for_code

Who defines the registration decides the ceiling (is_registration_fixed). Either way the request is the other half, so a code prompt never grants past what the app asked for. A resolved code request builds its prompt here.

An authorization-code prompt for requested_scopes. A fixed (server-defined) registration is its own ceiling; any other client is trusted on first use, so its ceiling also takes in what this request asked for — its registration is widened with the grant.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn for_code(
    requested_scopes: &[String],
    maybe_existing_client: Option<&Client>,
    registration_is_fixed: bool,
) -> Self {
    let registered_client_scopes = maybe_existing_client
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|existing_client| existing_client.allowed_scopes.iter().cloned());
    let registration_ceiling_scopes = if registration_is_fixed {
        registered_client_scopes.collect()
    } else {
        registered_client_scopes
            .chain(requested_scopes.iter().cloned())
            .collect()
    };
    ApprovableScopes {
        requested_scopes: requested_scopes.to_vec(),
        registration_ceiling_scopes,
        flow: ApprovalFlow::Code {
            registration_is_fixed,
        },
    }
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn a_code_prompt_widens_the_allowance_only_for_a_registration_trusted_on_first_use() {
    let requested = owned_scopes(&["patient/Patient.r", "openid"]);
    let registered = client("app", &["openid"]);
    let approved = || owned_scopes(&["patient/Patient.r", "openid"]);

    let trusted_on_first_use = ApprovableScopes::for_code(&requested, Some(&registered), false);
    assert_eq!(
        trusted_on_first_use.grantable_subset(approved()),
        ["patient/Patient.r", "openid"]
    );
    let unknown = ApprovableScopes::for_code(&requested, None, false);
    assert_eq!(
        unknown.grantable_subset(approved()),
        ["patient/Patient.r", "openid"]
    );

    let fixed = ApprovableScopes::for_code(&requested, Some(&registered), true);
    assert_eq!(fixed.grantable_subset(approved()), ["openid"]);
}
}

fn main() {
pub(crate) fn grantable_subset(&self, owner_approved_scopes: Vec<String>) -> Vec<String> {
    let requested: HashSet<&str> = self.requested_scopes.iter().map(String::as_str).collect();
    let ceiling: HashSet<&str> = self
        .registration_ceiling_scopes
        .iter()
        .map(String::as_str)
        .collect();
    grantable_scopes(owner_approved_scopes, &requested, &ceiling)
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/delegated_scopes.rs lines 163–171 · authorization-server in the code index

missing_approval_scopes

One function answers “may this approver approve?” for every place that asks, so the consent card, the approve route and /oauth/authorize never disagree.

The prompt’s approval scopes the approver_grant does not cover, rendered, in order; empty when it may approve. Shared by the approve paths (through DelegatedScopes::clamp), the consent read (missingApprovalScopes), and /oauth/authorize’s choice between the consent card and the wait page, so the three never disagree.

The approval scopes, and who takes them:

  • wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.u: every approval, to decide the request at all.
  • wildflower/Grant.c: a code or device approval, which records a standing grant; a browser pairing records none.
  • wildflower/Client.c and wildflower/Client.u: a code approval for a client trusted on first use, which creates or widens its registration, whichever the row needs when the approval lands; a server-defined registration takes neither.
  • Each held access (is_held_access) the request asks for that the prompt may grant: a code approval, which approves the request as asked, else it goes to the Owner.

A device or pairing prompt is expandable, so its approver may grant whatever it holds, and DelegatedScopes::clamp bounds that scope by scope instead. The Owner’s scopes lack no approval scope on any prompt.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn missing_approval_scopes(&self, approver_grant: &Grant) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut approval_scopes = consent_decider_scopes();
    if self.flow.would_record_grant() {
        approval_scopes.extend(grant_creating_approval_scopes());
    }
    if self.flow.would_write_registration() {
        approval_scopes.extend(client_registering_approval_scopes());
    }
    let uncovered_approval_scopes: Vec<Scope> = approval_scopes
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|required| !approver_grant.covers(required))
        .collect();
    let mut missing = render_scopes(&uncovered_approval_scopes);
    if self.flow.would_approve_as_asked() {
        missing.extend(uncovered_held_access(
            &self.grantable_subset(self.requested_scopes.clone()),
            approver_grant,
        ));
    }
    missing
}
}

delegable_scopes

Where a pairing card’s ticks start. Its promise is that the card, approved untouched, passes clamp below.

Everything the approver holding approver_grant may delegate on this prompt, which the pairing card’s ticks start from: each requested scope and each of the approver’s own scopes the prompt may grant, less any held access (is_held_access) the approver does not cover. Approving it untouched passes DelegatedScopes::clamp’s approver check, so a pairing card that starts from the Owner’s scopes starts an approver holding less from all it holds instead.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn delegable_scopes(&self, approver_grant: &Grant) -> Vec<String> {
    let candidates = self
        .requested_scopes
        .iter()
        .cloned()
        .chain(approver_grant.render())
        .collect();
    let approver_may_pass_on = may_pass_on(approver_grant);
    self.grantable_subset(candidates)
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|rendered| approver_may_pass_on(&Scope::from(rendered.as_str())))
        .collect()
}
}

DelegatedScopes

A scope set an approver has approved and is entitled to delegate. Holding one is proof that the approver held the prompt’s approval scopes, and that every held access (is_held_access) in it is covered by the approver’s own grant, so the writers that record grants, write registrations, and issue codes accept nothing else. The fields are private and there is no other constructor.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) struct DelegatedScopes {
    /// The ticks that survived the prompt's ceiling, every held access among
    /// them covered by the approver: what the request's approval, the standing
    /// grant and a widened registration record as they are. A code issued
    /// under them is further bounded by the browser session.
    scopes: Vec<String>,
    /// Whether the approval behind the proof creates or widens the client's
    /// registration: only a code approval for a client trusted on first use,
    /// whose approver held `wildflower/Client.c` and `wildflower/Client.u`.
    /// The grant recorder asks it whether to write the `clients` row.
    writes_registration: bool,
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/delegated_scopes.rs lines 247–258 · authorization-server in the code index

clamp

The one constructor. It runs missing_approval_scopes first, then grantable_subset, then uncovered_held_access against the approver’s grant. A held access the approver lacks fails the whole approval, rather than being dropped in silence, so the Owner sees the refusal instead of a narrower grant than they ticked.

The approval rule, in three steps:

  1. Require that the approver_grant holds the approvable prompt’s approval scopes (missing_approval_scopes), whatever was ticked, even nothing.
  2. Clamp the owner_approved_scopes to the approvable scopes’ grantable subset: Ok(None) when nothing survives, and the caller denies rather than recording an empty grant.
  3. Require that the approver_grant covers every held access (is_held_access) that survives, in either spelling; one it lacks fails the whole approval, naming it.

Identity and session markers (openid, offline_access, …) are no held access and pass the approver check; a resource scope or wildflower/launch the approver lacks fails the whole approval (a 403) rather than being silently dropped. Coverage is checked across both SMART spellings via Scope::as_alternate_canonical_form, the twinning the token minter applies.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::InsufficientScope naming the approval scopes the approver lacks, checked first, whatever was ticked; then AuthorizationServerError::InsufficientApproverScope naming the held access the approver cannot delegate.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn clamp(
    approver_grant: &Grant,
    owner_approved_scopes: Vec<String>,
    approvable: &ApprovableScopes,
) -> Result<Option<Self>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let missing_scopes = approvable.missing_approval_scopes(approver_grant);
    if !missing_scopes.is_empty() {
        return Err(AuthorizationServerError::InsufficientScope { missing_scopes });
    }
    let grantable = approvable.grantable_subset(owner_approved_scopes);
    if grantable.is_empty() {
        return Ok(None);
    }
    let approver_missing_scopes = uncovered_held_access(&grantable, approver_grant);
    if approver_missing_scopes.is_empty() {
        Ok(Some(DelegatedScopes {
            scopes: grantable,
            writes_registration: approvable.flow.would_write_registration(),
        }))
    } else {
        Err(AuthorizationServerError::InsufficientApproverScope {
            approver_missing_scopes,
        })
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/delegated_scopes.rs lines 1110–1134 · authorization-server in the code index

session_bounded_scopes

A code carries only what both the app’s authority and the browser the request was made in allow. The request’s approval and the standing grant keep the authorized scopes; only the code is narrowed. So a browser paired read-only earns no app write access, whoever approved the request.

The authorized scopes narrowed to what the browser session holding session_grant also holds: an authorization code carries only what both the client’s authority and the browser the request was made in allow.

Held access (is_held_access) the session covers, by the rule DelegatedScopes::clamp holds an approver to (either SMART spelling, system/* covering patient/* and user/*), stays as authorized. Held access the session covers only in part narrows to the parts it holds: its intersection with each session scope (intersection_in_either_spelling), so system/*.cruds against a session holding system/Patient.cruds yields system/Patient.cruds. A part is spelled in the authorized scope’s grammar where one spells it, and in letters where no word does. wildflower/launch has no parts, so it stays only when the session holds it. Identity and session markers are no held access, so they pass through.

One scope’s parts are collapsed (Grant::collapse), so overlapping session scopes yield the broadest part once, and the result keeps each scope’s first occurrence, in order. A session that covers everything authorized changes nothing but exact duplicates.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn session_bounded_scopes(authorized: &[String], session_grant: &Grant) -> Vec<String> {
    let session_covers = coverage_in_either_spelling(session_grant);
    let mut already_bounded = HashSet::new();
    let bounded: Vec<Scope> = authorized
        .iter()
        .map(|rendered| Scope::from(rendered.as_str()))
        .flat_map(|authorized_scope| {
            if !is_held_access(&authorized_scope) || session_covers(&authorized_scope) {
                vec![authorized_scope]
            } else {
                let mut parts = Grant::new(
                    session_grant
                        .scopes
                        .iter()
                        .filter_map(|session_scope| {
                            intersection_in_either_spelling(&authorized_scope, session_scope)
                        })
                        .collect(),
                );
                parts.collapse();
                parts.scopes
            }
        })
        .filter(|scope| already_bounded.insert(scope.clone()))
        .collect();
    render_scopes(&bounded)
}
}

intersection_in_either_spelling

The broadest scope both authorized_scope and session_scope cover (Scope::intersection) when each also counts in its alternate canonical form, spelled in the authorized scope’s grammar where one exists: patient/Observation.rs against patient/Observation.read is patient/Observation.rs, and patient/*.read against patient/Patient.rs is patient/Patient.read. patient/*.read against patient/Patient.r has no word spelling, so it is the letter patient/Patient.r.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn intersection_in_either_spelling(
    authorized_scope: &Scope,
    session_scope: &Scope,
) -> Option<Scope> {
    let authorized_spellings = [
        Some(authorized_scope.clone()),
        authorized_scope.as_alternate_canonical_form(),
    ];
    // The session's letter form first, so a letter-spelled authorized scope
    // intersects to a letter bag rather than the session's word.
    let session_spellings = [
        session_scope.as_alternate_canonical_form(),
        Some(session_scope.clone()),
    ];
    authorized_spellings
        .iter()
        .flatten()
        .find_map(|authorized_spelling| {
            session_spellings
                .iter()
                .flatten()
                .find_map(|session_spelling| authorized_spelling.intersection(session_spelling))
        })
}
}

The browser is told what it lacks before a narrowed code is issued. The shortfall and the bound are two views of one rule: the shortfall names, as requested, each scope the bound would drop or narrow.

What a code issued in the browser session holding session_grant would not carry of the requested scopes, in the request’s order: for each held access (is_held_access) the session does not cover, the part of it the session lacks (Grant::uncovered_part, in either SMART spelling), whether session_bounded_scopes drops the scope or narrows it to the part the session holds. A session holding system/*.cuds and system/Patient.r lacks system/MedicationRequest.r of system/MedicationRequest.rs, and nothing of system/Patient.rs. Empty when the session holds all the request asks for.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn session_shortfall(requested: &[String], session_grant: &Grant) -> Vec<String> {
    let session_lacks = uncovered_part_in_either_spelling(session_grant);
    let lacking: Vec<Scope> = requested
        .iter()
        .map(|rendered| Scope::from(rendered.as_str()))
        .filter(is_held_access)
        .filter_map(|requested_scope| session_lacks(&requested_scope))
        .collect();
    render_scopes(&lacking)
}
}

Standing Grant

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/standing_grant.rs

Once the Owner has approved an app, its next request for the same thing shouldn’t ask again. A standing grant records what the Owner approved for an app at one redirect, and /oauth/authorize may issue a code on it with nobody asked. That fast path is a code issued with no human in the loop, so it needs a proof of its own.

The Grant page lists what it takes for a grant to skip the Owner. This proof holds the first two: the request changes nothing in the app’s registration, and the standing grant covers every scope it asks for. However well an old grant covers a request from a new app, at a new redirect or for a new scope, the Owner hasn’t seen that combination, so it goes back to them. The other two, the browser session and the launch’s patient, are checked by /oauth/authorize beside the proof: it takes the fast path only when the request admits the grant’s patient, and the code is still bounded by the browser session.

A grant that covers only some of the scopes isn’t a proof, but the Owner’s earlier yes still counts: the consent card opens with those scopes already ticked.

domain::authority::standing_grant

Each test stores one grant with the standing-grant fixtures.

GrantCoverage

How far a standing grant covers a request. Only Full is a proof; the other two carry what the consent prompt pre-ticks.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) enum GrantCoverage {
    /// No standing grant for this `(client, redirect_uri)`, or the request is
    /// outside the registration.
    Uncovered,
    /// A grant covers some of the requested scopes — the prompt pre-ticks them,
    /// the Owner decides the rest.
    Partial {
        /// The requested scopes the grant covers, in request order; the
        /// parked request records them so the consent card opens with them
        /// ticked.
        pre_approved_scopes: Vec<String>,
    },
    /// Every requested scope is covered: the fast path.
    Full(StandingGrantCoverage),
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/standing_grant.rs lines 21–35 · authorization-server in the code index

resolve

The one constructor of the proof. /oauth/authorize resolves it in the scope that parks the request, and again when the browser goes on past the limited page.

Look up the standing grant for (requested_client_id, requested_redirect_uri) and compute which of requested_scopes it covers. A request that would change its registration never resolves past GrantCoverage::Uncovered, whatever the grant says. /oauth/authorize resolves it in the scope that parks the request, and again when the browser goes on past the limited page.

“Covers” is wildflowerhealthio_scopes::allowed_scope_covers, not string equality: a standing grant is a set of permissions, so patient/*.cruds answers for a later patient/Observation.r, and a grant the approval collapsed (.r + .s recorded as .rs) still answers for either half.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure on a store failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn resolve(
    tx: &mut impl GrantsTx,
    presented_client_change: &PresentedClientChange,
    requested_client_id: &str,
    requested_redirect_uri: &Url,
    requested_scopes: &[String],
) -> Result<GrantCoverage, AuthorizationServerError> {
    if presented_client_change.would_change_registration() {
        return Ok(GrantCoverage::Uncovered);
    }
    let Some(grant) =
        tx.grant_by_client_and_redirect(requested_client_id, requested_redirect_uri)?
    else {
        return Ok(GrantCoverage::Uncovered);
    };
    let pre_approved_scopes: Vec<String> = requested_scopes
        .iter()
        .filter(|requested| {
            grant.scopes.iter().any(|granted| {
                wildflowerhealthio_scopes::allowed_scope_covers(granted, requested)
            })
        })
        .cloned()
        .collect();
    // `pre_approved_scopes` is `requested_scopes` filtered, so equal lengths
    // means nothing was filtered out.
    if pre_approved_scopes.len() == requested_scopes.len() {
        Ok(GrantCoverage::Full(StandingGrantCoverage {
            grant_id: grant.id,
            covered_scopes: pre_approved_scopes,
            patient: grant.patient,
        }))
    } else {
        Ok(GrantCoverage::Partial {
            pre_approved_scopes,
        })
    }
}
}

Redemption

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/redemption.rs

An app’s back end comes to /oauth/token holding something it was given earlier: an authorization code, a device code, or a refresh token. It has already proved who it is with an authenticated client. Before an access token is minted for it, the thing it holds is redeemed into a proof, one per grant type. Each proof has one constructor, and that constructor is the whole redemption rule for its grant type: the single-use claim, the bindings to the app and redirect, the expiry, the PKCE check.

A proof’s scopes are copied from the record it redeemed, never from the request. The code carries the scopes its approval recorded; the device request carries the scopes the Owner granted; the refresh family carries the scopes it was started with. So a token can hold only what the consent behind it recorded.

Some refusals come after a write: a code is spent before its bindings are checked, a pending device poll is stamped before it is answered. Those refusals are the inner Err of a nested result, so the token exchange’s scope commits what it wrote rather than rolling it back. Only a store failure is the outer Err, and the token-exchange errors are the inner one’s vocabulary.

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/redemption.rs lines 147–158 · authorization-server in the code index

redeem

The code is taken out of the store in one step (AuthorizationCodesTx::redeem_authorization_code), so of two redemptions racing for one code, only one gets it back. A code that comes back missing may be a replay, so every refresh family started from it is expired (RefreshTokensTx::expire_refresh_token_families_for_authorization_code) before the refusal. A standing grant revoked between approval and redemption just leaves the proof’s grant_id empty.

Check the presented request is well formed, then atomically read-and-consume the code and verify every binding. A code is spent the moment it is presented, and only then checked, so of two redemptions racing for one code only one gets it, and a code that fails a binding can’t be retried into a token. A malformed request is refused before the code is touched. A code that is gone (redeemed or never issued) is a possible replay: any refresh family minted from it is revoked before the refusal (RFC 6749 §4.1.2). The binding failures all collapse to invalid_grant on the wire (the reason is logged), so a response never reveals which check failed.

The refusals, as the inner Err: TokenExchangeError::InvalidCodeVerifier (RFC 7636 §4.1 length) or TokenExchangeError::InvalidRedirectUri for a malformed request, and TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant with the specific reason.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure on a store failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn redeem(
    tx: &mut (impl AuthorizationCodesTx + RefreshTokensTx + GrantsTx),
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    presented: &PresentedAuthorizationCode<'_>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Result<Self, TokenExchangeError>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    if !is_valid_code_verifier_length(presented.code_verifier) {
        return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidCodeVerifier));
    }
    let Ok(redirect_uri) = Url::parse(presented.redirect_uri) else {
        return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidRedirectUri));
    };
    // A concurrent redemption of the same code can only succeed once, so
    // any racer past this point sees `None` (RFC 6749 §10.5).
    let Some(code) = tx.redeem_authorization_code(presented.code)? else {
        tx.expire_refresh_token_families_for_authorization_code(
            &token_storage_hash(presented.code),
            now,
        )?;
        return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::CodeNotFoundOrRedeemed,
        )));
    };
    if let Err(reason) =
        check_code_bindings(&code, authenticated_client, &redirect_uri, presented, now)
    {
        return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(reason)));
    }
    // The standing grant behind this exchange, recorded on the family; a
    // grant revoked between approval and redemption just leaves it `None`.
    let grant_id = tx
        .grant_by_client_and_redirect(authenticated_client.client_id(), &redirect_uri)?
        .map(|grant| grant.id);
    Ok(Ok(RedeemedAuthorizationCode {
        token_scopes: token_scope_spellings(&code.granted_scopes),
        code,
        grant_id,
    }))
}
}

fn main() {
fn a_code_redeems_once_with_its_recorded_claims() {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    let now = Utc::now();
    let client = authenticated(&store, "app");
    let code = issued_code(&store, "app", now);
    let redemption = PresentedAuthorizationCode {
        code: &code,
        code_verifier: VERIFIER,
        redirect_uri: REDIRECT,
    };
    let proof = RedeemedAuthorizationCode::redeem(&mut store.tx(), &client, &redemption, now)
        .unwrap()
        .expect("redeems");
    assert_eq!(proof.client_id(), "app");
    assert_eq!(proof.patient(), Some("pat-1"));
    assert_eq!(proof.granted_scopes(), ["patient/Patient.read"]);
    assert_eq!(
        proof.token_scopes(),
        ["patient/Patient.read", "patient/Patient.rs"]

    assert_eq!(proof.authorization_code(), code);

        Some(code.as_str())

fn main() {
fn a_code_is_refused_for_each_broken_binding() {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    let now = Utc::now();
    let app = authenticated(&store, "app");
    let other = authenticated(&store, "other");

    let code = issued_code(&store, "app", now);
    let wrong_client = PresentedAuthorizationCode {
        code: &code,
        code_verifier: VERIFIER,
        redirect_uri: REDIRECT,
    };
    assert!(matches!(
        reason(
            RedeemedAuthorizationCode::redeem(&mut store.tx(), &other, &wrong_client, now)
                .unwrap()
        ),
        InvalidGrantReason::CodeClientMismatch { .. }
    ));

    let code = issued_code(&store, "app", now);
    let wrong_redirect = PresentedAuthorizationCode {
        code: &code,
        code_verifier: VERIFIER,
        redirect_uri: "https://elsewhere.example/cb",
    };
    assert!(matches!(
        reason(
            RedeemedAuthorizationCode::redeem(&mut store.tx(), &app, &wrong_redirect, now)
                .unwrap()
        ),
        InvalidGrantReason::CodeRedirectMismatch { .. }
    ));

    let code = issued_code(
        &store,
        "app",
        now - AUTHORIZATION_CODE_TTL - Duration::seconds(1),
    );
    let expired = PresentedAuthorizationCode {
        code: &code,
        code_verifier: VERIFIER,
        redirect_uri: REDIRECT,
    };
    assert!(matches!(
        reason(
            RedeemedAuthorizationCode::redeem(&mut store.tx(), &app, &expired, now).unwrap()
        ),
        InvalidGrantReason::CodeExpired { .. }
    ));

    let code = issued_code(&store, "app", now);
    let bad_verifier = PresentedAuthorizationCode {
        code: &code,
        code_verifier: "not-the-verifier-not-the-verifier-not-the-verif",
        redirect_uri: REDIRECT,
    };
    assert!(matches!(
        reason(
            RedeemedAuthorizationCode::redeem(&mut store.tx(), &app, &bad_verifier, now)
                .unwrap()
        ),
        InvalidGrantReason::PkceMismatch { .. }
    ));
}
}

check_code_bindings

Each failure is its own invalid_grant reason, for the log; the wire answer is invalid_grant whichever failed. The code is already spent, so none of them can be retried into a token.

Why the consumed code may not be redeemed by authenticated_client with redirect_uri and the presented verifier at now, if anything: it must be the client’s, for that redirect, unexpired, and its PKCE challenge must match the verifier. Each failure is its own InvalidGrantReason, for the log; the code is already spent, so none can be retried into a token.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn check_code_bindings(
    code: &AuthorizationCode,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    redirect_uri: &Url,
    presented: &PresentedAuthorizationCode<'_>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<(), InvalidGrantReason> {
    if code.client_id != authenticated_client.client_id() {
        return Err(InvalidGrantReason::CodeClientMismatch {
            code_client_id: code.client_id.clone(),
            presented_client_id: authenticated_client.client_id().to_owned(),
        });
    }
    if code.redirect_uri != *redirect_uri {
        return Err(InvalidGrantReason::CodeRedirectMismatch {
            code_redirect_uri: code.redirect_uri.to_string(),
            presented_redirect_uri: redirect_uri.to_string(),
        });
    }
    if code.expires_at < now {
        return Err(InvalidGrantReason::CodeExpired {
            expires_at: code.expires_at,
        });
    }
    let computed = compute_code_challenge(presented.code_verifier);
    if !bool::from(code.code_challenge.as_bytes().ct_eq(computed.as_bytes())) {
        return Err(InvalidGrantReason::PkceMismatch {
            client_id: authenticated_client.client_id().to_owned(),
        });
    }
    Ok(())
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/redemption.rs lines 260–273 · authorization-server in the code index

consume

A device request is claimed once. The claim is the request’s own claim transition, written with the guarded replace under the scope’s write lock, so of two polls racing for one approval, one wins. The standing grant is found by the device’s grant name.

Resolve the device request for device_code, require it to be this client’s, unexpired, and approved (stamping the poll and throttling a still-pending one per §3.5), then claim it, single use, under the scope’s write lock, so two concurrent polls can’t both mint. Once claimed, the standing device grant is looked up by the client and the device’s grant name (device_grant_name) and recorded on the proof.

Each poll is answered by the request’s state:

  • unknown, another client’s, or not a device request: invalid_grant, the three alike;
  • past its expiry, whatever its status: expired_token;
  • pending, polled again within DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL of the last poll: slow_down, and the poll is not stamped;
  • pending otherwise: authorization_pending, and the poll is stamped;
  • denied: access_denied;
  • already claimed: expired_token, since the device code has done its work;
  • approved: claimed, and the proof returned; a poll that loses the claim to a concurrent one is invalid_grant.

The refusals, as the inner Err: the §3.5 poll outcomes (ExpiredToken, AuthorizationPending, AccessDenied, SlowDown), with an already-claimed request answering ExpiredToken; TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant for an unknown request, or one whose guarded claim loses a race to a concurrent poll.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure on a store failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn consume(
    tx: &mut (impl AuthorizationRequestsTx + GrantsTx),
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    device_code: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Result<Self, TokenExchangeError>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    // One outcome collapses "no such device_code", "wrong client", and
    // "not a device request".
    let Some(request) = tx
        .device_request_by_id(device_code)?
        .filter(|request| request.client_id == authenticated_client.client_id())
    else {
        return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::DeviceRequestNotFound {
                presented_client_id: authenticated_client.client_id().to_owned(),
            },
        )));
    };
    if request.is_expired_at(now) {
        return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::ExpiredToken));
    }
    let approval = match &request.state {
        PolledState::Pending => {
            if request.is_polled_too_soon_at(now) {
                return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::SlowDown));
            }
            if let Ok(stamped) = request.stamp_poll(now) {
                tx.replace_device_request(&request, &stamped)?;
            }
            return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::AuthorizationPending));
        }
        PolledState::Denied => return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::AccessDenied)),
        // A claimed request already minted its token: as RFC 8628 §3.5
        // has it, the device code has expired.
        PolledState::Claimed(_) => return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::ExpiredToken)),
        PolledState::Approved(approval) => approval.clone(),
    };
    let claimed = request.claim(now).map_err(|_| {
        AuthorizationServerError::infrastructure(
            "claiming a device request",
            "an approved, unexpired request is not claimable",
        )
    })?;
    if !tx.replace_device_request(&request, &claimed)? {
        return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::DeviceCodeAlreadyRedeemed {
                client_id: request.client_id.clone(),
            },
        )));
    }
    let grant_name =
        device_grant_name(request.device_name.as_deref(), authenticated_client.name());
    let grant_id = tx
        .device_grant_by_client_and_device_name(&request.client_id, grant_name)?
        .map(|grant| grant.id);
    Ok(Ok(ConsumedDeviceRequest {
        token_scopes: token_scope_spellings(&approval.granted_scopes),
        client_id: request.client_id.clone(),
        approval,
        grant_id,
    }))
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn a_device_request_reports_its_status_and_is_claimed_once() {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    let now = Utc::now();
    let client = authenticated(&store, "client");
    let stranger = authenticated(&store, "stranger");
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_device_request(&device_request("dev", "CODE", RequestStatus::Pending))
        .unwrap();

    assert!(matches!(
        ConsumedDeviceRequest::consume(&mut store.tx(), &client, "dev", now).unwrap(),
        Err(TokenExchangeError::AuthorizationPending)
    ));
    assert!(matches!(
        ConsumedDeviceRequest::consume(
            &mut store.tx(),
            &client,
            "dev",
            now + Duration::seconds(1)
        )
        .unwrap(),
        Err(TokenExchangeError::SlowDown)
    ));
    assert!(matches!(
        reason(ConsumedDeviceRequest::consume(&mut store.tx(), &stranger, "dev", now).unwrap()),
        InvalidGrantReason::DeviceRequestNotFound { .. }
    ));

    approve_stored(&store, "dev", &["openid"], None);
    let later = now + DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL;
    let proof = ConsumedDeviceRequest::consume(&mut store.tx(), &client, "dev", later)
        .unwrap()
        .expect("claimed");
    assert_eq!(proof.client_id(), "client");
    assert_eq!(proof.granted_scopes(), ["openid"]);
    assert_eq!(
        GrantRedemption::DeviceCode(&proof).authorization_code(),
        None
    );
    assert!(matches!(
        ConsumedDeviceRequest::consume(&mut store.tx(), &client, "dev", later).unwrap(),
        Err(TokenExchangeError::ExpiredToken)
    ));
}
}

ValidatedRefreshToken

It reads its refresh token family. It is not consumed yet: the refresh-family writer consumes it, by the hash it carries, when it rotates the token into its successor.

A refresh token that resolved to a live family owned by the presenting client (RFC 6749 §6). Not yet consumed: the refresh-family writer rotates it.

Built in two scopes. validate runs the whole validation in a read scope, the client’s revocation epoch included: the epoch lives on the revocation store, another connection to the same file, so it can’t be read under the exchange’s write lock without risking a lock-order stall. revalidate then re-runs the store-only half inside the write scope that rotates, because the family may have ended between the two.

    /// The storage hash of the token as presented, by which the refresh-family

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/redemption.rs lines 412–422 · authorization-server in the code index

validate

The epoch is the app’s revocation epoch: bumping it revokes every token the app held at that instant, so a family begun before it is refused like an access token issued before it.

Resolve the presented token’s family and require it to be this client’s, unexpired, not minted under a revoked browser session, and begun no earlier than its client’s revocation epoch. A valid token presented by the wrong client is answered exactly like an unknown one so a stranger can’t probe validity, and is refused before any consume so it can’t burn the rightful client’s token. A family begun at the epoch itself still validates. Bumping a client’s revocation epoch revokes every token it held at that instant, so a family begun before it is refused like an access token issued before it. Runs in a read scope, outside the write lock (see the type’s doc).

Errors

TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant with the specific reason; TokenExchangeError::Store on a store failure, the revocation store’s included, so an unreadable epoch never admits a family.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn validate(
    tx: &mut (impl RefreshTokensTx + BrowserSessionsTx),
    revocation: &dyn RevocationCheck,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    presented_refresh_token: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Self, TokenExchangeError> {
    let validated = Self::live_family(
        tx,
        authenticated_client,
        token_storage_hash(presented_refresh_token),
        now,
    )?;
    // Bumping a client's revocation epoch revokes every token it held at
    // that instant, refresh families included: a family begun before the
    // epoch is refused like an access token issued before it. The family
    // has no `jti` of its own, so only the epoch applies.
    let family_predates_client_epoch = revocation
        .is_revoked(
            None,
            Some(validated.family.issued_at),
            &validated.family.client_id,
        )
        .map_err(|error| {
            AuthorizationServerError::infrastructure(
                "refresh-token revocation epoch check failed",
                error,
            )
        })?;
    if family_predates_client_epoch {
        return Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenClientRevoked {
                family_id: validated.family.family_id,
            },
        ));
    }
    Ok(validated)
}
}

fn main() {
fn a_refresh_token_validates_for_its_client_while_the_family_lives() {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();

    let client = authenticated(&store, "client");

    live_family(&store, "client", now);

            .expect("validates");
    assert_eq!(proof.family_id(), "fam");
    assert_eq!(proof.presented_hash(), token_storage_hash("live"));

            &mut store.tx(),
            &NothingRevoked,
            &stranger,
            "live",
            now
        )),
        InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenClientMismatch { .. }
    ));
    assert_eq!(
        reason(ValidatedRefreshToken::validate(
            &mut store.tx(),
            &NothingRevoked,
            &client,
            "live",

fn main() {
fn a_refresh_token_is_refused_once_its_session_is_revoked() {
    let now = Utc::now();
    let session = BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), now);

    store.tx().insert_browser_session(&session).unwrap();

    assert_eq!(proof.sid(), Some(session.sid.as_str()));

        )),

    let client = authenticated(&store, "client");
    live_family_under(&store, "client", Some("no-such-sid"), now);

        reason(ValidatedRefreshToken::validate(

            &NothingRevoked,
            &client,

fn main() {
fn a_refresh_token_is_refused_once_its_client_epoch_passes_the_family() {

    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    let client = authenticated(&store, "client");

        .bump_subject_epoch("client", now)
        .expect("bump to the family's start");

        .expect("a family begun at the epoch validates");

        .bump_subject_epoch("other-client", now + Duration::seconds(1))
        .expect("bump another client");
    ValidatedRefreshToken::validate(&mut store.tx(), &revocation_store, &client, "live", now)

    revocation_store
        .bump_subject_epoch("client", now + Duration::seconds(1))
        .expect("bump past the family's start");
    assert_eq!(
        reason(ValidatedRefreshToken::validate(
            &mut store.tx(),
            &revocation_store,
            &client,
            "live",
            now

        InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenClientRevoked {

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn live_family(
    tx: &mut (impl RefreshTokensTx + BrowserSessionsTx),
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    presented_hash: String,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<Self, TokenExchangeError> {
    let Some((_, family)) = tx.refresh_token_with_family_by_hash(&presented_hash)? else {
        return Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenNotFound,
        ));
    };
    if family.client_id != authenticated_client.client_id() {
        return Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenClientMismatch {
                family_client_id: family.client_id,
                presented_client_id: authenticated_client.client_id().to_owned(),
            },
        ));
    }
    // Covers both natural deadline passage and prior revocation — revoking
    // pulls `expires_at` back to the revocation instant rather than
    // deleting rows, so the lineage stays auditable.
    if family.expires_at <= now {
        return Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenExpired,
        ));
    }
    // Revoking a browser session ends every family minted under it. A
    // family with no session (the device flow) has none to check.
    if let Some(sid) = family.sid.as_deref() {
        if tx.is_browser_session_revoked(sid)? {
            return Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
                InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenSessionRevoked {
                    family_id: family.family_id,
                },
            ));
        }
    }
    Ok(ValidatedRefreshToken {
        token_scopes: token_scope_spellings(&family.scopes),
        family,
        presented_hash,
    })
}
}

Same-Device Sign-In

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/same_device_sign_in.rs

The Owner’s browser signs in without a password. The base, the host app on the device that runs the server, mints a one-time same-device sign-in code in-process and opens GET /oauth/sign-in with it. Only the base can mint a code, and the base runs on the server’s own device, so redeeming one is proof the browser is on that device, and is the Owner’s.

A redeemed same-device sign-in code is that proof. It is the authority a same-device browser session is started under and its access token minted under. The sign-in capability redeems it inside its write scope, then hands it to the browser-session writer to store the session and to the access-token minter to mint the token, so the session and its token land together or not at all.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn redeem(
    codes: &SameDeviceSignInCodes,
    presented: &str,
    owner_grant: &Grant,
    session_ttl: Duration,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Option<Self> {
    codes
        .take(presented, now)
        .then(|| RedeemedSameDeviceSignInCode {
            session: BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(
                owner_grant.render(),
                session_ttl,
                now,
            ),
        })
}
}

}
}

Browser Pairing

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/browser_pairing.rs

A browser that isn’t on the server’s own device pairs. Its page starts a pairing request and shows the Owner a code; the Owner approves it on the device page, choosing what the browser may hold; the page, polling all along, then picks up its session. Only the page that started the pairing holds the pairing code the request is keyed on, so a claim is proof that the browser now polling is the one the Owner approved.

A claimed browser pairing is that proof. It is the authority a paired browser session is started under and its access token minted under. Approving the pairing starts no session; claiming it does. The pairing capability claims it inside the poll’s write scope, then hands it to the browser-session writer to store the session and to the access-token minter to mint the token. A poll that loses the claim is answered as expired.

claim

The one constructor. The claim is the request’s own claim transition, written with the guarded replace, so an approved pairing starts one session at most. The session is a new paired session, named as the Owner renamed the browser or as it named itself.

Claim pairing_request, as read, in the caller’s write scope tx. When this call wins the claim, the proof holds a new paired session named after the request’s browser, with the scopes the Owner granted, lasting session_ttl from now. None when the pairing isn’t approved and unexpired, or a concurrent poll claimed it first.

Errors
