#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn load_code_request_awaiting_limited_page(
    tx: &mut impl AuthorizationRequestsTx,
    id: &str,
    sid: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<CodeRequest, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let not_found = || AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound { id: id.to_owned() };
    tx.code_request_by_id(id)?
        .filter(|request| request.is_awaiting_limited_page_at(now) && request.sid == sid)
        .ok_or_else(not_found)
}
}

The missing scopes come from session_shortfall. openid isn’t held access, so a session never lacks it.

What request id asks for that the browser session sid doesn’t hold, and the app asking, in a read scope. The missing scopes come from session_shortfall against the session’s grant as its row holds it now (browser_session_grant), the same check /oauth/authorize made when it parked the request.

Errors

See load_code_request_awaiting_limited_page; AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound too once the session has ended, since no code is issued under it; the store’s.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn read(
    &self,
    id: &str,
    sid: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<SessionShortfallView, AuthorizationServerError> {
    self.store.read(|tx| {
        let request = load_code_request_awaiting_limited_page(tx, id, sid, now)?;
        let session_grant = browser_session_grant(tx, sid, &self.stale_session_cutoff, now)?
            .ok_or_else(|| AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound {
                id: id.to_owned(),
            })?;
        let client_name = tx
            .client_by_id(&request.client_id)?
            .map_or_else(|| request.client_id.clone(), |client| client.name);
        Ok(SessionShortfallView {
            client_name,
            missing_scopes: session_shortfall(&request.requested_scopes, &session_grant),
        })
    })
}
}

cancel

The denial is the request’s own deny_on_limited_page, written through the guarded replace. In the race test, the Cancel’s denial, built from its earlier read, is still a valid transition on paper, but its replace finds the row gone on past the page and writes nothing.

Deny request id, made in the browser session sid, and return the client callback carrying error=access_denied. The denial holds only while the request still waits on the page, so a Continue that went on with it meanwhile wins and this answers not found. The Owner was never told of a request still waiting here, so nothing is republished. A Cancel isn’t remembered: unlike a Continue it records nothing for the session and the client, so the browser’s next request for the client stops at the page again.

Errors

See load_code_request_awaiting_limited_page; the store’s.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn cancel(
    &self,
    id: &str,
    sid: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<String, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let not_found =
        || AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound { id: id.to_owned() };
    let cancelled = self.store.write(|tx| {
        let request = load_code_request_awaiting_limited_page(tx, id, sid, now)?;
        let cancelled = request.deny_on_limited_page(now).map_err(|_| not_found())?;
        if tx.replace_code_request(&request, &cancelled)? {
            Ok(cancelled)
        } else {
            Err(not_found())
        }
    })?;
    Ok(build_client_error_redirect_url(
        &cancelled.redirect_uri,
        OAuthErrorCode::AccessDenied,
        REQUEST_DECLINED_DESCRIPTION,
        &cancelled.client_state,
    ))
}
}

Client Authenticator

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/client_authenticator.rs

An app that calls /oauth/token, /oauth/device_authorization or /oauth/revoke speaks for itself, not for a person. Before it may do anything there, the server checks it is who it says it is, from the credentials it presents. The client authenticator is the one door to that check. It turns those credentials into the AuthenticatedClient proof, and every client-gated capability takes that proof, never a bare client_id. The token-style request extractor, which all three endpoints use, goes through it before their handlers run.

The authenticator holds the store and nothing else, so a handler holding one can do nothing but authenticate. The rule itself lives on the proof’s constructor, which has the tests.

Device Authorizer

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/device_authorizer.rs

A device with no browser of its own can’t send the Owner to a consent card. It asks through the device flow (RFC 8628) instead: it calls POST /oauth/device_authorization and gets two codes back, a secret device_code it keeps and polls /oauth/token with, and a short user_code the Owner confirms at the server’s device page. The device authorizer starts that flow. It parks a pending device request and republishes the Owner prompt, so the host notifies the Owner.

Starting a device authorization grants nothing. The scopes it records are what the device asked for. The Owner’s approval on the device page decides what the device gets, and the token exchanger’s poll mints it. Only an app that has authenticated may start one. Unlike /oauth/authorize, this door doesn’t park a request outside the app’s registration for the Owner: it refuses it.

The tests start authorizations for an authenticated fixture app.

start

The scope check is the authenticated client’s, by coverage.

Check the requested scopes against the client’s allowlist (coverage- aware: a broad grant admits a narrower request it covers), mint the code pair, park the request under device_name (the name the approver sees and the grant is keyed on; None falls back to the client name at approval), and republish the Owner prompt so the host raises the popup.

Errors

DeviceAuthorizationError::ScopeNotAllowed, DeviceAuthorizationError::UserCodeExhausted, or a store failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn start(
    &self,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    requested_scopes: Vec<String>,
    device_name: Option<String>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<DeviceCodes, DeviceAuthorizationError> {
    if !authenticated_client.allows_scopes(&requested_scopes) {
        return Err(DeviceAuthorizationError::ScopeNotAllowed);
    }
    // 256-bit CSPRNG opaque token per RFC 6749 §10.10, like an
    // authorization code.
    let device_code = generate_authorization_code();
    let user_code = self
        .store
        .write(|tx| -> Result<_, DeviceAuthorizationError> {
            let user_code = generate_unique_user_code(tx)?
                .ok_or(DeviceAuthorizationError::UserCodeExhausted)?;
            tx.insert_device_request(&DeviceRequest::new(
                NewDeviceRequestArgs {
                    id: device_code.clone(),
                    client_id: authenticated_client.client_id().to_owned(),
                    requested_scopes,
                    ttl: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_TTL,
                    user_code: user_code.clone(),
                    device_name,
                },
                now,
            ))?;
            Ok(user_code)
        })?;
    // A fresh pending request is now the Owner prompt; republish so the
    // host notifies it.
    self.owner_approval.republish_active();
    Ok(DeviceCodes {
        device_code,
        user_code,
        expires_in: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_TTL.num_seconds(),
        interval: DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL.num_seconds(),
    })
}
}

generate_unique_user_code

A browser pairing draws its user_code here too.

A random user_code that collides with no existing request in tx — pending or terminal, of any flow: reusing a code attached to a denied/expired row would let that stale row shadow the new request at the consent-side lookup. None when every candidate collided.

Errors

The store’s, when reading a candidate’s request fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) fn generate_unique_user_code(
    tx: &mut impl AuthorizationRequestsTx,
) -> Result<Option<String>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    for _ in 0..MAX_USER_CODE_GENERATION_ATTEMPTS {
        let candidate = {
            let mut rng = rand::rng();
            generate_oauth_user_code(&mut rng)
        };
        if tx.polled_request_by_user_code(&candidate)?.is_none() {
            return Ok(Some(candidate));
        }
    }
    Ok(None)
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/device_authorizer.rs lines 161–174 · authorization-server in the code index

Browser Pairing

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/browser_pairing.rs

A browser that isn’t the Owner’s, a laptop in the kitchen say, gets a browser session by pairing. It opens the pairing page, /oauth/pair, which starts a pairing, shows a user_code, and polls. The Owner confirms that code at the device page and unticks whatever the browser shouldn’t have. The first poll after the approval hands the browser its paired session’s token, which it keeps as its browser session cookie.

Pairing is no OAuth flow. No app redeems it at /oauth/token, and it records no grant and no refresh family. Underneath it is a pairing request, asked for by the browser-session client, the one client every browser session’s token is issued to. It borrows the device flow’s codes, lifetime and page: its user_code is drawn as a device’s is, and it lives the device flow’s five minutes. The poll is bound to the request by its pairing code, a 256-bit secret only the page that started the pairing holds, as a device holds its device_code; the user_code on screen identifies the request to the Owner, but can’t collect the session.

The first poll after the approval claims the pairing through the ClaimedBrowserPairing proof, the browser session writer stores the paired session, and the access token minter signs its token, all in the poll’s one write scope. If storing or minting fails, the claim rolls back with them and the next poll tries again.

The tests pair over the pairing fixtures.

start

A next is allowed by the sign-in destinations, so an approved browser is sent on to the server’s own /oauth/authorize, never off the server.

Start a pairing that goes on to next once approved, named user_agent_name (the name the browser’s user agent suggests, if any), and republish the Owner prompt so the host notifies it. A next that isn’t a path on this server, or a disabled browser-session client (no session token could be issued to it), starts nothing. The request is parked pending under its pairing code, with a unique user_code drawn as the device flow’s are, for DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_TTL.

Errors

BrowserPairingStartError::NextNotAllowed, BrowserPairingStartError::BrowserSessionClientDisabled, BrowserPairingStartError::UserCodeExhausted, or a store failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn start(
    &self,
    next: &str,
    user_agent_name: Option<String>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<StartedBrowserPairing, BrowserPairingStartError> {
    let next = self
        .destinations
        .allow_on_this_server(next)
        .ok_or(BrowserPairingStartError::NextNotAllowed)?;
    // 256-bit CSPRNG opaque token, like a `device_code`.
    let pairing_code = generate_authorization_code();
    let browser_name = user_agent_name.unwrap_or_else(|| UNRECOGNIZED_BROWSER_NAME.to_owned());
    let user_code = self.store.write(|tx| {
        if is_browser_session_client_disabled(tx)? {
            return Err(BrowserPairingStartError::BrowserSessionClientDisabled);
        }
        let user_code = generate_unique_user_code(tx)?
            .ok_or(BrowserPairingStartError::UserCodeExhausted)?;
        tx.insert_pairing_request(&PairingRequest::new(
            NewPairingRequestArgs {
                id: pairing_code.clone(),
                client_id: BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID.to_owned(),
                requested_scopes: pairing_requested_scopes(),
                ttl: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_TTL,
                user_code: user_code.clone(),
                browser_name: browser_name.clone(),
            },
            now,
        ))?;
        Ok(user_code)
    })?;
    self.owner_approval.republish_active();
    Ok(StartedBrowserPairing {
        pairing_code,
        user_code,
        browser_name,
        next,
        expires_in: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_TTL.num_seconds(),
        interval: DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL.num_seconds(),
    })
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/browser_pairing.rs lines 466–492 · authorization-server in the code index

poll

Poll the pairing pairing_code names at now, from a page that now names its browser browser_name (blank keeps the name it has). The whole poll is one write scope. A pairing past its expiry is Expired whatever its status; otherwise its status decides:

  • pending: throttled to the poll interval (SlowDown records nothing), then the poll is stamped and the name recorded; Pending;
  • approved: the first poll claims it, stores the paired session it starts and mints the session’s token, together or not at all; Approved with the token;
  • denied: Denied;
  • claimed: an earlier poll started the session; Expired.
Errors

BrowserPairingPollError::NotFound when no pairing has the code; a store, session or minting failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn poll(
    &self,
    pairing_code: &str,
    browser_name: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<BrowserPairingStatus, BrowserPairingPollError> {
    let polled = self.store.write(|tx| {
        let Some(request) = tx.pairing_request_by_id(pairing_code)? else {
            return Err(BrowserPairingPollError::NotFound);
        };
        if request.is_expired_at(now) {
            return Ok(PolledPairing::Answered(BrowserPairingStatus::Expired));
        }
        match request.state {
            PolledState::Pending => record_poll(tx, &request, browser_name, now),
            PolledState::Approved(_) => self.claim_paired_session(tx, &request, now),
            PolledState::Denied => Ok(PolledPairing::Answered(BrowserPairingStatus::Denied)),
            PolledState::Claimed(_) => {
                Ok(PolledPairing::Answered(BrowserPairingStatus::Expired))
            }
        }
    })?;
    match polled {
        PolledPairing::Answered(status) => Ok(status),
        PolledPairing::Renamed => {
            self.owner_approval.republish_active();
            Ok(BrowserPairingStatus::Pending)
        }
        PolledPairing::Claimed { session_token } => {
            Ok(BrowserPairingStatus::Approved { session_token })
        }
    }
}
}

While pending, a poll is throttled to the interval, records the name the page now gives (blank keeps the last one), and republishes only for a new name.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn a_pending_poll_is_throttled_and_records_the_browser_s_name() {
    let (pairing, owner_approval, _) = pairing();
    let now = Utc::now();
    let started = pairing
        .start(NEXT, Some("Firefox on Linux".to_owned()), now)
        .unwrap();
    let poll = |name: &str, at| pairing.poll(&started.pairing_code, name, at).unwrap();
    let name = || {
        pairing
            .store
            .tx()
            .pairing_request_by_id(&started.pairing_code)
            .unwrap()
            .map(|pairing_request| pairing_request.browser_name)
    };
    assert!(matches!(
        poll("Firefox on Linux", now),
        BrowserPairingStatus::Pending
    ));
    assert_eq!(
        owner_approval.count(),
        1,
        "the same name republishes nothing"
    );
    assert!(matches!(
        poll("Kitchen laptop", now + Duration::seconds(1)),
        BrowserPairingStatus::SlowDown
    ));
    assert_eq!(name().as_deref(), Some("Firefox on Linux"));
    let later = now + DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL;
    assert!(matches!(
        poll("  Kitchen laptop ", later),
        BrowserPairingStatus::Pending
    ));
    assert_eq!(name().as_deref(), Some("Kitchen laptop"));
    assert_eq!(owner_approval.count(), 2);
    assert!(matches!(
        poll(" ", later + DEVICE_CODE_POLL_INTERVAL),
        BrowserPairingStatus::Pending
    ));
    assert_eq!(name().as_deref(), Some("Kitchen laptop"));
}
}

Once approved, the first poll starts a 24 h paired session holding exactly the approved scopes, under the name the Owner approved, and mints its token for the browser-session client; the next poll finds it spent.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn the_first_poll_after_approval_starts_the_paired_session() {
    let (pairing, _, signing_key) = pairing();
    let started = pairing.start(NEXT, None, Utc::now()).unwrap();
    approve(
        &pairing.store,
        &started.pairing_code,
        &["wildflower/launch", "system/Patient.rs"],
    );
    let now = Utc::now();
    let BrowserPairingStatus::Approved { session_token } = pairing
        .poll(&started.pairing_code, "ignored once approved", now)
        .unwrap()
    else {
        panic!("approved");
    };
    let claims = verify_access_token(
        &session_token,
        &[signing_key],
        &AccessTokenVerifyOptions {
            expected_issuer: SERVER_ORIGIN,
            accepted_audiences: &[SERVER_ORIGIN.to_owned()],
        },
    )
    .expect("a token this server accepts");
    assert_eq!(claims.subject, BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID);
    assert_eq!(
        claims.scope.as_deref(),
        Some("wildflower/launch system/Patient.rs")
    );
    assert_eq!(
        claims
            .expires_at
            .zip(claims.issued_at)
            .map(|(exp, iat)| exp - iat),
        Some(PAIRED_SESSION_TTL)
    );
    let sid = claims.sid.expect("names its session");
    let session = pairing
        .store
        .tx()
        .browser_session_by_sid(&sid)
        .unwrap()
        .expect("the session is stored");
    assert_eq!(session.kind, BrowserSessionKind::Paired);
    assert_eq!(session.name.as_deref(), Some("Ruth's laptop"));
    assert_eq!(session.scopes, ["wildflower/launch", "system/Patient.rs"]);
    assert_eq!(session.expires_at - session.created_at, PAIRED_SESSION_TTL);
    assert!(matches!(
        pairing.poll(&started.pairing_code, "", now).unwrap(),
        BrowserPairingStatus::Expired
    ));
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn claim_paired_session(
    &self,
    tx: &mut impl GrantTx,
    pairing_request: &PairingRequest,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<PolledPairing, BrowserPairingPollError> {
    let Some(claimed_pairing) =
        ClaimedBrowserPairing::claim(tx, pairing_request, PAIRED_SESSION_TTL, now)?
    else {
        return Ok(PolledPairing::Answered(BrowserPairingStatus::Expired));
    };
    BrowserSessionWriter::within(tx)
        .start_paired_session(&claimed_pairing)
        .map_err(BrowserPairingPollError::SessionNotStored)?;
    let session_token =
        AccessTokenMinter::with_active_key(tx, &self.server_origin, PAIRED_SESSION_TTL)
            .and_then(|minter| minter.mint(TokenEntitlement::BrowserPairing(&claimed_pairing)))
            .map_err(BrowserPairingPollError::Issuance)?;
    Ok(PolledPairing::Claimed { session_token })
}
}

record_poll

The stamp is the pairing’s own stamp_poll.

Throttle and stamp a poll of the pending pairing request in tx, recording browser_name when it is a new one (blank keeps the name it has).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn record_poll(
    tx: &mut impl AuthorizationRequestsTx,
    request: &PairingRequest,
    browser_name: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<PolledPairing, BrowserPairingPollError> {
    if request.is_polled_too_soon_at(now) {
        return Ok(PolledPairing::Answered(BrowserPairingStatus::SlowDown));
    }
    let browser_name = Some(browser_name.trim())
        .filter(|browser_name| !browser_name.is_empty())
        .unwrap_or(&request.browser_name);
    if let Ok(stamped) = request.stamp_poll(browser_name, now) {
        tx.replace_pairing_request(request, &stamped)?;
    }
    if request.browser_name == browser_name {
        Ok(PolledPairing::Answered(BrowserPairingStatus::Pending))
    } else {
        Ok(PolledPairing::Renamed)
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/browser_pairing.rs lines 344–353 · authorization-server in the code index

Same-Device Sign-In

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/same_device_sign_in.rs

The Owner’s own browser doesn’t pair. The base app, running on the same device as the server, mints a one-time sign-in code in-process and opens GET /oauth/sign-in?code=…&next=… in a browser. Only the base can mint a code, so redeeming one proves the browser is on the Owner’s device. The sign-in starts a same-device browser session holding the Owner’s scopes, hands the browser that session’s token for its cookie, and sends it on to next.

The codes live in memory, not in the store, and redeeming one takes it out for good, even when the write scope later rolls back. So everything that can refuse a sign-in without the code’s fault runs before the code is touched, and a refused next or a disabled client leaves the code redeemable. A failure after the code is taken spends it: if the session can’t be stored or the token can’t be minted, no session remains, and signing in again takes a new code. Before the session’s write scope commits, the codes remember it by the code that started it, so the base can end it once the server’s launch views have closed, and no session lands that its code doesn’t find. A code the base withdrew before then, as its view closed, signs nobody in: the scope rolls back and the token is never handed out, so a closed view’s late sign-in can’t replace the cookie a view still open holds.

The redemption is the RedeemedSameDeviceSignInCode proof; the browser session writer stores the session it carries, and the access token minter signs its token.

The tests sign in over the sign-in fixtures.

sign_in

Where a sign-in may go next is the sign-in destinations.

Redeem presented_code at now for a same-device session and its token, both lasting SAME_DEVICE_SESSION_TTL, to go on to next. A next that isn’t allowed, or a disabled browser-session client, is refused before the code is touched, so the code stays redeemable. The session is stored and its token signed in one write scope, which also has the codes remember the session by the code before it commits, so the base can end it once the view it opened closes, and no session lands that its code doesn’t find. A code the base withdrew before then, as its view closed, signs nobody in: the scope rolls back, and the token is never handed out. A failure after this call takes the code spends it: the code leaves memory even when the scope rolls back, so signing in again takes a new code. A failure before then leaves the code as it stood, so a second presentation of a code mid-sign-in can’t clear its withdrawal.

Errors

SameDeviceSignInError::Refused for a next that isn’t allowed (SignInRefusal::RedirectNotAllowed), a disabled browser-session client (SignInRefusal::BrowserSessionClientDisabled), or a code that is unknown, spent, expired or withdrawn (SignInRefusal::CodeNotRedeemable); SameDeviceSignInError::Store when the browser-session client can’t be read; SameDeviceSignInError::SessionNotStored when the session can’t be stored; SameDeviceSignInError::Issuance when minting fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn sign_in(
    &self,
    presented_code: &str,
    next: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<SignedIn, SameDeviceSignInError> {
    let redirect = self
        .destinations
        .allow(next)
        .ok_or(SameDeviceSignInError::Refused(
            SignInRefusal::RedirectNotAllowed,
        ))?;
    let mut code_taken = false;
    let stored = self.store.write(|tx| {
        if is_browser_session_client_disabled(tx)? {
            return Err(SameDeviceSignInError::Refused(
                SignInRefusal::BrowserSessionClientDisabled,
            ));
        }
        let redeemed_sign_in_code = RedeemedSameDeviceSignInCode::redeem(
            &self.codes,
            presented_code,
            &self.owner_grant,
            SAME_DEVICE_SESSION_TTL,
            now,
        )
        .ok_or(SameDeviceSignInError::Refused(
            SignInRefusal::CodeNotRedeemable,
        ))?;
        code_taken = true;
        BrowserSessionWriter::within(tx)
            .start_same_device_session(&redeemed_sign_in_code)
            .map_err(SameDeviceSignInError::SessionNotStored)?;
        let session_token = AccessTokenMinter::with_active_key(
            tx,
            &self.server_origin,
            SAME_DEVICE_SESSION_TTL,
        )
        .and_then(|minter| {
            minter.mint(TokenEntitlement::SameDeviceSignIn(&redeemed_sign_in_code))
        })
        .map_err(SameDeviceSignInError::Issuance)?;
        if !self
            .codes
            .session_stored(presented_code, redeemed_sign_in_code.session())
        {
            return Err(SameDeviceSignInError::Refused(
                SignInRefusal::CodeNotRedeemable,
            ));
        }
        Ok(session_token)
    });
    let session_token = match stored {
        Ok(session_token) => session_token,
        Err(error) => {
            if code_taken {
                self.codes.session_not_stored(presented_code);
            }
            return Err(error);
        }
    };
    Ok(SignedIn {
        session_token,
        redirect,
    })
}
}

fn main() {
fn a_code_signs_the_owner_in_for_eight_hours() {

            accepted_audiences: &[SERVER_ORIGIN.to_owned()],

            .zip(claims.issued_at)
            .map(|(exp, iat)| exp - iat),
        Some(SAME_DEVICE_SESSION_TTL),
        "the token lives eight hours"

}

fn main() {
fn a_code_withdrawn_before_its_scope_commits_finds_its_session() {
    let now = Utc::now();
    let (sign_in, _signing_key) = sign_in_with_a_code(now);
    // Withdrawn at the end of the write scope, before it commits: the
    // view closed mid-sign-in.
    let withdrawing = WithdrawingStore {
        store: sign_in.store.clone(),
        codes: Arc::clone(&sign_in.codes),
    };
    let sign_in = SameDeviceSignIn::new(
        withdrawing,
        Arc::clone(&sign_in.codes),
        Arc::clone(&sign_in.destinations),
        Arc::clone(&sign_in.server_origin),
        sign_in.owner_grant.clone(),
    );
    sign_in.sign_in("code-1", "/", now).expect("signed in");
    let sessions = sign_in
        .store
        .store
        .tx()
        .live_browser_sessions(now)
        .expect("read");
    assert_eq!(
        sessions
            .iter()
            .map(|session| Some(session.sid.clone()))
            .collect::<Vec<_>>(),
        [sign_in.codes.signed_in_sid("code-1")],
        "the one session stands, found by its code"
    );
}
}

Same-Device Session Ender

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/same_device_session_ender.rs

A same-device sign-in hands the browser a launch opened an Owner session. On Android that browser is a Custom Tab, which shares the user’s Chrome cookies, and on a desktop it is the default browser’s own tab, so the session lands where any tab on the server’s domain holds it. So an Owner session lasts only as long as the server’s launch views stay open.

  • When the server’s last launch view closes, the base ends the sessions the codes of its views signed in since they last all closed. On iOS and Android a server’s views share one cookie jar: a stacked consent view’s sign-in replaces the cookie the launch view under it holds, so ending a closed view’s session at its own close could leave a view still open with a dead cookie. The base holds each code, a SameDeviceSignInCode, across the server’s runs, and ends the sessions through the run up then, with the OAuth bindings’ minter. Leaving the app with a view open and coming back isn’t a close, and keeps them.
  • When a view closes, its code is withdrawn: unredeemed, it is no longer redeemable, and still signing in, it signs nobody in.
  • When the server starts, its run’s start cuts off every same-device session but those of the launch views still open, whose codes the base hands setup, so the restart a return from a suspend brings on iOS keeps an open view signed in. It writes nothing for the others: the StaleSessionCutoff setup builds leaves them no longer live, so the token verifier refuses their cookies, as it does an expired session’s, and the Browsers list leaves them out. So a store that can’t be written as the server starts doesn’t keep it from starting. A desktop hears no close, so the base counts its views’ codes until the app exits: the server’s restarts keep the desktop browser signed in, and the first start after the app’s next start ends its sessions. A paired browser’s session isn’t a launch’s, and stands.

Ending a session expires it rather than revoking it. Its expires_at moves back to now: the session’s own token, the cookie, stops working at once (the token verifier refuses it), and the browser is sent to pairing until the base’s next launch signs it in again. A refresh-token family an app was issued under the session isn’t revoked with it, so it keeps refreshing as its client’s refresh policy says. A code forgets its session only once the expiry has landed. When the store fails, the base drops the codes all the same: the server’s next start exempts from its cutoff only the sessions of the views open then, so those sessions go stale.

end_sessions_signed_in_with

Withdraw each of sign_in_codes, and expire, at now, the sessions they signed browsers in with, returning how many were ended. A code that signed nobody in, or whose session was ended already, ends nothing. Each code forgets its session only once the write lands, so a failed write can be tried again with the same codes.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure on a store failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn end_sessions_signed_in_with(
    &self,
    sign_in_codes: &[SameDeviceSignInCode],
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<usize, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let sids: Vec<String> = sign_in_codes
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|sign_in_code| {
            sign_in_code.withdraw();
            sign_in_code.signed_in_sid()
        })
        .collect();
    let ended = self.store.write(|tx| {
        sids.iter().try_fold(0, |ended, sid| {
            Ok::<_, AuthorizationServerError>(
                ended + usize::from(tx.expire_browser_session(sid, now)?),
            )
        })
    })?;
    for sign_in_code in sign_in_codes {
        sign_in_code.forget_session();
    }
    Ok(ended)
}
}

Ending by codes expires exactly the sessions those codes signed in, at now, without revoking them; another code’s session stands, and the same codes end nothing a second time.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn codes_end_only_their_own_sessions() {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    let codes = Arc::new(SameDeviceSignInCodes::new());
    let signed_in_at = Utc::now();
    let closed = stored_same_device_session(&store, signed_in_at);
    let still_open = stored_same_device_session(&store, signed_in_at);
    let closed_code = signed_in_code(&codes, "closed-code", &closed, signed_in_at);
    signed_in_code(&codes, "open-code", &still_open, signed_in_at);
    let unredeemed_code = SameDeviceSignInCode::new("unredeemed-code".to_owned(), codes);
    let ender = SameDeviceSessionEnder::new(store.clone());
    let now = signed_in_at + Duration::minutes(10);
    let closed_codes = [closed_code, unredeemed_code];

    assert_eq!(
        ender
            .end_sessions_signed_in_with(&closed_codes, now)
            .expect("end"),
        1
    );
    assert_eq!(
        ender
            .end_sessions_signed_in_with(&closed_codes, now)
            .expect("end again"),
        0
    );

    assert_eq!(
        stored(&store, &closed.sid),
        BrowserSession {
            expires_at: now,
            ..closed
        },
        "expired, not revoked"
    );
    assert_eq!(stored(&store, &still_open.sid), still_open);
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/same_device_session_ender.rs lines 150–168 · authorization-server in the code index

Token Exchanger

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/token_exchanger.rs

POST /oauth/token is where an app turns what it was given into an access token it can call the FHIR server with. It has three ways in: an authorization code the Owner’s approval issued, a device request the Owner approved, or a refresh token from an earlier exchange. The token exchanger runs all three, always for an app that has authenticated.

Every exchange has the same spine. The app must be registered for the grant type it uses, checked before any scope opens, so a refused app spends nothing. Then, inside a write scope: obtain the redemption proof from the Redemption authority, load the signing key, start or rotate the refresh family through the refresh family writer, and sign the token through the access token minter. The proof is the hand-off between checking and writing, so a token is never minted for a grant that didn’t redeem.

Signing runs inside the scope, so a signing failure undoes the exchange: the code stays unspent, the device request unclaimed, the refresh token unrotated, and the app can try again. A refusal is different. Some refusals must keep what they wrote (the spent code of a failed redemption, the stamped poll of a device that polled too early, the ended family of a replayed refresh token), so a refusal comes back inside the scope’s answer, and the scope commits.

The tests exchange through an exchanger over a fresh fake, with codes issued for a fixed PKCE verifier.

exchange_refresh_token

An epoch bumped between the two scopes doesn’t stop this one rotation, as the epoch isn’t read again; but the family still began before the epoch, so its next refresh is refused.

Trade a live refresh token for a fresh access token and the refresh token’s successor (RFC 6749 §6, OAuth 2.1 rotation). The family keeps its scopes and absolute deadline — rotation never extends its life.

The one exchange with two scopes. A read scope validates the token, its client’s revocation epoch included: the epoch lives on the revocation store, another connection to the same file, so reading it under our write lock could stall both connections for the busy timeout. The write scope then re-validates the store-only facts, since the family may have ended between the two, rotates, and mints. An epoch bumped between the two scopes doesn’t stop this one rotation, as the epoch isn’t read again; but the family still began before the epoch, so its next refresh is refused.

Errors

TokenExchangeError::UnauthorizedGrantType, the validation’s InvalidGrant, a replay (RefreshTokenReplayed, after which the family is revoked), or a minting / store failure.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn exchange_refresh_token(
    &self,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    presented_refresh_token: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<IssuedTokens, TokenExchangeError> {
    ensure_grant_type_allowed(authenticated_client, AllowedGrantType::RefreshToken)?;
    let validated_refresh_token = self.store.read(|tx| {
        ValidatedRefreshToken::validate(
            tx,
            self.revocation.as_ref(),
            authenticated_client,
            presented_refresh_token,
            now,
        )
    })?;
    self.store.write(|tx| {
        self.rotate_refresh_token_in(tx, authenticated_client, validated_refresh_token, now)
    })?
}
}

fn main() {
fn a_refresh_exchange_rotates_and_a_replay_revokes_the_family() {
    let exchanger = exchanger();
    seed_fixture_browser_session(&exchanger.store);
    let client = authenticated(&exchanger.store, "app", &AllowedGrantType::ALL);
    let plain = issue_code(&exchanger.store, "app", &["openid", "offline_access"]);
    let now = Utc::now();
    let first = exchanger
        .exchange_authorization_code(
            &client,
            &PresentedAuthorizationCode {
                code: &plain,
                code_verifier: VERIFIER,
                redirect_uri: "https://example.com/cb",
            },
            now,
        )
        .unwrap()
        .refresh_token
        .unwrap();

    let rotated = exchanger
        .exchange_refresh_token(&client, &first, now)
        .expect("rotates");
    let successor = rotated.refresh_token.expect("successor issued");
    assert_eq!(rotated.granted_scopes, ["openid", "offline_access"]);

    let replay = exchanger.exchange_refresh_token(&client, &first, now + Duration::seconds(1));
    assert!(matches!(
        replay,
        Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenReplayed { .. }
        ))
    ));
    let after_revoke =
        exchanger.exchange_refresh_token(&client, &successor, now + Duration::seconds(2));
    assert!(matches!(
        after_revoke,
        Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
            InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenExpired
        ))
    ));
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn redeem_code_in(
    &self,
    tx: &mut impl GrantTx,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    presented: &PresentedAuthorizationCode<'_>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> ExchangeOutcome {
    let redeemed_code =
        match RedeemedAuthorizationCode::redeem(tx, authenticated_client, presented, now)? {
            Ok(redeemed_code) => redeemed_code,
            Err(refusal) => return Ok(Err(refusal)),
        };
    let redemption = GrantRedemption::AuthorizationCode(&redeemed_code);
    let (minter, refresh_token) = self.prepare_issuance(tx, redemption, now)?;
    issue(
        &minter,
        TokenEntitlement::AuthorizationCode(&redeemed_code),
        redemption.granted_scopes(),
        redeemed_code.patient(),
        refresh_token,
    )
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/token_exchanger.rs lines 186–210 · authorization-server in the code index

rotate_refresh_token_in

exchange_refresh_token’s write half, inside its write scope tx: re-validate the token validated in the read scope, rotate it, and mint. A refusal is the inner Err, so the scope keeps a replayed family’s end.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn rotate_refresh_token_in(
    &self,
    tx: &mut impl GrantTx,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    validated_refresh_token: ValidatedRefreshToken,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> ExchangeOutcome {
    let validated_refresh_token =
        match validated_refresh_token.revalidate(tx, authenticated_client, now) {
            Ok(validated_refresh_token) => validated_refresh_token,
            Err(TokenExchangeError::Store(error)) => return Err(error.into()),
            Err(refusal) => return Ok(Err(refusal)),
        };
    let minter = AccessTokenMinter::with_active_key(tx, &self.server_origin, ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL)?;
    let successor =
        match RefreshFamilyWriter::within(tx).rotate(&validated_refresh_token, now)? {
            Ok(successor) => successor,
            Err(refusal) => return Ok(Err(refusal)),
        };
    issue(
        &minter,
        TokenEntitlement::RefreshToken(&validated_refresh_token),
        validated_refresh_token.granted_scopes(),
        validated_refresh_token.patient(),
        Some(successor),
    )
}
}

Client Token Revoker

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/client_token_revoker.rs

POST /oauth/revoke (RFC 7009) is how an app gives up a token it holds, when its user signs out of it, say. The app authenticates first, as it does at /oauth/token. An app can only revoke its own tokens. A refresh token ends its whole family; an access token is denylisted by its jti until it expires, in the host’s revocation store, through the Revocation port.

Anything else is left alone and answered alike: a token the server doesn’t know, one already dead, one minted by another server, one issued to another app. The answer is the same empty success every time, so an app learns nothing about a token that isn’t its own. Ending a family touches no access token already minted from it; those live out their own fifteen minutes.

The tests revoke into a real in-memory revocation store, over the revoker fixtures.

revoke

Revoke presented_token if it is one of authenticated_client’s. The token’s type is told from the token itself, so the request’s token_type_hint is never needed: a refresh token is found by its storage hash and its family ended in the one write scope, and anything else is tried as an access token once the scope has closed.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure when the refresh-token, signing-key or revocation store can’t be read or written, or when an access token can’t be verified for want of a usable key (no signing keys stored, or a key’s material unreadable). Nothing about the token itself is an error.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn revoke(
    &self,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    presented_token: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError> {
    let presented_hash = token_storage_hash(presented_token);
    let presented = self
        .store
        .write(|tx| -> Result<_, AuthorizationServerError> {
            match tx.refresh_token_with_family_by_hash(&presented_hash)? {
                Some((_, family)) => {
                    end_refresh_family(tx, authenticated_client, &family, now)?;
                    Ok(PresentedToken::RefreshToken)
                }
                None => Ok(PresentedToken::NoRefreshToken {
                    signing_keys: tx.all_signing_keys()?,
                }),
            }
        })?;
    match presented {
        PresentedToken::RefreshToken => Ok(()),
        PresentedToken::NoRefreshToken { signing_keys } => {
            self.denylist_access_token(authenticated_client, presented_token, &signing_keys)
        }
    }
}
}

fn main() {
fn a_refresh_token_ends_its_family_only_for_its_own_client() {
    let (revoker, _) = revoker();
    let now = Utc::now();
    let app = authenticated(&revoker.store, "app");
    let stranger = authenticated(&revoker.store, "stranger");
    plant_family(&revoker.store, "app", "refresh", now);

    revoker.revoke(&stranger, "refresh", now).unwrap();
    assert!(family_expires_at(&revoker.store, "refresh") > now);

    revoker.revoke(&app, "refresh", now).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(family_expires_at(&revoker.store, "refresh"), now);

    revoker
        .revoke(&app, "refresh", now + Duration::minutes(1))
        .unwrap();
    assert_eq!(
        family_expires_at(&revoker.store, "refresh"),
        now,
        "revoking an ended family doesn't move its end"
    );
}
}

denylist_access_token

The check is verify_access_token, with the server’s origin as issuer and audience.

Denylist a presented access token until its own expiry when this server minted it for the client, verified against signing_keys. A token that fails verification (forged, expired, another server’s) can’t be used anyway, so there is nothing to revoke.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn denylist_access_token(
    &self,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    presented_token: &str,
    signing_keys: &[SigningKey],
) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError> {
    let claims = match verify_access_token(
        presented_token,
        signing_keys,
        &AccessTokenVerifyOptions {
            expected_issuer: &self.server_origin,
            accepted_audiences: &[self.server_origin.to_string()],
        },
    ) {
        Ok(claims) => claims,
        Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected) => return Ok(()),
        Err(error) => {
            return Err(AuthorizationServerError::infrastructure(
                "access-token verification failed during revocation",
                error,
            ))
        }
    };
    if claims.subject != authenticated_client.client_id() {
        tracing::info!(
            token_client_id = %claims.subject,
            presented_client_id = authenticated_client.client_id(),
            "revocation presented another client's access token; left alone"
        );
        return Ok(());
    }
    // Every token this server mints carries both; verification tolerates
    // one without a `jti`, which can't be denylisted on its own.
    let (Some(jti), Some(expires_at)) = (claims.jti.as_deref(), claims.expires_at) else {
        return Ok(());
    };
    self.revocation
        .revoke_jti(jti, expires_at, CLIENT_REVOCATION_REASON)
        .map_err(|error| AuthorizationServerError::infrastructure("revoke_jti failed", error))
}
}

fn main() {
fn end_refresh_family(
    tx: &mut impl RefreshTokensTx,
    authenticated_client: &AuthenticatedClient,
    family: &RefreshTokenFamily,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError> {
    if family.client_id != authenticated_client.client_id() {
        tracing::info!(
            family_id = %family.family_id,
            presented_client_id = authenticated_client.client_id(),
            "revocation presented another client's refresh token; left alone"
        );
        return Ok(());
    }
    if family.expires_at <= now {
        return Ok(());
    }
    tx.expire_refresh_token_family(&family.family_id, now)
}
}

Public Keys Reader

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/oauth/public_keys_reader.rs

Every token this server mints is signed with one of its signing keys. Anyone checking a token, the FHIR server or an app, needs the public half of that key. The public keys reader is the read behind GET /.well-known/jwks.json, the server’s JSON Web Key Set. It is public, and its one power is this read. It hands out public JWKs only: the private material stays inside the signing key they are projected from.

A key rotated out signs nothing new, but it stays in the set, so a token it signed can still be checked.

Session

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/mod.rs

The session capabilities are what a caller does with its own credential: checking it, reading it back, ending it. Every other capability acts on a request, a grant or a client the caller names; these act only on the token or the browser session the caller already holds. That is why none of them takes a scope. The Owner, an app and a browser with the narrowest pairing can all log out and read what they hold, and a scope gate here would lock out exactly the under-scoped callers who need to.

The first of them is how the server learns what a caller holds at all. Every access token the server accepts passes through the token verifier: the /authorization bearer gate, the bearer gate the host layers over its FHIR and other routes, the browser-session cookie checks, and the FHIR server’s own check, in process. The rest of the part builds on its answer.

The capabilities reach a handler two ways. Those that act on the bearer the gate verified, the session ender and the session reader, come through the shared Authenticated<…> extractor, which builds them from the verified claims and checks no scope. Those that act on a browser’s cookie rather than a bearer, the browser session ender and the browser session use recorder, and the verifier itself, are built from the state alone; their callers verify the cookie’s token first. The Session Bindings page shows each one’s construction.

In this part

  • Token Verifier: the one access-token check, signature to revocation, that every gate runs.
  • Session Reader: a caller reading back its own scopes and its browser session’s expiry.
  • Session Ender: logout, denylisting the presented token.
  • Browser Session Ender: sign-out, revoking the browser session the cookie holds.
  • Browser Session Use Recorder: moving a browser session’s last_seen_at when its cookie is accepted.

Token Verifier

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/token_verifier.rs

The token verifier answers one question for every request that presents an access token: is this a live token this server minted for itself? It is the single place that question is answered, so a token is accepted or refused the same way wherever it is presented.

Its answer is the token’s VerifiedClaims, or an AccessTokenVerifyError saying why not. Revocation comes last: a token is first proven genuine by verify_access_token against the stored keys, and only then asked whether it has since been withdrawn: by its browser session, in the grant store, and by its jti or its subject’s epoch, in the host’s revocation store. A logout denylists a jti; an Owner’s revoke or a grant’s revoke moves a subject’s epoch; signing a browser out revokes its session. A browser session’s own token, the one its cookie holds, lasts only as long as the session: the host ends the Owner’s same-device session by expiring it, before its token would expire, and the verifier refuses the token from then on. It refuses the token of a same-device session the stale-session cutoff makes stale the same way. The tokens apps were issued under the session don’t end with its expiry, only with its revocation.

The tests verify against a fake store with one signing key, and a recording revocation check.

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/token_verifier.rs lines 42–54 · authorization-server in the code index

verify

Verify token: its iss and aud must both be this server’s origin, so a token another server minted is refused by construction. See docs/Origins/Explanation.md.

Revocation is the last gate: the token is cryptographically valid, but a logout / owner revoke / grant revoke may have denylisted its jti or bumped the subject’s epoch since it was minted, or revoked the browser session its sid names. A sid that names no session row reads as revoked, so a token naming a session the server never had is refused too. A browser session’s own token is also refused once the session is no longer live, which can be before the token expires. Both authN gates, the browser-session cookie checks, and through InProcessTokenVerifier the FHIR server, funnel through here, so it runs the complete check (per-jti denylist, per-subject epoch and browser session). A token with no sid has no session to check. Every store failure fails closed, never admitting the token, and the gates answer it with a 500, not a 401.

Errors

AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected for a bad, expired, wrong-issuer or wrong-audience token, or a browser session’s own token once the session is no longer live; AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked for a revoked one; the server-side variants when the key, revocation or browser-session store can’t be read.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn verify(&self, token: &str) -> Result<VerifiedClaims, AccessTokenVerifyError> {
    // A connection that can't be checked out at all fails like the key
    // read that is the scope's first statement.
    let claims = self
        .store
        .read(|tx| Ok(self.verify_signed_and_session_live(tx, token)))
        .map_err(AccessTokenVerifyError::KeyStoreUnavailable)??;
    let revoked = self
        .revocation
        .is_revoked(claims.jti.as_deref(), claims.issued_at, &claims.subject)
        .map_err(AccessTokenVerifyError::RevocationStoreUnavailable)?;
    if revoked {
        return Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked);
    }
    Ok(claims)
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn revocation_is_the_last_gate_and_fails_closed() {
    let (store, key) = store_with_key();
    let token = mint(&key, ORIGIN, ORIGIN);
    let jti = verify_access_token(
        &token,
        &store.tx().all_signing_keys().unwrap(),
        &AccessTokenVerifyOptions {
            expected_issuer: ORIGIN,
            accepted_audiences: &[ORIGIN.to_owned()],
        },
    )
    .unwrap()
    .jti
    .expect("minted tokens carry a jti");

    let revoked = TokenVerifier::new(
        FakeGrantStore::default(),
        Arc::new(FakeRevocation {
            revoked_jtis: vec![jti],
            ..FakeRevocation::default()
        }),
        ORIGIN.into(),
        Arc::new(StaleSessionCutoff::none()),
    );
    // Re-seed the key so the revoked verifier can check the signature.
    revoked.store.tx().insert_signing_key(&key).unwrap();
    assert!(matches!(
        revoked.verify(&token),
        Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked)
    ));

    let failing = TokenVerifier::new(
        store,
        Arc::new(FakeRevocation {
            fail: true,
            ..FakeRevocation::default()
        }),
        ORIGIN.into(),
        Arc::new(StaleSessionCutoff::none()),
    );
    assert!(matches!(
        failing.verify(&token),
        Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::RevocationStoreUnavailable(_))
    ));
}
}

verify_signed_and_session_live

Verify token’s signature, iss and aud against the keys in tx, and refuse it when the browser session its sid names is revoked or has no row, or, for the session’s own token, is no longer live.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn verify_signed_and_session_live(
    &self,
    tx: &mut (impl SigningKeysTx + BrowserSessionsTx),
    token: &str,
) -> Result<VerifiedClaims, AccessTokenVerifyError> {
    let keys = tx
        .all_signing_keys()
        .map_err(AccessTokenVerifyError::KeyStoreUnavailable)?;
    let claims = verify_access_token(
        token,
        &keys,
        &AccessTokenVerifyOptions {
            expected_issuer: &self.server_origin,
            accepted_audiences: &[self.server_origin.to_string()],
        },
    )?;
    if let Some(sid) = claims.sid.as_deref() {
        if claims.subject == BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID {
            ensure_own_session_live(tx, sid, &self.stale_session_cutoff, Utc::now())?;
        } else if tx
            .is_browser_session_revoked(sid)
            .map_err(AccessTokenVerifyError::BrowserSessionStoreUnavailable)?
        {
            return Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked);
        }
    }
    Ok(claims)
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/token_verifier.rs lines 102–129 · authorization-server in the code index

ensure_own_session_live

Refuse a browser session’s own token, the one its cookie holds, once the session sid is no longer live at now under stale_session_cutoff: Revoked when the session is revoked or has no row, TokenRejected when it is otherwise not live. A session can end before its token does: the host ends a same-device session by expiring it, and the cutoff makes one stale. The tokens apps were issued under the session outlive its ending, and only its revocation ends them.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn ensure_own_session_live(
    tx: &mut impl BrowserSessionsTx,
    sid: &str,
    stale_session_cutoff: &StaleSessionCutoff,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<(), AccessTokenVerifyError> {
    let session = tx
        .browser_session_by_sid(sid)
        .map_err(AccessTokenVerifyError::BrowserSessionStoreUnavailable)?;
    match session {
        None => Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked),
        Some(session) if session.revoked_at.is_some() => Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked),
        Some(session) if !session.is_live_at(now, stale_session_cutoff) => {
            Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected)
        }
        Some(_) => Ok(()),
    }
}
}

Session Reader

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/session_reader.rs

The session reader is a caller reading back its own session: the scopes the token it presented carries, and, for a token minted under a browser session, when that session ends. Every answer comes from the caller’s verified claims or from the one browser session their sid names, so the read discloses nothing about anyone else, and it needs no scope.

That matters for who calls it. The device-login screen reads the session’s real scopes to seed its scope picker, and the server’s own pages read the browser session’s expiry to show how long the browser stays signed in. A caller that has just been refused for a missing scope is exactly the one that needs to read what it does hold. GET /authorization/session builds one, and so does the browsers list, which reads the caller’s sid to mark the caller’s own browser.

The test reads claims under a stored session or none.

Session Ender

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/session_ender.rs

The session ender is logout: a caller giving up the access token it presented. The token is signed and carries its own expiry, so the caller forgetting it would leave any copy usable until then. Logout closes that window by putting the token’s jti on the denylist the token verifier checks. It does not revoke the browser session the token may name; that is sign-out.

It is built from the caller’s verified claims, so it can revoke nothing but the token that was presented, and it takes no scope: anyone holding a valid token may end it. POST /authorization/logout builds one.

The test logs out through a recording revocation port.

The denylisting itself is revoke_session_token.

Denylist the presented token’s jti until its exp, so a leaked copy can’t outlive the logout. Best-effort by design (see revoke_session_token): a token with no jti or exp has nothing to denylist, and a store hiccup is logged, never surfaced — the logout’s redirect must not be blocked. It does not revoke the browser session the token may name; that is BrowserSessionEnder’s sign-out.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn end(&self) {
    let (Some(jti), Some(expires_at)) = (self.claims.jti.as_deref(), self.claims.expires_at)
    else {
        return;
    };
    revoke_session_token(self.revocation.as_ref(), jti, expires_at);
}
}

Browser Session Ender

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/browser_session_ender.rs

The browser session ender is sign-out: a browser ending the browser session it holds, from the Sign out button on the server’s own pages. Where logout withdraws one token, sign-out withdraws the whole session, and with it everything minted under it: the session cookie’s token, and every app token and refresh family that carries its sid. From then on the token verifier refuses every token naming it.

It acts on the session named by the claims of the browser’s own cookie, which POST /oauth/sign-out passes in only for a token the token verifier accepted, so a browser can end no session but its own. No bearer and no scope is involved. A failed write leaves the cookie in place, as the handler answers it with a 500.

The test ends sessions named by claims under a chosen sid.

Browser Session Use Recorder

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/browser_session_use_recorder.rs

The Owner’s list of browsers shows when each was last in use, so the Owner can tell a browser they still use from one to revoke. That time is the browser session’s last_seen_at. One of the things that moves it is the server accepting the browser’s session cookie, and the recorder records that, once the host’s cookie-to-bearer layer has accepted a cookie.

A browser sends its cookie on nearly every request from the server’s pages, and writing on each would make every page load a database write. So last_seen_at moves at most once every LAST_SEEN_RESOLUTION per session. Two things hold that: the in-memory LastSeenThrottle, shared by every request, lets one use per session per window through to the store, and the store’s update is itself conditional, so the window holds even when the throttle is empty after a restart.

The tests record uses named by claims under a chosen sid.

record_cookie_use

Record that the cookie holding the browser session session_claims name (their sid) was accepted at now: its last_seen_at moves to now unless it moved within the last LAST_SEEN_RESOLUTION. Claims with no sid name no session and record nothing.

Errors

AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure when the update fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn record_cookie_use(
    &self,
    session_claims: &VerifiedClaims,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError> {
    let Some(sid) = session_claims.sid.as_deref() else {
        return Ok(());
    };
    if !self.throttle.admit(sid, now) {
        return Ok(());
    }
    self.store
        .write(|tx| tx.touch_browser_session_last_seen(sid, now, now - LAST_SEEN_RESOLUTION))
        .inspect_err(|_| self.throttle.forget(sid))?;
    Ok(())
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/session/browser_session_use_recorder.rs lines 44–59 · authorization-server in the code index

A use moves last_seen_at; another inside the window leaves it, and one after the window moves it again.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn a_cookie_use_moves_last_seen_at_most_once_a_window() {
    let signed_in_at = Utc::now() - Duration::hours(1);
    let session =
        BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), signed_in_at);
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    store.tx().insert_browser_session(&session).expect("insert");
    let recorder = BrowserSessionUseRecorder::new(store, Arc::new(LastSeenThrottle::new()));
    let session_claims = claims(Some(&session.sid));

    let first_use = Utc::now();
    recorder
        .record_cookie_use(&session_claims, first_use)
        .expect("recorded");
    assert_eq!(last_seen(&recorder.store, &session.sid), first_use);

    recorder
        .record_cookie_use(&session_claims, first_use + Duration::minutes(4))
        .expect("recorded");
    assert_eq!(last_seen(&recorder.store, &session.sid), first_use);

    let after_the_window = first_use + LAST_SEEN_RESOLUTION;
    recorder
        .record_cookie_use(&session_claims, after_the_window)
        .expect("recorded");
    assert_eq!(last_seen(&recorder.store, &session.sid), after_the_window);
}
}

starter stores the requesting session as a paired session holding all the Owner holds, so it falls short of nothing until a test narrows it with narrow_requesting_session. The stored session is what the starter checks for a shortfall and what the approval bounds the code by; the request’s session_token_grant only decides whether the browser can decide the request on the consent card.

A starter over store, seeded with an active signing key and the standing paired session REQUESTING_SID, holding all the Owner holds, and the approval port it republishes through.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn starter(
    store: FakeGrantStore,
) -> (
    CodeAuthorizationStarter<FakeGrantStore>,
    Arc<RecordingOwnerApproval>,
) {
    seed_active_signing_key(&store);
    store
        .tx()
        .insert_browser_session(&BrowserSession {
            sid: REQUESTING_SID.to_owned(),
            ..BrowserSession::new_paired_session(
                "Firefox on Linux".to_owned(),
                crate::owner_scopes(),
                Duration::hours(24),
                Utc::now(),
            )
        })
        .unwrap();
    let owner_approval = Arc::new(RecordingOwnerApproval::default());
    let code_authorization_starter = CodeAuthorizationStarter::new(
        store,
        owner_approval.clone(),
        SERVER_ORIGIN.into(),
        Arc::new(StaleSessionCutoff::none()),
    );
    (code_authorization_starter, owner_approval)
}
}

        .tx()

            Url::parse(SERVER_ORIGIN).expect("server origin"),
            LauncherBase::parse("https://site.example/launcher/").expect("launcher"),
            AuthorizationAppBase::parse("https://site.example/authorization/")
                .expect("authorization app"),
            Url::parse("https://site.example/launcher/").expect("launcher URL"),
            Url::parse("https://site.example/authorization/").expect("authorization URL"),
        )),
        SERVER_ORIGIN.into(),
    );
    (pairing, owner_approval, signing_key)
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn issue_code(store: &FakeGrantStore, client_id: &str, scopes: &[&str]) -> String {
    let code = generate_authorization_code();
    let now = Utc::now();
    store
        .tx()
        .issue_authorization_code(&AuthorizationCode {
            code: code.clone(),
            request_id: "req".to_owned(),
            client_id: client_id.to_owned(),
            redirect_uri: url::Url::parse("https://example.com/cb").unwrap(),
            code_challenge: compute_code_challenge(VERIFIER),
            granted_scopes: scopes.iter().map(|s| (*s).to_owned()).collect(),
            patient: None,
            issued_at: now,
            expires_at: now + AUTHORIZATION_CODE_TTL,
            sid: FIXTURE_SID.to_owned(),
        })
        .unwrap();
    code

fn is_jti_denylisted(revocation_store: &RevocationStore, access_token: &str) -> bool {
    let payload = access_token.split('.').nth(1).expect("a JWT");
    let claims: serde_json::Value =
        serde_json::from_slice(&base64::url_safe_no_pad_decode(payload).expect("base64url"))
            .unwrap();
    revocation_store
        .is_revoked_by_jti(claims["jti"].as_str().expect("jti"))
        .unwrap()
}
}

HTTP

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/state.rs

The HTTP layer is how the server’s callers reach the capabilities: a browser at the front door, an app’s back end at the token endpoint, the Owner’s pages at /authorization, and the host, which layers this crate’s bearer gate over its own routes. Everything axum-shaped lives under src/http/, and it decides nothing about access on its own. A handler parses the request, acquires one capability through an extractor, calls it, and renders the outcome. The rules live in the capabilities and the domain below them.

Three surfaces

The server answers on three groups of paths, each behind a different gate.

PathsWho calls itWhat stands in front
/.well-known/jwks.json, /oauth/* APIAnyone: a browser starting a request, an app’s back end, devicesNo bearer. The authorization start limit on the two routes that start a request; client authentication where it’s due.
/oauth/* pagesThe person at the browserNo bearer. The wait page, consent card, limited page, device and pairing pages, sign-in and sign-out.
/authorization/*The Owner’s pages, and any app holding wildflower/* scopesThe session gate (a valid, unrevoked bearer), then a scope gate per route, all cache-suppressed.

Three gates stand between a request and a capability, each on the Middleware page. The session gate, require_valid_session, wraps all of /authorization and proves who the caller is. The bearer gate, authorization_server_auth_middleware, is the same check, packaged for the host to put over its FHIR server and other routes. The authorization start limit, limit_authorization_starts, sits on the two routes anyone can call to start a request that may raise the Owner’s approval popup.

Past the session gate, what the caller may do is decided per route, by the extractor the handler takes. A handler never names the router state. Scoped<F> builds a capability only when the caller’s claims cover its scopes; Authenticated<F> builds one from the claims whole, for a caller acting on its own session; and Live<F> builds one from the state alone, for the front door, whose capabilities are gated by the proofs their methods take. A failure comes back as a domain error, and Errors and Wire Shapes renders it.

http

The middleware, the extractors and the routes are private to this module. What the crate exports from it is the router, the state, the bearer gate and its ensure_bearer_header helper, and the browser-session cookie functions the host’s cookie-to-bearer layer calls (see Browser Session Cookie). Every integration test spins the router up over an in-memory store.

router

Build the authorization server’s public HTTP surface. Routes live at /.well-known/jwks.json, /oauth/*, and /authorization/* (authenticated bearer JWT + per-resource scope gates) — the module owns its mount paths so the caller just .merge()s. The host’s tunnel listener serves it to remote visitors, behind these bearer and session gates.

Three pieces join over the shared state:

  • the documented pre-auth routes, JWKS and the /oauth API, with the authorization start limit layered on the two routes that start a request;
  • the /oauth pages, which need the launcher base for where sign-out sends a browser;
  • the /authorization routes, merged from each resource’s router, with the deferred start limit on the ask-owner route, then the session gate, then cache suppression outermost, so the session gate’s own 401s carry no-store too.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn router(state: Arc<AuthorizationServerState>) -> Router {
    let (documented, _spec) = documented_public_router(|routes, start_route| {
        routes.layer(axum_middleware::from_fn_with_state(
            (state.clone(), start_route),
            middleware::limit_authorization_starts,
        ))
    })
    .split_for_parts();
    let (clients, _spec) = routes::clients::openapi_router().split_for_parts();
    let access = Router::new()
        .merge(clients)
        .merge(routes::grants::router())
        .merge(routes::browser_sessions::router())
        .merge(routes::oauth_consents::router(|route| {
            route.layer(axum_middleware::from_fn_with_state(
                state.clone(),
                middleware::defer_authorization_start_limit,
            ))
        }))
        .merge(routes::devices::router())
        .merge(routes::logout::router())
        .merge(routes::revocations::router())
        .merge(routes::session::router())
        .layer(axum_middleware::from_fn_with_state(
            state.clone(),
            middleware::require_valid_session,
        ))
        // Outermost, so the session gate's 401s are cache-suppressed too.
        .layer(axum_middleware::from_fn(middleware::cache_suppress));

    Router::new()
        .merge(documented)
        .nest(
            routes::oauth::OAUTH_MOUNT,
            routes::oauth::page_router(&state.launcher_base),
        )
        .nest("/authorization", access)
        .with_state(state)
}
}

openapi_spec

A change to a wire type fails the snapshot test until the snapshot is regenerated, so the TypeScript client and the server-docs console never read a stale spec.

The authorization server OAuth + discovery + client-management OpenAPI document, collected from the very routes that serve traffic. info is set explicitly so the committed snapshot doesn’t churn with the crate version. It generates the committed snapshot the TS spec-drift test guards and the published server-docs console renders.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn openapi_spec() -> utoipa::openapi::OpenApi {
    use utoipa::Modify as _;

    let (_router, mut spec) = documented_router().split_for_parts();
    spec.info = utoipa::openapi::Info::new("Wildflower Authorization OAuth API", "0.0.0");
    // Every documented `/authorization` operation is scope-gated (the ungated
    // `/authorization/session` isn't documented), so the gated paths are read off the
    // spec rather than listed by hand.
    let gated_paths: Vec<String> = spec
        .paths
        .paths
        .keys()
        .filter(|path| path.starts_with("/authorization/"))
        .cloned()
        .collect();
    wildflowerhealthio_scope_capabilities::InsufficientScopeResponses::for_paths(gated_paths)
        .modify(&mut spec);
    spec
}
}

Browser Session Cookie

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/browser_session_cookie.rs

A browser the server has let in holds its browser session in a cookie, __Host-browser_session. The cookie’s value is the browser’s access token itself, issued to the browser-session client and naming the session as its sid. Nothing about the cookie is stored server-side: what signs the browser out is whatever the token verifier refuses: a revoked jti, a revoked subject, a revoked browser session, or, for the session’s own token, an expired one. The host ends the Owner’s same-device sessions by expiring them once the server’s last launch view closes, and a server start cuts off every same-device session but those of the launch views still open, so the verifier refuses the others as it does an expired one; a paired browser’s session lasts through a restart.

The server sets the cookie when it signs a browser in: the Owner’s at same-device sign-in, an approved browser’s on the pairing page’s poll. From then on two kinds of reader use it:

  • The host’s cookie-to-bearer layer, in front of everything, turns the cookie of a request from the server’s own pages into that request’s bearer, so the gates check it like any other token. It asks this file whether the session still stands, records the use, and clears the cookie once the session has ended.
  • The front door reads it directly: /oauth/authorize sends a browser with no standing session to pairing and issues an app’s code under the session it finds; the wait page’s status poll and the limited page’s calls read it to know whose browser is asking; the start limit reads it to decide whether to defer; sign-out reads it to know which session to end.

A browser can also hold the FHIR web UI’s hfs_session. When both ride a request, the host’s layer presents hfs_session’s bearer, unless the page names the browser session with the SESSION_HEADER.

http::browser_session_cookie

BROWSER_SESSION_COOKIE

The browser session cookie. The __Host- prefix holds a browser to accepting it only Secure, with Path=/ and no Domain, so it is this server’s alone, set over https, and no sibling subdomain can set or shadow it.

standing_browser_session

Does this cookie value still hold a browser session? A token the verifier refuses as rejected or revoked is None, not an error; only a store that can’t be read is an error, so the caller can tell “signed out” from “can’t tell”. The host’s cookie-to-bearer layer calls this with the cookie’s value.

The verified claims of the browser session a browser session cookie holds, or None once the session has ended: the gates would refuse session_token as a bad, expired or revoked token (by its jti, its subject or its browser session) or one whose session has expired, checked by the same TokenVerifier the gates run, or it is no browser session’s token at all. Their sid names the browser session.

Errors

authorization-server-rust/src/http/browser_session_cookie.rs lines 103–108 · authorization-server in the code index

standing_session_claims

The decision itself, over any store, which the test drives directly. Any token but a browser-session client’s under a session holds none, even one the gates would accept: an app’s token copied into the cookie doesn’t make a browser session. The tests mint real tokens and verify them against the fake store.

The verified claims of session_token, or None when it holds no standing browser session: token_verifier refuses it for good (bad, expired or revoked), or it is some other token, not issued to the browser-session client under a browser session (its sid).

Errors

The server-side AccessTokenVerifyErrors, when a store can’t be read.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn standing_session_claims<S: GrantStore>(
    token_verifier: &TokenVerifier<S>,
    session_token: &str,
) -> Result<Option<VerifiedClaims>, AccessTokenVerifyError> {
    match token_verifier.verify(session_token) {
        Ok(claims) if claims.subject == BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID && claims.sid.is_some() => {
            Ok(Some(claims))
        }
        Ok(_) | Err(AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected | AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked) => {
            Ok(None)
        }
        Err(error) => Err(error),
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/browser_session_cookie.rs lines 170–183 · authorization-server in the code index

Only a token issued to the browser-session client under a standing browser session is one: another client’s token the gates would accept, even under that session, and a browser-session client’s token with no session, hold no browser session.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn only_a_browser_session_token_holds_a_browser_session() {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    let key = seed_active_signing_key(&store);
    let session =
        BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), Utc::now());
    store.tx().insert_browser_session(&session).expect("insert");
    let verifier = TokenVerifier::new(
        store,
        Arc::new(NothingRevoked),
        ORIGIN.into(),
        Arc::new(StaleSessionCutoff::none()),
    );

    let browser_session_token = mint(&key, BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID, Some(&session.sid));
    let claims = standing_session_claims(&verifier, &browser_session_token)
        .expect("checked")
        .expect("a browser session");
    assert_eq!(claims.sid.as_deref(), Some(session.sid.as_str()));
    for (token, case) in [
        (mint(&key, "another-client", None), "another client's token"),
        (
            mint(&key, "another-client", Some(&session.sid)),
            "another client's token under the session",
        ),
        (
            mint(&key, BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID, None),
            "a browser-session client token without a sid",
        ),
    ] {
        assert!(
            standing_session_claims(&verifier, &token)
                .expect("checked")
                .is_none(),
            "{case} holds no browser session"
        );
    }
}
}

fn main() {
pub(crate) fn carried_browser_session(

    headers: &HeaderMap,
) -> Result<Option<VerifiedClaims>, AccessTokenVerifyError> {

authorization-server-rust/src/http/browser_session_cookie.rs lines 136–144 · authorization-server in the code index

browser_session_token

It parses every Cookie header, so a browser sending its cookies in one header or several is read the same, and matches the name exactly. The test builds its headers with cookie_headers.

The browser session cookie’s value among headers’ Cookies, if the browser sent it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn browser_session_token(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Option<String> {
    headers
        .get_all(header::COOKIE)
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|cookie_header| cookie_header.to_str().ok())
        .flat_map(Cookie::split_parse)
        .filter_map(Result::ok)
        .find(|cookie| cookie.name() == BROWSER_SESSION_COOKIE)
        .map(|cookie| cookie.value().to_owned())
}
}

fn the_session_token_is_read_from_among_the_browser_s_cookies() {

        (&["hfs_session=s-1"][..], None),

    ] {

authorization-server-rust/src/http/browser_session_cookie.rs lines 342–364 · authorization-server in the code index

can_decide_consents

The Owner’s session can; a browser paired with less can’t. This is a necessary condition, not the whole one: whether a given request goes to the consent card also depends on the session holding that request’s approval scopes, which /oauth/authorize works out per request. The start limit uses it to decide whether a start can wait to be counted (see limit_authorization_starts).

Whether the browser session claims describe can decide consents: its grant covers both loading a request on the consent card (consent_reader_scopes) and deciding it (consent_decider_scopes). A request such a browser starts is sent to the consent card and decided there when the session also holds that request’s approval scopes (as /oauth/authorize works out per request); otherwise it goes to the wait page and is raised for the Owner, and only then does its start spend from the authorization start limit.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn can_decide_consents(claims: &VerifiedClaims) -> bool {
    let granted = claims.granted();
    consent_reader_scopes()
        .iter()
        .chain(&consent_decider_scopes())
        .all(|required| granted.covers(required))
}
}
