A browser session decides consents only when it can both read a request for the consent card and update it to decide it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn deciding_consents_takes_reading_and_updating_requests() {
    let store = FakeGrantStore::default();
    let key = seed_active_signing_key(&store);
    let session =
        BrowserSession::new_same_device_session(vec![], Duration::hours(8), Utc::now());
    store.tx().insert_browser_session(&session).expect("insert");
    let verifier = TokenVerifier::new(
        store,
        Arc::new(NothingRevoked),
        ORIGIN.into(),
        Arc::new(StaleSessionCutoff::none()),
    );

    for (scopes, expected) in [
        (
            &[
                "wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.r",
                "wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.u",
            ][..],
            true,
        ),
        (&["wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.ru"][..], true),
        (&["wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.r"][..], false),
        (&["wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.u"][..], false),
    ] {
        let token = mint_scoped(&key, BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID, Some(&session.sid), scopes);
        let claims = standing_session_claims(&verifier, &token)
            .expect("checked")
            .expect("a browser session");
        assert_eq!(can_decide_consents(&claims), expected, "{scopes:?}");
    }
}
}

Errors and Wire Shapes

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/errors.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/wire_representations.rs

These two files are how the server’s answers look on the wire. They render; they decide nothing. The vocabulary of failure is the domain’s AuthorizationServerError, and a handler that gets one back from a capability returns it with ?; this page is where it becomes a status and a body. The same goes for success: the JSON shapes that more than one route sends or reads have one home here, so two surfaces can’t drift apart.

Two rules run through the page. A server-side failure is an opaque 500: the detail goes to the operator’s log, never to the caller. A refused credential is a bare 401 that names, for the host’s request log only, why it was refused.

http::errors

verify_error_response

Both bearer gates answer through it (see verify_request_claims). The tests read the refusal on a response with stamped_refusal.

Map a token-AccessTokenVerifyError to its HTTP response, shared by the auth middlewares. Server-side failures (no keys configured, the key, revocation or browser-session store can’t be read, a configured key’s material is corrupt) are operator problems, so they log and return 500; only a genuinely rejected or revoked token is a 401, stamped with the matching RequestRefusal. Written as an exhaustive match so a new AccessTokenVerifyError variant forces a deliberate status choice rather than silently defaulting to 401.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn verify_error_response(context: &str, err: AccessTokenVerifyError) -> Response {
    match err {
        AccessTokenVerifyError::NoSigningKeysConfigured
        | AccessTokenVerifyError::KeyStoreUnavailable(_)
        | AccessTokenVerifyError::RevocationStoreUnavailable(_)
        | AccessTokenVerifyError::BrowserSessionStoreUnavailable(_)
        | AccessTokenVerifyError::SigningKeyUnreadable(_) => internal_error(context, err),
        AccessTokenVerifyError::TokenRejected => unauthorized(RequestRefusal::TokenRejected),
        AccessTokenVerifyError::Revoked => unauthorized(RequestRefusal::Revoked),
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/errors.rs lines 57–60 · authorization-server in the code index

AuthorizationServerError

Every /authorization route renders the domain’s failures the same way. Each body carries error, the variant’s name, and one key, the identifier the caller sent. Each “not found” is a 404. Each refusal of an otherwise valid request is a 409 of the same shape. A missing scope, the caller’s or, on an approval, the approver’s, is the shared 403 listing the scopes lacking, from scope-capabilities-rust. An infrastructure failure is the logged, empty 500.

into_response

Render the domain’s failure vocabulary onto the wire, the same way from every /authorization route. Every JSON body carries error, the variant’s name, and one key, the identifier the caller sent:

  • each *NotFound variant is a 404 naming what wasn’t found: id for an OAuth consent, an authorization request or a grant, userCode for a device consent, sid for a browser session, clientId for a client;
  • a refusal of an otherwise valid request is a 409 of the same shape: EssentialClient (clientId), a request to disable a client the Owner needs to get in; RegistrationNotAcknowledged (id), an approval outside the app’s registration without the Owner’s acknowledgement; and LaunchPatientMismatch (id), an approval naming a patient other than the one the app’s launch binds;
  • a missing scope, the caller’s (InsufficientScope) or on an approval the approver’s (InsufficientApproverScope), is the shared 403 listing the scopes lacking;
  • an Infrastructure failure is logged (via the shared InternalError) and answered as an opaque, empty 500.

This is the whole of the HTTP layer’s error knowledge for the /authorization surface; the handlers just ? a Result<_, AuthorizationServerError> from a domain action.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn into_response(self) -> Response {
    match self {
        AuthorizationServerError::OAuthConsentNotFound { id } => (
            StatusCode::NOT_FOUND,
            Json(OAuthConsentNotFoundBody {
                error: "OAuthConsentNotFound",
                id,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::DeviceConsentNotFound { user_code } => (
            StatusCode::NOT_FOUND,
            Json(DeviceConsentNotFoundBody {
                error: "DeviceConsentNotFound",
                user_code,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::GrantNotFound { id } => (
            StatusCode::NOT_FOUND,
            Json(GrantNotFoundBody {
                error: "GrantNotFound",
                id,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::BrowserSessionNotFound { sid } => (
            StatusCode::NOT_FOUND,
            Json(BrowserSessionNotFoundBody {
                error: "BrowserSessionNotFound",
                sid,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::ClientNotFound { client_id } => (
            StatusCode::NOT_FOUND,
            Json(ClientNotFoundBody {
                error: "ClientNotFound",
                client_id,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::EssentialClient { client_id } => (
            StatusCode::CONFLICT,
            Json(EssentialClientBody {
                error: "EssentialClient",
                client_id,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound { id } => (
            StatusCode::NOT_FOUND,
            Json(AuthorizationRequestNotFoundBody {
                error: "AuthorizationRequestNotFound",
                id,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::RegistrationNotAcknowledged { id } => (
            StatusCode::CONFLICT,
            Json(RegistrationNotAcknowledgedBody {
                error: "RegistrationNotAcknowledged",
                id,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::LaunchPatientMismatch { id } => (
            StatusCode::CONFLICT,
            Json(LaunchPatientMismatchBody {
                error: "LaunchPatientMismatch",
                id,
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        AuthorizationServerError::InsufficientScope { missing_scopes } => {
            insufficient_scope(missing_scopes)
        }
        AuthorizationServerError::InsufficientApproverScope {
            approver_missing_scopes,
        } => insufficient_scope(approver_missing_scopes),
        AuthorizationServerError::Infrastructure { context, source } => {
            InternalError::new(context, source).into_response()
        }
    }
}
}

Error pages

Two front-door routes answer the person at the browser with a page rather than JSON or a redirect: /oauth/authorize, when it may not send the browser back to the app, and /oauth/sign-in, when it refuses to sign a browser in.

oauth_error_html

OAuth lets the server redirect an error to the app only once the redirect is trusted. A refusal made before that, a malformed or unregistered redirect_uri for one, leaves nothing safe to redirect to, so the browser gets a 400 with this page. Its sentence is the AuthorizeRefusal’s own description, the same sentence a trusted redirect carries as its error_description.

The local page /oauth/authorize renders for a refusal it may not redirect.

http::wire_representations

CacheSuppressed

OAuth requires it of every token response, success or error, and the server applies it more widely. Making it a wrapper makes it part of the value rather than a step a handler can forget; cache_suppress applies it as one layer to all of /authorization.

Wrapper that stamps the RFC 6749 §5.1/§5.2 cache-suppression headers (Cache-Control: no-store, Pragma: no-cache) onto the wrapped response. Token- and device-authorization-endpoint responses — success or error — must never be cached; wrapping makes that part of the value instead of a step a call site can forget. The same wrapper renders the authorize-status poll (its Approved redirect carries a redeemable code), the start limit’s 429, sign-out and, applied as a blanket layer, every Owner /authorization/* response. The headers are inserted, not appended, so nothing ends up with either twice.

ConsentResult

The consent card is the requesting browser itself, so it follows the redirect directly rather than polling.

Result the approving surface sees after approving or denying a consent prompt: {"status":"approved"} or {"status":"denied"}, with a redirect for a code-flow decision.

A code-flow decision carries the client callback URL (code + state, or error=access_denied + state, appended to the client’s redirect_uri) so the approving surface can complete the flow directly when it is the requesting browser (the consent card) — no separate poll of /oauth/authorize/{id} needed. Device-flow decisions have no client redirect_uri, so redirect is None and (thanks to skip_serializing_if) omitted from the wire entirely.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) enum ConsentResult {
    /// The request was approved: a code-flow request's code is issued, a
    /// device's grant stands, a pairing's browser may now sign in.
    Approved {
        /// The app's callback carrying the code and the app's `state`, for
        /// the consent card to leave for; absent for a device-page decision,
        /// whose device or browser polls for its result.
        redirect: Option<String>,
    },
    /// The request was denied: declined, or an approval that granted
    /// nothing. A code-flow approval is a deny too when the requesting
    /// browser's session has ended or the app was disabled since.
    Denied {
        /// The app's callback carrying `error=access_denied` and the app's
        /// `state`; absent for a device-page decision.
        redirect: Option<String>,
    },
}
}

Extractors

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/extractors/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/extractors/live.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/extractors/launcher_pages.rs

A handler reaches the server’s data only through an extractor that hands it a capability. It never takes the router state itself, so it can’t open the store, mint a token or read a field of the state behind a gate’s back; the source guard handlers_reach_the_state_only_through_capabilities fails the build if one tries.

There are three capability extractors:

  • Scoped<F> builds F from the state and the claims the session gate stored, and only when those claims cover F’s required scopes. A token short of one is a 403 listing the scopes it lacks, and the handler never runs.
  • Authenticated<F> builds F from the state and the claims whole, with no gate beyond the session gate: for a caller acting on its own session, logging out or reading its own scopes.
  • Live<F> builds F from the state alone, with no gate at extraction.

Scoped and Authenticated come from the shared scope-capabilities-rust crate. Both fail closed with a 500 when they find no claims, since that means a route was mounted without its gate. Live lives here, beside LauncherPages, which hands a handler the one piece of configuration it may need.

Live

The door to the capabilities no principal unlocks. The front door’s capabilities, starting an authorization, exchanging a code, pairing a browser, verifying a token, serve callers who hold no bearer yet. Their gate is not a scope: it is the proof their methods demand (an authenticated client, a redeemable code), checked when the method is called. F is built through its FromState, on the Live Bindings page.

Middleware

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/middleware/mod.rs

The middleware are the gates a request passes before a handler sees it. Each enforces one rule:

  • Only a live token of this server’s gets past a bearer gate. Two gates check it, the session gate on /authorization and the bearer gate the host layers over its own routes, and both run one pipeline, so they can’t disagree about a token.
  • Starting requests that may reach the Owner is rate-limited. Anyone who knows the server’s domain can start an authorization request, and each one raised for the Owner pops up on the Owner’s device. The start limit asks the host whether to admit each one.
  • Nothing on /authorization is cached. Every response there is privileged.

Middleware verify tokens only through the token verifier, never against a store; the source guard middleware_verifies_only_through_the_token_verifier holds that. The Request Caller, Authorization Start Limit and Cache Suppression integration tests hold these gates end to end.

http::middleware::require_auth

try_bearer_token_from_headers

Extract the access token from the request’s Authorization: Bearer header — the only credential the server accepts. The scheme match is case-insensitive; None when the header is absent, not UTF-8, or another scheme. The returned slice borrows the header, so a request pays no per-request JWT copy on the way to verification.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn try_bearer_token_from_headers(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Option<&str> {
    let value = headers.get(header::AUTHORIZATION)?.to_str().ok()?;
    let prefix = "bearer ";
    // Case-insensitive prefix check against just the scheme bytes — avoids
    // lowercasing (and reallocating) the whole header, which carries the
    // full JWT. The returned slice borrows the header, so no copy is made.
    if !value
        .get(..prefix.len())
        .is_some_and(|p| p.eq_ignore_ascii_case(prefix))
    {
        return None;
    }
    Some(value[prefix.len()..].trim())
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/middleware/require_auth.rs lines 102–115 · authorization-server in the code index

verify_request_claims

The one pipeline both bearer gates run. The verifier holds this server’s origin as the only iss and aud it accepts, and a failure renders through verify_error_response.

The shared authN pipeline both claims-inserting gates run: extract the Authorization: Bearer access token, verify it through the TokenVerifier (signature, iss/aud against the server’s origin, revocation), and map each failure to its response — a missing token is a 401 stamped RequestRefusal::MissingToken, a verify failure whatever errors::verify_error_response maps it to (a rejected or revoked token’s 401 stamped with that refusal). Extracted so require_valid_session and authorization_server_auth_middleware cannot drift in how a token becomes claims; they differ only in the extension type they insert (and the bearer gate’s exempt paths).

The error is the prepared failure Response, boxed so the happy-path Ok stays small (the Response is large — clippy::result_large_err).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn verify_request_claims(
    state: &Arc<AuthorizationServerState>,
    headers: &HeaderMap,
    log_context: &'static str,
) -> Result<VerifiedClaims, Box<Response>> {
    let Some(token) = try_bearer_token_from_headers(headers) else {
        return Err(Box::new(errors::unauthorized(RequestRefusal::MissingToken)));
    };
    // The token must name the server's origin. See
    // `docs/Origins/Explanation.md`.
    LiveTokenVerifier::from_state(state)
        .verify(token)
        .map_err(|e| Box::new(errors::verify_error_response(log_context, e)))
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/middleware/require_auth.rs lines 82–95 · authorization-server in the code index

require_valid_session

The session gate on /authorization. It stores the VerifiedClaims in the request, so a token is verified once per request, here, and the Scoped<…> and Authenticated<…> extractors read them.

The /authorization authN gate: verify the request carries a valid, non-revoked bearer token and stash the resulting VerifiedClaims in the request’s extensions for the scope-gated capability extractors (domain::capabilities) to read — a missing/invalid token is a 401.

This layer only proves who the caller is (authN); what they may do (authZ) is decided per-route by the Scoped<…> extractor, which reads these claims and checks the covering scope, returning a 403 with the missing scopes on failure. An Owner token (covering WILDFLOWER_WIDEST_SCOPES) still covers every per-resource scope, so it passes every gate.

This is one of the pair of claims-inserting authN gates (see docs/Authorization/Scope-Gated Endpoints How-To.md, “Wiring the claims”): this one guards the authorization server’s own /authorization router and inserts the domain VerifiedClaims; its sibling authorization_server_auth_middleware wraps the host’s downstream slice routers and inserts the framework-neutral ScopeClaims. Both run the same verify_request_claims pipeline.

Both also stamp the verified OAuth client on the response as a RequestCaller extension, so the host can say which app is using the server over the tunnel. The 401s verify_request_claims answers instead carry a RequestRefusal saying why.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub async fn require_valid_session(
    State(state): State<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    mut req: Request<Body>,
    next: Next,
) -> Response {
    let claims = match verify_request_claims(&state, &headers, "require_valid_session failed") {
        Ok(claims) => claims,
        Err(response) => return *response,
    };
    let caller = RequestCaller {
        client_id: claims.subject.clone(),
    };
    // Hand the verified claims (incl. the `scope` claim) to the handler layer.
    // The scope-gated extractors read them from here rather than re-verifying —
    // authN runs exactly once, at this layer.
    req.extensions_mut().insert(claims);
    let mut response = next.run(req).await;
    // Name the verified caller on the response, for the host's forwarded-request
    // observer (see `wildflowerhealthio_shared_structures::request_caller`).
    response.extensions_mut().insert(caller);
    response
}
}

http::middleware::require_valid_bearer_token

authorization_server_auth_middleware

The bearer gate the host puts in front of its own routes: the FHIR server, where the paths a client may read without a token are exempt, and the imaging viewer, where none are. A verified request carries the token’s scopes on as ScopeClaims, the framework-neutral form the host’s own Scoped<…> capabilities read.

The downstream-slice authN middleware — 401 for a missing/invalid bearer token, except exempt_paths which pass through (pass &[] to gate every path). Inserts ScopeClaims for downstream Scoped<…> capabilities, and stamps the response with the verified RequestCaller (an exempt path’s response carries none; a 401 carries the RequestRefusal verify_request_claims stamped instead). Clone — build once, clone per router. See docs/Authorization/Scope-Gated Endpoints How-To.md.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn authorization_server_auth_middleware(
    state: Arc<AuthorizationServerState>,
    exempt_paths: &[&str],
) -> AuthorizationServerAuthMiddleware {
    let gate = BearerGate {
        state,
        exempt: exempt_paths
            .iter()
            .map(|p| p.trim_end_matches('/').to_string())
            .collect(),
    };
    let handler: BearerGateFn = |State(gate), headers, mut req, next| {
        Box::pin(async move {
            if is_exempt(req.uri().path(), &gate.exempt) {
                return next.run(req).await;
            }
            let claims = match verify_request_claims(
                &gate.state,
                &headers,
                "access-token verification failed",
            ) {
                Ok(verified) => verified,
                Err(response) => return *response,
            };
            req.extensions_mut()
                .insert(wildflowerhealthio_scope_capabilities::ScopeClaims::new(
                    claims.scope.clone(),
                ));
            let mut response = next.run(req).await;
            // Name the verified caller on the response, as `require_valid_session`
            // does, for the host's forwarded-request observer.
            response.extensions_mut().insert(RequestCaller {
                client_id: claims.subject,
            });
            response
        })
    };
    axum::middleware::from_fn_with_state(gate, handler)
}
}

http::middleware::authorization_start_limit

The limit sits on the two routes that start a request, GET /oauth/authorize and POST /oauth/device_authorization, on every method axum serves them on, and on no other route. The authorization server doesn’t decide who is over the limit: it knows only the request. The host, which knows the connection a request arrived on, does, through the AuthorizationStartGate port, with an allowance per visitor and one overall.

What spends from the limit is a request raised for the Owner, and only that. Most starts ask the gate at once, before the request is even parsed, so every attempt counts, however malformed. Two kinds of start can’t yet know whether they will reach the Owner, so the layer defers the question and the route asks once it knows:

  • A browser whose session can decide consents, the Owner’s own browser typically. A request it decides on its own consent card raises nothing for the Owner. One it can’t decide, and every device request, does, and asks then.
  • An /oauth/authorize request carrying no browser session. The endpoint sends that browser to pairing and parks nothing, so it costs the Owner no popup, and a flood of them can’t spend the allowance a paired browser’s requests need.

A session the store can’t vouch for, because a store can’t be read, doesn’t defer; it asks the gate like any other start. A request parked on the browser’s limited page has spent by the time it is parked, so going on from that page asks nothing more. Asking the Owner about a request from the consent card raises it without starting one, so it spends from the same limit, when it actually raises one.

fn main() {
pub(crate) async fn defer_authorization_start_limit(
    State(state): State<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>>,
    mut request: Request,
    next: Next,
) -> Response {
    let deferred_start_limit = DeferredStartLimit {
        gate: state.authorization_start_gate.clone(),
        request_extensions: request.extensions().clone(),
    };
    request.extensions_mut().insert(deferred_start_limit);
    next.run(request).await
}
}

limit_authorization_starts

It reads the request’s browser session through carried_browser_session.

Pass request on with a DeferredStartLimit for the route to ask when it carries a live browser session that can decide consents, or when it is a start_route of AuthorizationStartRoute::Authorize that carries no live browser session; pass it on when the state’s AuthorizationStartGate admits it; answer it 429 Too Many Requests, uncached, otherwise.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) async fn limit_authorization_starts(
    State((state, start_route)): State<(Arc<AuthorizationServerState>, AuthorizationStartRoute)>,
    mut request: Request,
    next: Next,
) -> Response {
    let token_verifier = LiveTokenVerifier::from_state(&state);
    let defers = match carried_browser_session(&token_verifier, request.headers()) {
        Ok(Some(claims)) => can_decide_consents(&claims),
        Ok(None) => matches!(start_route, AuthorizationStartRoute::Authorize),
        Err(_) => false,
    };
    if defers {
        let deferred_start_limit = DeferredStartLimit {
            gate: state.authorization_start_gate.clone(),
            request_extensions: request.extensions().clone(),
        };
        request.extensions_mut().insert(deferred_start_limit);
        return next.run(request).await;
    }
    if state.authorization_start_gate.admit(request.extensions()) {
        return next.run(request).await;
    }
    start_limited_response()
}
}

cache_suppress

Every /authorization response is no-store. Each one carries something privileged: a pending consent, a device prompt, the standing grants, the caller’s session, the outcome of an approval. The layer is outermost on the /authorization router, so a new route, a 404 and the session gate’s own 401 all carry it.

Wrap every response flowing through this layer in CacheSuppressed, stamping Cache-Control: no-store + Pragma: no-cache. The headers are inserted (not appended), so a handler that had already set either can’t end up with a duplicate.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub async fn cache_suppress(req: Request<Body>, next: Next) -> Response {
    CacheSuppressed(next.run(req).await).into_response()
}

Routes

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/mod.rs

The routes are where a caller meets the server. Each handler is thin: it reads the request, takes the capability its extractor grants (Live for an operation anyone may ask for, Scoped or Authenticated for one that wants a bearer), calls one operation, and renders the outcome. The rules live below it, in the capabilities and the domain; what a route adds is who may call it and what each outcome looks like on the wire.

The folder tree mirrors the URL tree. A path with one route is a file named for its operation (well_known_jwks, logout, revocations, session). A segment with several routes is a folder whose mod.rs is its route table (oauth, oauth_consents, devices, grants, clients, browser_sessions), with one file per handler.

The HTTP layer’s router mounts the routes in two groups, and the group decides the gate:

  • /.well-known/jwks.json and /oauth/* are reached before anyone holds a token. They answer what the request itself proves: a browser session cookie, a client’s credentials, a code.
  • /authorization/* is the Owner’s surface. Every route sits behind the session gate and cache suppression. Most then demand a scope through their Scoped<…> capability; the session read and logout are self-service, Authenticated<…>. The Owner’s UI calls them on its bearer, and the server’s own consent card and device page on the browser session’s, which the host’s cookie-to-bearer layer presents for them.

Pages

  • Authorize: the front door of the code flow.
  • Authorization Pages: the wait page, the React pages, the status poll and the limited page’s calls.
  • Token Endpoint: client authentication, the token exchange and token revocation.
  • Device Authorization: a device asking for its codes.
  • Pairing and Sign-In: how a browser gets a browser session, and gives it up.
  • Consent Routes: reading and deciding a code request or a device request.
  • Owner Resource Routes: the Owner’s grants, apps and browsers.
  • Session Routes: the caller’s own session, logout, token revocation and the public keys.

OAuth Router

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/openapi.rs

Everything under /oauth is reached before anyone holds a bearer token. An app’s browser arrives at the front door, an app’s back end trades a code for tokens, a device asks for a code to show its user, a browser asks to be paired. None of them is the Owner, so none of these routes sits behind the /authorization session gate. Each answers its caller from what the request itself proves: a browser session cookie, a client’s credentials, a code.

The oauth folder holds two route tables, mounted side by side under the same prefix. The API table is documented; the page table isn’t. An app or a device talks to the API routes, and the OpenAPI spec is collected from them. A browser shows the pages, which are no API surface, so they stay out of the spec. The HTTP layer’s router mounts both.

openapi_router

Two routes start an authorization request, and only those two are limited by limit_authorization_starts, each named by its AuthorizationStartRoute.

The /oauth/* routes as an OpenApiRouter, so the OpenAPI spec is collected from the same handlers that serve traffic. Mounted under /oauth by crate::http; routes! reads each handler’s #[utoipa::path] for its method + path. The routes:

  • GET /oauth/authorize: the front door of the authorization-code flow;
  • GET /oauth/authorize/{id}: the wait page’s status poll;
  • GET /oauth/authorize/{id}/session-shortfall, POST /oauth/authorize/{id}/continue and POST /oauth/authorize/{id}/cancel: the limited page’s calls;
  • POST /oauth/token and POST /oauth/revoke: the token endpoint and revocation;
  • POST /oauth/device_authorization: a device asking for its codes;
  • POST /oauth/pair/start and POST /oauth/pair/poll: the pairing page’s calls.

limit_authorization_starts wraps the two routes that start an authorization request, /authorize and /device_authorization, each named by its AuthorizationStartRoute, in the limit on how fast they are started (see limit_authorization_starts), so it covers every method axum serves them on, HEAD /oauth/authorize included; the spec, which serves nothing, leaves them as they are. Only those two are limited: anyone who knows the server’s domain can start a request, and one raised for the Owner pops up on the Owner’s device.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn openapi_router(
    limit_authorization_starts: impl Fn(
        UtoipaMethodRouter<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>>,
        AuthorizationStartRoute,
    ) -> UtoipaMethodRouter<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>>,
) -> OpenApiRouter<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>> {
    OpenApiRouter::new()
        .routes(limit_authorization_starts(
            routes!(authorize::handle_authorize_request),
            AuthorizationStartRoute::Authorize,
        ))
        .routes(routes!(
            authorization_status::handle_authorization_status_request
        ))
        .routes(routes!(session_shortfall::handle_session_shortfall_read))
        .routes(routes!(
            session_shortfall::handle_session_shortfall_continue
        ))
        .routes(routes!(session_shortfall::handle_session_shortfall_cancel))
        .routes(routes!(token_exchange::handle_token_request))
        .routes(routes!(token_revocation::handle_token_revocation_request))
        .routes(limit_authorization_starts(
            routes!(device_authorization::handle_device_authorization_request),
            AuthorizationStartRoute::DeviceAuthorization,
        ))
        .routes(routes!(browser_pairing::handle_browser_pairing_start))
        .routes(routes!(browser_pairing::handle_browser_pairing_poll))
}
}

The token-style handlers parse a body without client credentials: the TokenRequest extractor reads client_id and client_secret from the same form body, or from Authorization: Basic, on its own. What arrives on the wire still carries them, so the spec models each body with the credentials put back. These types are never built; they exist for #[utoipa::path] to name.

TokenRequestBody

POST /oauth/token request body — the grant_type-tagged union of the three grants the endpoint dispatches (mirrors super::token_exchange::TokenPayload plus the body credentials). Form-urlencoded (RFC 6749 §3.2). client_id/client_secret are optional: a confidential client may instead authenticate via Authorization: Basic (RFC 6749 §2.3.1) and omit them from the body — resolve_client_credentials accepts either source.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) enum TokenRequestBody {
    /// Redeem an authorization code with its PKCE verifier (RFC 6749 §4.1.3).
    AuthorizationCode {
        /// The client's id, for `client_secret_post` or a public client;
        /// omitted when it authenticates by `Authorization: Basic`.
        client_id: Option<String>,
        /// A confidential client's secret, for `client_secret_post`; never
        /// beside a Basic header.
        client_secret: Option<String>,
        /// The code `/oauth/authorize` sent to the client's redirect.
        code: String,
        /// The PKCE verifier whose S256 hash is the request's
        /// `code_challenge` (RFC 7636 §4.5).
        code_verifier: String,
        /// The same `redirect_uri` the authorization request named.
        redirect_uri: String,
    },
    /// Poll with a device code until the Owner decides (RFC 8628 §3.4).
    DeviceCode {
        /// The client's id, for `client_secret_post` or a public client;
        /// omitted when it authenticates by `Authorization: Basic`.
        client_id: Option<String>,
        /// A confidential client's secret, for `client_secret_post`; never
        /// beside a Basic header.
        client_secret: Option<String>,
        /// The `device_code` `/oauth/device_authorization` answered with.
        device_code: String,
    },
    /// Trade a live refresh token for a fresh access token and the refresh
    /// token's successor (RFC 6749 §6).
    RefreshToken {
        /// The client's id, for `client_secret_post` or a public client;
        /// omitted when it authenticates by `Authorization: Basic`.
        client_id: Option<String>,
        /// A confidential client's secret, for `client_secret_post`; never
        /// beside a Basic header.
        client_secret: Option<String>,
        /// The refresh token being rotated; it is spent by the trade.
        refresh_token: String,
    },
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/openapi.rs lines 129–134 · authorization-server in the code index

Authorize

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/authorize.rs

GET /oauth/authorize is the front door of the authorization-code flow. Nothing in the server calls it. An app finds it in the FHIR server’s .well-known/smart-configuration and sends the person’s browser here, with PKCE and a state. Everything the endpoint answers is for that browser: a redirect onward, or a page saying why it can’t.

No browser session, no authorization. A browser that carries no live browser session is sent to the pairing page first, and nothing is parked, consumed or raised. A browser with one has its request handed to the code authorization starter, which validates it, parks it as a code request made in that session, and says where the browser goes next:

  • back to the app with a code, when a standing grant skips the Owner: the request changes nothing in the app’s registration, the grant covers every requested scope, and the session holds what the request needs or has gone on past the limited page for this app before;
  • to the limited page, when the session holds less than the request asks for and hasn’t gone on for this app;
  • to the consent card, when the browser decides the request itself;
  • to the wait page otherwise, with the request raised for the Owner.

A request that fails once its redirect is trusted goes back to the app with error and state. One that fails while its redirect isn’t trusted gets a local 400 page, since redirecting there would be an open redirect. The Grant Flows, OAuth Endpoints, Session Required and Consent Card integration tests hold the endpoint to each of these answers.

http::routes::oauth::authorize

AuthorizeParams

A query missing any of the seven required parameters fails to deserialize, and axum answers its own 400 before the handler runs. The starter checks the values. A launch names a launch context.

Query parameters accepted at /oauth/authorize per RFC 6749 §4.1.1 + RFC 7636 (PKCE). Stricter than the base spec: state is required (the spec merely recommends it), and PKCE with S256 is mandatory — both matching the OAuth 2.1 direction. The optional SMART App Launch extensions (launch, aud) are documented on their fields below.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct AuthorizeParams {
    /// The response the client wants; only `code` is supported, anything else
    /// is `unsupported_response_type`.
    pub response_type: String,
    /// The PKCE transform (RFC 7636 §4.3); only `S256` is accepted.
    pub code_challenge_method: String,
    /// The client asking. An unknown one is trusted on first use and carried
    /// to the Owner's prompt as a registration warning; a disabled one is
    /// refused on a local page.
    pub client_id: String,
    /// The scopes asked for, space-separated (RFC 6749 §3.3). Scopes outside a
    /// trusted-on-first-use client's registration are carried to the Owner's
    /// prompt; outside a server-defined registration they are refused.
    pub scope: String,
    /// The PKCE challenge, `BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))`, which the code
    /// remembers so `POST /oauth/token` can check the verifier (RFC 7636 §4.2).
    pub code_challenge: String,
    /// Where the browser goes back to with the code or the error. It must be
    /// an http(s) URL; until it is trusted (registered for this client), a
    /// failure renders the local page rather than redirecting there.
    pub redirect_uri: String,
    /// The client's opaque value, carried back unchanged on every redirect to
    /// it. Required here, though RFC 6749 only recommends it.
    pub state: String,
    /// SMART App Launch `launch` value, handed to the app in its launch URL
    /// and forwarded here. It must name a launch this server minted for this
    /// `client_id` that is unused and unexpired (five minutes); it is consumed,
    /// so it works once, and the request carries the launch's context
    /// (including any patient it binds) to the consent. Any other value is
    /// `invalid_request`, its `error_description` saying why. A browser
    /// without a session is sent to pairing before the launch is
    /// read, so pairing never spends it. Absent, the request is plain OAuth.
    pub launch: Option<String>,
    /// SMART App Launch audience: the FHIR server the app expects to call with
    /// the token. When present it must be this server's origin
    /// (`https://<domain>`), which is also its FHIR base, else
    /// `invalid_request`. The minted token's `aud` is the server's origin.
    pub aud: Option<String>,
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/authorize.rs lines 146–186 · authorization-server in the code index

handle_authorize_request

It reads the browser session through carried_browser_session before anything else, and passes the starter whether the session can decide consents. may_raise_for_owner asks the deferred start limit, when the layer deferred one; with nothing deferred, the layer has already asked.

The authorization endpoint (RFC 6749 §3.1), the public front door of the OAuth flow. It issues nothing to a browser without a browser session: such a browser is sent to the pairing page first. For a browser with one it validates the request, then either auto-issues an authorization code (when an existing grant pre-approves every requested scope) or parks the user-agent on the consent card or the wait page while the Owner decides.

Nothing in-process calls this route. Registered clients (e.g. SMART-on-FHIR apps) discover it via the FHIR server’s .well-known/smart-configuration (authorization_endpoint) and send the user’s browser here with PKCE params to start an authorization-code flow:

  1. Browser lands here. The browser session cookie is read before anything else: a browser without a live browser session is 302’d to the pairing page, /oauth/pair?next=<this request's path and query>, and nothing is parked, notified or consumed. Once the Owner approves the pairing, the page sends the browser back here with its new session. A browser with a session has its request parked as an AuthorizationRequest (5-minute TTL), made in that session (sid). A SMART App Launch’s aud and launch are checked first (see their fields), and the launch is consumed onto the request.
  2. A request asking for more than the browser’s session holds (scopes a code issued in that session would not carry in full) waits on the limited page at /oauth/authorize/{id}/limited, which says what the session lacks and offers Continue or Cancel: POST /oauth/authorize/{id}/continue goes on as below, POST /oauth/authorize/{id}/cancel answers the client access_denied. Until then the Owner isn’t asked about it. Once a browser session has pressed Continue for a client, its later requests for that client skip the page, whatever the session then lacks. What the session holds is read from its browser_sessions row.
  3. Unless every requested scope is pre-approved by an existing grant for this (client, redirect_uri) pair, the request joins the pending-consent queue and the browser is 302’d to a page this authorization server serves beside the endpoint, on the origin the browser used. A browser whose session can decide consents and holds the request’s approval scopes goes to the consent card at /oauth/authorize/{id}/consent, where it decides in place; the request records that it can be decided there (decidable_in_requesting_browser). Any other goes to the wait page at /oauth/authorize/{id}/wait, and the Owner is notified (the host webview’s popup). The wait page polls GET /oauth/authorize/{id} (a custom extension, not part of any RFC), which answers the browser session the request was made in and a session that can decide it on the consent card, until the Owner decides — in the popup, in a signed-in launcher, or on the consent card once that browser can decide it. Either way the code is issued under the session the request was made in, not the approver’s. RFC 6749 leaves the owner-interaction mechanism unspecified, so both pages are spec-legal; likewise §4.1 explicitly allows skipping consent on a previously established authorization decision, which is what the grant fast path implements.
  4. Approval 302s the browser back to the client’s redirect_uri with code + state (§4.1.2); the client then redeems the short-lived code at POST /oauth/token (§4.1.3) with its PKCE verifier.

Clients without a server-defined registration are trusted on first use: an unknown client_id, an unregistered redirect_uri, and scopes outside the registration are all carried to the Owner’s prompt as a registration warning rather than rejected here, and nothing is written to the clients table until the Owner approves. Such a request never takes the grant fast path, and while its redirect is untrusted every other failure renders the local HTML page instead of redirecting. A server-defined registration (the host app’s, the FHIR server UI’s) keeps the strict treatment, and a disabled client is rejected either way. Once the redirect is trusted, a failure goes back to the client’s redirect_uri with error, error_description and state (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1) instead.

The start limit is asked only when it must be: its layer defers a request from a browser that can decide consents, and one carrying no session, and the starter asks the deferred limit only before it raises the request for the Owner or parks it for the limited page.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_authorize_request(
    code_authorization_starter: Live<LiveCodeAuthorizationStarter>,
    token_verifier: Live<LiveTokenVerifier>,
    deferred_start_limit: Option<Extension<DeferredStartLimit>>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    OriginalUri(authorize_uri): OriginalUri,
    Query(params): Query<AuthorizeParams>,
) -> Result<Response, AuthorizeError> {
    // The start limit's layer deferred it for a browser that can decide
    // consents, and for one without a session (sent to pairing below, so it
    // never asks): asked only if the request is raised for the Owner.
    let may_raise_for_owner = || {
        deferred_start_limit
            .as_ref()
            .is_none_or(|Extension(deferred_start_limit)| deferred_start_limit.admits())
    };
    let browser_session = carried_browser_session(&token_verifier, &headers).map_err(|error| {
        AuthorizeError::Internal(InternalError::new(
            "verify a browser session at /oauth/authorize",
            error,
        ))
    })?;
    // No browser session, no authorization: pair this browser first, then
    // come back to this very request. Nothing is parked, notified or consumed.
    let Some((browser_session, browser_sid)) = browser_session
        .as_ref()
        .and_then(|claims| Some((claims, claims.sid.as_deref()?)))
    else {
        return Ok(found_redirect(&pairing_page_location(
            authorize_uri
                .path_and_query()
                .map_or(authorize_uri.path(), |path_and_query| {
                    path_and_query.as_str()
                }),
        )));
    };
    let session_token_grant = browser_session.granted();
    let next_step = code_authorization_starter.start(
        &AuthorizeRequest {
            response_type: &params.response_type,
            code_challenge_method: &params.code_challenge_method,
            client_id: &params.client_id,
            scope: &params.scope,
            code_challenge: &params.code_challenge,
            redirect_uri: &params.redirect_uri,
            client_state: &params.state,
            launch: params.launch.as_deref(),
            aud: params.aud.as_deref(),
            session_token_grant: &session_token_grant,
            can_decide_consents: can_decide_consents(browser_session),
            may_raise_for_owner: &may_raise_for_owner,
            sid: browser_sid,
        },
        FreshIds {
            request_id: Uuid::new_v4().to_string(),
            code: generate_authorization_code(),
        },
        chrono::Utc::now(),
    )?;
    Ok(found_redirect(&next_step_location(next_step, "")))
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/authorize.rs lines 272–332 · authorization-server in the code index

next_step_location

The pages’ locations come from consent_page_location, wait_page_location and limited_page_location; the app’s from the domain’s build_client_redirect_url.

Where next_step sends the browser: straight back to the client with the fresh code when fully pre-approved (RFC 6749 §4.1.2), else to a page for the request, relative to /oauth/ (request_page_location) after page_prefix: empty for /oauth/authorize’s own Location, which the browser resolves against the endpoint, and /oauth/ for the limited page’s Continue, which the page follows from elsewhere.

The Owner decides on the consent card when this browser can decide the request, and else from this authorization server’s wait page, which waits for whichever surface — the host popup, a signed-in launcher’s consent list, or the consent card — decides first. A browser whose session holds less than the app asks for is first told so on the limited page, which goes on or cancels.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) fn next_step_location(next_step: AuthorizeNextStep, page_prefix: &str) -> String {
    let request_page = match next_step {
        AuthorizeNextStep::RedirectToClient {
            redirect_uri,
            code,
            client_state,
        } => return build_client_redirect_url(&redirect_uri, &code, &client_state),
        AuthorizeNextStep::AwaitOwner {
            request_id,
            decidable_in_requesting_browser: true,
        } => consent_page_location(&request_id),
        AuthorizeNextStep::AwaitOwner {
            request_id,
            decidable_in_requesting_browser: false,
        } => wait_page_location(&request_id),
        AuthorizeNextStep::ConfirmSessionShortfall { request_id } => {
            limited_page_location(&request_id)
        }
    };
    format!("{page_prefix}{request_page}")
}
}

AuthorizeError

Error half of the /oauth/authorize handler’s Result. Each variant renders one of the endpoint’s failure responses through IntoResponse, so a fallible step bails with ? instead of a match + return at every call site — the authorization-endpoint analogue of TokenError (and, on the Owner /authorization surface, AuthorizationServerError). Kept small (no embedded Response) so Result<_, AuthorizeError> doesn’t trip clippy::result_large_err.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) enum AuthorizeError {
    /// A failure on a request whose `redirect_uri` is not trusted — a disabled
    /// client, a malformed or non-http(s) URI, an unregistered redirect for a
    /// server-defined registration, or (because the client is new to this authorization server or
    /// the redirect is not on its registration) any later validation failure.
    /// Renders a `400` with the server's own HTML error page
    /// ([`oauth_error_html`]) — redirecting to an unvouched-for URI would be
    /// an open redirect (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1).
    LocalPage(AuthorizeRefusal),
    /// A spec'd error once `redirect_uri` is validated — 302 back to the
    /// client. Carries the already-built `Location` (the client `redirect_uri`
    /// merged with `error` + `error_description` + `state`, RFC 6749
    /// §4.1.2.1) rather than the `Url`, keeping the variant small enough to
    /// dodge `clippy::result_large_err`.
    Redirect {
        /// The client's `redirect_uri` with the error, its description and
        /// the client's `state` in its query.
        location: String,
    },
    /// No active signing key: without token-mint capability the endpoint can't
    /// proceed, so it 503s rather than parking a request it can never complete.
    /// Nothing is parked.
    ServiceUnavailable,
    /// The authorization start limit refused a request that would be raised
    /// for the Owner — the `429` the limit's layer answers.
    StartLimited,
    /// A logged, opaque 500 — see [`InternalError`]. A store failure, or a
    /// request the fast path found no longer pending when it came to approve
    /// it.
    Internal(InternalError),
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/authorize.rs lines 51–81 · authorization-server in the code index

from

The starter’s failures map onto it. A redirectable one has its Location built here, with build_client_error_redirect_url. A request the fast path found no longer pending, and a store failure, are both logged 500s.

Render the flow’s failure vocabulary onto the endpoint’s responses: a local page while the redirect is untrusted, a 302 with error + error_description + state back to a validated redirect (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1), a 503 with no signing key, the start limit’s 429, and a logged opaque 500 for the rest.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn from(error: AuthorizationStartError) -> Self {
    match error {
        AuthorizationStartError::NoActiveSigningKey => AuthorizeError::ServiceUnavailable,
        AuthorizationStartError::StartLimited => AuthorizeError::StartLimited,
        AuthorizationStartError::LocalPage(kind) => {
            if kind == AuthorizeRefusal::RedirectUriNotAllowed {
                tracing::warn!("redirect_uri not on a server-defined registration");
            }
            AuthorizeError::LocalPage(kind)
        }
        AuthorizationStartError::Redirectable {
            redirect_uri,
            error,
            description,
            client_state,
        } => AuthorizeError::Redirect {
            location: build_client_error_redirect_url(
                &redirect_uri,
                error,
                description,
                &client_state,
            ),
        },
        AuthorizationStartError::RequestNotPending => {
            AuthorizeError::Internal(InternalError::new(
                "approve_authorization_request",
                "authorization request was not pending",
            ))
        }
        AuthorizationStartError::Store(error) => AuthorizeError::Internal(InternalError::new(
            "store operation failed at /oauth/authorize",
            error,
        )),
    }
}
}

While a request waits, the browser waits on a page this server serves, on its own origin, so the address bar names the server being approved. /oauth/authorize sends the browser to one of three pages beside it: the wait page while the Owner decides elsewhere, the consent card when this browser decides itself, the limited page when its session holds less than the app asks for. Two more pages are reached another way: the device page, where the Owner confirms a device’s code, and the pairing page, where a browser without a session asks for one.

The pages are static. Each is the same bytes for every request, and reads the request id or code from its own URL, so nothing a caller sends can reach the markup. What changes is answered by JSON routes beside them: the status poll the wait page drives, and the three calls the limited page makes. All of it is uncached, and all of it is locked down by the same security headers.

http::routes::oauth::pages

content_security_policy

A page loads only from this origin, talks only to this origin, and can’t be framed. The one thing that differs between pages is where their forms may go: the wait page has no form, and the React pages’ Sign out form posts here and is redirected on to the launcher.

The Content-Security-Policy of a page whose forms may submit to, and follow redirects to, form_targets (a form-action source list, NO_FORM_TARGETS for none). Everything a page loads (its scripts, stylesheets and fonts) comes from this origin, it can only talk back to it, and nothing may frame it. The top-level navigation to the client’s redirect is not a fetch, so connect-src doesn’t constrain it. A router builds it once and hands it to page_security_headers for each request.

Panics

When form_targets holds a byte a header value can’t, which a source list of keywords and origins never does.

pub(super) fn content_security_policy(form_targets: &str) -> HeaderValue {

        "default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; font-src 'self'; \
         connect-src 'self'; base-uri 'none'; form-action {form_targets}; \
         frame-ancestors 'none'"
    ))
    .expect("a source list of keywords and origins is a valid header value")
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/pages.rs line 14 · authorization-server in the code index

page_security_headers

Every page and asset is checked for them by assert_locked_down.

The headers every file of a page carries: its content_type, its content_security_policy (built by content_security_policy), no Referer on anything it loads from or leaves for another origin, and no sniffing a type other than the one declared. The referrer policy is same-origin, not no-referrer: under no-referrer a browser sends a form POST with Origin: null, which the host’s cookie→bearer layer refuses, so the pages’ Sign out would fail.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) fn page_security_headers(
    content_type: &'static str,
    content_security_policy: &HeaderValue,
) -> [(HeaderName, HeaderValue); 4] {
    [
        (header::CONTENT_TYPE, HeaderValue::from_static(content_type)),
        (
            header::CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY,
            content_security_policy.clone(),
        ),
        (
            header::REFERRER_POLICY,
            HeaderValue::from_static("same-origin"),
        ),
        (
            header::X_CONTENT_TYPE_OPTIONS,
            HeaderValue::from_static("nosniff"),
        ),
    ]
}
}

http::routes::oauth::wait_page

The wait page is where a browser waits while the Owner decides somewhere else: in the host’s popup, in a signed-in launcher, or on a consent card. Its script polls the status until the request is decided, then follows the redirect the poll hands back. That redirect is the only address off this origin the page ever leaves for. While the request is pending, the page also checks whether this browser has since signed in as the Owner and, if so, switches to the consent card beside it. Its three files are embedded as they are, with nothing interpolated; the script has no unit tests, and the Wait Page integration tests pin how its files are served.

router

The wait page’s routes, relative to the /oauth mount. The page references its assets as ../wait.js and ../wait.css, which resolve to these two siblings whatever prefix the authorization server is mounted under.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn router() -> Router<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>> {
    let policy = content_security_policy(NO_FORM_TARGETS);
    let script_policy = policy.clone();
    let stylesheet_policy = policy.clone();
    Router::new()
        .route(
            "/authorize/{id}/wait",
            get(move || async move { wait_page(&policy) }),
        )
        .route(
            "/authorize/wait.js",
            get(move || async move { wait_page_script(&script_policy) }),
        )
        .route(
            "/authorize/wait.css",
            get(move || async move { wait_page_stylesheet(&stylesheet_policy) }),
        )
}
}

http::routes::oauth::authorization_pages

The consent card, the limited page, the device page and the pairing page are the build of authorization-server-web, embedded in the binary when it is compiled. The consent card and the device page call /authorization/* and FHIR on the browser session’s bearer, which the host’s cookie-to-bearer layer presents for them. The pairing page calls /oauth/pair/*, which needs no session. The limited page calls /oauth/authorize/{id}/*, on the browser session’s cookie.

The unit tests serve a fake build laid out as Vite lays it out, with a launcher on another origin.

router_for

The routes above, serving pages, whose forms may submit to form_targets. The policy is built once, here. They read no router state.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn router_for<S: Clone + Send + Sync + 'static>(
    pages: &'static Dir<'static>,
    form_targets: &str,
) -> Router<S> {
    let policy = content_security_policy(form_targets);
    let consent_policy = policy.clone();
    let limited_policy = policy.clone();
    let device_policy = policy.clone();
    let pair_policy = policy.clone();
    Router::new()
        .route(
            "/authorize/{id}/consent",
            get(move || async move { page(pages, CONSENT_PAGE, &consent_policy) }),
        )
        .route(
            "/authorize/{id}/limited",
            get(move || async move { page(pages, LIMITED_PAGE, &limited_policy) }),
        )
        .route(
            DEVICE_PAGE_ROUTE,
            get(move || async move { page(pages, DEVICE_PAGE, &device_policy) }),
        )
        .route(
            "/pair",
            get(move || async move { page(pages, PAIR_PAGE, &pair_policy) }),
        )
        .route(
            "/assets/{*file}",
            get(move |Path(file): Path<String>| async move { asset(pages, &file, &policy) }),
        )
}
}

asset

An asset is cached for a year without revalidating, since Vite’s file names carry a hash of their contents and never change under a name. Anything but a script, a stylesheet or a font is a 404, even when the build holds it.

The hashed script, stylesheet or font file under pages’ assets/, cached as immutable, under policy, or 404.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn asset(pages: &'static Dir<'static>, file: &str, policy: &HeaderValue) -> Response {
    let Some(content_type) = asset_content_type(file) else {
        return StatusCode::NOT_FOUND.into_response();
    };
    let Some(asset) = pages.get_file(format!("{ASSETS_DIR}/{file}")) else {
        return StatusCode::NOT_FOUND.into_response();
    };
    (
        [(header::CACHE_CONTROL, IMMUTABLE)],
        page_security_headers(content_type, policy),
        asset.contents(),
    )
        .into_response()
}
}

fn main() {
fn asset_content_type(file: &str) -> Option<&'static str> {
    match FilePath::new(file)
        .extension()
        .and_then(|extension| extension.to_str())
    {
        Some("js") => Some("text/javascript; charset=utf-8"),
        Some("css") => Some("text/css; charset=utf-8"),
        Some("woff2") => Some("font/woff2"),
        _ => None,
    }
}
}

The pairing redirect resolves beside /oauth/authorize to the pairing page, and its next decodes back to the authorize request’s own path and query, whatever they hold.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn the_pairing_location_resolves_to_the_pairing_page_carrying_next() {
    let authorize =
        Url::parse("https://ruth.relay.example/oauth/authorize?x=1").expect("valid url");
    for next in [
        "/oauth/authorize?client_id=app&scope=a%20b&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp%2Fcb",
        "/oauth/authorize?state=a&b#c+d",
    ] {
        let resolved = authorize
            .join(&pairing_page_location(next))
            .expect("resolves");
        assert_eq!(resolved.path(), "/oauth/pair");
        let nexts: Vec<String> = resolved
            .query_pairs()
            .filter(|(name, _)| name == NEXT_PARAM)
            .map(|(_, value)| value.into_owned())
            .collect();
        assert_eq!(nexts, [next]);
    }
}
}

http::routes::oauth::authorization_status

AuthorizationStatus

Polling response for the wait page watching an authorization request as it moves from Pending toward approval or denial: where the request stands, and once it is decided, where to send the browser.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum AuthorizationStatus {
    /// `{"status":"pending"}`: undecided and unexpired, whether it waits for
    /// the Owner or still sits on its browser's limited page. The wait page
    /// keeps polling.
    Pending,
    /// `{"status":"denied","redirect":…}`: the Owner declined, or the
    /// browser session the request was made in was revoked; the poll can't
    /// tell the two apart, so every denial reads as declined.
    Denied {
        /// Client callback URL carrying `error=access_denied`, an
        /// `error_description` and `state` for code-flow requests (RFC 6749
        /// §4.1.2.1) so the wait page can complete the flow. Always set: only
        /// code-flow requests are polled here.
        redirect: Option<String>,
    },
    /// `{"status":"approved","redirect":…}`: the request was approved and
    /// its code issued.
    Approved {
        /// Client callback URL carrying the redeemable `code` and `state`
        /// (RFC 6749 §4.1.2). The wait page follows it.
        redirect: String,
    },
    /// `{"status":"error","message":…}`: the request passed its expiry
    /// undecided, so it can't be decided any more. The wait page stops and
    /// shows the message.
    Error {
        /// What the wait page shows: "Authorization request expired".
        message: String,
    },
}
}

fn into_response(self) -> Response {

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/authorization_status.rs lines 71–73 · authorization-server in the code index

handle_authorization_status_request

A leaked request id collects nothing. The authorization status reader enforces who may read; the handler passes it the browser session the cookie carries.

Return the current status of the pending authorization request, including the final redirect URL once approved. The caller’s browser session (its __Host-browser_session cookie) is answered when the request was made in it, or when its grant covers wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.r and .u, the scopes that decide the request on the consent card. Any other caller, with another session or none, gets the same 404 as an unknown id, so a leaked request id can’t collect the code.

The answers, by where the request stands:

  • pending: 200 AuthorizationStatus::Pending;
  • pending past its expiry: 200 AuthorizationStatus::Error;
  • denied: 200 AuthorizationStatus::Denied, with the client’s access_denied callback;
  • approved: 200 AuthorizationStatus::Approved, with the client’s callback carrying the code;
  • unknown, or not readable by this caller: 404 AuthorizationRequestNotFound;
  • approved but with no code: 500 server_error, an invariant the store broke.

Only code requests are answered here; a device and a pairing have polls of their own.

The error side is axum::response::ErrorResponse because two error shapes share the handler: the Owner-surface AuthorizationServerError (its AuthorizationRequestNotFound 404 / logged 500) and the OAuth-shaped OAuthErrorResponse server_error — ? converts either through its IntoResponse.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_authorization_status_request(
    reader: Live<LiveAuthorizationStatusReader>,
    token_verifier: Live<LiveTokenVerifier>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    Path(id): Path<String>,
) -> axum::response::Result<AuthorizationStatus> {
    let polling_browser_session =
        carried_browser_session(&token_verifier, &headers).map_err(|error| {
            InternalError::new("verify a browser session at /oauth/authorize/{id}", error)
        })?;
    let poller = polling_browser_session.and_then(|claims| {
        let grant = claims.granted();
        claims.sid.map(|sid| PollingBrowserSession { sid, grant })
    });
    let view = reader.status(&id, poller.as_ref(), Utc::now()).map_err(
        |error| -> axum::response::ErrorResponse {
            match error {
                AuthorizationStatusError::NotFound { id } => {
                    AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound { id }.into()
                }
                AuthorizationStatusError::ApprovedWithoutCode => {
                    OAuthErrorResponse::server_error("Authorization code missing").into()
                }
                AuthorizationStatusError::Store(error) => error.into(),
            }
        },
    )?;
    Ok(match view {
        AuthorizationStatusView::Pending => AuthorizationStatus::Pending,
        AuthorizationStatusView::Expired => AuthorizationStatus::Error {
            message: "Authorization request expired".to_string(),
        },
        // Build the client callback so the user-agent waiting at the client's
        // redirect_uri receives `error=access_denied`, an `error_description`
        // and `state`, and stops hanging. The poll can't tell an Owner's
        // decline from a revoked browser session, so every denial reads as
        // declined.
        AuthorizationStatusView::Denied {
            redirect_uri,
            client_state,
        } => AuthorizationStatus::Denied {
            redirect: Some(build_client_error_redirect_url(
                &redirect_uri,
                OAuthErrorCode::AccessDenied,
                REQUEST_DECLINED_DESCRIPTION,
                &client_state,
            )),
        },
        AuthorizationStatusView::Approved {
            redirect_uri,
            code,
            client_state,
        } => AuthorizationStatus::Approved {
            redirect: build_client_redirect_url(&redirect_uri, &code, &client_state),
        },
    })
}
}

http::routes::oauth::session_shortfall

A browser whose session holds less than an app asks for is told so on the limited page before anyone else is bothered. The page makes three calls on its own origin: read what the session lacks, go on, or cancel. Each answers only the browser session the request was made in; any other browser, with another session or none, gets the same 404 as an unknown id.

The two posts carry no body, so another page could send them as a simple request. What refuses one is the host’s cookie-to-bearer layer, which answers 403 to a write carrying the cookie from any origin but the server’s. Every answer is uncached, since a Continue may carry the app’s redirect with a code. The Session Shortfall integration tests hold all three.

fn requesting_sid(

handle_session_shortfall_continue

The request takes the branch /oauth/authorize would have taken had the session held everything, and next_step_location builds the location, under /oauth/, since the page follows it from elsewhere. Any other failure renders as /oauth/authorize would render it (AuthorizeError).

Go on with request id although this browser’s session holds less than it asks for: issue a code under a standing grant that covers it, or else ask the Owner, on the consent card when this browser can decide it and on the wait page otherwise, with the request’s five minutes started again. The request spent from the authorization start limit when /oauth/authorize parked it, so going on spends nothing. This browser session’s later requests for the same app skip the limited page. A client disabled since the request parked ends it: the request is denied and the app is sent access_denied.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_session_shortfall_continue(
    code_authorization_starter: Live<LiveCodeAuthorizationStarter>,
    token_verifier: Live<LiveTokenVerifier>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    Path(id): Path<String>,
) -> Result<Response, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let sid = requesting_sid(&token_verifier, &headers, &id)?;
    let next_step = code_authorization_starter.continue_past_session_shortfall(
        &id,
        &sid,
        generate_authorization_code(),
        Utc::now(),
    );
    let location = match next_step {
        Ok(next_step) => next_step_location(next_step, &format!("{OAUTH_MOUNT}/")),
        Err(AuthorizationStartError::Store(
            error @ AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound { .. },
        )) => return Err(error),
        // Cancelled between this Continue's acknowledgement and its fast-path
        // approval: no longer waiting here, like any other request that isn't.
        Err(AuthorizationStartError::RequestNotPending) => {
            return Err(AuthorizationServerError::AuthorizationRequestNotFound { id })
        }
        Err(error) => match AuthorizeError::from(error) {
            AuthorizeError::Redirect { location } => location,
            other => return Ok(other.into_response()),
        },
    };
    Ok(next_location(location))
}
}

Cancel request id: deny it and send the browser back to the app with error=access_denied. Cancel isn’t remembered: this session’s next request for the app stops at the limited page again.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_session_shortfall_cancel(
    session_shortfall: Live<LiveSessionShortfall>,
    token_verifier: Live<LiveTokenVerifier>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    Path(id): Path<String>,
) -> Result<Response, AuthorizationServerError> {

Pairing and Sign-In

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/browser_pairing.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/sign_in.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/sign_out.rs

A browser needs a browser session before it can ask for anything, and it holds one as its browser session cookie. There are two ways to get one, and one way to give it up. A browser that isn’t the Owner’s asks to be paired: it shows a code, and the Owner approves it from somewhere they are already signed in. The Owner’s own browser, on the device the server runs on, is signed in by the base app with a one-time same-device sign-in code. Either kind of browser signs out from the Sign out button on the server’s pages.

Wildflower has no accounts and no passwords. RFC 6749 leaves how a person signs in to an authorization server to the server (§3.1): here, holding the device the server runs on is what makes someone the Owner, and the Owner’s approval is what lets any other browser in. The Browser Pairing, Same-Device Sign-In and Browser Sessions integration tests hold these routes end to end.

http::routes::oauth::browser_pairing

The pairing page makes two calls on its own origin: start a pairing request, then poll it until the Owner decides. Pairing is no OAuth flow, so the bodies are JSON, not form-encoded. A JSON body needs a CORS preflight from any other origin, and the server’s CORS policy never allows credentials, so only the server’s own pages can have a poll’s cookie set.

handle_browser_pairing_start

The browser is named by device_name_from_user_agent, a name the page may change while it polls. The start goes through the browser pairing capability, which parks the pairing and republishes the Owner prompt, so the host notifies the Owner.

Start a browser pairing for this browser, named after its User-Agent, and raise the Owner’s notification. The body’s next is where the browser goes once paired, in practice the /oauth/authorize request it was sent away from.

The answer’s pairing code is the page’s secret, and the user code is for the Owner, who confirms it on the device page: only the page that started the pairing can collect the session. The refusals:

  • next is no path on this server: 400, BrowserPairingNextNotAllowed.
  • The browser-session client is disabled: 403, BrowserSessionClientDisabled.
  • No unused user code could be generated, or a store failed: a logged 500.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_browser_pairing_start(
    pairing: Live<LiveBrowserPairing>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    Json(body): Json<BrowserPairingStartBody>,
) -> Response {
    let user_agent_name = headers
        .get(header::USER_AGENT)
        .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
        .and_then(device_name_from_user_agent);
    let response = match pairing.start(&body.next, user_agent_name, Utc::now()) {
        Ok(started) => Json(StartedBrowserPairingBody::from(started)).into_response(),
        Err(BrowserPairingStartError::NextNotAllowed) => (
            StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST,
            Json(BrowserPairingRefused {
                error: "BrowserPairingNextNotAllowed",
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        Err(BrowserPairingStartError::BrowserSessionClientDisabled) => (
            StatusCode::FORBIDDEN,
            Json(BrowserPairingRefused {
                error: "BrowserSessionClientDisabled",
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        Err(BrowserPairingStartError::UserCodeExhausted) => InternalError::new(
            "start a browser pairing",
            "exhausted every user_code generation attempt",
        )
        .into_response(),
        Err(BrowserPairingStartError::Store(error)) => {
            InternalError::new("start a browser pairing", error).into_response()
        }
    };
    CacheSuppressed(response).into_response()
}
}

handle_browser_pairing_poll

The poll that finds the pairing approved hands the browser its session. The capability claims the request, stores the approved browser session and mints its token, and the answer sets that token as the cookie through browser_session_set_cookie.

Poll a browser pairing. The poll that finds it approved starts the browser’s paired session and sets it as the browser’s __Host-browser_session cookie. A blank browser_name keeps the name the pairing has. An unknown pairing code is a 404; a store failure, a session that couldn’t be stored, and a token that couldn’t be minted are each a logged 500.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_browser_pairing_poll(
    pairing: Live<LiveBrowserPairing>,
    Json(body): Json<BrowserPairingPollBody>,
) -> Response {
    let response = match pairing.poll(&body.pairing_code, &body.browser_name, Utc::now()) {
        Ok(BrowserPairingStatus::Approved { session_token }) => (
            [(
                header::SET_COOKIE,
                browser_session_set_cookie(&session_token, PAIRED_SESSION_TTL),
            )],
            Json(BrowserPairingStatusBody::Approved),
        )
            .into_response(),
        Ok(BrowserPairingStatus::Pending) => {
            Json(BrowserPairingStatusBody::Pending).into_response()
        }
        Ok(BrowserPairingStatus::SlowDown) => {
            Json(BrowserPairingStatusBody::SlowDown).into_response()
        }
        Ok(BrowserPairingStatus::Denied) => Json(BrowserPairingStatusBody::Denied).into_response(),
        Ok(BrowserPairingStatus::Expired) => {
            Json(BrowserPairingStatusBody::Expired).into_response()
        }
        Err(BrowserPairingPollError::NotFound) => (
            StatusCode::NOT_FOUND,
            Json(BrowserPairingNotFound {
                error: "BrowserPairingNotFound",
            }),
        )
            .into_response(),
        Err(BrowserPairingPollError::Store(error)) => {
            InternalError::new("poll a browser pairing", error).into_response()
        }
        Err(BrowserPairingPollError::SessionNotStored(error)) => {
            InternalError::new("store a paired browser session", error).into_response()
        }
        Err(BrowserPairingPollError::Issuance(error)) => {
            InternalError::new("mint a paired browser session's token", error).into_response()
        }
    };
    CacheSuppressed(response).into_response()
}
}

pub(super) enum BrowserPairingStatusBody {
    /// The Owner hasn't decided yet; the page polls again after its interval.

handle_sign_in

The code goes to the same-device sign-in capability, which answers an Owner session’s token and the redirect.

Redeem the code for a same-device session’s token, hand the browser the token as its __Host-browser_session cookie, and 303 it on to next. A next that isn’t allowed, a disabled browser-session client, or a code that is unknown, spent or expired, gets the error page, with no cookie and no redirect.

Every answer is uncached and sends no Referer on, since the request’s own URL carries the code.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn handle_sign_in(
    same_device_sign_in: Live<LiveSameDeviceSignIn>,
    Query(params): Query<SignInParams>,
) -> Response {
    let response = match same_device_sign_in.sign_in(&params.code, &params.next, Utc::now()) {
        Ok(SignedIn {
            session_token,
            redirect,
        }) => (
            StatusCode::SEE_OTHER,
            [
                (header::LOCATION, redirect.location().to_owned()),
                (
                    header::SET_COOKIE,
                    browser_session_set_cookie(&session_token, SAME_DEVICE_SESSION_TTL),
                ),
            ],
        )
            .into_response(),
        Err(SameDeviceSignInError::Refused(refusal)) => refusal_page(refusal),
        Err(SameDeviceSignInError::Store(error)) => {
            InternalError::new("read the browser-session client", error).into_response()
        }
        Err(SameDeviceSignInError::SessionNotStored(error)) => {
            InternalError::new("store the same-device session", error).into_response()
        }
        Err(SameDeviceSignInError::Issuance(error)) => {
            InternalError::new("mint the same-device session's token", error).into_response()
        }
    };
    (
        [(header::REFERRER_POLICY, "no-referrer")],
        CacheSuppressed(response),
    )
        .into_response()
}
}
