http::routes::oauth::sign_out

A browser ends its own browser session from the Sign out form on the server’s pages. The cookie alone authenticates it; no bearer is involved. A browser always leaves signed out: one with no cookie, or whose session already ended, has nothing to revoke and gets the same answer.

Nothing here checks where the form came from. The host’s cookie-to-bearer layer refuses a write carrying the cookie from any origin but the server’s own, so another page can’t sign a browser out.

handle_sign_out

The browser session ender revokes the session, which ends everything minted under it, and the answer clears the cookie with browser_session_clearing_set_cookie.

Revoke the browser session the request’s cookie holds, if it holds a standing one, then clear the cookie and 303 to the launcher’s root. The 303 turns the form’s POST into a GET. A browser session that can’t be checked or revoked, because a store can’t be read or written, is a 500 that leaves the cookie as it was.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn handle_sign_out(
    token_verifier: Live<LiveTokenVerifier>,
    browser_session_ender: Live<LiveBrowserSessionEnder>,
    pages: LauncherPages,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Response {
    let session_claims = match carried_browser_session(&token_verifier, &headers) {
        Ok(session_claims) => session_claims,
        Err(error) => {
            return InternalError::new("check the browser session to sign out", error)
                .into_response()
        }
    };
    if let Some(session_claims) = session_claims {
        if let Err(error) = browser_session_ender.end(&session_claims, Utc::now()) {
            return InternalError::new("revoke the browser session", error).into_response();
        }
    }
    CacheSuppressed((
        StatusCode::SEE_OTHER,
        [
            (header::LOCATION, pages.root_url().to_owned()),
            (header::SET_COOKIE, browser_session_clearing_set_cookie()),
        ],
    ))
    .into_response()
}
}

A device with no good browser of its own, a command line or a TV app, asks for access the RFC 8628 way. The device gets two codes: one to poll with, one for a person to type. It shows the user code and the device page’s address; the Owner opens the page, confirms the code, and decides. Meanwhile the device polls the token endpoint with its device code until the decision lands. The request it parks is a device request.

POST /oauth/device_authorization is the first step. Its caller is the device’s client, authenticated by the TokenRequest extractor as at the token endpoint. Every device request is raised for the Owner, so every one spends from the authorization start limit. The Device Code and OAuth Endpoints integration tests hold the route end to end.

http::routes::oauth::device_authorization

DeviceAuthorizationPayload

Body of an RFC 8628 device authorization request. Client credentials are not parsed here — RFC 8628 §3.1 inherits RFC 6749 §3.2.1 client authentication, so the TokenRequest extractor owns both the Basic header and the body client_id/client_secret fields.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct DeviceAuthorizationPayload {
    /// The scopes the device asks for, space-separated (RFC 6749 §3.3).
    /// Absent asks for none. Each must be one the client may ask for, else the
    /// request is `invalid_scope`.
    pub scope: Option<String>,
    /// Non-standard RFC 8628 extension: a human-chosen name for the device being paired,
    /// surfaced to the approver. Absent for strict RFC clients.
    pub device_name: Option<String>,
}
}

verification_uri is the device page; verification_uri_complete is the page with the code filled in.

Body returned by /oauth/device_authorization per RFC 8628 §3.2.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct DeviceAuthorizationResponse {
    /// The secret the device polls `/oauth/token` with until the Owner
    /// decides. Only the device holds it.
    pub device_code: String,
    /// The short code the device shows its user, which the Owner confirms on
    /// the device page before deciding.
    pub user_code: String,
    /// This server's device verification page, `{origin}/oauth/device`.
    pub verification_uri: String,
    /// The device verification page with the code filled in,
    /// `{origin}/oauth/device?user_code={user_code}`. The Owner still confirms
    /// the code before the page reads the request.
    pub verification_uri_complete: String,
    /// Seconds until the request expires; a poll after that is
    /// `expired_token`.
    pub expires_in: i64,
    /// Seconds the device waits between polls; polling sooner is answered
    /// `slow_down` (RFC 8628 §3.5).
    pub interval: i64,
}
}

handle_device_authorization_request

The start limit is asked through StartLimitAskedNow: a start the layer deferred for a browser that can decide consents is asked now, since a device request is raised for the Owner whoever sends it.

Issue a (device_code, user_code) pair for the client to poll on while the user pairs the device. Ok carries the §5.1 cache suppression via DeviceAuthorizationResponse, Err via TokenError.

The extractors run in order: the start limit first, before the body is read, since every device request is raised for the Owner whoever sends it (a refusal is the 429); then the User-Agent; then TokenRequest, last because it consumes the body, which checks the content type, parses the payload and authenticates the client.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_device_authorization_request(
    authorizer: Live<LiveDeviceAuthorizer>,
    // Every device request is raised for the Owner, so a start limit the
    // layer deferred (for a browser that can decide consents) is asked now,
    // before the body is parsed.
    _start_limit: StartLimitAskedNow,
    headers: HeaderMap,
    request: TokenRequest<DeviceAuthorizationPayload>,
) -> Response {
    // `HeaderMap` is a `FromRequestParts` extractor, so it must precede the
    // body-consuming `TokenRequest`.
    let user_agent = headers
        .get(header::USER_AGENT)
        .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok());
    device_authorization(&authorizer, user_agent, request).into_response()
}
}

device_authorization

The request goes to the device authorizer, which parks it.

Parse the request, hand it to the LiveDeviceAuthorizer, and frame the RFC 8628 §3.2 response with the authorizer’s device verification page, surfacing every failure as a TokenError:

  • a scope the client may not ask for: 400 invalid_scope, “Scope not allowed for client”;
  • no unused user code could be generated: a logged, uncached 500;
  • a store failure: a logged, uncached 500.

The name the approver sees is the one the client chose, trimmed, when it isn’t blank; else one guessed from the User-Agent when that names a browser or a system; else none, and the approval falls back to the client’s name.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn device_authorization(
    authorizer: &LiveDeviceAuthorizer,
    user_agent: Option<&str>,
    request: TokenRequest<DeviceAuthorizationPayload>,
) -> Result<DeviceAuthorizationResponse, TokenError> {
    let TokenRequest {
        payload,
        authenticated_client,
    } = request;
    let requested_scopes: Vec<String> = payload
        .scope
        .as_deref()
        .unwrap_or("")
        .split_whitespace()
        .map(str::to_string)
        .collect();
    // The name the approver sees and the grant is keyed on. Prefer the name the
    // client chose (normalizing an all-whitespace/empty name to `None`); when it
    // didn't name itself, infer a friendly one from its User-Agent. If neither
    // yields a name, approval falls back to the client name so the upsert key
    // stays total.
    let device_name = payload
        .device_name
        .as_deref()
        .map(str::trim)
        .filter(|name| !name.is_empty())
        .map(str::to_string)
        .or_else(|| user_agent.and_then(device_name_from_user_agent));
    let device_codes = authorizer
        .start(
            &authenticated_client,
            requested_scopes,
            device_name,
            Utc::now(),
        )
        .map_err(|error| match error {
            DeviceAuthorizationError::ScopeNotAllowed => TokenError::bad_request(
                OAuthErrorCode::InvalidScope,
                Some("Scope not allowed for client"),
            ),
            DeviceAuthorizationError::UserCodeExhausted => TokenError::internal(
                "user_code generation failed",
                "exhausted every user_code generation attempt",
            ),
            DeviceAuthorizationError::Store(error) => TokenError::from(error),
        })?;
    let device_page = authorizer.device_page();
    Ok(DeviceAuthorizationResponse {
        device_code: device_codes.device_code,
        verification_uri_complete: device_page_url_with_code(device_page, &device_codes.user_code)
            .into(),
        verification_uri: device_page.as_str().to_owned(),
        user_code: device_codes.user_code,
        expires_in: device_codes.expires_in,
        interval: device_codes.interval,
    })
}
}

http::routes::oauth::device_name_hint

A raw agent string is never shown as a name. The hint names a device that didn’t name itself, and a browser starting a pairing. It is a small substring check, not an agent database, and the more specific token is tested first, since agents embed the tokens of what they derive from: Chromium forks carry Chrome/, Chrome carries Safari/, and the iOS and Android agents carry Mac OS X and Linux.

device_name_from_user_agent

Derive a friendly device name from a User-Agent, or None when nothing recognizable is present (the caller then falls back to the client name).

"Chrome on macOS" when both a browser and OS are known; the single known half otherwise ("iPhone", "Firefox"); None when neither is.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) fn device_name_from_user_agent(user_agent: &str) -> Option<String> {
    match (browser(user_agent), operating_system(user_agent)) {
        (Some(browser), Some(os)) => Some(format!("{browser} on {os}")),
        (Some(browser), None) => Some(browser.to_owned()),
        (None, Some(os)) => Some(os.to_owned()),
        (None, None) => None,
    }
}
}

browser

The browser family a UA advertises, or None if none is recognized.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn browser(user_agent: &str) -> Option<&'static str> {
    // Chromium forks embed `Chrome/`, and Chrome itself embeds `Safari/`, so the
    // fork tokens (`Edg`, `OPR`, `CriOS`) must be tested before `Chrome`, and
    // `Chrome` before `Safari`.
    if user_agent.contains("Edg/") || user_agent.contains("EdgiOS/") {
        Some("Edge")
    } else if user_agent.contains("OPR/") || user_agent.contains("Opera") {
        Some("Opera")
    } else if user_agent.contains("CriOS/") || user_agent.contains("Chrome/") {
        Some("Chrome")
    } else if user_agent.contains("FxiOS/") || user_agent.contains("Firefox/") {
        Some("Firefox")
    } else if user_agent.contains("Safari/") {
        Some("Safari")
    } else {
        None
    }
}
}

operating_system

The operating system / device family a UA advertises, or None.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn operating_system(user_agent: &str) -> Option<&'static str> {
    // iOS and Android UAs also carry the desktop tokens they derive from
    // (`like Mac OS X`, `Linux`), so the mobile tokens are tested first.
    if user_agent.contains("iPhone") {
        Some("iPhone")
    } else if user_agent.contains("iPad") {
        Some("iPad")
    } else if user_agent.contains("Android") {
        Some("Android")
    } else if user_agent.contains("CrOS") {
        Some("ChromeOS")
    } else if user_agent.contains("Macintosh") || user_agent.contains("Mac OS X") {
        Some("macOS")
    } else if user_agent.contains("Windows") {
        Some("Windows")
    } else if user_agent.contains("Linux") {
        Some("Linux")
    } else {
        None
    }
}
}

The token endpoint is where an app’s back end, not a browser, gets its tokens. It trades an authorization code, a device code or a refresh token for an access token (RFC 6749 §3.2, RFC 8628 §3.4), and POST /oauth/revoke beside it takes one of the app’s tokens back (RFC 7009). Every call is made by a client, and the client is authenticated before the handler runs. A public client proves itself by its client_id alone, a confidential one by its secret too.

Three routes take this shape: /oauth/token, /oauth/revoke and /oauth/device_authorization, on the next page. Each reads a form-encoded body through one extractor, TokenRequest, which hands the handler the parsed body and an AuthenticatedClient proof. A handler can’t act for a client whose secret was never checked, because it never sees raw credentials. Every answer, success or error, is uncached (RFC 6749 §5.1). The Client Auth, Grant Flows and Token Revocation integration tests hold the routes end to end.

http::routes::oauth::token_request

TokenRequest

An RFC 6749 token-style request, extracted once into its payload (the endpoint’s own body, generic per endpoint) and the authenticated_client.

Centralizes what the token-style endpoints otherwise repeat inline: the RFC 6749 §3.2 Content-Type check, reading the body, the §2.3.1 credential dance (resolve_client_credentials, which reconciles the Authorization: Basic header with body client_id / client_secret), and §2.3 client authentication through the LiveClientAuthenticator. On any failure the rejection is a TokenError, so it renders the same cache-suppressed §5.2 error shape as the rest of the surface; an authentication failure carries presented_via so a Basic attempt gets its WWW-Authenticate challenge.

The body is read once; the grant payload and the credential fields are then each deserialized from it (two cheap serde_urlencoded passes over the same small string — they pull disjoint, differently-shaped fields, so a single pass would buy nothing but coupling).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) struct TokenRequest<P> {
    /// The endpoint's own body, parsed from the form: it ignores
    /// `client_id` and `client_secret`, which the credential parse reads.
    pub payload: P,
    /// The verified client — the proof every client-gated operation takes.
    pub authenticated_client: AuthenticatedClient,
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/token_request.rs lines 41–47 · authorization-server in the code index

from_request

The payload is parsed before the credentials, so a malformed body reads as malformed, not as “Missing client_id”. The client is authenticated through the client authenticator.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn from_request(
    req: Request,
    state: &Arc<AuthorizationServerState>,
) -> Result<Self, Self::Rejection> {
    require_form_urlencoded_content_type(req.headers())?;
    // `resolve_client_credentials` needs only the `Authorization` header
    // value; capture it (owned) before the body read consumes the request.
    let authorization = req
        .headers()
        .get(AUTHORIZATION)
        .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
        .map(str::to_owned);
    let body = String::from_request(req, state).await.map_err(|_| {
        TokenError::bad_request(OAuthErrorCode::InvalidRequest, Some("Invalid request body"))
    })?;
    // Parse the grant payload before resolving credentials so a structurally
    // malformed body still reads as such, not as "Missing client_id".
    let payload: P = serde_urlencoded::from_str(&body).map_err(|_| {
        TokenError::bad_request(OAuthErrorCode::InvalidRequest, Some("Malformed payload"))
    })?;
    let presented = resolve_client_credentials(authorization.as_deref(), &body)?;
    let authenticated_client = LiveClientAuthenticator::from_state(state)
        .authenticate(&presented.credentials)
        .map_err(|error| ClientAuthenticationFailure {
            error,
            presented_via: presented.presented_via,
        })?;
    Ok(TokenRequest {
        payload,
        authenticated_client,
    })
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/token_request.rs line 22 · authorization-server in the code index

require_form_urlencoded_content_type

The tests build their headers with headers_with_content_type.

Reject unless the request carries Content-Type: application/x-www-form- urlencoded (RFC 6749 §3.2). Matches the media type only, tolerating a ; charset=… parameter and case differences per RFC 7231 §3.1.1.1.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn require_form_urlencoded_content_type(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Result<(), TokenError> {
    let is_form = headers
        .get(CONTENT_TYPE)
        .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
        .and_then(|value| value.split(';').next())
        .is_some_and(|media_type| media_type.trim().eq_ignore_ascii_case(FORM_URLENCODED));
    if is_form {
        Ok(())
    } else {
        Err(TokenError::bad_request(
            OAuthErrorCode::InvalidRequest,
            Some("Content-Type must be application/x-www-form-urlencoded"),
        ))
    }
}
}

http::routes::oauth::client_auth

A client presents its credentials one of two ways (RFC 6749 §2.3.1): the HTTP Basic Authorization header, or client_id and client_secret in the form body. The header wins; the body is the fallback; a secret both ways is refused, since §2.3 forbids more than one authentication method per request. Checking the credentials is the domain’s job; this file only reads them. The tests build the expected answer with presented and a Basic header with basic_authorization.

resolve_client_credentials

Resolve the client credentials for a token-style request from the request’s Authorization header value (None when absent) and the raw application/x-www-form-urlencoded body.

Precedence per RFC 6749 §2.3.1: a Basic Authorization header wins; body client_id/client_secret are the fallback. A body client_id alongside Basic is tolerated when it matches the Basic userid (some client libraries always send it); a body client_secret alongside Basic is a second authentication method and is rejected (§2.3).

Errors

  • ResolveClientCredentialsError::MalformedBasic when a Basic header is present but undecodable.
  • ResolveClientCredentialsError::InvalidRequest when credentials are presented both ways, the body client_id contradicts the Basic userid, or no client_id is present at all.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn resolve_client_credentials(
    authorization: Option<&str>,
    form_body: &str,
) -> Result<PresentedCredentials, ResolveClientCredentialsError> {
    // A structurally unparseable body simply contributes no credentials; the
    // grant-payload parse is responsible for rejecting malformed bodies. `mut`
    // so the success path can `take` the fields out (the zero-on-drop structs
    // forbid moving fields by plain access).
    let mut body: BodyClientCredentials = serde_urlencoded::from_str(form_body).unwrap_or_default();
    let basic =
        decode_basic_authorization_header(authorization).map_err(|MalformedBasicHeader| {
            ResolveClientCredentialsError::MalformedBasic(OAuthError::new(
                OAuthErrorCode::InvalidClient,
                Some("Malformed Basic authorization header"),
            ))
        })?;
    match basic {
        Some(mut basic) => {
            if body.client_secret.is_some() {
                return Err(ResolveClientCredentialsError::InvalidRequest(
                    OAuthError::new(
                        OAuthErrorCode::InvalidRequest,
                        Some("Multiple client authentication methods presented"),
                    ),
                ));
            }
            if body
                .client_id
                .as_deref()
                .is_some_and(|body_client_id| body_client_id != basic.client_id)
            {
                return Err(ResolveClientCredentialsError::InvalidRequest(
                    OAuthError::new(
                        OAuthErrorCode::InvalidRequest,
                        Some("client_id does not match Basic authorization header"),
                    ),
                ));
            }
            // `take` moves the fields out without a plain-access move, which the
            // zero-on-drop `BasicCredentials` forbids; the emptied `basic`
            // scrubs its now-empty buffers on drop.
            Ok(PresentedCredentials {
                credentials: ClientCredentials {
                    client_id: std::mem::take(&mut basic.client_id),
                    client_secret: Some(std::mem::take(&mut basic.client_secret)),
                },
                presented_via: ClientAuthenticationMethod::HttpBasic,
            })
        }
        None => match body.client_id.take() {
            Some(client_id) => Ok(PresentedCredentials {
                credentials: ClientCredentials {
                    client_id,
                    client_secret: body.client_secret.take(),
                },
                presented_via: ClientAuthenticationMethod::RequestBody,
            }),
            None => Err(ResolveClientCredentialsError::InvalidRequest(
                OAuthError::new(OAuthErrorCode::InvalidRequest, Some("Missing client_id")),
            )),
        },
    }
}
}

decode_basic_authorization_header

Decode the Authorization header value as Basic credentials per RFC 6749 §2.3.1: base64 → UTF-8 → split at the first colon → form-urlencoded-decode each half.

Ok(None) means no Basic attempt (authorization is None, or a different scheme such as Bearer — mirroring try_bearer_token_from_headers); Err(MalformedBasicHeader) means the client attempted Basic but the header is undecodable.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn decode_basic_authorization_header(
    authorization: Option<&str>,
) -> Result<Option<BasicCredentials>, MalformedBasicHeader> {
    let Some(value) = authorization else {
        return Ok(None);
    };
    let prefix = "basic ";
    // Case-insensitive prefix check against just the scheme bytes, matching
    // `try_bearer_token_from_headers` in `middleware/require_auth.rs`.
    if !value
        .get(..prefix.len())
        .is_some_and(|p| p.eq_ignore_ascii_case(prefix))
    {
        return Ok(None);
    }
    try_decode_basic_payload(value[prefix.len()..].trim()).map(Some)
}
}

try_decode_basic_payload

The fallible tail of decode_basic_authorization_header, split out so every decode failure collapses to the same MalformedBasicHeader.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn try_decode_basic_payload(
    encoded_payload: &str,
) -> Result<BasicCredentials, MalformedBasicHeader> {
    let decoded_bytes =
        base64::standard_decode(encoded_payload).map_err(|_| MalformedBasicHeader)?;
    // The decoded `id:secret` pair holds the plaintext secret; `Zeroizing` scrubs
    // it when this frame returns. `from_utf8` reuses `decoded_bytes`' buffer, so
    // wrapping the resulting string covers the raw bytes too. On the invalid-UTF-8
    // path `from_utf8` hands the bytes back inside the `FromUtf8Error`, which would
    // otherwise drop them unscrubbed — zeroize them before discarding the error.
    let decoded_pair = Zeroizing::new(String::from_utf8(decoded_bytes).map_err(|e| {
        e.into_bytes().zeroize();
        MalformedBasicHeader
    })?);
    let (encoded_client_id, encoded_client_secret) =
        decoded_pair.split_once(':').ok_or(MalformedBasicHeader)?;
    Ok(BasicCredentials {
        client_id: form_urlencoded_decode_credential_component(encoded_client_id)
            .ok_or(MalformedBasicHeader)?,
        client_secret: form_urlencoded_decode_credential_component(encoded_client_secret)
            .ok_or(MalformedBasicHeader)?,
    })
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/client_auth.rs lines 397–404 · authorization-server in the code index

form_urlencoded_decode_credential_component

Each half was form-encoded before the pair was base64-encoded, so + is a space and %2B a plus.

Decode one application/x-www-form-urlencoded value (+ → space, then percent-decode), per the encoding RFC 6749 §2.3.1 applies to each Basic credential half before base64.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn form_urlencoded_decode_credential_component(encoded_component: &str) -> Option<String> {
    // `+` → space first is safe: `%2B` contains no literal `+`, so an encoded
    // plus still round-trips through the percent-decode step. `plus_decoded` is a
    // full copy of the (possibly secret) component half, so wrap it in `Zeroizing`
    // to scrub it when this frame returns rather than leaving it on the heap. The
    // returned `String` is moved on into `BasicCredentials`, whose own drop scrubs
    // it.
    let plus_decoded = Zeroizing::new(encoded_component.replace('+', " "));
    percent_encoding::percent_decode_str(&plus_decoded)
        .decode_utf8()
        .ok()
        .map(std::borrow::Cow::into_owned)
}
}

A Basic header that won’t decode (bad base64, no colon, bytes that aren’t UTF-8, a percent-escape to a bad byte) is a failed authentication: a 401 carrying the WWW-Authenticate: Basic challenge.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn malformed_basic_header_is_invalid_client_with_challenge() {
    let malformed_payloads = [
        "Basic !!!not-base64!!!".to_string(),
        // valid base64 of a colon-less payload
        format!(
            "Basic {}",
            base64::standard_encode("no-colon-here".as_bytes())
        ),
        // valid base64 of invalid UTF-8 bytes
        format!(
            "Basic {}",
            base64::standard_encode(&[0xff, 0xfe, b':', b'x'])
        ),
        // a percent-escape that decodes to an invalid UTF-8 byte
        format!(
            "Basic {}",
            base64::standard_encode("app%ff:secret".as_bytes())
        ),
    ];
    for authorization in malformed_payloads {
        let err = resolve_client_credentials(Some(&authorization), "").unwrap_err();
        assert!(
            matches!(err, ResolveClientCredentialsError::MalformedBasic(_)),
            "expected MalformedBasic for {authorization:?}, got {err:?}"
        );
        let response = err.into_response();
        assert_eq!(response.status(), StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED);
        assert_eq!(
            response
                .headers()
                .get(header::WWW_AUTHENTICATE)
                .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok()),
            Some(BASIC_AUTH_CHALLENGE)
        );
    }
}
}

TokenError

Error half of the token / device-authorization / revocation endpoints’ Result-returning handlers (the OAuth-surface analogue of the Owner /authorization surface’s AuthorizationServerError). Every variant renders the matching RFC 6749 §5.2 response, cache-suppressed per §5.1, through IntoResponse — so a fallible step bails with ? instead of a match + return at each call site. Kept small (no embedded Response) so Result<_, TokenError> doesn’t trip clippy::result_large_err.

It is also the TokenRequest extractor’s rejection. Beyond the constructors, the rest come by conversion: a credential error and an authentication failure keep their own rendering, a store failure becomes the logged opaque 500, and a failed exchange maps onto RFC 6749 §5.2 and RFC 8628 §3.5.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum TokenError {
    /// An OAuth error body at its status: the §5.2 400s (`invalid_grant`,
    /// `unauthorized_client`, `invalid_request`, `invalid_scope`, `slow_down`,
    /// …) and the JSON-bodied 500 from a token-mint failure.
    Oauth(OAuthErrorResponse),
    /// Client-credential resolution failure (RFC 6749 §2.3) — renders its own
    /// response, possibly with a `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` challenge.
    ResolveCredentials(ResolveClientCredentialsError),
    /// Client-authentication failure — renders its own response, possibly with
    /// a `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` challenge.
    ClientAuth(ClientAuthenticationFailure),
    /// A logged, opaque, cache-suppressed 500 (e.g. a store read failed) —
    /// see [`InternalError`].
    Internal(InternalError),
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/internal.rs lines 243–250 · authorization-server in the code index

Conversions

The rest come by conversion. A credential error and an authentication failure keep their own rendering. A store failure (AuthorizationServerError) becomes the logged, opaque 500. A failed exchange (TokenExchangeError) maps onto RFC 6749 §5.2 and RFC 8628 §3.5: a wrong grant type is 400 unauthorized_client; a bad verifier and an InvalidGrantReason are 400 invalid_grant; a bad redirect_uri is 400 invalid_request; a device poll’s states are 400 with their own codes; a token that couldn’t be signed is 500 server_error.

invalid_grant_description

The wire doesn’t say which check refused a code. Wrong client, wrong redirect_uri, expired, wrong verifier and already redeemed all read “Invalid authorization grant”, since telling them apart would leak facts about a code that may be another client’s. The reason carries no secret, so it is logged, and the operator can still tell them apart.

The one wire description each family of refusal shares (see From<TokenExchangeError>).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn invalid_grant_description(reason: &InvalidGrantReason) -> &'static str {
    match reason {
        InvalidGrantReason::CodeNotFoundOrRedeemed
        | InvalidGrantReason::CodeClientMismatch { .. }
        | InvalidGrantReason::CodeRedirectMismatch { .. }
        | InvalidGrantReason::CodeExpired { .. }
        | InvalidGrantReason::PkceMismatch { .. } => "Invalid authorization grant",
        InvalidGrantReason::DeviceRequestNotFound { .. } => "Unknown device_code",
        InvalidGrantReason::DeviceCodeAlreadyRedeemed { .. } => "Device code already redeemed",
        InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenNotFound
        | InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenClientMismatch { .. }
        | InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenVanished { .. } => "Invalid refresh_token parameter",
        InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenExpired => "Refresh token has expired",
        InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenReplayed { .. }
        | InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenSessionRevoked { .. }
        | InvalidGrantReason::RefreshTokenClientRevoked { .. } => "Refresh token has been revoked",
    }
}
}

        ClientAuthenticationError::UnknownClient => "Unknown client_id",
        ClientAuthenticationError::Disabled => "Client is disabled",
        ClientAuthenticationError::SecretNotConfigured => "Client secret not configured",
        ClientAuthenticationError::SecretRequired => "Client secret required",
        ClientAuthenticationError::SecretMismatch => "Invalid client_secret",
        ClientAuthenticationError::Verification(error) => {
            tracing::error!(%error, "client secret verification failed");
            return server_error();
        }
        ClientAuthenticationError::Store(error) => {
            tracing::error!(%error, "client_by_id lookup failed");
            return server_error();
        }
    };
    let unauthorized = OAuthErrorResponse::new(
        StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED,
        OAuthErrorCode::InvalidClient,
        Some(description),
    );
    match self.presented_via {
        ClientAuthenticationMethod::HttpBasic => (
            [(header::WWW_AUTHENTICATE, BASIC_AUTH_CHALLENGE)],
            unauthorized,
        )
            .into_response(),
        ClientAuthenticationMethod::RequestBody => unauthorized.into_response(),
    }
}
}

TokenPayload

Body of an RFC 6749 / RFC 8628 token endpoint request, dispatched by the wire-level grant_type field. Client credentials are not parsed here — they may also arrive via the Authorization: Basic header, so the TokenRequest extractor owns both sources (any body client_id/client_secret fields are simply ignored by this enum).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum TokenPayload {
    /// Authorization-code grant — the client redeems a previously-issued
    /// `code` (RFC 6749 §4.1.3) along with the PKCE verifier.
    AuthorizationCode {
        /// The code `/oauth/authorize` sent to the client's redirect; it is
        /// redeemable once, by the client it was issued to.
        code: String,
        /// The PKCE verifier whose S256 hash is the request's
        /// `code_challenge` (RFC 7636 §4.5).
        code_verifier: String,
        /// Must be the `redirect_uri` the authorization request named
        /// (RFC 6749 §4.1.3).
        redirect_uri: String,
    },
    /// Device-code grant — the client polls with the `device_code` it was
    /// handed at `/device_authorization` (RFC 8628 §3.4).
    DeviceCode {
        /// The `device_code` `/oauth/device_authorization` answered with.
        device_code: String,
    },
    /// Refresh-token grant — the client trades its live refresh token for a
    /// fresh access token plus the refresh token's successor (RFC 6749 §6).
    RefreshToken {
        /// The refresh token being rotated; the trade spends it.
        refresh_token: String,
    },
}
}

fn main() {
fn token_payload_tolerates_unparsed_client_credential_fields() {
    let payload: TokenPayload = serde_urlencoded::from_str(
        "grant_type=refresh_token&client_id=app&client_secret=s3cret&refresh_token=tok",
    )
    .expect("unknown fields are ignored");

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/token_exchange/mod.rs lines 134–143 · authorization-server in the code index

handle_token_request

Each exchange goes to the token exchanger, with the authenticated client.

POST /oauth/token (RFC 6749 §3.2, RFC 8628 §3.4): hand the body’s grant to the matching exchange for the authenticated client, an authorization code with its PKCE verifier, a device code while the device polls, or a refresh token for an access token and its successor. A grant_type the endpoint doesn’t take fails to parse, so it is the extractor’s 400 invalid_request, “Malformed payload”.

Either outcome is uncached (§5.1): Ok through TokenResponse, Err through TokenError.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_token_request(
    exchanger: Live<LiveTokenExchanger>,
    request: TokenRequest<TokenPayload>,
) -> Response {
    let TokenRequest {
        payload,
        authenticated_client,
    } = request;
    let now = Utc::now();
    let exchanged = match payload {
        TokenPayload::AuthorizationCode {
            code,
            code_verifier,
            redirect_uri,
        } => exchanger.exchange_authorization_code(
            &authenticated_client,
            &PresentedAuthorizationCode {
                code: &code,
                code_verifier: &code_verifier,
                redirect_uri: &redirect_uri,
            },
            now,
        ),
        TokenPayload::DeviceCode { device_code } => {
            exchanger.exchange_device_code(&authenticated_client, &device_code, now)
        }
        TokenPayload::RefreshToken { refresh_token } => {
            exchanger.exchange_refresh_token(&authenticated_client, &refresh_token, now)
        }
    };
    let token = match exchanged {
        Ok(token) => token,
        Err(error) => return TokenError::from(error).into_response(),
    };
    token_response(token).into_response()
}
}

fn main() {
fn token_response(token: IssuedTokens) -> TokenResponse {
    TokenResponse {
        access_token: token.access_token,
        token_type: "Bearer".to_string(),
        expires_in: token.expires_in,
        scope: token.granted_scopes.join(" "),
        refresh_token: token.refresh_token,
        patient: token.patient,
    }
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_token_revocation_request(
    revoker: Live<LiveClientTokenRevoker>,
    request: TokenRequest<TokenRevocationPayload>,
) -> Result<StatusCode, TokenError> {
    let TokenRequest {
        payload,
        authenticated_client,
    } = request;

Consent Routes

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth_consents/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth_consents/get.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth_consents/approve.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth_consents/deny.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth_consents/ask_owner.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/devices/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/devices/get.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/devices/approve.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/devices/deny.rs

A request that needs a decision is a consent prompt, and these routes are where it is read and decided. There are two surfaces. The code-flow prompt is an app’s code request, keyed by the request’s id, which the consent card shows. The device page’s prompt is keyed by the short user code the device page asks for: a device’s request through the device flow, or a browser asking to be paired (the polled requests).

Both surfaces live under /authorization, behind the session gate, and no answer is cached. Each handler acquires its capability through Scoped<…>: reading a prompt takes wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.r, deciding one takes wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.u, and a token without the scope gets a 403 naming it. The Owner holds both. A paired browser holds only what its pairing granted, so it may be able to read a prompt it can’t decide.

The rules of a decision (what an approval may grant, the acknowledgement, the patient, the race with another surface) belong to the capability: OAuth Consents for the code flow and Device Consents for the device page. The routes read the body, pass the server’s clock, and put the outcome on the wire, as a ConsentResult. The Consent Card, Approval Scopes and Device Code integration tests hold them end to end.

http::routes::oauth_consents

router

Asking the Owner raises a request for the Owner’s attention, so that route alone is wrapped in the deferred start limit the caller passes in.

The /oauth-consents route table. defer_start_limit wraps the ask-owner route, which raises a request for the Owner and so spends from the authorization start limit (see defer_authorization_start_limit).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn router(
    defer_start_limit: impl Fn(
        MethodRouter<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>>,
    ) -> MethodRouter<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>>,
) -> Router<Arc<AuthorizationServerState>> {
    Router::new()
        .route("/oauth-consents/{id}", get::route())
        .route("/oauth-consents/{id}/approve", approve::route())
        .route("/oauth-consents/{id}/deny", deny::route())
        .route(
            "/oauth-consents/{id}/ask-owner",
            defer_start_limit(ask_owner::route()),
        )
}
}

fn main() {
async fn handle_get_oauth_consent(
    consents: Scoped<LiveConsentReader>,
    Path(id): Path<String>,
) -> Result<Json<OAuthConsent>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let OAuthConsentView {
        pending_request,

        presented_client_change,
        missing_approval_scopes,
    } = consents.oauth_consent(&id, Utc::now())?;

            .approval()
            .and_then(|approval| approval.patient.clone()),

        client_name,
        scopes: pending_request.requested_scopes,
        redirect_uri: pending_request.redirect_uri,
        pre_approved_scopes: pending_request.pre_approved_scopes,
        registration: presented_client_change.into(),
        missing_approval_scopes,
    }))
}
}

from

Render the domain change onto the wire.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn from(registration: PresentedClientChange) -> Self {
    match registration {
        PresentedClientChange::NoChange => ClientRegistrationBody::Registered,
        PresentedClientChange::WouldCreate => ClientRegistrationBody::New,
        PresentedClientChange::WouldWiden {
            redirect_uri_is_new,
            unregistered_requested_scopes: new_scopes,
        } => ClientRegistrationBody::Changed {
            redirect_uri_is_new,
            new_scopes,
        },
    }
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth_consents/approve.rs lines 29–40 · authorization-server in the code index

handle_approve_oauth_consent

POST /authorization/oauth-consents/{id}/approve — the Owner approves a consent prompt, granting a (narrowed) scope set and minting the authorization code the polling endpoint hands back to the client. Gated by LiveConsentDecider (scope wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.u), which also carries the approver’s own scopes: an approval delegating a resource scope beyond them is rejected with a 403. Approving a prompt whose client, redirect, or scopes are outside the current registration without acknowledged_registration_change is rejected with a 409 and writes nothing, as is an approval naming a patient other than the one the request’s SMART launch binds. The write scope lives in the consent capability’s approve_oauth_consent.

The answers:

  • 200, "status":"approved": the code is issued; redirect is the app’s callback carrying it and the app’s state, for the card to leave for.
  • 200, "status":"denied": nothing was granted, the requesting browser’s session has ended, or the app was disabled since; the request is denied and redirect carries access_denied.
  • 403: the approver lacks an approval scope, or a ticked resource scope is beyond their own grant. Nothing is written.
  • 409: the registration change wasn’t acknowledged, or the body names a patient other than the one the launch bound. Nothing is written.
  • 404: no live code-flow prompt has this id.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn handle_approve_oauth_consent(
    consents: Scoped<LiveConsentDecider>,
    Path(id): Path<String>,
    Json(body): Json<ApproveOAuthConsentBody>,
) -> Result<Json<ConsentResult>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let outcome = consents.approve_oauth_consent(
        &id,
        ApproveOAuthConsentInput {
            owner_approved_scopes: body.approved_scopes,
            patient: body.patient,
            acknowledged_registration_change: body.acknowledged_registration_change,
        },
        generate_authorization_code,
        Utc::now(),
    )?;
    Ok(Json(outcome.into()))
}
}

handle_ask_owner

A browser that can read a prompt but not approve it hands it to the Owner. The capability asks the start limit the layer deferred onto the request, and only when it is about to raise.

POST /authorization/oauth-consents/{id}/ask-owner — a browser that can read a consent prompt but not approve it hands it to the server’s Owner (scope wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.r, as reading it takes): the request no longer counts as decidable in the browser that made it, so the host notifies the Owner. Decides nothing. Raising a request spends from the authorization start limit, as starting one the Owner is asked about does: 429 Too Many Requests when refused, the request left as it was. Raising one already raised spends nothing. 204 No Content, or 404 once the request is no longer pending.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn handle_ask_owner(
    consents: Scoped<LiveConsentRaiser>,
    Extension(deferred_start_limit): Extension<DeferredStartLimit>,
    Path(id): Path<String>,
) -> Result<Response, AuthorizationServerError> {
    Ok(
        match consents.raise_for_owner(&id, || deferred_start_limit.admits(), Utc::now())? {
            OwnerRaising::Raised | OwnerRaising::AlreadyRaised => {
                StatusCode::NO_CONTENT.into_response()
            }
            OwnerRaising::StartLimited => start_limited_response(),
        },
    )
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn handle_get_device_consent(
    consents: Scoped<LiveConsentReader>,
    Path(user_code): Path<String>,
) -> Result<Json<DeviceConsent>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let DeviceConsentView {
        request,
        client_name,
        starting_scopes,
        approvable_scopes,
        missing_approval_scopes,
    } = consents.device_consent(&user_code, Utc::now())?;
    let (kind, device_name) = match &request {
        PolledRequest::Pairing(pairing_request) => (
            DeviceConsentKind::Browser,
            Some(pairing_request.browser_name.clone()),
        ),
        PolledRequest::Device(device_request) => (
            DeviceConsentKind::Device,
            device_request.device_name.clone(),
        ),
    };
    Ok(Json(DeviceConsent {
        kind,
        user_code,
        client_id: request.client_id().to_owned(),
        client_name,
        device_name,
        starting_scopes,
        allowed_scopes: approvable_scopes,
        missing_approval_scopes,
    }))
}
}

These routes are the Owner’s view of what they have let in, and the switches to take it back: the standing grants apps hold, the apps themselves, and the browsers the server has signed in. The Owner’s access-management screens call them with the Owner’s token.

They live under /authorization, behind require_valid_session, and are uncached. Each handler takes its capability through Scoped<…>, which needs one scope per resource and permission: wildflower/Grant.r and .d, wildflower/Client.r and .u, wildflower/BrowserSession.r and .d. A token without it gets a 403 naming the missing scope, before the handler runs. The Owner’s scopes cover every one of them. The capability is the only way to the store, so the scope can’t be skipped.

PATCH /authorization/clients/{clientId} — disable (stamped with the server’s now, whatever time is sent) or re-enable a client by writing its disabledAt; answers with the client as stored. A disabled client is refused at /oauth/authorize and /oauth/token. Idempotent (a client that already has a disabledAt keeps it). #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) async fn handle_update_client(
    clients: Scoped<LiveClientsDisabler>,
    Path(client_id): Path<String>,
    Json(body): Json<UpdateClientBody>,
) -> Result<Json<ClientBody>, AuthorizationServerError> {
    let stamp = body.disabled_at.map(|_sent| Utc::now());
    let updated = clients.set_disabled_at(&client_id, stamp)?;
    Ok(Json(updated.into()))
}
}

Session Routes

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/session.rs

Four routes are about tokens themselves rather than what they unlock. A caller reads back its own session and ends it. The Owner revokes tokens, by id or by app. Anyone fetches the public keys that verify every token this server signs.

The first three live under /authorization, behind require_valid_session: no valid, unrevoked bearer token, no answer but a 401. The session read and logout are self-service: a caller acting on its own session needs no scope, so they take their capability through Authenticated<…>, which hands over the caller’s verified claims and nothing else. Revoking other tokens is an Owner’s power, and takes wildflower/Token.d through Scoped<…>. The key set is public, and sits outside /authorization.

http::routes::session

GET /authorization/session — the caller reading back their own session.

Self-service, authN-only, exactly like logout: every field is derived from the token the caller already presented, or from the browser session it was minted under, so the response can’t disclose anything about another caller, and no Scoped<…> capability gates it — the /authorization mount’s require_valid_session gate is the whole authorization it needs. That is load-bearing rather than merely convenient: the callers who need this most are under-scoped sessions (one that just took a 403 InsufficientScope), and any admin scope gate would lock exactly those out of reading their own scopes.

The device-login screen reads it to seed the scope picker from the session’s real scopes rather than a hard-coded preset — the device flow mints a whole new grant, so a step-up seeded from anything narrower silently drops access the caller already had. The server’s own pages read it for when this browser’s session expires, which they show as “Signed in until”. See the Scope-Gated Endpoints How-To.

http::routes::logout

POST /authorization/logout — ends the caller’s session by revoking the presented access token and redirecting to the hosted launcher.

Self-service, authN-only: logout is a caller ending their own session, not an admin resource operation, so it takes no scope — the /authorization mount’s require_valid_session gate (any valid, non-revoked bearer) is the whole authorization it needs, and it acts on the already-verified claims through the authenticated-only LiveSessionEnder rather than re-verifying. The access token is a stateless JWT that keeps its own short TTL; the client forgetting it ends the session in that client, so logout also revokes the presented token’s jti in the shared store, closing the window a leaked copy could otherwise ride until exp.

handle_logout

The session ender is built from the claims require_valid_session already verified, and end denylists the token’s jti. Denylisting is best-effort: a token with no jti or expiry has nothing to denylist, and a store failure is logged, never answered. Either way the browser goes to the hosted launcher with a 303 See Other, which turns the POST into a GET.

POST /authorization/logout: denylist the presented token’s jti through Authenticated<LiveSessionEnder>, then answer 303 See Other to the hosted launcher’s root.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn handle_logout(session: Authenticated<LiveSessionEnder>, pages: LauncherPages) -> Response {
    // Revoke the presented session token so a leaked copy can't outlive the
    // logout. Best-effort by design: a store hiccup must never fail the logout.
    session.end();
    // `303 See Other` → the hosted launcher's root (this server serves no UI of
    // its own); `303` downgrades a `POST` logout to a `GET`.
    Redirect::to(pages.root_url()).into_response()
}
}

http::routes::revocations

POST /authorization/revocations — the token-revocation control surface. Acquired through the LiveTokenRevoker facade (scope wildflower/Token.d): a caller must cover the Token delete scope — which an owner’s wildflower/*.cruds does — to revoke, else a 403.

Two modes, exactly one per request:

  • Per-token — { "jti": "…", "expiresAt": "<RFC3339>" } denylists a single token until its own expiry (the expiresAt lets the background sweep drop the row once the token would have expired anyway).
  • Bulk, per subject — { "subject": "<client_id>" } bumps the subject’s revocation epoch to just past now (see revoke_subject_as_of_now), invalidating every token that subject holds issued at or before the call — including one minted in the current (second-granular) second. subject is the sub claim (the client_id), so revocation is per client, not per device.

The daily sweep keeps a denylisted jti until the longest token this server mints, issued at the moment of revocation, would have expired (see setup_authorization_server). So an expiresAt that is too early can’t free a live token.

fn main() {
fn into_revocation(self) -> Result<Revocation, RevocationError> {
    match (self.jti, self.subject) {
        (Some(jti), None) => {
            let expires_at = self.expires_at.ok_or_else(|| {
                RevocationError::bad_request(
                    "MissingExpiresAt",
                    "revoking by `jti` requires `expiresAt` (the token's own expiry)",
                )
            })?;
            Ok(Revocation::Token { jti, expires_at })
        }
        (None, Some(subject)) => Ok(Revocation::Subject { subject }),
        (Some(_), Some(_)) => Err(RevocationError::bad_request(
            "AmbiguousRevocation",
            "provide exactly one of `jti` or `subject`, not both",
        )),
        (None, None) => Err(RevocationError::bad_request(
            "EmptyRevocation",
            "provide either `jti` (with `expiresAt`) or `subject`",
        )),
    }
}
}

enum Revocation {

handle_create_revocation

Each mode goes through the token revoker: revoke_jti or revoke_subject. A jti whose expiresAt has already passed is refused too: the token is already dead, and denylisting it would only leave a dead row.

POST /authorization/revocations, through Scoped<LiveTokenRevoker> (wildflower/Token.d): denylist one token or bump a subject’s epoch. 204 No Content on success; 400 with error and detail for a body that names neither mode, both, a jti without expiresAt, or an expiresAt already past.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn handle_create_revocation(
    tokens: Scoped<LiveTokenRevoker>,
    Json(request): Json<RevocationRequest>,
) -> Result<StatusCode, RevocationError> {
    match request.into_revocation()? {
        Revocation::Token { jti, expires_at } => {
            // Reject an `expiresAt` already in the past: the token is expired
            // (so verification rejects it anyway) and denylisting it just leaves
            // a dead row. A clear 400 surfaces the stale/mistyped value rather
            // than silently no-op'ing. (A too-early-but-future `expiresAt` can't
            // prematurely un-revoke a live token — the store's `purge_expired`
            // retention floor guards that.)
            if expires_at <= Utc::now() {
                return Err(RevocationError::bad_request(
                    "ExpiresAtInPast",
                    "`expiresAt` is in the past; the token has already expired",
                ));
            }
            tokens.revoke_jti(&jti, expires_at)?;
        }
        Revocation::Subject { subject } => tokens.revoke_subject(&subject)?,
    }
    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}
}

Assembly

The layers before this one are written against traits: the domain against the store port, the capabilities against any GrantStore, the routes against Live… names. Assembly is where the concrete pieces are chosen and the server is handed to the host: the SQLite store, the shared revocation store, the host’s configuration and its say over who may start requests. Nothing here decides what anyone may do. It decides what each rule is built from.

Setup is the one call the host makes at boot, setup_authorization_server, and what it takes and gives back: the configuration, the constants naming the server’s own clients and the Owner’s authority, the background sweeps it starts, and what the crate root re-exports for the host.

Live Bindings is the shared state every request is served from, and the rule that binds a generic capability to the concrete store: each binding lifts only the handles its capability needs out of that state.

Access Bindings are the Owner’s /authorization capabilities, one per resource and permission, each behind the scope its extractor checks before the capability exists.

OAuth Bindings are the /oauth front door’s capabilities, which no token unlocks, and three in-process handles for the host: the launch minter, the sign-in code minter and the pending-consent watcher.

Session Bindings are the capabilities about the caller’s own token: the token verifier every gate runs, and hands to the host’s FHIR server, and the self-service reads and revokes that need a token but no scope.

Ports and Adapters are what the domain needs from outside the store, notifying the host of a pending consent, revoking and checking tokens, and asking whether a request may start, and what implements each.

Seeding is what exists at boot and why: the signing key, the server’s own clients, and in debug builds the first-party apps’ dev clients.

Setup

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/lib.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/config.rs

The authorization server isn’t a process of its own. It is one slice of the Wildflower host, and the host builds it once, at boot, with one call: setup_authorization_server. The host hands over what only it has: the shared database, the shared revocation store, its configuration, a channel to hear about the Owner prompt on, and its say over how fast requests may start. It gets back a router to merge, the shared state its own gates need, and four in-process handles.

This page is that seam: the configuration, the constants that name the server’s own clients and the Owner’s authority, the call itself, the background sweeps it starts, and what the crate root re-exports for the host.

crate

The Wildflower authorization server: the OAuth 2.0 and SMART App Launch authorization server in front of the Owner’s FHIR server. It decides which apps, devices and browsers may reach the Owner’s data, asks the Owner when it must, and signs the access tokens the FHIR server checks.

The host builds one with setup_authorization_server and merges its router: /oauth/* for apps, devices and browsers on their way in, /authorization/* for the Owner’s own pages, and /.well-known/jwks.json for anyone checking a token. domain holds the rules, db the SQLite store, and http the routes that adapt between the two.

Every signed-in browser’s token is issued to the browser-session client. So revoking this subject signs every browser out, while one browser is signed out by revoking its session (its token’s sid) or its token’s jti. Neither sign-in nor pairing is an OAuth flow, so the client is seeded with no grant type, and /oauth/token never mints its token.

client_id of the browser-session client: the browsers the server has signed in. The Owner’s is signed in by the host app on its own device with a same-device sign-in code at /oauth/sign-in; any other browser pairs at /oauth/pair, showing a code the Owner approves. Each such browser holds a token issued to this client (its sub), so revoking the client’s subject signs every browser out, and one browser is signed out by revoking its browser session (its token’s sid) or its token’s jti. Like WILDFLOWER_HOST_APP_CLIENT_ID, it is an essential client: it can’t be disabled. Seeded at boot by crate::setup_authorization_server with OWNER_SCOPES, the most a browser session may hold, and no grant type; it takes part in no OAuth flow, since neither sign-in nor pairing is one.

The Owner’s authority

A token covering the widest scopes covers every per-resource scope an /authorization route asks for, so the Owner passes every gate. The Owner’s scopes add wildflower/launch, which is a known scope rather than a resource scope, so the wildflower/* wildcard doesn’t cover it and it has to be listed.

The maximal-access scopes that mark an Owner: full system FHIR access (system/*.cruds) and full Wildflower-resource access (wildflower/*.cruds). An Owner token covers every one of these, so it covers every per-resource /authorization/* scope the scope-gated extractors require — the fail-closed owner default.

];

authorization-server-rust/src/lib.rs lines 155–157 · authorization-server in the code index

setup_authorization_server

Build the server over the host’s database, and start it working. In order:

  1. Open and seed the store (open_and_seed_store): run the migrations, make sure a signing key is active, and rewrite the server’s own clients.
  2. Build the shared state (AuthorizationServerState) from the config, with a stale-session cutoff at the run’s start. The host ends an Owner session once the server’s last launch view closes, so one no open view holds is one whose ending was missed, as across the app’s exit, or failed. The run’s start cuts off the Owner sessions earlier runs signed in, except those the host’s launch views still open hold: setup is handed those views’ sign-in codes, whichever run minted them, and exempts the sessions they signed in, so the restart a return from a suspend brings on iOS keeps an open view signed in. The others are stale, and nothing is written for them, so a store that can’t be written then doesn’t keep the server from starting. Paired sessions stand.
  3. Publish the Owner prompt on owner_approval_tx. The channel’s value doesn’t survive a restart, but the row does, so a request left pending across a restart is in the server’s first status, and the host notifies about it.
  4. Start the background sweeps below.
  5. Build the router, whose routes are at /.well-known/jwks.json, /oauth/* and /authorization/*. The host merges it as it is.
  6. Build the in-process handles the host keeps.

The host builds revocation_store once and passes the same store to the FHIR server’s adapter, so the authorization server’s gates and the FHIR server read one denylist. Where no visitor can reach the server, the host passes AdmitEveryAuthorizationStart as the start gate.

Build the authorization-server-rust HTTP surface over the host-owned diesel connection pool (the same app-wide wildflowerhealthio_persistence::open_pool pool the other diesel-backed slices ride). Runs idempotent bootstrap (schema migrations, signing-key seed, essential-client seed), and:

  • publishes the OwnerPrompt, the newest request awaiting the Owner (device-code and authorization-code requests and browser pairings alike), on owner_approval_tx. On the Tauri host, the server’s run reports it as its detail, which the base’s server status carries and from which the host notifies each new request. Seeding at boot means a request that was pending across an app restart is still reported (the row survived in SQLite, the in-memory watch value didn’t);
  • cuts off, at the run’s start, the same-device sessions earlier runs signed in, except those open_views_sign_in_codes signed in: the codes of the host’s launch views still open, whichever run minted them. The host ends a same-device session once the last of the server’s launch views has closed, so a session no open view holds is one whose ending was missed, as across the app’s exit, or failed. So the StaleSessionCutoff invalidates sessions before the run’s start, with the open views’ sessions exempt: it makes the others stale, writing nothing, so a store that can’t be written doesn’t keep the server from starting, and the browser is sent through sign-in again, which the host’s next launch does. Paired sessions stand;
  • returns a Router whose routes are at /.well-known/jwks.json, /oauth/*, and /authorization/* (authenticated bearer JWT + per-resource scope gates via the Scoped<…> extractors) — the slice owns its mount paths so the caller just .merge()s;
  • returns the Arc<AuthorizationServerState> the caller passes to authorization_server_auth_middleware to gate fhir-r4-rust;
  • returns the LaunchContextMinter an in-process launcher mints each SMART App Launch launch value through, which /oauth/authorize then consumes;
  • returns the SameDeviceSignInCodeMinter the host mints each same-device sign-in code through, which /oauth/sign-in then redeems, and which ends the sessions codes signed in when the host asks;
  • returns the PendingConsentWatcher the host waits on for a pending consent it opened to be decided or expire;
  • returns the InProcessTokenVerifier the host’s FHIR server verifies each bearer through, in-process.

authorization_start_gate says whether a request may start an authorization request (GET /oauth/authorize, POST /oauth/device_authorization): asked for every one that carries no live browser session, which is answered 429 when it refuses. Pass AdmitEveryAuthorizationStart where no visitor reaches the server.

Every token this server mints carries the server’s origin (AuthorizationServerConfig::server_origin) as both iss and aud, and the bearer gates accept no other. See docs/Origins/Explanation.md.

revocation_store is the shared token-revocation store the host builds once on the shared database and threads into both this setup and fhir-r4-rust’s HFS adapter, so the auth gate and the FHIR server read one denylist/epoch store.

Errors

Returns an error if opening and seeding the store fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn setup_authorization_server(
    pool: DieselPool,
    revocation_store: RevocationStore,
    config: &AuthorizationServerConfig,
    owner_approval_tx: watch::Sender<Option<OwnerPrompt>>,
    authorization_start_gate: Arc<dyn AuthorizationStartGate>,
    open_views_sign_in_codes: &[SameDeviceSignInCode],
) -> anyhow::Result<AuthorizationServer> {
    let store = seeding::open_and_seed_store(
        pool,
        &config.host_app_client_scopes,
        &config.fhir_ui_client_id,
        &config.server_origin,
    )?;
    let server_origin: Arc<str> =
        wildflowerhealthio_shared_structures::origin_string(&config.server_origin).into();
    let same_device_sign_in_codes = Arc::new(SameDeviceSignInCodes::new());
    let stale_session_cutoff = Arc::new(StaleSessionCutoff::new(
        Utc::now(),
        open_views_sign_in_codes
            .iter()
            .filter_map(SameDeviceSignInCode::signed_in_sid)
            .collect(),
    ));
    let (pending_consents_recomputed_tx, pending_consents_recomputed_rx) = watch::channel(());
    let state = Arc::new(AuthorizationServerState {
        store: store.clone(),
        revocation_store: revocation_store.clone(),
        server_origin: server_origin.clone(),
        device_page: Arc::new(http::device_page_url(&config.server_origin)),
        launcher_base: config.launcher_base.clone(),
        owner_approval_tx,
        pending_consents_recomputed_tx,
        owner_grant: Grant::new(OWNER_SCOPES.to_vec()),
        same_device_sign_in_codes: same_device_sign_in_codes.clone(),
        sign_in_destinations: Arc::new(SignInDestinations::new(
            config.server_origin.clone(),
            config.launcher_base.clone(),
            config.authorization_app_base.clone(),
            config.launcher_url.clone(),
            config.authorization_url.clone(),
        )),
        authorization_start_gate,
        last_seen_throttle: Arc::new(LastSeenThrottle::new()),
        stale_session_cutoff,
    });
    // Publish the Owner prompt from SQLite so a request that was
    // pending across an app restart is reported in the run's first detail —
    // the `watch` value itself doesn't survive the process, but the row
    // does.
    ports::OwnerApproval::republish_active(state.as_ref());
    spawn_device_consent_reaper(state.clone());
    // Reclaim the authorization server rows past their retention window: once at startup, then
    // daily.
    spawn_retention_sweep(store);
    // Reclaim expired denylist rows: once at startup, then daily.
    spawn_revocation_purge(revocation_store);
    let router = http::router(state.clone());
    let launch_context_minter = LaunchContextMinter::new(state.store.clone());
    let in_process_token_verifier = InProcessTokenVerifier::new(&state);
    let same_device_sign_in_code_minter =
        SameDeviceSignInCodeMinter::new(same_device_sign_in_codes, state.store.clone());
    let pending_consent_watcher =
        PendingConsentWatcher::new(state.store.clone(), pending_consents_recomputed_rx);
    Ok(AuthorizationServer {
        router,
        state,
        launch_context_minter,
        same_device_sign_in_code_minter,
        pending_consent_watcher,
        in_process_token_verifier,
    })
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/lib.rs lines 191–215 · authorization-server in the code index

The background sweeps

setup_authorization_server starts three loops on the runtime. None changes what the server honours: each either reclaims rows the read paths already refuse, or republishes what the store already says. After a long pause such as a suspend, each runs once rather than catching up on the ticks it missed.

The reaper republishes the Owner prompt, because republishing otherwise happens only after a write, and an idle server would go on advertising a request that has expired.

How often the background reaper recomputes the OwnerPrompt, so the watch channel drops a request whose expires_at has passed without any HTTP mutation arriving to trigger a republish. Picked well under the 5-minute DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_TTL so a freshly-expired request clears within seconds; the recompute is two LIMIT 1 reads, one per request table, and the watch sender suppresses no-op publishes.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
const DEVICE_CONSENT_REAPER_INTERVAL: std::time::Duration = std::time::Duration::from_secs(15);
}

authorization-server-rust/src/lib.rs line 187 · authorization-server in the code index

Spawn the background reaper that periodically recomputes the OwnerPrompt. Mutation-driven republishing alone leaves the watch advertising a request whose row has expired in the meantime — without this task, an idle host stays stuck on the now-expired request until some unrelated handler happens to write. The reaper drops the stale request within DEVICE_CONSENT_REAPER_INTERVAL, and send_if_modified suppresses ticks that leave it unchanged so an idle server publishes nothing.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn spawn_device_consent_reaper(state: Arc<AuthorizationServerState>) {
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let mut ticks = interval(DEVICE_CONSENT_REAPER_INTERVAL);
        // A long pause (suspend/resume, debugger break) must not cause a
        // burst of catch-up republishes — one tick after the gap is the
        // right behaviour.
        ticks.set_missed_tick_behavior(MissedTickBehavior::Delay);
        // The first tick fires immediately; the boot-time republish in
        // `setup_authorization_server` already covered that, so consume it before
        // the loop.
        ticks.tick().await;
        loop {
            ticks.tick().await;
            ports::OwnerApproval::republish_active(state.as_ref());
        }
    });
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/lib.rs line 179 · authorization-server in the code index

Spawn the background sweep that deletes the authorization server rows past their retention window — once at startup (the interval’s immediate first tick), then every RETENTION_SWEEP_INTERVAL. The windows and their rationale live in domain::retention.

Space reclamation only: every row it touches is already past expires_at (or, for a browser session, its revoked_at) and rejected by the read paths, so nothing here changes what the server honours. A failed sweep is logged and retried next tick.

Runs on spawn_blocking rather than a runtime worker: pool.get() alone can park for r2d2’s 30s connection timeout, and the sweep then holds one write transaction across a delete per table.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn spawn_retention_sweep(store: SqliteGrantStore) {
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let mut ticks = interval(RETENTION_SWEEP_INTERVAL);
        // A long pause (suspend/resume) must not queue up catch-up sweeps —
        // one tick after the gap reclaims the same rows anyway.
        ticks.set_missed_tick_behavior(MissedTickBehavior::Delay);
        loop {
            // First tick is immediate → startup sweep; then daily.
            ticks.tick().await;
            // Cheap clone (the pool is an `Arc` inside) so the loop keeps its own
            // handle for the next tick.
            let sweep_store = store.clone();
            let swept = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || {
                domain::retention::purge_expired(&sweep_store, Utc::now())
            })
            .await;
            match swept {
                Ok(Ok(purged)) if !purged.is_empty() => tracing::info!(
                    refresh_token_families = purged.refresh_token_families,
                    code_authorization_requests = purged.code_authorization_requests,
                    user_code_requests = purged.user_code_requests,
                    authorization_codes = purged.authorization_codes,
                    browser_sessions = purged.browser_sessions,
                    "swept the authorization server rows past their retention window",
                ),
                Ok(Ok(_)) => {}
                Ok(Err(error)) => {
                    tracing::warn!(%error, "the authorization server retention sweep failed")
                }
                Err(error) => {
                    tracing::warn!(%error, "the authorization server retention sweep task failed")
                }
            }
        }
    });
}
}

How often the background sweep drops denylist rows whose token has already expired (mirrors the refresh-token/device-code reaping cadence). The first sweep runs at startup; thereafter daily. A revoked-then-expired jti is rejected by expiry validation regardless, so this only reclaims space.

const REVOCATION_PURGE_INTERVAL: std::time::Duration = std::time::Duration::from_secs(24 * 60 * 60);
}

authorization-server-rust/src/lib.rs line 172 · authorization-server in the code index

Spawn the background sweep that purges expired rows from the revocation denylist — once at startup (the interval’s immediate first tick) then every REVOCATION_PURGE_INTERVAL. Purely space reclamation: an expired jti is already rejected by expiry validation, denylisted or not.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn spawn_revocation_purge(revocation_store: RevocationStore) {
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let mut ticks = interval(REVOCATION_PURGE_INTERVAL);
        ticks.set_missed_tick_behavior(MissedTickBehavior::Delay);
        loop {
            // First tick is immediate → startup purge; then daily.
            ticks.tick().await;
            // Retention floor = the longest access token we mint (a browser
            // session's token lives as long as the session, at most a day,
            // past the 15-min OAuth `ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL`), so a denylist row is
            // never dropped while its token could still be live — even if the
            // `/authorization/revocations` caller supplied a too-early
            // `expiresAt`. See `RevocationStore::purge_expired`.
            match revocation_store.purge_expired(Utc::now(), LONGEST_BROWSER_SESSION_TTL) {
                Ok(purged) if purged > 0 => {
                    tracing::info!(purged, "swept expired revoked jtis");
                }
                Ok(_) => {}
                Err(error) => tracing::warn!(%error, "revoked-jti sweep failed"),
            }
        }
    });
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/lib.rs lines 355–377 · authorization-server in the code index

What the crate root re-exports

The host imports the crate root, not its modules. Beyond the items above, the root re-exports:

  • the store: SqliteGrantStore, the persistence port GrantStore and GrantTx, and DieselPool, so the host can name the pool type without depending on diesel;
  • the Owner prompt: OwnerPrompt, what the host is told about, and ConsentKey, what it waits on;
  • the gates and cookies: authorization_server_auth_middleware and AuthorizationServerAuthMiddleware, ensure_bearer_header, AuthorizationServerState, and the browser-session cookie’s name, header and helpers;
  • the in-process handles: LaunchContextMinter, SameDeviceSignInCodeMinter, PendingConsentWatcher, InProcessTokenVerifier;
  • the start gate: AuthorizationStartGate, which the host implements, and AdmitEveryAuthorizationStart;
  • grantable_admin_scopes, every admin scope the /authorization surface enforces;
  • in debug builds only, seed_dev_app_clients.

The modules config, crypto_util, db, domain and http stay public too: the integration tests reach into some of them, and the crate’s public doc links point into them.

Live Bindings

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/live_bindings/mod.rs

Covers authorization-server-rust/src/live_bindings/state.rs

The capabilities in domain/ are generic over the store, so their unit tests run against the in-memory fake. The live bindings are where they meet the real thing: each names a capability over the concrete SqliteGrantStore, and says how to build it from the server’s shared state. A handler never names the state. It names a Live… binding in its extractor, and the extractor builds the capability, or refuses the request first.

A binding lifts only the handles its capability needs out of the state, never the whole state, so domain/ depends neither on http nor on the concrete adapters. The bindings come in three groups, one page each, by how a handler acquires them:

GroupAcquired throughUnlocked by
AccessScoped<…>The caller’s scopes, checked before the capability exists.
OAuthLive<…>Nothing: the /oauth front door. Where there is a gate, it is a proof the method takes.
SessionAuthenticated<…>, Live<…>A verified token alone, for a caller acting on its own session; or nothing, for the token verifier itself.

The OAuth and Session groups also hold the in-process handles setup_authorization_server gives the host.

live_bindings::state

The shared authorization server runtime state — the router state every handler is built over, and the composition point that wires the concrete adapters (SqliteGrantStore, RevocationStore) to the domain ports. It lives at the crate root (not under crate::http) deliberately: the scope-gated capabilities in domain/ are built from it, and domain/ must not depend on crate::http. The struct itself is axum-free.

The port trait impls that adapt this state to the domain seams live in crate::adapters, and the bindings that name the concrete SqliteGrantStore live in the sibling crate::live_bindings modules — so the generic, store-agnostic capabilities in domain/ never mention a concrete adapter.

AuthorizationServerState

Everything the server shares across requests, built once by setup_authorization_server. The host gets it back inside an Arc and passes it to its bearer gate without looking inside.

Shared state threaded through every authorization server handler and lifted into the scope-gated capabilities. Opaque to callers outside the crate — the host receives one (inside an Arc) from crate::setup_authorization_server and passes it back into crate::authorization_server_auth_middleware without looking inside.

    /// [`TokenVerifier`](crate::domain::capabilities::session::TokenVerifier))

live_bindings

The composition layer — where the generic, store-agnostic capabilities in crate::domain::capabilities meet the concrete SqliteGrantStore and the Arc<AuthorizationServerState> router state. It lives at the crate root (not under crate::http) so domain/ can be built from it without depending on the transport layer.

  • state holds the AuthorizationServerState struct.
  • crate::adapters holds the port trait impls that adapt the state / revocation store to the domain seams.
  • access binds the scope-gated /authorization capabilities (FixedScopeCapability / Capability), acquired through Scoped<…>: the caller’s scopes unlock each, checked before the capability exists.
  • oauth binds the pre-auth /oauth front door (FromState, acquired through Live<…>), which no claims unlock: where there is a gate, it is a proof the method takes, such as an authenticated client. It also holds the in-process faces crate::setup_authorization_server hands out: the LaunchContextMinter (the launchers outside the authorization server mint launches through it), the SameDeviceSignInCodeMinter (the host mints /oauth/sign-in codes through it, and ends the sessions they signed in) and the PendingConsentWatcher (the host waits on a consent through it).
  • session binds the token verifier both authN gates run (and its in-process face, the InProcessTokenVerifier the host’s FHIR server verifies bearers with), which nothing unlocks, and the caller’s-own-session capabilities (AuthenticatedCapability, acquired through Authenticated<…>), which a verified token alone unlocks.

Each binding lifts the store and port handles out of the state (never the whole state), so domain/ stays free of both crate::http and the concrete adapter types. The Live… aliases are what the handlers name in Scoped<…>, Authenticated<…>, or Live<…>.

FromState

Handlers acquire one through the Live<F> extractor; the auth middleware and the token request’s extractor build theirs directly.

A live capability built from the router state alone — the pre-auth front-door bindings and the token verifier, which no claims unlock (their gate, where they have one, is the proof their methods take). Handlers acquire them through the Live<F> extractor in http, so they never name the state; the auth middleware and the token-request extractor build theirs directly.
