A test-only revoke cascade over the store primitives: deletes the grant of either kind and expires the client’s refresh-token families in one write scope, then answers GrantNotFound when no grant row was deleted. The families are expired even on that miss, and no revocation epoch is bumped, so it is a fixture for these db tests, not GrantsRevoker::revoke.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn revoke_grant(
    store: &SqliteGrantStore,
    grant_id: &str,
    client_id: &str,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Result<(), AuthorizationServerError> {
    let removed = store.write(|tx| -> Result<bool, AuthorizationServerError> {
        let removed_code = tx.delete_authorization_code_grant(grant_id)?;
        let removed_device = tx.delete_device_grant(grant_id)?;
        tx.expire_refresh_token_families_for_client(client_id, now)?;
        Ok(removed_code || removed_device)
    })?;
    if removed {
        Ok(())
    } else {
        Err(AuthorizationServerError::GrantNotFound {
            id: grant_id.to_owned(),
        })
    }
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn upsert_code_grant(
    store: &SqliteGrantStore,
    client_id: &str,
    redirect: &Url,
    scopes: &[String],
    patient: Option<&str>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) {
    store
        .write(
            |tx| match tx.grant_by_client_and_redirect(client_id, redirect)? {
                Some(mut grant) => {
                    grant.absorb_reapproval(scopes, patient, now);
                    tx.update_authorization_code_grant(&grant)
                }
                None => tx.create_authorization_code_grant(&AuthorizationCodeGrant {
                    id: Uuid::new_v4().to_string(),
                    client_id: client_id.to_owned(),
                    scopes: scopes.to_vec(),
                    granted_at: now,
                    last_used_at: None,
                    patient: patient.map(str::to_owned),
                    redirect_uri: redirect.clone(),
                }),
            },
        )
        .expect("upsert code grant");
}
}

The create-or-union device-grant upsert transaction, inlined here so the db test drives the real adapter’s grant primitives directly instead of reaching up into a domain capability. Mirrors domain::capabilities::writers::GrantRecorder::record_device_grant.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn upsert_device_grant(
    store: &SqliteGrantStore,
    client_id: &str,
    device_name: &str,
    scopes: &[String],
    patient: Option<&str>,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) {
    store
        .write(|tx| {
            match tx.device_grant_by_client_and_device_name(client_id, device_name)? {
                Some(mut grant) => {
                    grant.absorb_reapproval(scopes, patient, now);
                    tx.update_device_grant(&grant)
                }
                None => tx.create_device_grant(&DeviceGrant {
                    id: Uuid::new_v4().to_string(),
                    client_id: client_id.to_owned(),
                    scopes: scopes.to_vec(),
                    granted_at: now,
                    last_used_at: None,
                    patient: patient.map(str::to_owned),
                    device_name: device_name.to_owned(),
                }),
            }
        })
        .expect("upsert device grant");
}
}

The mechanisms underneath the rules: encodings, digests, random secrets, the user code a person types, PKCE, secret hashing, and the public key’s wire shape. They know nothing of the product and depend on nothing else in the crate. The rules that use them (what a token claims, when a secret matches, what a code may be redeemed for) live in the Domain. Constant-time comparison is left to the subtle crate where it is needed.

crypto_util::base64

The two RFC 4648 alphabets the server needs, named for their exact wire format so they can’t be confused, and the only place a base64 engine is built. URL-safe without padding is the web’s: opaque tokens, digests, and JWT and JWK key material. Standard with padding is only for HTTP Basic credentials at the token endpoint. The decoders’ DecodeError is re-exported here, so no other module names the base64 crate.

crypto_util::sha256

as_base64_no_pad

The at-rest form of a high-entropy secret: a digest can’t be reversed, so a leaked database yields nothing presentable. It is also the PKCE S256 transform, which compute_code_challenge’s test checks against RFC 7636’s example.

SHA-256 of input, base64url-encoded without padding.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn as_base64_no_pad(input: &[u8]) -> String {
    let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
    hasher.update(input);
    base64::url_safe_no_pad_encode(&hasher.finalize())
}
}

Every secret the server hands out that must be impossible to guess is 32 bytes from the OS’s secure generator, URL-safe base64 without padding. The value carries no structure. One construction serves authorization codes and device codes, refresh tokens, SMART launch values and same-device sign-in codes; each has its own name, so a call site says which it is minting.

generate_authorization_code

Generate an opaque, URL-safe authorization/device code from 32 CSPRNG bytes, base64url-encoded without padding. Suitable for OAuth authorization_code and device_code values where unguessability is the only requirement (the value carries no structure).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(crate) fn generate_authorization_code() -> String {
    let mut bytes = [0u8; TOKEN_BYTES];
    rand::rng().fill_bytes(&mut bytes);
    base64::url_safe_no_pad_encode(&bytes)
}
}

authorization-server-rust/src/crypto_util/random_token.rs lines 20–24 · authorization-server in the code index

A token is 43 unpadded base64url characters that decode back to exactly 32 bytes.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn encodes_32_bytes_as_unpadded_base64url() {
    let code = generate_authorization_code();
    // 32 bytes -> 43 base64url chars, no padding.
    assert_eq!(code.len(), 43);
    assert!(!code.contains('='));
    assert!(code
        .bytes()
        .all(|b| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b == b'-' || b == b'_'));
    // Round-trips back to exactly 32 bytes.
    let decoded = base64::url_safe_no_pad_decode(&code).expect("valid base64url");
    assert_eq!(decoded.len(), TOKEN_BYTES);
}
}

The alphabet holds only uppercase consonants: no vowels, no Y, and no digit a reader could mistake for a letter.

fn main() {
fn alphabet_is_unambiguous_consonants() {
    // No vowels, no 0/1/I/O confusables, no Y.
    for &c in ALPHABET {
        let c = c as char;
        assert!(c.is_ascii_uppercase());
        assert!(!matches!(c, 'A' | 'E' | 'I' | 'O' | 'U' | 'Y'));
        assert!(!matches!(c, '0' | '1'));
    }
}

generate_oauth_user_code

The random source is a parameter, so a test can seed it.

Generate a device-flow user code (e.g. BCDF-GHJK) using the unambiguous consonant alphabet.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn generate_oauth_user_code<R: RngExt + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) -> String {
    let mut chars =
        std::iter::repeat_with(|| ALPHABET[rng.random_range(0..ALPHABET.len())] as char);
    let dash_count = BLOCK_COUNT - 1;
    let letter_count = BLOCK_COUNT * BLOCK_LENGTH;
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(letter_count + dash_count);
    for block_idx in 0..BLOCK_COUNT {
        if block_idx > 0 {
            out.push('-');
        }
        out.extend((&mut chars).take(BLOCK_LENGTH));
    }
    out
}
}

is_valid_oauth_user_code

Return true if s matches the user-code shape: BLOCK_COUNT blocks of BLOCK_LENGTH ALPHABET chars joined by -.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn is_valid_oauth_user_code(s: &str) -> bool {
    let mut blocks_seen = 0usize;
    for part in s.split('-') {
        if blocks_seen >= BLOCK_COUNT
            || part.len() != BLOCK_LENGTH
            || !part.bytes().all(|b| ALPHABET.contains(&b))
        {
            return false;
        }
        blocks_seen += 1;
    }
    blocks_seen == BLOCK_COUNT
}
}

crypto_util::pkce

Proof that the app redeeming a code is the app that asked for it (RFC 7636). The app sends /oauth/authorize a challenge, the S256 digest of a secret verifier it keeps, and sends the verifier itself to /oauth/token. The challenge’s shape is checked at /oauth/authorize, the verifier’s length at /oauth/token, and the challenge derived from the verifier is compared with the one the code carries.

is_valid_code_verifier_length

True when code_verifier has an RFC 7636 §4.1-legal length (43–128 chars). Counts Unicode scalar values, matching how the verifier arrives on the wire.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn is_valid_code_verifier_length(code_verifier: &str) -> bool {
    (CODE_VERIFIER_MIN_LEN..=CODE_VERIFIER_MAX_LEN).contains(&code_verifier.chars().count())
}
}

is_valid_s256_code_challenge

True when s is a syntactically valid S256 code_challenge: exactly 43 base64url characters ([A-Za-z0-9-_], no padding) per RFC 7636 §4.2/§4.3. RFC 7636’s ABNF also lists . and ~, but the SHA-256/base64url form the only supported method (S256) produces never contains them.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn is_valid_s256_code_challenge(s: &str) -> bool {
    s.len() == S256_CODE_CHALLENGE_LEN
        && s.bytes()
            .all(|b| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b == b'-' || b == b'_')
}
}

    assert!(!is_valid_s256_code_challenge(&format!(
        "{}=",
        "a".repeat(42)
    )));
    assert!(!is_valid_s256_code_challenge(&format!(
        "{}.",
        "a".repeat(42)
    )));
}
}

hash_client_secret

Hash a plaintext client secret into an argon2id PHC string suitable for storage in clients.secret_hash. Each call uses a fresh random salt, so the same secret hashes to a different string every time.

Errors

Returns ClientSecretError::Hash if the argon2id hashing step fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn hash_client_secret(secret: &str) -> Result<String, ClientSecretError> {
    Argon2::default()
        .hash_password(secret.as_bytes())
        .map(|hash| hash.to_string())
        .map_err(ClientSecretError::Hash)
}
}

verify_client_secret

Verify a presented plaintext secret against a stored argon2id PHC string.

Returns Ok(true) on a match, Ok(false) on a mismatch, and Err only if the stored value cannot be parsed as a PHC hash. The comparison is constant-time internally.

Errors

Returns ClientSecretError::MalformedHash if stored_phc is not a parseable PHC hash string (or verification fails for a non-mismatch reason).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn verify_client_secret(presented: &str, stored_phc: &str) -> Result<bool, ClientSecretError> {
    let parsed =
        PasswordHash::new(stored_phc).map_err(|e| ClientSecretError::MalformedHash(e.into()))?;
    match Argon2::default().verify_password(presented.as_bytes(), &parsed) {
        Ok(()) => Ok(true),
        Err(argon2::password_hash::Error::PasswordInvalid) => Ok(false),
        Err(e) => Err(ClientSecretError::MalformedHash(e)),
    }
}
}

Integration Tests

The domain chapters show each rule on its own, against the fake store. The integration tests hold the whole server to its promises through the surface the outside world sees: HTTP. Each test is one promise, stated in the terms an app, a browser or the Owner would use (“a disabled client is refused”, “a launch works once”), and checked by sending requests to the real router over a real database.

Nothing listens on a port. Each test builds the server’s axum router over a fresh in-memory SQLite database, sends it requests one at a time with tower’s oneshot, and reads the responses. Every store, migration, seed, capability and route is the production one. The stand-ins are few: the database lives in memory, the tests mint their own tokens instead of earning them through a flow, and the authorization start gate admits everything unless a test passes its own.

How they are run

All the files under tests/integration/ build into one test binary, integration. Its main.rs only declares the modules, one per file, plus common, the fixtures they share.

cargo test -p wildflowerhealthio-authorization-server --test integration

How to read the sub-chapters

Each sub-chapter covers one test file. It opens with the part of the server’s promise that file holds it to, then gives each test a section: its doc comment states the promise, then comes the test, then the domain and capability sections the promise rests on. The first test on a page to use a fixture links it on the Test Fixtures page, which holds the shared fixtures and each file’s own helpers.

The files follow the order the Domain part builds its concepts in. The first ones hold the server to its tokens: the signing key and the bearer gates (Smoke, Bearer Only, Scope Gating, Request Caller) and revoking them (Revocation). Then the Owner’s own browser signs in (Same-Device Sign-In), and clients authenticate and are managed (Client Auth, Client Management). The authorization-code flow comes next, end to end in Grant Flows, then door by door and page by page. The polled requests follow: devices and paired browsers. Last come what ends a browser’s or an app’s access, and the rules laid across the whole surface: cache suppression and the limit on starting requests.

Smoke

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/smoke.rs

The server’s most basic promises. It publishes its public signing key and nothing private. Every gated route needs a bearer token minted by this server for this server: a token’s iss and aud must both be the server’s origin.

Two gates check bearers. require_valid_session guards the server’s own /authorization routes. authorization_server_auth_middleware wraps the host’s other routers, with the paths it lets through untouched. Both read the token as verify_access_token does, with the key the Signing Key page explains.

This file’s own helpers are on the Test Fixtures page, with the shared ones.

integration::smoke

jwks_endpoint_returns_seeded_key

The JWKS publishes the seeded key’s public half, for verifying only, and no private component.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn jwks_endpoint_returns_seeded_key() {
    let (g, _owner_token, _db) = spin_up();
    let req = build_request(Request::get("/.well-known/jwks.json"), Body::empty());
    let res = g.router.oneshot(req).await.expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let body = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    // The kid/n/e are key-material-derived, so thread them through from the
    // actual key; everything else (kty/alg/key_ops and — crucially — the
    // *absence* of any private field like d/p/q) is pinned by comparing the
    // entire body against one literal.
    let key = &body["keys"][0];
    let kid = key["kid"].clone();
    let n = key["n"].clone();
    let e = key["e"].clone();
    assert_eq!(
        body,
        serde_json::json!({
            "keys": [{
                "kid": kid,
                "kty": "RSA",
                "alg": "RS256",
                "key_ops": ["verify"],
                "n": n,
                "e": e,
            }]
        })
    );
}
}

bearer_gate_exempts_listed_paths_but_gates_the_rest

The bearer gate serves an exempt path without a token, and gates a path that only shares its prefix and every other path.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn bearer_gate_exempts_listed_paths_but_gates_the_rest() {
    use axum::routing::get;
    use axum::Router;
    use wildflowerhealthio_authorization_server::authorization_server_auth_middleware;

    let (g, _owner_token, _db) = spin_up();
    // A trivial downstream router wrapped in the bearer gate with only the
    // discovery path exempted — exercises the real middleware wiring (full path,
    // exact match) rather than just the `is_exempt` helper.
    let inner = Router::new()
        .route("/metadata", get(|| async { "ok" }))
        .route("/metadata-x", get(|| async { "ok" }))
        .route("/Patient", get(|| async { "ok" }));
    let gated = inner.layer(authorization_server_auth_middleware(
        g.state.clone(),
        &["/metadata"],
    ));

    let status = |path: &'static str| {
        let gated = gated.clone();
        async move {
            gated
                .oneshot(Request::get(path).body(Body::empty()).unwrap())
                .await
                .expect("oneshot")
                .status()
        }
    };

    // Exempt path: served without any bearer token.
    assert_eq!(status("/metadata").await, StatusCode::OK);
    // A path that merely shares a prefix is NOT exempt — still gated.
    assert_eq!(status("/metadata-x").await, StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED);
    // A normal resource path is gated — 401 without a token.
    assert_eq!(status("/Patient").await, StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED);
}
}

Bearer Only

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/bearer_only.rs

The bearer gates read the Authorization: Bearer header and nothing else. No grant hands a token back as a cookie, a token carried in a wf_auth cookie authenticates nothing, and logout sets no cookies. The one cookie the server sets is the browser session’s, from same-device sign-in (Same-Device Sign-In) and from the pairing poll (Browser Pairing). It reaches the gates only through the host’s cookie-to-bearer layer, which presents its token as the request’s bearer.

Scope Gating

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/scope_gating.rs

The /authorization surface checks two things in turn. The session gate proves who the caller is: no valid token is a 401 (Smoke). Each route then asks for the scope its capability needs. A valid token without that scope is a 403 naming the missing scope, decided before the handler runs. A wildcard covers every resource it names, by allowed_scope_covers. Logout and the session read are self-service and take no scope.

Request Caller

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/request_caller.rs

The host shows the Owner which app is using the server. It learns that from the response: both bearer gates stamp a verified request’s response with the token’s client, as a RequestCaller, and a request they refuse with a RequestRefusal saying why. A path the gate exempts carries neither.

The two gates are require_valid_session, on the /authorization routes (the “session gate”), and authorization_server_auth_middleware, on the host’s other routers (the “bearer gate”). Both verify through verify_request_claims.

This file’s own helpers are on the Test Fixtures page, with the shared ones.

fn main() {
async fn the_bearer_gate_stamps_why_it_refused_each_401() {
    let (g, _owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    let router = bearer_gated_router(&g);
    let revoked_token = mint_scoped_token(&db, &["patient/*.rs"]);
    revoke(&db, &revoked_token);

    for (token, refusal) in [
        (None, RequestRefusal::MissingToken),
        (Some("not-a-jwt"), RequestRefusal::TokenRejected),
        (Some(revoked_token.as_str()), RequestRefusal::Revoked),

            .clone()
            .oneshot(get_with_bearer("/Patient", token))
            .await
            .expect("oneshot");
        assert_eq!(response.status(), StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED);
        assert_eq!(stamped_refusal(&response), Some(refusal));

    let exempt = router
        .oneshot(get_with_bearer("/metadata", None))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(
        stamped_refusal(&exempt),
        None,
        "an exempt path is not refused"
    );
}
}

Revocation

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/revocation.rs

An access token is a signed JWT that stays valid until it expires. Revocation is how the server stops one early. It keeps two records, in a revocation store shared with the FHIR server:

  • The jti denylist ends one token: the row lives until the token would have expired anyway.
  • The subject epoch ends a cohort: every token issued to a subject (its sub, the client_id) before the epoch is revoked.

Every /authorization bearer gate checks both, and a revoked token is 401, the same as no token. Revocation is written in three places: the Owner’s POST /authorization/revocations, logout, and revoking a grant. Token Revocation covers an app revoking its own tokens.

This file’s own helpers are on the Test Fixtures page, with the shared ones.

fn main() {
async fn revocations_endpoint_rejects_invalid_bodies() {

    let bad_bodies = [
        // jti without the required expiresAt
        serde_json::json!({ "jti": "abc" }),
        // both modes at once
        serde_json::json!({ "jti": "abc", "expiresAt": Utc::now().to_rfc3339(), "subject": "c" }),
        // neither mode
        serde_json::json!({}),
        // jti with an expiresAt already in the past (stale/mistyped)
        serde_json::json!({
            "jti": "abc",

        }),

            .router
            .clone()
            .oneshot(owner_revocation_request(&owner_token, body.clone()))
            .await
            .expect("oneshot");
        assert_eq!(
            res.status(),
            StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST,
            "invalid revocation body must 400: {body}"

revoking_a_grant_bumps_the_client_revocation_epoch

Revoking an authorization-code grant bumps its client’s revocation epoch, so the client’s live access tokens end with the standing consent.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn revoking_a_grant_bumps_the_client_revocation_epoch() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    // Seed a client + a grant for it.
    seed_client_with_redirect(&db, "granted-client", "https://app.example/cb", &["read"]);
    let store = store_handle(&db);
    store
        .write(|tx| {
            tx.create_authorization_code_grant(
                &wildflowerhealthio_authorization_server::domain::grant::AuthorizationCodeGrant {
                    id: "grant-1".to_string(),
                    client_id: "granted-client".to_string(),
                    scopes: vec!["read".to_string()],
                    granted_at: Utc::now(),
                    last_used_at: None,
                    patient: None,
                    redirect_uri: Url::parse("https://app.example/cb").expect("url"),
                },
            )
        })
        .expect("create grant");
    // Revoke it.
    let res = g
        .router
        .clone()
        .oneshot(build_request(
            Request::delete("/authorization/grants/grant-1")
                .header("host", "127.0.0.1")
                .header("authorization", format!("Bearer {owner_token}")),
            Body::empty(),
        ))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::NO_CONTENT);
    // The client's live access tokens are now revoked via the epoch — a token
    // it holds issued an hour ago reads back revoked.
    assert!(
        revocation_store_handle(&db)
            .is_revoked(
                None,
                Some(Utc::now() - Duration::hours(1)),
                "granted-client"
            )
            .expect("query"),
        "grant revoke must bump the client's revocation epoch"
    );
}
}

Same-Device Sign-In

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/same_device_sign_in.rs

The Owner’s own browser doesn’t pair. The base app, running on the same device as the server, mints a one-time sign-in code in-process and opens GET /oauth/sign-in?code=…&next=… in a browser. Only the base can mint a code, so redeeming one proves the browser is on the Owner’s device. The sign-in starts a same-device browser session holding the Owner’s scopes, hands the browser its token as the __Host-browser_session cookie, and sends it on to an allowed next.

A code signs in once. A refused sign-in renders an error page, with no cookie and no redirect. The flow is SameDeviceSignIn::sign_in, and the proof it mints under is RedeemedSameDeviceSignInCode::redeem.

This file’s own helpers are on the Test Fixtures page, with the shared ones.

A sign-in code signs a browser in once: the first use answers a 303, uncached, with the browser session cookie, and a second use gets the error page.

async fn a_code_signs_in_once() {
    let (g, _owner_token, _db) = spin_up();
    let code = g.same_device_sign_in_code_minter.mint();

    let signed_in = sign_in(&g, code.as_str(), "/").await;
    assert_eq!(signed_in.status(), StatusCode::SEE_OTHER);
    assert_cache_suppressed(&signed_in, "the sign-in");
    browser_session_token(&signed_in);

    assert_refused(sign_in(&g, code.as_str(), "/").await, "a spent code").await;
}
}

async fn the_cookie_holds_an_eight_hour_owner_token() {

    );

        claims["exp"].as_i64().expect("exp") - claims["iat"].as_i64().expect("iat"),
        8 * 60 * 60

    assert!(claims["jti"].as_str().is_some_and(|jti| !jti.is_empty()));

            .clone()
            .oneshot(owner_grants_probe(&owner_token))
            .await
            .expect("oneshot")
            .status(),

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn a_browser_session_is_revoked_by_its_jti() {
    let (g, owner_token, _db) = spin_up();
    let session = |token: String| {
        let router = g.router.clone();
        async move {
            router
                .oneshot(build_request(
                    Request::get("/authorization/session")
                        .header("authorization", format!("Bearer {token}")),
                    Body::empty(),
                ))
                .await
                .expect("oneshot")
        }
    };
    let first = browser_session_token(
        &sign_in(&g, g.same_device_sign_in_code_minter.mint().as_str(), "/").await,
    );
    let second = browser_session_token(
        &sign_in(&g, g.same_device_sign_in_code_minter.mint().as_str(), "/").await,
    );
    assert_ne!(jti_of(&first), jti_of(&second));

    let res = session(first.clone()).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    assert_eq!(
        body_json(res.into_body()).await["scopes"],
        serde_json::json!(wildflowerhealthio_authorization_server::owner_scopes())
    );

    let res = g
        .router
        .clone()
        .oneshot(owner_revocation_request(
            &owner_token,
            serde_json::json!({
                "jti": jti_of(&first),
                "expiresAt": (Utc::now() + Duration::hours(8)).to_rfc3339(),
            }),
        ))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::NO_CONTENT);

    assert_eq!(session(first).await.status(), StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED);
    assert_eq!(session(second).await.status(), StatusCode::OK);

                .expect("oneshot")

        .clone()

Same-Device Session Ending

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/same_device_session_ending.rs

An Owner session a launch’s sign-in started lasts only as long as the server’s launch views stay open. The base ends it by the sign-in code it opened the view with, through the server’s current run, once the server’s last launch view closes (SameDeviceSignInCodeMinter::end_signed_in_sessions), and a server start cuts off every same-device session but those of the launch views still open. Ending a session expires it, and a session the start cut off is stale, so the token verifier refuses it as an expired one: the browser’s cookie no longer counts, so /oauth/authorize sends the browser to pairing, and the next launch’s code signs it in again. A paired browser’s session survives a start. The flow is the same-device session ender.

This file’s own helpers are on the Test Fixtures page, with the shared ones.

integration::same_device_session_ending

closing_a_launch_ends_only_its_session

Ending a launch’s code ends exactly the session it signed in: that session is expired, not revoked, its cookie no longer reaches the consent card, and its token no longer passes the bearer gate. Another launch’s session stands, and ending by the same code again ends nothing.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn closing_a_launch_ends_only_its_session() {
    let (g, _owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    let (closed_code, closed_token) = launch(&g).await;
    let (_open_code, open_token) = launch(&g).await;
    assert!(is_consent_card(
        &authorize_destination(&g, &closed_token).await
    ));
    let closed_codes = [closed_code];

    assert_eq!(
        g.same_device_sign_in_code_minter
            .end_signed_in_sessions(&closed_codes)
            .expect("end"),
        1
    );
    assert_eq!(
        g.same_device_sign_in_code_minter
            .end_signed_in_sessions(&closed_codes)
            .expect("end again"),
        0,
        "ended already"
    );

    let closed_session = stored_session(&db, &sid_of(&closed_token));
    assert!(closed_session.expires_at <= Utc::now(), "expired");
    assert_eq!(closed_session.revoked_at, None, "not revoked");
    assert!(is_pairing_page(
        &authorize_destination(&g, &closed_token).await
    ));
    assert_eq!(
        g.router
            .clone()
            .oneshot(owner_grants_probe(&closed_token))
            .await
            .expect("oneshot")
            .status(),
        StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED
    );

    assert!(row_stands(
        &stored_session(&db, &sid_of(&open_token)),
        Utc::now()
    ));
    assert!(is_consent_card(
        &authorize_destination(&g, &open_token).await
    ));
}
}

a_restart_ends_same_device_sessions_but_open_views_and_paired_ones

A server start cuts off the same-device sessions an earlier run signed in, except the session of a launch view still open, so another’s cookie no longer reaches the consent card, while a paired session stands. The start writes nothing: the other session’s row is left as it was. That view’s session is ended later through the new run, by the code the earlier run minted. A launch on the new run signs the browser in again.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn a_restart_ends_same_device_sessions_but_open_views_and_paired_ones() {
    let (g, _owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    let (_closed_code, closed_token) = launch(&g).await;
    let (open_code, open_token) = launch(&g).await;
    assert!(is_consent_card(
        &authorize_destination(&g, &closed_token).await
    ));

    let restarted = restart(&db, std::slice::from_ref(&open_code));

    assert!(
        row_stands(&stored_session(&db, &sid_of(&closed_token)), Utc::now()),
        "left as it was"
    );
    assert!(is_pairing_page(
        &authorize_destination(&restarted, &closed_token).await
    ));
    assert!(is_consent_card(
        &authorize_destination(&restarted, &open_token).await
    ));
    assert!(row_stands(
        &stored_session(&db, &db.paired_browser_sid),
        Utc::now()
    ));
    assert!(restarted
        .in_process_token_verifier
        .verify(&db.paired_browser_token)
        .is_ok());

    assert_eq!(
        restarted
            .same_device_sign_in_code_minter
            .end_signed_in_sessions(&[open_code])
            .expect("end"),
        1
    );
    assert!(is_pairing_page(
        &authorize_destination(&restarted, &open_token).await
    ));

    let (_code, signed_in_again) = launch(&restarted).await;
    assert!(is_consent_card(
        &authorize_destination(&restarted, &signed_in_again).await
    ));
}
}

Client Auth

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/client_auth.rs

A confidential client proves who it is with its credentials, sent one of two ways: an Authorization: Basic header (client_secret_basic) or client_id and client_secret in the form body (client_secret_post). A request presents exactly one method, and a failed Basic attempt is answered with a Basic challenge. The same rules hold at the token endpoint and the device-authorization endpoint.

Reading the presented credentials is resolve_client_credentials; checking them is AuthenticatedClient::authenticate.

Happy path for client_secret_basic: credentials only in the header, the grant redeems and mints a token (RFC 6749 §2.3.1).

        &g.router,
        "/oauth/token",
        "grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=conf-token".to_string(),
        &basic_authorization(CONFIDENTIAL_CLIENT_ID, CONFIDENTIAL_CLIENT_SECRET),

        .is_empty());

    let res = post_form_with_authorization(

        "/oauth/token",
        "grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=conf-token".to_string(),
        &authorization,
    )
    .await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
}
}

Client Management

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/client_management.rs

The other half of trusting a client on first use: the Owner can see every client the server trusts and take that trust back. GET /authorization/clients lists them; PATCH /authorization/clients/{id} with disabledAt disables or re-enables one. A disabled client is refused at both OAuth front doors at once, and re-enabling it restores it with its registration intact. The essential clients can’t be disabled: that would leave the Owner no way in.

The write goes through ClientsDisabler::set_disabled_at.

This file’s own helpers are on the Test Fixtures page, with the shared ones.

integration::client_management

list_shows_seeded_and_trusted_on_first_use_clients_without_secrets

The list shows the essential clients, the seeded SMART apps and a client created by a trust-on-first-use approval exactly as registered, ordered by id, and no row carries a secret.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn list_shows_seeded_and_trusted_on_first_use_clients_without_secrets() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_confidential_client(&db, "conf-app", "a-secret", &["read"]);

    // Trust a brand-new app on first use.
    let res = get_authorize(
        &g.router,
        &db.paired_browser_token,
        &authorize_query("brand-new-app", "read"),
    )
    .await;
    let request_id = parked_request_id(&res);
    let res = approve_oauth_consent(
        &g,
        &owner_token,
        &request_id,
        r#"{"approvedScopes":["read"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":true}"#.to_string(),
    )
    .await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);

    let clients = listed_clients(&g, &owner_token).await;

    // Seeded by boot (the host) and by migration (a SMART app).
    let host =
        find_client(&clients, WILDFLOWER_HOST_APP_CLIENT_ID).expect("the host client is listed");
    assert_eq!(host["essential"], true);
    let browser_session_client = find_client(&clients, BROWSER_SESSION_CLIENT_ID)
        .expect("the browser-session client is listed");
    assert_eq!(browser_session_client["essential"], true);
    assert!(find_client(&clients, "941de68e6b59eb9dcc32df8ede89e636").is_some());

    // Created by the TOFU approval, exactly as it was registered.
    let tofu = find_client(&clients, "brand-new-app").expect("the TOFU client is listed");
    assert_eq!(
        tofu,
        &serde_json::json!({
            "clientId": "brand-new-app",
            "name": "brand-new-app",
            "kind": "public",
            "redirectUris": ["https://app.example/cb"],
            "allowedScopes": ["read"],
            "allowedGrantTypes": [
                "authorization_code",
                "refresh_token",
                "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code",
            ],
            "registeredAt": tofu["registeredAt"],
            "disabledAt": null,
            "essential": false,
        }),
    );
    assert!(tofu["registeredAt"].is_string());

    // Ordered by id, and the secret hash never leaves the server.
    let ids: Vec<&str> = clients
        .iter()
        .map(|c| c["clientId"].as_str().expect("clientId"))
        .collect();
    let mut sorted = ids.clone();
    sorted.sort_unstable();
    assert_eq!(ids, sorted);
    let confidential = find_client(&clients, "conf-app").expect("the confidential client");
    assert_eq!(confidential["kind"], "confidential");
    for client in &clients {
        let fields = client.as_object().expect("a JSON object");
        assert!(
            !fields.keys().any(|k| k.to_lowercase().contains("secret")),
            "no secret field on {}",
            client["clientId"],
        );
    }
}
}

a_disabled_client_is_refused_at_authorize_until_re_enabled

A disabled client’s /oauth/authorize gets a local error page, never a redirect to the client or a prompt for the Owner. Re-enabled, its registration is intact and the same request parks again.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn a_disabled_client_is_refused_at_authorize_until_re_enabled() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_client_with_redirect(&db, "test-app", "https://app.example/cb", &["read"]);
    let query = authorize_query("test-app", "read");

    // Enabled: the request parks for the Owner.
    parked_request_id(&get_authorize(&g.router, &db.paired_browser_token, &query).await);

    // The PATCH answers with the client as stored — the same row the list shows.
    let res = disable_client(&g, &owner_token, "test-app", Utc::now()).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let patched = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert!(patched["disabledAt"].is_string());
    let listed = listed_clients(&g, &owner_token).await;
    assert_eq!(find_client(&listed, "test-app"), Some(&patched));

    // Disabled: a local error page, never a redirect to the client or a prompt.
    let res = get_authorize(&g.router, &db.paired_browser_token, &query).await;
    assert_ne!(res.status(), StatusCode::FOUND);
    assert!(body_string(res.into_body())
        .await
        .contains("Disabled client"));

    let res = enable_client(&g, &owner_token, "test-app").await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);

    // Re-enabled with its registration intact: the same request parks again.
    parked_request_id(&get_authorize(&g.router, &db.paired_browser_token, &query).await);
    let row = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(row["disabledAt"], Value::Null);
    assert_eq!(
        row["redirectUris"],
        serde_json::json!(["https://app.example/cb"])
    );
    assert_eq!(row["allowedScopes"], serde_json::json!(["read"]));
}
}

A disabled client is invalid_client at /oauth/token, and the refused attempt spends nothing: once re-enabled, the same refresh token redeems.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn a_disabled_client_is_refused_at_token_until_re_enabled() {
    let (g, db) = spin_up_with_confidential_client();
    let owner = mint_scoped_token(&db, &["wildflower/Client.u"]);

    let res = disable_client(&g, &owner, CONFIDENTIAL_CLIENT_ID, Utc::now()).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);

    let res = refresh_as_confidential_client(&g).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED);
    let body = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(body["error"], "invalid_client");
    assert_eq!(body["error_description"], "Client is disabled");

    let res = enable_client(&g, &owner, CONFIDENTIAL_CLIENT_ID).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);

    // The refused attempt consumed nothing: the same refresh token now redeems.
    let res = refresh_as_confidential_client(&g).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    assert_eq!(body_json(res.into_body()).await["token_type"], "Bearer");
}
}

any_sent_disabled_at_disables_now_with_the_servers_time

Whatever time is sent — long past or an hour ahead — the client is disabled now, stamped with the server’s clock: a disable can be neither backdated nor scheduled.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn any_sent_disabled_at_disables_now_with_the_servers_time() {
    let (g, db) = spin_up_with_confidential_client();
    let owner = mint_scoped_token(&db, &["wildflower/Client.u"]);

    for sent in [
        Utc::now() - Duration::days(365),
        Utc::now() + Duration::hours(1),
    ] {
        let before = Utc::now();
        let res = disable_client(&g, &owner, CONFIDENTIAL_CLIENT_ID, sent).await;
        let after = Utc::now();
        assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
        let answered = disabled_at_of(&body_json(res.into_body()).await).expect("disabled");
        assert!(
            (before..=after).contains(&answered),
            "stamped with the server's now, not the time sent ({sent})"
        );
        assert_eq!(
            stored_disabled_at(&db, CONFIDENTIAL_CLIENT_ID),
            Some(answered)

        let res = refresh_as_confidential_client(&g).await;
        assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED, "refused at once");

        let res = enable_client(&g, &owner, CONFIDENTIAL_CLIENT_ID).await;
        assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);

}

Grant Flows

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/grant_flows.rs

These tests hold the server to its main promise: an app reaches the Owner’s FHIR server only after the Owner said yes, now or in a standing grant, and never with more than the Owner and the browser it runs in hold. They drive the whole authorization-code flow over HTTP, from /oauth/authorize to /oauth/token, so this page starts with that flow as a story. The entities it moves through have their own pages: the code request, the grant, the authorization code, the browser session and the client.

The story

The Owner has paired their laptop browser. They open Wildflower Strength, a SMART app, in that browser. Strength asks for patient/Observation.rs and launch/patient.

The front door: no session, no request

The browser lands on GET /oauth/authorize. The first check is about the browser, not the app: does it carry a browser session?

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// No browser session, no authorization: pair this browser first, then
// come back to this very request. Nothing is parked, notified or consumed.
let Some((browser_session, browser_sid)) = browser_session
    .as_ref()
    .and_then(|claims| Some((claims, claims.sid.as_deref()?)))
else {
    return Ok(found_redirect(&pairing_page_location(
        authorize_uri
            .path_and_query()
            .map_or(authorize_uri.path(), |path_and_query| {
                path_and_query.as_str()
            }),
    )));
};
}

authorization-server-rust/src/http/routes/oauth/authorize.rs lines 294–307 · authorization-server in the code index

A code is always issued under a browser session (its sid). Without one there is nothing to issue under and nothing to revoke later, so the browser is sent to pair first, with this request’s path and query as where to come back to. Nothing is written yet, so the detour spends no SMART launch value.

Everything after this point runs in one write scope, in CodeAuthorizationStarter::start. Telling the Owner’s popup about a new request happens after the scope closes.

Three questions decide where the browser goes

The starter first validates the request: a signing key to mint with, a client that isn’t disabled, PKCE, and the client’s registration. A server-defined registration holds the request to its redirects and scopes. Any other client is trusted on first use: whatever steps outside its registration is carried to the Owner as a presented client change. Then three questions about the request pick the next step:

#![allow(unused)]

pub(crate) enum AuthorizeNextStep {
    RedirectToClient {
        redirect_uri: Url,
        code: String,
        client_state: String,
    },
    AwaitOwner {
        request_id: String,
        decidable_in_requesting_browser: bool,
    },
    ConfirmSessionShortfall {
        request_id: String,
    },
}
}

The second half of waits_on_limited_page means the limited page is shown once per browser per app: once this browser has pressed Continue for Strength, its later Strength requests skip the page, whatever the session lacks. Continue and Cancel are the code request’s own transitions, CodeRequest::acknowledge_session_shortfall and CodeRequest::deny_on_limited_page.

Every one of these paths, the fast path included, parks a code request first. From then on the request changes only through its own transitions, each written as a guarded replace on its status (the Authorization Request page), so the first decision wins.

The Owner decides

Strength’s request is pending. The laptop isn’t the Owner, so it went to the wait page, and the host app on the Owner’s phone shows the request as the Owner prompt. The Owner ticks scopes and taps Approve, which arrives at ConsentDecider::approve_oauth_consent. Before anything is written, the approval must earn a proof:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let maybe_delegated_scopes = DelegatedScopes::clamp(
    &self.approver_grant,
    input.owner_approved_scopes,
    resolved.approvable_scopes(),
)?;
if resolved
    .presented_client_change()
    .would_change_registration()
    && !input.acknowledged_registration_change
{
    return Err(AuthorizationServerError::RegistrationNotAcknowledged {
        id: id.to_owned(),
    });
}
if !pending_request.admits_patient(input.patient.as_deref()) {
    return Err(AuthorizationServerError::LaunchPatientMismatch { id: id.to_owned() });
}
let Some(delegated_scopes) = maybe_delegated_scopes else {
    deny_pending_request(tx, &pending_request, now, id)?;
    return Ok(denial_outcome(
        &pending_request,
        REQUEST_DECLINED_DESCRIPTION,
    ));
};
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/access/consents/oauth.rs lines 200–223 · authorization-server in the code index

You can’t give away what you don’t hold. DelegatedScopes::clamp is the whole rule:

  1. The approver must hold the prompt’s approval scopes: the power to decide a request, to record a grant, to write the registration of a client trusted on first use, and every resource scope (or wildflower/launch) the request asks for. Missing any is a 403 that names them, whatever was ticked (Approval Scopes).
  2. The ticks are clamped to what the prompt may grant: each must be covered by a requested scope and by the client’s registration, which for a client trusted on first use takes in what it asked for.
  3. Every resource scope that survives must be covered by the approver’s own grant.

If nothing survives, the request is denied. Before that, a request that would change the app’s registration needs the Owner to acknowledge so (a 409 otherwise). And when the SMART launch pinned a patient, the approval must name that patient (CodeRequest::admits_patient).

Approving and issuing the code

Both paths to a code go through one writer method, RequestApprover::approve_for_code: the Owner’s approval above, and the fast path below. It takes a CodeAuthority, an enum with exactly two variants. That enum is the complete answer to “what can cause a code to be issued?”

fn main() {
pub(crate) enum CodeAuthority<'a> {
    OwnerDelegated(&'a DelegatedScopes),
    StandingGrant(&'a StandingGrantCoverage),
}
}

let Some(browser_session) = self
    .tx
    .browser_session_by_sid(&request.sid)?
    .filter(|browser_session| browser_session.is_live_at(now, stale_session_cutoff))
else {
    let Ok(denied) = request.deny(now) else {
        return Ok(CodeApproval::RequestNotPending);
    };
    return Ok(if self.tx.replace_code_request(request, &denied)? {
        CodeApproval::BrowserSessionEnded
    } else {
        CodeApproval::RequestNotPending
    });
};
let approval = Approval {
    granted_scopes: authorized_scopes.to_vec(),
    patient: patient.map(str::to_owned),
};
let Ok(approved) = request.approve(approval, now) else {
    return Ok(CodeApproval::RequestNotPending);
};
if !self.tx.replace_code_request(request, &approved)? {
    return Ok(CodeApproval::RequestNotPending);
}
let authorization_code = AuthorizationCode {
    code,
    request_id: request.id.clone(),
    client_id: request.client_id.clone(),
    redirect_uri: request.redirect_uri.clone(),
    code_challenge: request.code_challenge.clone(),

    ),
    patient: patient.map(str::to_owned),
    issued_at: now,
    expires_at: now + AUTHORIZATION_CODE_TTL,
    sid: browser_session.sid,
};

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/capabilities/writers/request_approver.rs lines 125–164 · authorization-server in the code index

Three rules, in the order they run:

  1. The requesting browser must still be live. If the laptop was signed out while the Owner decided, the approval becomes a denial and Strength hears access_denied. There’s no session left to issue under.
  2. The request records what the authority allowed (the approval’s granted scopes): the Owner’s delegated scopes, or the requested scopes the standing grant covered (CodeRequest::approve).
  3. The code carries that, intersected with the browser’s session (session_bounded_scopes). A browser paired read-only earns its apps read-only access, whoever approved. The code also carries the sid, so revoking the laptop later ends everything Strength earned there.

On the Owner’s path, the same write scope then records the grant for (Strength, its redirect), unioned into any grant already there, and for a client trusted on first use creates or widens its registration (GrantRecorder::record_code_grant). The code, the grant and the registration land together or not at all. The grant is what lets the next request’s second question answer yes. On the fast path, the same scope stamps the standing grant’s last_used_at instead.

The fast path

The fast path is the one place a code is issued with no person deciding:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn fast_path_coverage(
    request: &CodeRequest,
    coverage: GrantCoverage,
) -> Option<StandingGrantCoverage> {
    match coverage {
        GrantCoverage::Full(standing_grant_coverage)
            if request.admits_patient(standing_grant_coverage.patient()) =>
        {
            Some(standing_grant_coverage)
        }
        _ => None,
    }
}
}

GrantCoverage::resolve answers Full only when the request makes no change to the client’s registration (its presented client change is NoChange) and the standing grant for that client and redirect covers every requested scope. Coverage is by permission, not spelling (allowed_scope_covers): a grant for patient/Observation.rs answers a request for patient/Observation.r. A request that is new or steps outside the registration never takes the fast path, however well an old grant covers it: the Owner hasn’t seen that combination. The browser session’s part was settled by the first question: a request still waiting on its limited page never gets this far.

Redemption: the code is spent once

The browser is sent back to Strength’s redirect with ?code=…&state=…. Strength posts the code and its PKCE verifier to /oauth/token, which builds the proof RedeemedAuthorizationCode:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// A concurrent redemption of the same code can only succeed once, so
// any racer past this point sees `None` (RFC 6749 §10.5).
let Some(code) = tx.redeem_authorization_code(presented.code)? else {
    tx.expire_refresh_token_families_for_authorization_code(
        &token_storage_hash(presented.code),
        now,
    )?;
    return Ok(Err(TokenExchangeError::InvalidGrant(
        InvalidGrantReason::CodeNotFoundOrRedeemed,
    )));
};
}

authorization-server-rust/src/domain/authority/redemption.rs lines 192–202 · authorization-server in the code index

A code presented twice means someone else has seen it. The second presentation fails, and it also expires every refresh family the first redemption started. The attacker gets nothing, and the real app has to ask again.

The code is consumed before its bindings are checked: same client, same redirect, not expired, and the PKCE verifier matching the challenge. A code that fails any of them is spent all the same, and every failure reads invalid_grant on the wire. The token then carries the code’s scopes, which the session already bounded. Its scope claim adds each SMART scope’s other spelling (with_alternate_canonical_forms), so the FHIR server can read either.

Where the story lands

Follow the scopes and each step can only narrow them:

asked for      ∩ registration           → approvable          (the Owner decides)
approvable     ∩ Owner's ticks, ⊆ Owner → DelegatedScopes     (the Owner decides)
DelegatedScopes                         → Approval on request (approving: the record)
DelegatedScopes ∩ browser session       → code's scopes       (approving: what's issued)
code's scopes                           → token's scopes      (redemption)

On the fast path the standing grant’s coverage stands in for DelegatedScopes. When you review a change to this crate, ask which arrow it touches. If it touches none, it shouldn’t be able to change what anyone can access. If it touches one, the proof or writer at that arrow is where to look.

integration::grant_flows

auth_code_grant_happy_path_end_to_end

An app the Owner approves ends up with a signed bearer token for exactly the approved scope: /oauth/authorize parks the browser on the wait page, the Owner approves, the approve response and the wait page’s poll hand back the same code (the poll’s answer uncached), and /oauth/token redeems it. No offline_access was granted, so no refresh token comes back.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn auth_code_grant_happy_path_end_to_end() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_client_with_redirect(&db, "test-app", "https://app.example/cb", &["read"]);
    let challenge = compute_code_challenge(CODE_VERIFIER);

    // 1. /authorize parks a pending request and 302s to the wait page.
    let query = format!(
        "response_type=code&code_challenge_method=S256&client_id=test-app&scope=read&\
         code_challenge={challenge}&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb&state=xyz"
    );
    let res = g
        .router
        .clone()
        .oneshot(build_request(
            Request::get(format!("/oauth/authorize?{query}"))
                .header("cookie", browser_session_cookie(&db.paired_browser_token)),
            Body::empty(),
        ))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::FOUND);
    let polling = res
        .headers()
        .get("location")
        .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok())
        .expect("location")
        .to_string();
    let request_id = polling_request_id(&polling);

    // 2. Owner approves the requested scope via the consent endpoint.
    let approve = build_request(
        Request::post(format!(
            "/authorization/oauth-consents/{request_id}/approve"
        ))
        .header("host", "127.0.0.1")
        .header("authorization", format!("Bearer {owner_token}"))
        .header("content-type", "application/json"),
        Body::from(r#"{"approvedScopes":["read"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":false}"#),
    );
    let res = g.router.clone().oneshot(approve).await.expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    // The approve response's inline-completion redirect must target the client's
    // `redirect_uri` and carry both the redeemable `code` and the client's `state`.
    let approve_body = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(approve_body["status"], "approved");
    let approve_redirect = approve_body["redirect"].as_str().expect("approve redirect");
    assert!(
        approve_redirect.starts_with("https://app.example/cb"),
        "approve redirect should target the client redirect_uri, got {approve_redirect}"
    );
    let (approve_code, approve_state) = {
        let url = Url::parse(approve_redirect).expect("approve redirect url");
        let code = url
            .query_pairs()
            .find(|(k, _)| k == "code")
            .map(|(_, v)| v.into_owned())
            .expect("approve code param");
        let state = url
            .query_pairs()
            .find(|(k, _)| k == "state")
            .map(|(_, v)| v.into_owned())
            .expect("approve state param");
        (code, state)
    };
    assert_eq!(approve_state, "xyz");

    // 3. The status poll now reports Approved and hands back the client
    //    redirect carrying the redeemable `code`. It must agree with the code
    //    the approve response already returned.
    let res = get_authorization_status(&g.router, &db.paired_browser_token, &request_id).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    // The Approved redirect carries a redeemable code, so no cache may keep it.
    assert_cache_suppressed(&res, "the Approved status poll");
    let status = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(status["status"], "approved");
    let redirect = status["redirect"].as_str().expect("redirect");
    let code = Url::parse(redirect)
        .expect("redirect url")
        .query_pairs()
        .find(|(k, _)| k == "code")
        .map(|(_, v)| v.into_owned())
        .expect("code param");
    assert_eq!(
        code, approve_code,
        "approve-response code and poll code must agree"
    );

    // 4. /token redeems the code with the matching PKCE verifier.
    let body = format!(
        "grant_type=authorization_code&client_id=test-app&code={code}&\
         code_verifier={CODE_VERIFIER}&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb"
    );
    let res = g
        .router
        .clone()
        .oneshot(build_request(
            Request::post("/oauth/token")
                .header("content-type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"),
            Body::from(body),
        ))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let token = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(token["token_type"], "Bearer");
    assert_eq!(token["scope"], "read");
    assert!(!token["access_token"]
        .as_str()
        .expect("access_token")
        .is_empty());
    // No `offline_access` in the grant → no standing credential.
    assert!(token.get("refresh_token").is_none());
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn auth_code_grant_owner_narrows_requested_scope() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    // The client is allowed the broader `.rs`; the request asks for `.rs`.
    seed_client_with_redirect(
        &db,
        "test-app",
        "https://app.example/cb",
        &["patient/Observation.rs"],
    );
    let (_, session_token) =
        paired_browser_session_holding(&db, &["wildflower/launch", "patient/Observation.rs"]);
    let challenge = compute_code_challenge(CODE_VERIFIER);

    // 1. /authorize parks a pending request for `patient/Observation.rs`.
    let query = format!(
        "response_type=code&code_challenge_method=S256&client_id=test-app&\
         scope=patient%2FObservation.rs&code_challenge={challenge}&\
         redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb&state=xyz"
    );
    let res = g
        .router
        .clone()
        .oneshot(build_request(
            Request::get(format!("/oauth/authorize?{query}"))
                .header("cookie", browser_session_cookie(&session_token)),
            Body::empty(),
        ))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::FOUND);
    let polling = res
        .headers()
        .get("location")
        .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok())
        .expect("location")
        .to_string();
    let request_id = polling_request_id(&polling);

    // 2. Owner approves the *narrowed* `.s` — tighter than the requested `.rs`.
    let approve = build_request(
        Request::post(format!(
            "/authorization/oauth-consents/{request_id}/approve"
        ))
        .header("host", "127.0.0.1")
        .header("authorization", format!("Bearer {owner_token}"))
        .header("content-type", "application/json"),
        Body::from(
            r#"{"approvedScopes":["patient/Observation.s"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":false}"#,
        ),
    );
    let res = g.router.clone().oneshot(approve).await.expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    // Approved (NOT denied): the narrowed scope is covered by the request.
    let approve_body = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(approve_body["status"], "approved");
    let code = Url::parse(approve_body["redirect"].as_str().expect("redirect"))
        .expect("redirect url")
        .query_pairs()
        .find(|(k, _)| k == "code")
        .map(|(_, v)| v.into_owned())
        .expect("code param");

    // 3. /token redeems the code; the grant carries the narrowed `.s`.
    let body = format!(
        "grant_type=authorization_code&client_id=test-app&code={code}&\
         code_verifier={CODE_VERIFIER}&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb"
    );
    let res = g
        .router
        .clone()
        .oneshot(build_request(
            Request::post("/oauth/token")
                .header("content-type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"),
            Body::from(body),
        ))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let token = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(token["scope"], "patient/Observation.s");
}
}

an_approver_lacking_a_requested_resource_scope_is_refused_and_the_request_stays_pending

The approver must hold every resource scope they approve: a token that may approve (wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.u and wildflower/Grant.c) but lacks one of the requested resource scopes is refused with a 403 InsufficientScope naming the uncovered scope. No code is issued: the request stays pending, so the status poll keeps waiting and an approver whose token does cover it (here the Owner) can still answer it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn an_approver_lacking_a_requested_resource_scope_is_refused_and_the_request_stays_pending() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_client_with_redirect(
        &db,
        "test-app",
        "https://app.example/cb",
        &["patient/Observation.rs", "patient/Condition.rs"],
    );
    let request_id = parked_request_id(
        &get_authorize(
            &g.router,
            &db.paired_browser_token,
            &authorize_query(
                "test-app",
                "patient%2FObservation.rs%20patient%2FCondition.rs",
            ),
        )
        .await,
    );
    let narrow_approver = mint_scoped_token(
        &db,
        &[
            "wildflower/AuthorizationRequest.u",
            "wildflower/Grant.c",
            "wildflower/Client.cu",
            "patient/Observation.rs",
        ],
    );
    let approve_body = r#"{"approvedScopes":["patient/Observation.rs","patient/Condition.rs"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":false}"#;

    let res =
        approve_oauth_consent(&g, &narrow_approver, &request_id, approve_body.to_string()).await;

    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::FORBIDDEN);
    let body = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(body["error"], "InsufficientScope");
    assert_eq!(
        body["missingScopes"],
        serde_json::json!(["patient/Condition.rs"])
    );
    let res = get_authorization_status(&g.router, &db.paired_browser_token, &request_id).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let status = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(status["status"], "pending", "no code was issued: {status}");
    assert!(
        status.get("redirect").is_none_or(Value::is_null),
        "{status}"
    );
    let res = approve_oauth_consent(&g, &owner_token, &request_id, approve_body.to_string()).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    assert_eq!(body_json(res.into_body()).await["status"], "approved");
}
}

HFS authorizes FHIR reads off the token’s scope claim, parsing only the SMART v2 letter grammar — so a v1-worded grant must be minted with its letter-form alternate alongside it. The app-facing TokenResponse.scope stays the granted set verbatim.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn minted_jwt_scope_claim_carries_alternate_canonical_forms() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_client_with_redirect(
        &db,
        "test-app",
        "https://app.example/cb",
        &["patient/Observation.read"],
    );
    let (_, session_token) =
        paired_browser_session_holding(&db, &["wildflower/launch", "patient/Observation.rs"]);
    let request_id = authorize_and_approve(
        &g,
        &owner_token,
        &session_token,
        "test-app",
        "patient%2FObservation.read",
        r#"{"approvedScopes":["patient/Observation.read"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":false}"#,
    )
    .await;

    // Poll the approved request for the client redirect carrying the code.
    let res = get_authorization_status(&g.router, &session_token, &request_id).await;
    let status = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    let redirect = status["redirect"].as_str().expect("redirect");
    let code = Url::parse(redirect)
        .expect("redirect url")
        .query_pairs()
        .find(|(k, _)| k == "code")
        .map(|(_, v)| v.into_owned())
        .expect("code param");

    // Redeem the code for a token.
    let body = format!(
        "grant_type=authorization_code&client_id=test-app&code={code}&\
         code_verifier={CODE_VERIFIER}&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb"
    );
    let res = g
        .router
        .clone()
        .oneshot(build_request(
            Request::post("/oauth/token")
                .header("content-type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"),
            Body::from(body),
        ))
        .await
        .expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let token = body_json(res.into_body()).await;

    // App-facing `scope` is the granted set, unexpanded.
    assert_eq!(token["scope"], "patient/Observation.read");

    // The signed JWT carries both the v1 word and its v2 letter twin.
    let access_token = token["access_token"].as_str().expect("access_token");
    let claims = decode_jwt_payload(access_token);
    let scope_claim = claims["scope"].as_str().expect("scope claim");
    let claim_scopes: Vec<&str> = scope_claim.split_whitespace().collect();
    assert!(
        claim_scopes.contains(&"patient/Observation.read")
            && claim_scopes.contains(&"patient/Observation.rs"),
        "JWT scope claim must carry both v1 and v2 forms, got {scope_claim:?}"
    );
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn reauthorizing_under_a_standing_grant_stamps_its_last_use() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_client_with_redirect(&db, "test-app", "https://app.example/cb", &["read"]);
    authorize_and_approve(
        &g,
        &owner_token,
        &db.paired_browser_token,

        "read",
        r#"{"approvedScopes":["read"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":false}"#,
    )
    .await;
    let last_used_at = || async {
        let res = g
            .router
            .clone()
            .oneshot(owner_grants_probe(&owner_token))
            .await
            .expect("oneshot");
        assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
        body_json(res.into_body()).await[0]["lastUsedAt"].clone()
    };
    assert_eq!(last_used_at().await, Value::Null);

    let before = Utc::now();
    let res = get_authorize(
        &g.router,
        &db.paired_browser_token,
        &authorize_query("test-app", "read"),
    )
    .await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::FOUND);
    assert!(
        location_of(&res).starts_with("https://app.example/cb?"),
        "the standing grant skipped the Owner"
    );

    let stamped: chrono::DateTime<Utc> = last_used_at()
        .await
        .as_str()
        .expect("lastUsedAt is set")
        .parse()
        .expect("an RFC 3339 instant");
    assert!(stamped >= before && stamped <= Utc::now());
}
}

auth_code_replay_revokes_issued_refresh_family

Replaying a consumed authorization code revokes the refresh-token family it minted (RFC 6749 §4.1.2 / OAuth 2.1 §4.1.2.1): the first redemption returns a rotating refresh token; replaying the same code is rejected AND kills that lineage, so the previously-issued refresh token can no longer be rotated.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn auth_code_replay_revokes_issued_refresh_family() {
    let (g, _owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_client_with_redirect(
        &db,
        "test-app",
        "https://app.example/cb",
        &["read", "offline_access"],
    );
    plant_authorization_code(
        &store_handle(&db),
        &db.paired_browser_sid,
        "test-app",
        &Url::parse("https://app.example/cb").unwrap(),
        &["read", "offline_access"],
        "reuse-code",
        Utc::now() + Duration::minutes(1),
    );
    let redeem = "grant_type=authorization_code&client_id=test-app&code=reuse-code&\
                  code_verifier=verifierverifierverifierverifierverifierabc&\
                  redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb";

    // First redemption succeeds and hands back a rotating refresh token.
    let first = post_form(&g.router, "/oauth/token", redeem).await;
    assert_eq!(first.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let refresh_token = body_json(first.into_body())
        .await
        .get("refresh_token")
        .and_then(Value::as_str)
        .expect("refresh_token issued with offline_access")
        .to_string();

    // Replaying the same code is rejected.
    let replay = post_form(&g.router, "/oauth/token", redeem).await;
    assert_eq!(replay.status(), StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST);

    // The refresh token from the first redemption is now revoked — rotating it
    // fails because the replay killed its family.
    let rotate_req = build_request(
        Request::post("/oauth/token").header("content-type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"),
        Body::from(format!(
            "grant_type=refresh_token&client_id=test-app&refresh_token={refresh_token}"
        )),
    );
    let rotate = g.router.clone().oneshot(rotate_req).await.expect("oneshot");
    assert_eq!(rotate.status(), StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST);
    assert_eq!(
        body_json(rotate.into_body()).await["error"],
        "invalid_grant"
    );
}
}

fn main() {
async fn consent_prompt_reports_the_presented_client_change() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();

    assert_eq!(
        consent["registration"],
        serde_json::json!({"status": "new"})
    );
    // A client with no row is still named on the prompt — by its `client_id`.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn approving_a_new_app_without_acknowledgement_is_rejected() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    let res = get_authorize(
        &g.router,
        &db.paired_browser_token,
        &authorize_query("brand-new-app", "read"),
    )
    .await;
    let request_id = parked_request_id(&res);

    let res = approve_oauth_consent(
        &g,
        &owner_token,
        &request_id,
        r#"{"approvedScopes":["read"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":false}"#.to_string(),
    )
    .await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::CONFLICT);
    assert_eq!(
        body_json(res.into_body()).await,
        serde_json::json!({
            "error": "RegistrationNotAcknowledged",
            "id": request_id,
        }),
    );

    assert!(store
        .read(|tx| tx.client_by_id("brand-new-app"))
        .unwrap()
        .is_none());
    assert!(store
        .read(|tx| tx.grant_by_client_and_redirect(
            "brand-new-app",

        ))
        .unwrap()
        .is_none());
    assert!(store
        .read(|tx| tx.authorization_code_by_request_id(&request_id))
        .unwrap()
        .is_none());
    // Still pending — the prompt loads again.
    let consent = get_oauth_consent(&g, &owner_token, &request_id).await;
    assert_eq!(
        consent["registration"],
        serde_json::json!({"status": "new"})

approving_a_new_app_registers_it_and_the_next_request_fast_paths

The whole trust-on-first-use loop: an acknowledged approval registers the app (public client, named by its id, the one redirect it used, the granted scopes), issues the code, and leaves a standing grant — so the same request a moment later is registered and takes the fast path straight back to the client.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn approving_a_new_app_registers_it_and_the_next_request_fast_paths() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    let res = get_authorize(
        &g.router,
        &db.paired_browser_token,
        &authorize_query("brand-new-app", "read"),
    )
    .await;
    let request_id = parked_request_id(&res);

    let res = approve_oauth_consent(
        &g,
        &owner_token,
        &request_id,
        r#"{"approvedScopes":["read"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":true}"#.to_string(),
    )
    .await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let approved = body_json(res.into_body()).await;
    assert_eq!(approved["status"], "approved");
    assert!(approved["redirect"]
        .as_str()
        .expect("approve redirect")
        .starts_with("https://app.example/cb?code="));

    let store = store_handle(&db);
    let registered = store
        .read(|tx| tx.client_by_id("brand-new-app"))
        .unwrap()
        .expect("the approval registers the client");
    assert_eq!(registered.name, "brand-new-app");
    assert_eq!(registered.kind, ClientKind::Public);
    assert_eq!(
        registered.redirect_uris,
        vec![Url::parse("https://app.example/cb").unwrap()],
    );
    assert_eq!(registered.allowed_scopes, vec!["read".to_string()]);
    assert_eq!(
        registered.allowed_grant_types,
        AllowedGrantType::ALL.to_vec()
    );
    assert!(registered.secret_hash.is_none());
    assert!(registered.disabled_at.is_none());
    assert!(store
        .read(|tx| tx.grant_by_client_and_redirect(
            "brand-new-app",
            &Url::parse("https://app.example/cb").unwrap(),
        ))
        .unwrap()
        .is_some());

    // Same client, same redirect, same scopes → `registered`, so the standing
    // grant pre-approves everything and `/authorize` 302s straight back.
    let res = get_authorize(
        &g.router,
        &db.paired_browser_token,
        &authorize_query("brand-new-app", "read"),
    )
    .await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::FOUND);
    let location = location_of(&res);
    assert!(
        location.starts_with("https://app.example/cb?code="),
        "the second request must fast-path back to the client, got {location}"
    );
}
}

approving_a_changed_app_widens_its_registration

Approving a known client’s changed request widens its registration in place: the new redirect is appended to the existing allowlist, the granted scopes are unioned, a requested-but-pruned scope is NOT added, and the row’s identity (registered_at, name) survives.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn approving_a_changed_app_widens_its_registration() {
    let (g, owner_token, db) = spin_up();
    seed_client_with_redirect(&db, "test-app", "https://elsewhere.example/cb", &["read"]);
    let store = store_handle(&db);
    let before = store
        .read(|tx| tx.client_by_id("test-app"))
        .unwrap()
        .unwrap();

    // A different redirect AND two scopes the registration doesn't cover.
    let res = get_authorize(
        &g.router,
        &db.paired_browser_token,
        &authorize_query("test-app", "read%20write%20pruned"),
    )
    .await;
    let request_id = parked_request_id(&res);
    let consent = get_oauth_consent(&g, &owner_token, &request_id).await;
    assert_eq!(
        consent["registration"],
        serde_json::json!({
            "status": "changed",
            "redirectUriIsNew": true,
            "newScopes": ["write", "pruned"],
        }),
    );

    let res = approve_oauth_consent(
        &g,
        &owner_token,
        &request_id,
        r#"{"approvedScopes":["read","write"],"acknowledgedRegistrationChange":true}"#.to_string(),
    )
    .await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);

    let after = store
        .read(|tx| tx.client_by_id("test-app"))
        .unwrap()
        .unwrap();
    assert_eq!(
        after.redirect_uris,
        vec![
            Url::parse("https://elsewhere.example/cb").unwrap(),
            Url::parse("https://app.example/cb").unwrap(),
        ],
    );
    // `pruned` was requested but not granted, so it is not registered.
    assert_eq!(
        after.allowed_scopes,
        vec!["read".to_string(), "write".to_string()],
    );
    assert_eq!(after.name, before.name);
    assert_eq!(after.registered_at, before.registered_at);
}
}

fn main() {
async fn a_changed_request_never_takes_the_fast_path() {

    let request_id = parked_request_id(&res);
    let consent = get_oauth_consent(&g, &owner_token, &request_id).await;

OAuth Endpoints

Covers authorization-server-rust/tests/integration/oauth_endpoints.rs

These tests hold the server’s three OAuth doors to their contract with apps: /oauth/authorize, where a browser starts an app’s request, /oauth/device_authorization, where a device starts one, and /oauth/token, where an app collects what it was granted. They are about what each door accepts, refuses and reports, more than about what happens once the Owner decides; Grant Flows follows the flows end to end.

Most of the file is /oauth/authorize, and most of that is one rule from RFC 6749: an error may be sent back to an app’s redirect only once that redirect is trusted. A redirect is trusted when a client the server already knows has it registered (Client::allows_redirect_uri). Until then, a failure renders a local error page (AuthorizeRefusal), because redirecting to an address nobody vouched for would be an open redirect. Clients without a server-defined registration are trusted on first use: an unknown client, a new redirect or a new scope is carried to the Owner’s prompt as a presented client change instead of refused.

The tests run in this order: what /oauth/authorize checks and how it fails, a request’s scopes against its client’s registration, telling the Owner about a parked request, SMART App Launch (launch context), the device door, and the token door.

This file’s own helpers are on the Test Fixtures page, with the shared ones.

Trust on first use: a client_id this authorization server has never seen isn’t rejected at the door. Its request is parked like any other and the browser is sent to wait for the Owner, and nothing is written to the clients table, so a request nobody approves leaves no trace of the app.

        &db.paired_browser_token,
        &authorize_query("ghost", "read"),
    )

    let res = get_authorization_status(&g.router, &db.paired_browser_token, &request_id).await;
    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    assert_eq!(body_json(res.into_body()).await["status"], "pending");
    assert!(
        store_handle(&db)
            .read(|tx| tx.client_by_id("ghost"))
            .expect("client query")
            .is_none(),
        "/authorize must not register an unknown client",
    );
}
}

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn authorize_unknown_client_renders_later_failures_locally() {
    let (g, _owner_token, db) = spin_up();

    for (query, expected) in [
        (
            "response_type=code&code_challenge_method=S256&client_id=ghost&scope=read&\
             code_challenge=abc&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb&state=xyz"
                .to_string(),
            "Invalid PKCE code challenge",
        ),
        (
            "response_type=code&code_challenge_method=plain&client_id=ghost&scope=read&\
             code_challenge=abc&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb&state=xyz"
                .to_string(),
            "Unsupported PKCE method",
        ),
        (
            format!(
                "response_type=token&code_challenge_method=S256&client_id=ghost&scope=read&\
                 code_challenge={challenge}&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcb&state=xyz"
            ),
            "Unsupported response type",
        ),
    ] {
        let res = get_authorize(&g.router, &db.paired_browser_token, &query).await;
        assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, "query = {query}");
        let body = body_string(res.into_body()).await;
        assert!(body.contains(expected), "body = {body}");

}
